descs.en: At sixteen she talked to him across a library table every day for a year, and he never answered. Ten years later he chairs the company her agency works for, and he has asked for her by name.

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
At sixteen, Tang Xi talked to Wang An Yu across a library table every lunchtime for a year, and he never said a word back. Then one summer she was gone.

Ten years later he chairs An-Tech, and she is the quiet account manager his outside agency sends to run his marketing. He asked for her by name. Before the second week is out, he has kissed her in a locked archive.

She doesn’t work for him, and she means to keep it that way: her rules, her career, her choices. He has spent ten years learning to speak. Now he has to learn not to decide everything for her.

Second chance · A school crush, grown up · Office romance without a boss · Ongoing

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
I didn’t want a boss chasing his employee. So she works for the agency, not for him, and the turning point is her taking herself off his account so they can meet as equals.

It’s charged and held back: years of looks finally spent, an office after hours, a tie loosened, glasses off. He’s in control until she uses the nickname. Then he isn’t.

chapters.title: The Girl in the Library
chapters.desc: In 2014 a loud girl sits opposite a silent boy in a Shanghai school library every lunchtime for a year. He never answers. Then one June she doesn’t come back.
chapters.content:
The first time Tang Xi spoke to Wang An Yu, in September 2014, he didn’t answer. The second time, he didn’t answer either. By the seventh, she had decided he was either extraordinarily rude or didn’t know how to speak, and by the end of the month she’d settled on both.

It was an unusual way to begin a friendship. But Tang Xi had never been good at leaving things alone, especially people who made her curious, and Wang An Yu, unfortunately for him, made her curious.

The library was at its busiest at lunchtime. Students filled nearly every table, some revising, most pretending to while they traded gossip, and every reminder from Mrs. Hua at the desk bought about thirty seconds of quiet. An Yu sat by the windows, where he had sat since twelve: white school shirt tucked in, sleeves folded twice to the elbow, a maths textbook open beside a notebook whose handwriting was so precise it looked printed.

A shadow fell across his page.

“Is this seat taken?”

He didn’t look up. Tang Xi counted three seconds, which felt generous.

“Okay. I’ll take that as a no.”

She pulled out the chair opposite him with a scrape that made two people turn round. An Yu turned a page. She set down the lunchbox she wasn’t supposed to have in there and leaned over to read his textbook upside down.

“Maths. Of course. What else would someone like you be doing at lunch?” Nothing. She tilted her head. “Do you know, I think you’re the only person in this school who actually looks happy doing maths.”

He picked up his pen.

“That’s a compliment, by the way.”

He went on writing.

“You’re welcome,” said Tang Xi.

For the next fifteen minutes she talked. She told him about her chemistry teacher, who had managed to tip an entire beaker of blue solution into his own shoe; about her deskmate, who had slept through history with his eyes open; about her growing suspicion that the canteen had cooked every dish since September from the same six ingredients. An Yu said nothing at all. He also didn’t ask her to leave, and Tang Xi decided that counted as encouragement.

She came back the next day, and the day after that. By Friday she had stopped asking whether the seat was taken.

✦ ✦ ✦

In October she arrived with two cartons of strawberry milk and put one in front of him.

“I got eighty-seven on my chemistry test. That’s three points higher than last time. You’re supposed to congratulate me.” He turned a page. “Wang An Yu. Are you listening?”

He was. She had become good at telling the difference between a boy who wasn’t listening and a boy who was refusing to show that he was, and she pushed the carton an inch closer.

“It’s not poisoned. Don’t look at me like that.” He looked at her, which was more than she usually got, and she grinned. “Well, I suppose you can’t be completely sure.”

Something moved at the corner of his mouth. She missed it; she was busy with her straw.

“The canteen had a promotion, buy one get one free. I don’t even like this flavour, and wasting food is terrible, so you can have it.”

An Yu looked at the carton, then at her, and without a word moved it a little closer to himself.

“Oh,” said Tang Xi, and rested her chin on her palm. “So you do accept things from strangers. Interesting.”

When the bell went she left first. He stayed another twenty minutes with the empty carton beside his notebook, and when he finally threw it away he remembered the flavour.

It became a habit, a peculiar one, since he had never agreed to it. She came at a quarter past twelve, twenty past if chemistry ran late, always sat opposite him and always brought something to talk about: a new pen, a ridiculous question on a physics worksheet, a boy from the next class who had confessed to three girls in one week, the new vending machine, her mother’s campaign to make her eat more vegetables. And, more and more often, him.

“Why do you always sit here? Is it the window? The way the sun lands on this table?” She considered him. “Or are you secretly in love with this chair?”

His eyes came up for three whole seconds before they went back down, and she laughed so loudly that Mrs. Hua said her name.

She had learned that his silences came in kinds. When he was concentrating, the silence was absolute. When he was reading, it was almost dismissive. And when she asked something truly ridiculous, it lasted just long enough for her to understand that he was choosing not to dignify it. She liked that one best. It meant he was listening.

✦ ✦ ✦

It rained one afternoon in November, and the library smelled of damp uniforms and old paper. Tang Xi propped her umbrella against her chair and said his name three times until he looked up.

“See? You know your name.” She looked pleased with herself for a full minute before she started. “I’ve been thinking. If you could go to any university at all, not just here, where would it be? London? Singapore? Switzerland?”

His pen stopped on the last one.

“Switzerland,” she said slowly. “So you have a preference. No, don’t tell me, I’ll guess. Somewhere quiet, with good libraries, where nobody bothers you.” She tilted her head, and for once she didn’t smile. “Somewhere without people like me.”

His eyes lifted. It had been light enough to pass as a joke and not quite light enough to be one. He looked at her, then at his book, and turned a page.

She broke into a smile again. “That’s fine. I’ll visit anyway. Even if you go to Switzerland, I’ll find the library.”

By December An Yu knew a number of things about Tang Xi that he hadn’t meant to learn. She hated the cold and never remembered a proper coat. She liked strawberry milk best and bought other flavours anyway because she liked trying things. When the weather turned she switched to jasmine tea, no sugar, after a whole lunchtime complaining that the canteen’s tea was syrup; she left a second cup beside his elbow every day for a week, and on the day she came back from the toilets to find it empty, she didn’t say a word, which for her was a kind of fireworks. She was better at maths than she pretended. She went quiet when a test came back bad. She tied her hair up when she meant business and hummed when she read. And she was never there before twenty past twelve on a Wednesday, because her chemistry teacher kept the class behind.

He knew her timetable better than some of his own. He came to the library at twelve now, not half past, so that he’d be there first.

✦ ✦ ✦

In January the teachers started talking about the gaokao as if it were a national emergency, and Tang Xi started spending longer in the library. Not because she had caught his feelings about maths. Because studying opposite him was strangely comforting. He never interrupted her, never sighed when she muttered, and never once made her feel stupid for not knowing something.

One afternoon she pushed a physics worksheet across the table. “I understand the first part. I don’t understand why they suddenly throw this formula at you.”

He took her pencil and worked it through in the margin in his small, neat hand, without explaining much: the necessary steps and a circle round the line she’d missed. She stared at it, then at him.

“Oh,” she said. “Oh! That’s actually simple.” She studied the page a while longer. “You’d make a good teacher. A very difficult one, probably, the kind who hands everyone a worksheet and expects them to work out their own lives. But a good one.” She folded the corner of the worksheet down carefully. “Thank you, Professor.”

He didn’t look up. When she started on the next question, though, he moved his textbook to one side to give her more room, and from then on she called him Professor whenever he corrected her, whenever he refused to answer, and whenever she wanted him to look up. He never told her to stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

By March even the gossips had brought revision notes. Tang Xi still talked, just less, and some days she spent the whole break with her lips moving silently over practice questions. An Yu noticed she’d stopped bringing stories. He also noticed she rubbed her eyes more.

One afternoon she was explaining why the male lead in a television drama was being completely unreasonable when her sentences got slower and slower, and then her cheek was on her folded arm and she was asleep, a loose strand of hair across her face.

When Mrs. Hua’s footsteps came along the row, An Yu shifted his chair until he was between the sleeping girl and the aisle.

“Your classmate?” Mrs. Hua asked.

He looked down at his book. She waited, smiled at nobody in particular and walked on.

Tang Xi woke twelve minutes later, blinking, and pressed her palms to her cheeks. “Did I fall asleep? That’s embarrassing. How long?” He turned a page. “An Yu. How long?”

He glanced at the clock and went back to reading.

“You’re not even going to tell me?” She laughed under her breath and packed her things. “Fine. Thank you for not waking me.”

He had known she would wake up eventually, and that she’d be embarrassed when she did. He hadn’t wanted to watch that.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first day in April that she didn’t come, he looked at the entrance at half past twelve and again at twenty to one, and didn’t leave. She came the next day with a stack of notes and dropped into the chair breathless.

“Student council. Don’t tell me you noticed.” He went back to his book. “I knew it. Anyway, good news. I’ve been selected for the academic programme. They said if I keep my grades up, I’ve got a real chance at my first-choice university.”

She waited, bright-eyed, for congratulations she must have known weren’t coming. He looked at her, and something round his eyes softened, so slightly that anyone who didn’t know where to look would have missed it.

Tang Xi saw it. Her smile got wider. “Thank you.”

In May she talked about her parents. Her father wanted a practical major; her mother wanted something that would take her abroad. She drew little stars in the corner of her notebook and said she wanted a job where she met different people and didn’t sit in the same office every day. Business, maybe, or international relations. Then she looked at him.

“What about you? Right. Switzerland.” She rested her chin on her hand and watched him write. “You really don’t like telling people things about yourself, do you? It’s all right. I think I’ve told you enough about me for both of us. Probably more than enough.”

The sun lay across the table, and for once she didn’t fill the silence. An Yu, who had grown used to the sound of her voice, found himself looking at the clock. It was only a quarter to one. She usually stayed till one.

✦ ✦ ✦

The end-of-year exams came and went, and the school breathed out. On the Monday after, Tang Xi came in later than usual, carrying a paper bag, and didn’t say anything for so long that he looked up first.

“I brought you something.” It was a packet of biscuits. “I checked the ingredients. Nothing suspicious. I know you don’t like sweet things, but these aren’t very sweet. Consider it an end-of-term present.” She took out a small notebook and leafed through it without reading it. “I’ll be busy for a while. And you’ve got your maths camp in July. I saw the form,” she said, before he could ask. “You leave it on the table.”

She tore a page out of the notebook and folded it while she talked, corner to corner, without looking at her hands. Her voice was quieter than usual. When he went to the shelves to find a reference book, he didn’t see where the paper went.

“Well. You’ve survived me for almost a year,” she said when he came back. “Congratulations.”

She stayed till Mrs. Hua rang the bell. She packed her books and pushed her chair in properly, which she had never once done, and looked at him.

“Good luck, Wang An Yu. Don’t study too much.”

She waited. He looked at her. She picked up her bag.

“See you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

That Thursday An Yu wasn’t at school. On Friday he came to the library at twelve and sat down, and at a quarter past the door opened and a group of first-years came in, loud, and none of them was her. At twenty past he checked the time. At half past he went back to his work, and he stayed until one.

He came the next week, and every day of it. By Friday he’d stopped looking at the door. It was summer; people were leaving; there was no reason for her to come. He understood that. He didn’t like it.

In the last week of June he was clearing his desk at home when a folded square of paper slid out of his maths textbook. He caught it before it hit the floor. It was a paper crane, its wings uneven, one side creased where it had been folded too hard, and there was writing on the inside.

For the person who never talks.
I hope you find something interesting to do when I’m not here.
— Tang Xi

He looked at it. Then he took a sheet of wax paper from the drawer, laid the crane between its folds, smoothed the edges so they wouldn’t tear, and put it back between the pages where she had left it.

That evening he sat at his desk with the camp forms in a neat pile and his phone beside them. He opened his contacts. There was no Tang Xi. He had never asked for her number. For almost a year she had sat opposite him every lunchtime, told him about her day, borrowed his pencils, stolen his quiet afternoons and made herself part of a routine he had never meant to have, and he had never once asked her to stay.

He wondered, for the first time, whether she had taken his silence for indifference. Whether she knew he came at twelve because she came at a quarter past. That he knew she sat facing the window because the afternoon sun made her sleepy. That he could pick her footsteps out from the corridor.

At sixteen he had thought there was no particular need to say things. People came and went, school ended, everyone ended up somewhere else, and he had been content with that until a girl with too much to say sat down opposite him, and then one day didn’t.

On Monday the library was quiet at a quarter past twelve. The chair opposite the window was empty, and Wang An Yu turned a page of his maths book, past the corner of wax paper, and kept reading.

chapters.title: He Asked for You by Name
chapters.desc: Northlight wins An-Tech, and its chairman has asked for one account manager by name. She hasn’t seen his face in ten years.
chapters.content:
The first thing Tang Xi learned about An-Tech was that its chairman didn’t like wasting time. The second was that he apparently knew her name. The third was that she had no idea why.

“Congratulations, everyone. We’ve officially won An-Tech.”

Applause went round Conference Room 2 at Northlight Agency at nine on Monday morning, the third of February. Somebody at the far end whistled. Somebody else immediately asked whether the client had confirmed the retainer terms, and the room dissolved into the usual mix of excitement and practical worry that followed a big win.

Tang Xi kept typing. On her screen was the revised onboarding document: technology company, privately founded, expanding fast, a ambitious communications plan for the coming year. She had spent three weeks on the pitch. Competitor analysis, audience segments, positioning, campaign proposals, projections; two late nights rebuilding the deck, and one memorable afternoon when the client asked for an entirely new direction forty-eight hours before the final presentation. It had been a hard account to win. A good one.

“Before everyone runs off to celebrate,” said Daniel, the managing director, “there’s one more thing. An-Tech wants a specific structure: a senior account manager as their single point of contact, with a dedicated team on strategy, creative and delivery.” He glanced at his notes. “And they’ve made a personnel request.”

Tang Xi’s fingers stopped.

Beside her, Rachel, the strategy director, leaned back. “A personnel request?”

“They’ve asked for Tang Xi.”

It wasn’t silence, exactly. Somebody was still shutting a laptop, and the air conditioning hummed. But it was quiet enough for Tang Xi to feel twenty-odd people turn towards her at once.

“Me?” she said.

“You specifically. The request came straight from their chairman. Wang An Yu.”

The name took longer than it should have to reach her. The room went on existing around it. Someone asked whether the chairman had worked with Northlight before; Daniel said he hadn’t. Rachel asked whether he meant the pitch team; Daniel said that was what they’d assumed, but the client had been clear: Tang Xi as account manager, not as one name on a slide. Tang Xi heard all of it, and for several seconds none of it seemed important. The cursor blinked at the end of a line she had typed herself.

Primary account manager: Tang Xi.

It had never looked so unfamiliar.

“Xi?” Rachel’s voice. “Are you all right?”

“Of course.” It came out quickly. Too quickly. She gave Rachel a smile. “Just surprised.”

“Well, be pleased. That’s a serious endorsement.”

“Your work on the pitch was excellent,” Daniel said. “They were particularly taken with your account strategy. Can you take it on?”

“Yes. Of course.”

“Good. Client servicing will send you the onboarding pack. Their chairman wants the first meeting this week.”

The meeting moved on to budgets, timelines and staff. Tang Xi went back to her notes, and her hands were perfectly steady, and nobody noticed she had typed the same sentence three times.

✦ ✦ ✦

Rachel turned up at her desk at a quarter to ten with two coffees and the face of a woman who had been patient for forty minutes and was finished with it.

“Okay, I have to ask. How does the chairman of a technology company know your name?”

“I don’t know.”

“Worked with them before?”

“No.”

“Met him at an event? LinkedIn?”

Tang Xi gave her a look, and Rachel laughed and pulled over the empty chair.

“I’m only establishing whether this is professional or something more interesting. Because I did some reading on him over the weekend. Wang An Yu, twenty-six, founder and chairman. Started An-Tech himself. Educated in Zurich and London, very low profile, almost no interviews, allergic to events.” She sipped her coffee and watched Tang Xi click through a file. “He’s also young.”

“Sounds busy.”

“Xi. You’re not listening. You’re being weird.”

“I’m working.”

“You’re always working.”

“Then you have your answer.”

Rachel gave up, laughing. “Fine. But if the chairman asked for you personally, I’d expect a very interesting introduction. And enjoy this a bit, will you? You earned it.”

When she’d gone back to her own desk, Tang Xi looked at her second screen, where Daniel’s forwarded client profile was open. In the top corner was a photograph: a man in a dark suit in front of a glass wall, one hand resting loosely on the other wrist. Composed. Not smiling. His glasses gave him an almost academic look, apart from the unmistakable authority in the way he stood. Underneath, in capitals: WANG AN YU — FOUNDER & CHAIRMAN, AN-TECH.

She hadn’t seen his face in ten years.

She remembered a boy by the library windows with a maths textbook open in front of him. The boy who never answered her questions, who took strawberry milk without acknowledging it, who had once looked at her for three whole seconds when she asked if he was secretly in love with his chair. She remembered his handwriting, and how he was never in a hurry. She remembered a paper crane.

She closed the photograph. Her phone buzzed.

Rachel (Lunch Police): Eat lunch today. New big client, new responsibilities. Don’t die on me.

Tang Xi: I won’t.

She put the phone down, and after a while she opened the profile again, scrolled to Key Stakeholders and read the name once more. It was strange. She had talked to him nearly every day for a year, and after ten years of silence he had found a way to speak to her without saying a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before half past eleven Vivian, Daniel’s assistant, came over with a tablet. “The client’s sent their preferred arrangements. They’d like the introductory meeting on Wednesday, at their office, with you there in person. And there’s one more note.”

Tang Xi took the tablet. The note was brief, professional and entirely reasonable for a major client with a dedicated account lead. She still read the last sentence twice.

Mr. Wang has asked that Ms. Tang remain his primary contact throughout the engagement, with decisions handled directly rather than routed through the corporate communications team.

“Is that a problem?” Vivian asked.

“No. That’s fine.”

When Vivian had gone, she opened a blank document and typed AN-TECH | ACCOUNT MANAGEMENT PLAN at the top.

Review the signed retainer and scope of work.
Confirm the client approval process.
Set up communication channels.
Arrange the first stakeholder meeting.
Review existing brand materials.
Check for conflicts of interest.
Draft the account roadmap.

She stopped at the last line, then added one more: Establish clear professional boundaries. It looked ridiculous sitting there in black and white, like a note to herself in a diary. She deleted it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunch Rachel sat down opposite her with the expression of someone carrying news.

“You won’t believe this. He asked for you before the final pitch.” Tang Xi’s chopsticks paused. “Daniel told me. During the early account conversations the client asked whether you’d be available to run it if we won.”

“How did they even know I was involved?”

“Your name was on the proposal, obviously. But Daniel says the chairman asked whether you’d be personally assigned.” Rachel leaned in. “Do you think he knows you?”

“No.”

It came before Rachel had finished the question. Rachel raised an eyebrow.

“I mean,” said Tang Xi, reaching for her water, “I’ve never worked with him.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“Eat your lunch.”

“I’m eating.”

“You’re investigating.”

“I can do both,” said Rachel, and for the next ten minutes, mercifully, they talked about staffing and whether they could hire another executive. It was ordinary, and Tang Xi was grateful for it. She was good at keeping her life in compartments. Work was work and the past was the past, and whatever Wang An Yu remembered about her, if he remembered anything, wasn’t something she intended to look into during office hours.

At ten to four the first official email arrived: Introductory Meeting — Northlight Agency, addressed to Daniel, Rachel and her, confirming Wednesday at ten and asking for an attendee list. It was signed with his name, Chairman, An-Tech, and nothing else. No greeting, no pleasantries.

She closed it, opened it again, and wrote back.

Dear Mr. Wang,
Thank you for confirming the arrangements. I will attend as primary account manager for An-Tech and look forward to discussing the account objectives and our proposed working structure.
Best regards,
Tang Xi

She read it through. Professional. Neutral. Appropriate. She sent it.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the forty-second floor of An-Tech’s building, the notification landed on a screen in a quiet office, where Wang An Yu was reading a financial report.

“Mr. Wang.” His assistant, Ding, stood in the doorway with a printed schedule. “Northlight have confirmed Wednesday. Their managing director, the strategy director, and Ms. Tang Xi, the account manager.”

The pen stopped. “Has she confirmed herself?”

“She replied a few minutes ago.” Ding put the schedule on the desk. “Corporate communications asked whether you’d like their director in the meeting too.”

“No. Keep it at ten. And send me the original pitch presentation.”

“Northlight’s?”

“Yes.”

When Ding had gone, An Yu read another page of the report without taking any of it in, then picked up his phone and opened his calendar. Wednesday, ten o’clock, Northlight Agency, Tang Xi. He remembered a girl who arrived at a quarter past twelve, a carton of strawberry milk, a voice that never ran out of things to say. He remembered an afternoon she fell asleep over a physics worksheet. And more clearly than he cared to, he remembered the last thing she’d said to him.

Good luck, Wang An Yu. The desk phone rang. It was the head of corporate communications, who wanted to know whether the chairman’s request for Ms. Tang came from her work for another client.

“No.”

A pause on the line. “Understood. Is there anything specific you’d like us to prepare for her?”

He looked out at the light on the buildings across the road. “Make sure she has the complete briefing before the meeting.”

He had asked for her by name, and he had known exactly what he was doing. There was no mistake and no doubt about whether it was the same Tang Xi. He hadn’t needed her photograph on the proposal or the profile attached to her CV. He had seen the name on the team page in January and read it four times.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past six Tang Xi stood in front of her wardrobe with a dark grey suit in one hand. Then she put it back and took out the black one, because black was more appropriate for a first meeting with a chairman, and because she wanted something to decide.

Her phone lit up on the bed: An-Tech — Additional Account Briefing Materials. Corporate profile, brand guidelines, communications history, a stakeholder list. She downloaded everything, and the stakeholder list opened first: senior management, department heads, communications director, legal, and at the top, his name.

She locked the phone. Her flat was quiet. She was used to quiet. Her friends said she was hard to read; colleagues thought her composed, a little reserved. She rarely spoke unless she had something to add, and she had long ago stopped being the girl who filled every silence because she could. She hadn’t become unhappy. She had grown up. People did.

She went to her desk and opened the bottom drawer, where she kept old notebooks, school certificates and a few photographs she had never got round to throwing out. She didn’t take anything out. She looked, and shut it.

Rachel (Lunch Police): Wednesday. Don’t be nervous. You’ll be great.

Tang Xi: I’m not nervous.

Rachel (Lunch Police): Liar.

The black suit hung on the wardrobe door. A meeting with the chairman of An-Tech, a man who had once spent a whole school year listening to her without saying a word. She wondered if he would recognise her, and then corrected herself. Of course he would. He’d asked for her by name. What she didn’t know was whether he remembered the girl who sat opposite him every lunchtime, or had simply found a capable account manager who happened to be called Tang Xi.

She preferred the second. It was safer, and much more professional.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to midnight An Yu was still in his office, his tie loose and his glasses on the desk beside the Northlight deck. He had finished reading it twenty minutes ago. He was looking at the small photograph on Tang Xi’s biography: a neutral blouse, hair neatly pinned, a pleasant, careful face. No bright smile. Nothing to suggest she had once talked through an entire lunch break without getting a single answer.

He closed it. Then he took out his wallet, where, since the week he asked for her, a square of wax paper had lived behind his cards, because a maths textbook was too big to carry and he had found he didn’t want to leave it at home.

At sixteen he hadn’t known how to ask a girl to stay. He hadn’t known that silence could be mistaken for not caring, or that he would one day remember the exact sound of someone’s voice with no way of hearing it again. Now he was twenty-six, with a company, meetings he chaired and contracts he negotiated and hundreds of people who did what he decided. He had learned to speak when he needed to, and to make people listen.

He put the wallet back in his jacket and switched off the lamp. On Wednesday morning she would walk into his building, and this time, when she spoke, he intended to answer.

chapters.title: The Quiet Account Manager
chapters.desc: The first meeting on the forty-second floor: a long look, “Ms. Tang”, slide thirty-one, and her tea exactly as she took it at sixteen.
chapters.epigraph: “Visibility is useful, Mr. Wang, but only when there’s a reason for it.”
chapters.content:
Tang Xi rehearsed the meeting three times in her head on Wednesday morning before she left the agency. Not because she was nervous. She liked to know what she was walking into. Forty slides, sixty minutes, three communication objectives, two campaign directions, a first budget split and a twelve-month roadmap; she knew which slides needed explaining, which numbers would draw questions, and which recommendations would have to be defended rather than presented. She had answers ready for anything An-Tech’s chairman might reasonably ask.

She hadn’t prepared for the man himself.

“Ms. Tang? Mr. Wang is ready for you.”

The forty-second floor was quieter than she’d expected. The windows ran floor to ceiling over the city, the reception area was all muted colours, and the staff who passed moved with an almost unnerving efficiency. Everything looked expensive without seeming interested in proving it. The receptionist opened a glass door with AN-TECH on it, and Tang Xi stepped through, with Daniel and Rachel behind her.

Wang An Yu was standing by the conference table, talking to a man from his management team. Charcoal suit, white shirt, dark tie, glasses straight on the bridge of his nose, one hand in his trouser pocket and a document in the other. He was taller than she remembered. Or she had forgotten what it felt like to look up at him.

The conversation stopped when the door opened. He turned, and his eyes landed on her and stayed there.

She had prepared for recognition. She had even prepared for him to pretend not to recognise her. She hadn’t prepared for this: not a glance, not the polite nod one gives a new supplier, but a look that went on so long it felt like a full minute, moving over her face, her pinned hair, the black suit she had changed her mind about twice. She kept her professional smile in place. She could feel Rachel beside her, waiting for introductions.

“Ms. Tang,” he said.

His voice was lower than it used to be. Calm and even, as if he had never spent a year listening to her without once returning the favour.

“Mr. Wang.”

“Welcome to An-Tech.”

“Thank you for having us.”

He held out his hand and she took it. His palm was warm, his grip firm without trying to prove anything.

“Please, sit.”

That was all. No surprise, no recognition, no mention of Shanghai or the library or the girl who had sat opposite him every lunchtime for a year. Just Mr. Wang and Ms. Tang. She took her seat and hated how perfectly polite he was.

✦ ✦ ✦

Daniel introduced himself, Rachel outlined the strategy team, and Tang Xi introduced herself as the account manager responsible for the day-to-day relationship. An Yu listened without interrupting and, when they’d finished, glanced at the screen.

“Please go ahead.”

She stood and clicked to the first slide. “Thank you for giving Northlight the chance to work with you. Over the past few weeks we’ve reviewed An-Tech’s communications, competitive position and business priorities, and our view is that the company has reached an important stage. The market position is established. The communications haven’t caught up with it.”

Her voice was clear and measured, with none of the breathless enthusiasm she used to carry into the library and none of the stories about her morning. She spoke like someone who had learned that being heard wasn’t the same as talking. Rather than a string of separate campaigns, she recommended one integrated year: audience perception, corporate reputation, leadership positioning, media relations, digital, each section leading into the next.

An Yu sat at the head of the table. Now and then he looked at the printed deck; now and then he made a note. Tang Xi looked at him no more than she had to. She had a job to do and meant to do it well, and by slide twelve she had found her rhythm. Rachel took over the creative direction at eighteen, Daniel the commercial structure at twenty-four. Everything was going smoothly until she noticed that he had stopped following the screen and was reading several pages ahead.

“...which brings us to the implementation timeline. We’d split the first quarter into three phases, starting with a communications audit and stakeholder alignment.”

He turned a page, then another. She clicked to slide twenty-eight, and he looked up.

“Ms. Tang. May I ask about slide thirty-one?”

Rachel glanced at her. They were on twenty-eight.

“Of course.”

“You recommend separating leadership visibility from the corporate reputation work in the first phase. Why?”

“Because they need different preparation.” She clicked forward to thirty-one. “Reputation can be strengthened through consistent external communications once the audit’s done and the key messages are set. Leadership visibility needs more care. We’d have to decide which executives should be out in front, what they’re expert in, and what they can talk about credibly.”

“Wouldn’t doing both at once save time?”

“It might shorten the preparation, but it risks inconsistency. If a senior executive goes public with a story that’s more ambitious than the company’s positioning can carry, you get a gap between how people see you and what the business is actually doing. More coverage doesn’t fix that.”

His eyes stayed on her. “And if the chairman is part of the leadership programme?”

She didn’t hesitate. “Then he gets his own strategy. His public profile carries different weight from anyone else’s. Anything involving him should be tied to the company’s long-term plans, not to this year’s campaign calendar.” She looked straight at him. “Visibility is useful, Mr. Wang, but only when there’s a reason for it.”

Something changed in his face for the first time that morning. Not a smile, but close to one.

“Go on,” he said.

By slide thirty-five it had become a real conversation. He asked about reporting, approvals and how resources would be split, and his questions were precise; he didn’t ask things to show that he knew the answers, and when he disagreed he said why. He was demanding without being unreasonable, which was almost worse. Tang Xi had expected him to be difficult. It would have been easier if he were.

“The monthly retainer,” he said, looking at the commercial proposal. “Does it cover campaign support outside the agreed scope?”

“Account management and strategic advice are included,” Daniel said. “Additional execution would be scoped separately.”

“Then I want the approval process for extra work written down. And I don’t want the team losing days to sign-offs for small changes.”

“We can set up an approval matrix,” said Tang Xi, writing. “The team will know which decisions sit with the account and which need your office.”

“Would you be responsible for that?”

“Yes.”

“Good. Put it in the revised scope.”

By the last slide she had almost forgotten she was sitting across from someone she’d known in a different life. Almost.

✦ ✦ ✦

When it was over, Daniel turned to An-Tech’s management representative to talk next steps, Rachel shut her laptop, and someone from the office came in with a tray: coffee for Daniel, coffee for Rachel, tea for the representative, and a cup set directly in front of Tang Xi.

Jasmine. No sugar. The scent was light and warm and familiar, and her fingers stopped on her notes.

She hadn’t ordered tea. Nobody had asked what she wanted. “Excuse me, I think there might be a mistake.”

“Mr. Wang asked for tea for you,” the woman said.

At the head of the table, An Yu was reading. He didn’t look up. “Is something wrong, Ms. Tang?”

She looked at him, and at the cup. “No. Thank you.”

It was exactly how she had taken it at sixteen. She remembered the winter afternoon she’d spent complaining that the canteen’s tea was syrup, and the week after, when she started bringing jasmine, no sugar, and leaving a second cup by his elbow. He never touched it while she was watching. Then one day she came back from the toilets and it was empty, and she never asked whether he liked it. She just kept bringing it.

The tea smelled exactly the same. She hated him a little for that.

“Is everything satisfactory?” he asked, a few minutes later.

“Yes, Mr. Wang.”

“The tea?”

She paused. “It’s lovely.”

He nodded and returned to the discussion, and that was all. No explanation. He hadn’t even looked at her when it arrived. She took a small sip and set the cup down, and decided that what she disliked about the meeting wasn’t the questions or the demanding client. It was that Wang An Yu had mastered the art of making her feel that something was happening while giving her nothing at all to confirm it.

“We’ll send the revised scope and account structure by Friday,” Daniel was saying, “and arrange formal onboarding once it’s approved.”

“Coordinate directly with Ms. Tang,” said An Yu. His gaze moved to her. “She’s the primary contact. Major strategic decisions come to my office. Routine matters shouldn’t wait. Do you have any concerns about that arrangement, Ms. Tang?”

Professionally, there was nothing she couldn’t manage. Personally—

She folded her notes together. “No, Mr. Wang. I think the expectations are clear.”

He stood, and everyone stood with him. Daniel shook his hand, then Rachel. When it was Tang Xi’s turn he held her hand a beat longer than he’d held theirs, and his thumb moved once against the side of it. A small thing. Possibly nothing.

“See you next week, Ms. Tang.”

“Certainly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Rachel waited until the conference room door had shut behind them. “Well. That was intense.”

Tang Xi pressed the button for the lift. “Was it?”

“He was reading eight slides ahead. He practically skipped half the deck.”

“He’d probably read the proposal beforehand.”

“Probably. He’s very particular.”

“He’s the chairman.”

“That explains the particular. It doesn’t explain the eye contact.” The lift doors opened, and Rachel followed her in. “I think he likes you.”

“He likes the proposal.”

“Professionally that’s the same thing. And did you notice the tea? He asked for jasmine for you specifically. Daniel and I got coffee.”

Tang Xi watched the floor numbers. “Maybe someone told him I prefer tea.”

“See? That’s nice.”

Tang Xi said nothing. She wasn’t sure what she wanted Rachel to say. Perhaps nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs, Ding came in to clear the conference room while An Yu stayed at the table with the meeting notes. When Ding reached Tang Xi’s place, he noticed the tea was almost untouched.

“Shall I have the same prepared for Ms. Tang next time?”

“No.”

Ding picked up the cup. He was nearly at the door when An Yu asked, without looking up, “Did she say anything about it?”

“She said it was lovely.”

An Yu nodded, and Ding left without knowing that his employer had remembered how a sixteen-year-old girl liked her tea, or that he had noticed she barely drank it, or that he had spent the morning watching a woman who used to talk to him without a second thought now weigh every word before she let it go.

He opened the account file. On the page listing contacts, someone from his team had written: Ms. Tang — primary contact. Under it, a reminder from the meeting: Confirm communication protocol with Ms. Tang. He uncapped his pen and wrote Direct contact, and after a moment, No intermediary.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the back of the car Tang Xi went through her notes while Rachel answered messages beside her.

“Did you get the feeling he knew our work before the pitch?” Rachel asked. “He knew your section better than you do.”

“That’s his job.”

“You’re very determined to make this boring.”

“It’s a client meeting.”

Her phone buzzed with an email from An-Tech’s executive office.

Dear Ms. Tang,
Thank you for today’s presentation. Mr. Wang has asked that all future account correspondence be directed to you.
Office of the Chairman

She read it once and locked the screen. Outside, the city slid past in its familiar colours, and she rested her head against the seat and thought about the tea, and slide thirty-one, and the way he had looked at her when she walked in, for what felt like a full minute, before he called her Ms. Tang.

Perhaps he remembered. Perhaps he didn’t. Perhaps someone had told him about the tea, and perhaps he’d read the proposal carefully because that was what a responsible chairman did. There was a perfectly reasonable explanation for everything, and Tang Xi preferred reasonable explanations. They were much easier to work with.

✦ ✦ ✦

In his office, An Yu took a call about the next meeting and asked his questions, and his voice was level and his attention exact. He had three hours of work before his next commitment. But just before the call ended his eyes went to the cup Ding had left on the side table. He had drunk the second cup for the first time ten years ago, the day she went to the toilets and he was sure she wouldn’t see. He had drunk every one after that.

And today she had taken three sips and thanked him the way she would thank a stranger. He had expected her to be different. He hadn’t expected her to be so careful with him.

chapters.title: The Archive Room
chapters.desc: Locked in the archive after ten, she asks whether he remembers her. He takes a paper crane out of his wallet.
chapters.epigraph: “So I wouldn’t leave before you came.”
chapters.content:
By half past nine on Friday night, Tang Xi had developed a personal dislike of An-Tech’s document management system. It wasn’t complicated. It was inconvenient, and apparently designed by someone who believed every document the company had ever produced deserved to exist in at least three formats.

“Why,” she muttered to a metal shelf, “does a company need four copies of the same quarterly report?”

Behind her, Wang An Yu turned a page. “Regulatory records.”

“I wasn’t asking you.”

“I know.”

It was the fourteenth of February, which she had remembered at nine that morning and forgotten by ten. The meeting with An-Tech’s communications department had finished hours ago, but a discrepancy in the old campaign records meant Northlight needed the original reports before it could finish the audit, the communications director had gone home, the rest of the floor had followed, and somehow she had ended up in the archive with the chairman himself. She had assumed he was showing her where things were kept. Then he took off his jacket, rolled up his sleeves and started pulling files, and she had to admit that even chairmen could be useful.

“Do you know where the 2021 annual communications report is?”

“Third shelf, left side.”

There it was. “And 2022?”

“Same section.”

“You know this room very well.”

“I work here.”

She turned round. “That’s a very reasonable explanation.”

His eyes came up from the folder, and she thought she saw something like amusement in them before it went.

“You’re welcome, Ms. Tang,” he said.

She turned back to the shelves before he could see her face. She hated that name. She hated even more that he had used her old joke to say it, as if to tell her he hadn’t forgotten a thing, and then gone back to his folder.

The archive was a narrow room lined with tall steel shelving, the aisle between just wide enough for two people to pass without touching, with a small table and a computer terminal at the far end and lighting that was functional rather than kind. Twenty minutes in, she put another folder on the stack. “That’s the last one.”

“You’re missing the supplementary report. Lower cabinet.”

The cabinet was locked. He reached past her to the access panel, it beeped, the lock clicked, and when she stood up with the folder he was watching her.

“What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re doing that thing again. Looking at me as if you’re about to say something.”

He considered her, then the cabinet. “I wasn’t aware I did that.”

“Right.” She put the folder down. “You’re still very good at that.”

His hand paused. “At what?”

She didn’t answer, and the only sound was the ventilation, until he said, “You’re standing in front of the door,” and she stepped aside and he walked past her close enough for his sleeve to brush her arm. It was an entirely ordinary thing, and she still found she was holding her breath.

✦ ✦ ✦

The door swung shut behind him with a mechanical click that she didn’t register, because she was busy checking the last report against the digital record. “The figures match. We’re done.”

She put the folders in the return tray, picked up her laptop and pressed the button by the door. Nothing happened. She pressed it again, and a small red light came on with a beep. ACCESS RESTRICTED.

“Mr. Wang?”

He checked the panel and the indicator above the frame. “The archive locks itself down after ten.” He looked at his watch. “It’s three minutes past.”

“Yes, I’m aware of the time.”

“Security has to release it centrally.”

“You’re telling me we’re locked in.”

“Temporarily.”

“Wonderful. I’ve always wanted to spend Friday night shut in a room full of old financial records.” She folded her arms. “Aren’t you going to say something reassuring?”

He thought about it, and said, quite seriously, “We won’t be here all night.”

She stared at him and then laughed, a real one, short and disbelieving and completely unplanned. His face softened. It was the first time that evening she had laughed like that, and he kept it.

He spoke to security through the panel. Forty minutes, they said: the patrol was on the lower floors. There was no signal on her phone, and when she held it up at different heights there was still none.

“There’s a signal by the door,” he said.

“Of course there is.”

She sat on the edge of the table. He stood a few feet away with his tie still perfectly knotted and his sleeves folded neatly to the elbow, and she found herself rehearsing a question. It was ridiculous. At sixteen she had asked him anything she liked, what he wanted, where he’d go, whether he was in love with his chair, and never worried about the answer. Now, at twenty-six, she was practising a single sentence in her head.

“Do you remember me?”

He didn’t move. The silence that followed wasn’t the comfortable kind.

“Never mind,” she said.

“Why are you asking?”

“Because I want to know.”

“Which part?”

She gave a short laugh with nothing funny in it. “That’s a convenient answer.” She slid off the table. “Look, it’s fine. It’s been ten years. We were children. We went to the same school and sat in the same library. It’s not something you’d need to remember. And even if you do, it doesn’t mean anything.”

“Doesn’t it?”

For the first time that evening her composure slipped. “I don’t know, Mr. Wang.”

“When you were sixteen,” he said, “you called me An Yu. You only said Wang An Yu when you were annoyed with me.”

Her lips parted. He remembered. Not just her: the details.

She looked away first. “That was a long time ago.”

“Yes.”

“So you remember. All of it?”

“Most of it.”

Something warm and uncomfortable settled in her chest. She wished he had said no. It would have been easier.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took out his wallet and drew a small square of wax paper from behind his cards, and unfolded it slowly. Inside was a flattened paper crane, wings uneven, one corner creased, the paper a little faded, the writing on the inside still legible.

Tang Xi stopped breathing. She had folded it on a Monday in June, talking about nothing, and slipped it into his maths book while he was at the shelves. Afterwards she had told herself it hadn’t mattered. He held it out. She didn’t take it.

“Where did you get that?”

“You gave it to me.”

“I know I did. I didn’t think you kept it.”

“It lived in my maths book for ten years. It’s been in my wallet since January.”

“Why?”

He looked down at it. “You told me to find something interesting to do when you weren’t there.”

Her throat tightened. She had written that as a joke, a silly goodbye present, and never imagined he would keep it. He folded the wax paper back along its old creases.

“Your handwriting was difficult to read,” he said. “The last line.”

She laughed, and it came out unsteady. “You could have asked.”

“I didn’t have your number.”

The words were simple. The way he said them made her chest ache, and she took a step closer.

“You could have asked someone.”

“I could have.”

“But you didn’t. Why?” He didn’t answer, and she looked at the crane and then at his face. “An Yu.”

It was the first time she had used his name since they met again. His expression changed, only slightly, but she saw it. She had always read his face better than he knew.

“I thought you threw it away,” she said. “I thought you never even noticed it was there.”

“I found it the last week of June. The week after you’d gone.”

“You knew I wasn’t coming back?”

“I knew you hadn’t come that week. I kept coming.”

“To the library?”

“Yes.”

For a moment she couldn’t think of anything to say, which was possibly the most extraordinary thing that had happened between them in ten years. “Why?”

“Because you came at a quarter past twelve. Later on Wednesdays, because your chemistry teacher kept you behind.”

“You knew that?”

“I learned your timetable.”

The room seemed to get smaller. “You learned my timetable? Why?”

“So I wouldn’t leave before you came.”

For ten years she had thought she was the only one who remembered those afternoons, the only one who’d carried a piece of that ordinary year into adulthood. He’d been there too, without telling her, and somehow that was much worse.

“You’re unfair,” she said. “You can’t just tell me things like that. I don’t know what to do with them.”

He put the crane down carefully on the table. “Then don’t do anything.”

“That’s easy for you to say. Do you know how often I thought about that library? I used to wonder whether you remembered me at all. You never said anything. I was practically talking to myself for a year.”

“You weren’t. I was listening.”

“You could have told me. Once.”

“I know.”

“You’re still terrible at this.”

He smiled then. Not the faint movement at the corner of his mouth she used to catch at school, but a real smile, small and unmistakable, the one she had once found so unfairly attractive that she forgot what she was saying halfway through a sentence. She had been sixteen. She was twenty-six. Apparently some things hadn’t improved.

“Are you going to keep calling me Ms. Tang?” she asked.

“Would you prefer I didn’t?”

“I haven’t decided.”

“Then I’ll wait.”

Her eyes went to his mouth without her permission. He noticed, of course, and his own gaze dropped to her lips and came back to her eyes, and neither of them moved. She knew she should say something clever to put the balance back, and for once she had nothing ready.

“Tang Xi,” he said.

Her name. Not Ms. Tang. He lifted one hand and stopped it just short of her face, a question without words, and that was what undid her: that even now, after ten years, he was waiting for her to choose. She closed the distance and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

For one second he didn’t move. Then his hand settled at her waist and the other found the back of her neck, his fingers sliding into her hair, and he kissed her back, and she forgot about the archive and the locked door and the fact that she had spent the whole week reminding herself that he was a client. His mouth was warm and tasted faintly of the tea he’d had at nine. He kissed carefully at first. She didn’t. She caught the front of his shirt and pulled, and he made a low sound against her mouth that she would have missed in any other room.

He drew back an inch. “You’re smiling.”

“I’m allowed.”

“You are,” he said, and kissed her again, and this time he didn’t wait for anything. He drew her in until there was no space between them, and she pushed her fingers into his hair, which was softer than she’d expected, and turned them both until his back met the files. A folder shifted on the shelf behind him. She had imagined this before, not seriously, but there had been nights over the years when she wondered what it would be like if the quiet boy in the library had ever looked at her the way he was looking at her now. It turned out to be hard to think.

He rested his forehead on hers. “Tang Xi. Look at me.”

His glasses had slipped, and his face was no longer entirely composed; there was restraint in his eyes and it was getting harder for him to hold. “You’re giving me instructions already?” she said.

“Would you prefer I didn’t?”

She caught his tie. “No. I quite like it.”

He loosened it himself when she tugged it, took off his glasses and put them on the table, and without them he looked less like the chairman on the forty-second floor and more like the boy she remembered, except that he wasn’t a boy any more and she wasn’t a girl.

“You’re staring,” he said.

“I’ve waited ten years to see you properly.”

Something moved in his face, and when he reached for her again she felt the weight of all those years in the way he held her, not hurried and not careless, only unwilling to let the moment end. He kissed the corner of her mouth, her cheek, her mouth again. When she laughed against him he asked what was funny and she said she had nothing to say, and he said that was unusual, and she told him not to get used to it.

“Can the cameras see in here?” she asked, when she needed air.

“Not into the aisles.”

“Good. I’d hate for the chairman to end up with an embarrassing recording.”

“Are you worried about my reputation?”

“Deeply.”

“You’re not very convincing.”

“Neither are you. You’re still holding me.”

“Do you want me to stop?” he asked, low.

“No.”

He lifted her onto the filing cabinet beside them, his hands steady at her waist, and a few loose papers slid across the top.

“Careful,” she said. “Those are important documents.”

“I know.”

“You’re kissing someone on top of company records.”

“You climbed up.”

“You lifted me.”

“Would you like me to put you down?”

She wrapped her arms round his neck. “Not particularly.”

“Then stop talking.”

“Make me,” said Tang Xi, and he looked at her for a long second and kissed her until she forgot what she’d been about to say.

✦ ✦ ✦

They had to stop when her bag, which she’d left on the floor by the door, started buzzing. She slid down and went to it. Three missed calls from Rachel, and a message.

Rachel (Lunch Police): Are you still at An-Tech? Daniel says the audit documents have to go in tonight. Please tell me you’re not still working.

“Work?” said An Yu.

“Apparently I have a job. Don’t look at me like you’ve got nothing to do with it.” She typed with her back to him.

Tang Xi: Still here. Checking the archive documents. Sending the files shortly. Don’t wait up.

Rachel (Lunch Police): At this hour? Xi. Go home.

She put the phone away and turned round. He was retying his tie. “We should finish the documents,” he said.

“You’re unbelievable.” She smoothed her blouse. He stepped forward and tucked a loose strand of hair behind her ear, so gently that she went still. “What are we doing, An Yu?”

It was a simple question, and neither of them was ready for it.

“I don’t know yet,” he said.

“Good. At least we’re equally confused.”

They went back to the table. She opened her laptop and checked the files and he stood beside her reading the last reports, and now and then his shoulder touched hers when he reached for a folder, and neither of them said so. His tie was still not quite straight. His hair wasn’t as neat as it had been. When he told her that hers was coming down, and stood behind her to gather it and help her pin it again, his fingers brushed the back of her neck and she lost her place on the page entirely.

At eleven there was a knock. “Mr. Wang? Security. Releasing the archive now.”

The officer looked at the chairman, then at Tang Xi, and wished them both a good evening with perfect neutrality. In the doorway, with the empty corridor beyond, An Yu said, “Good night, Ms. Tang,” and she nearly laughed. After the last hour he was still calling her that.

“Good night, Mr. Wang.”

“Tang Xi.” She turned. He was holding the crane in its wax paper. “You forgot something.”

“Keep it.”

“I intend to.”

She was nearly at the lifts when she heard him behind her, his jacket over his arm now.

“Your phone,” he said.

She handed it over without thinking, and he typed his number into it and saved it and gave it back. The contact read Wang An Yu, in full, like a business card.

“In case,” he said, “anything else locks itself.”

The lift came. She stepped in and he stayed outside, and just before the doors met she saw that he wasn’t looking at the floor display or at his phone. He was looking at her.

On the way down she opened the contact and changed his name to Professor.

✦ ✦ ✦

When An Yu got back to his office, a message was waiting from a number he didn’t know.

Unknown number: This is Tang Xi. You saved yourself in my phone like a business card.

Unknown number: Thank you for the records tonight. And for keeping the crane.

He saved the number as Twelve Fifteen.

An Yu: It’s going back in the book tomorrow. The wallet is creasing its wing.

Twelve Fifteen: One more thing. You still owe me an answer.

An Yu: Which question?

Twelve Fifteen: Whether you were secretly in love with that library chair.

He laughed, alone in an empty office, and for real.

An Yu: No. I was waiting for someone who sat opposite it.

The reply took longer this time.

Twelve Fifteen: You really should have said something ten years ago.

An Yu: I know.

In the back of a taxi on the ring road, Tang Xi read it three times. She managed major accounts, negotiated budgets and could sit through a four-hour presentation without losing her composure, and one text from Wang An Yu had reduced her to a girl staring at her phone. In the dark window her reflection looked back at her: hair not quite right, lipstick gone, blouse not as neat as it had been that morning. She touched her mouth and smiled at the glass.

chapters.title: Conflict of Interest
chapters.desc: She signs a form saying there is nothing to declare and goes to his flat that night. Afterwards she finds out his lawyers have read her contract.
chapters.content:
The first time Tang Xi lied about Wang An Yu, she did it in a meeting room with glass walls.

It was twenty past ten on Thursday morning. Northlight’s weekly account review had just broken up, and Rachel was halfway out of the door when Daniel said, “Xi, one moment,” with a formality he didn’t usually bother with. He closed his folder and turned a printed page towards her.

Client Relationship and Conflict of Interest Declaration. The same form every account manager signed on a new client.

“An-Tech is a significant account,” Daniel said. “The chairman asked for you personally, and you’ve been his main contact since day one. I don’t want anything to compromise that relationship or the agency’s position. Have you had any prior personal relationship with Mr. Wang?”

Her fingers rested on the edge of the paper. “Nothing beyond what I’ve disclosed. We were at the same school in Shanghai. We weren’t close.”

It was technically true. It was also a carefully built lie.

“Any ongoing personal relationship? Family connection, financial interest? Anything that could affect your judgement, or look as if it does?”

She understood every word. She also remembered a locked archive, a paper crane in wax paper, and the way he had said her name.

“No.”

It came out smoothly. Daniel watched her a moment longer and pushed the form across. “Sign here. If anything changes, you tell me, immediately. We can manage a conflict that’s been declared. What we can’t manage is hearing about one from the client, or worse, from outside the agency. Your reputation matters, Xi. Don’t put yourself where someone can question your work.”

“I won’t.”

Her signature was steady. Only when the glass door closed behind her did she notice she’d been holding her breath.

At a quarter past twelve her phone buzzed on her desk.

Professor: Are you free this evening?

Around her the office went on with its afternoon: keyboards, the coffee machine, Rachel laughing at something near the pantry.

Tang Xi: Is this about work?

Professor: No.

Tang Xi: Then why are you asking?

Professor: I’d like to see you.

She turned the phone over and read the same line of An-Tech’s communications calendar three times. Eight minutes later she turned it over again.

Tang Xi: What time?

✦ ✦ ✦

His flat took up the top floors of a residential tower above the city. She had expected something imposing, and it was, but it wasn’t showy: dark wood and pale stone, a wall of glass, furniture that didn’t try to impress anyone, no family photographs, almost nothing on any surface. The city lay beyond the windows, bright and restless.

“You’re late,” he said, closing the door behind her.

“By three minutes.”

“I noticed.”

He took her coat and hung it up. He was in a dark shirt with the sleeves folded to his forearms, his hair less formal than she had ever seen it, no tie, no jacket, no office between them, and it made him look different. Or it made her notice how much of him she had only ever seen under office lights.

There was a covered plate on the kitchen counter. “You cooked?”

“I ordered.”

“That’s less impressive.”

“I’ll make a note.”

She lifted the cover anyway. Something simple and still warm, and her expression softened before she could stop it. “You didn’t have to.”

“I wanted to.”

They ate at the island and talked about ordinary things: a difficult client Rachel was handling, an approval that kept slipping, a restaurant Tang Xi kept meaning to try. He listened and asked questions and remembered details, and it was almost unsettling how easily the conversation moved when neither of them was pretending to be in a meeting. When she carried her plate to the sink, he reached for it at the same time and their fingers met, and neither of them let go.

“You keep finding reasons to stand close to me,” she said.

He put the plate down. “Would you rather I didn’t?”

“No.”

“Then I’ll keep finding them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They ended up by the windows, her back to the glass, a glass of water in her hand that she didn’t want.

“Something’s bothering you,” he said.

“Am I that obvious?”

“To me.”

She looked out at the lights. “Daniel made me sign a conflict-of-interest declaration today.”

His face didn’t change. “About us.”

“Us?”

“Whatever you’d call this.”

“You make it sound simple.”

“It isn’t.”

“No.” She put the glass on the side table. “There are rules. If there’s a personal relationship with a client, we declare it, and the agency can reassign the account, put safeguards round it, or decide we can’t work together.”

“And what did you tell him?”

“That there was nothing to declare.” He said nothing, and she folded her arms. “I know.”

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You didn’t have to.”

“Do you want to declare it?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then you should think about it.”

She turned on him. “That’s easy for you to say. It’s your company. If anyone has to move, it won’t be you.” He didn’t interrupt, and her voice stayed level, which was what made it sound so serious. “My career is there. My team is there. I worked for years to get where I am. I don’t want people thinking I got this account because I used to know you. I don’t want Rachel wondering whether my work is mine, or Daniel second-guessing every call I make. I don’t want to be the woman who got close to the chairman and stopped being judged like everyone else.”

“You won’t be.”

“You can’t promise that.”

“I can’t promise what people will think. I can make sure the account never depends on you being close to me.”

“That isn’t the same thing. And you can’t decide everything will be fine because you’ve said so.”

“No,” he agreed, and she saw that there was no impatience in his face and no irritation at being argued with, only the certainty of a man who believed most problems would yield if he approached them correctly. She had to remind herself that she wasn’t one of his problems.

“An Yu. I don’t want you making decisions about my career without me.”

“I won’t.”

She nodded. Then, quieter, “Good.”

He came a step closer, not touching her, close enough that she could feel the warmth of him. “Stay a minute.”

“That sounds like an instruction.”

“An invitation.”

“You’re learning.”

His mouth curved, and she took the last step herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

She kissed him first. It was becoming a habit. His hand settled on her waist and the other came up to her cheek, and he kissed her slowly, without the hunger of the archive, as if they had nowhere else to be. She found the front of his shirt with both hands and leaned back to look at him.

“You’re very neat. Your shirt, your hair, everything.”

“Is that a complaint?”

“It’s a project.” She undid the top button.

His eyes dropped to her hands. “Xi. Are you sure?”

There was no performance in it, no assumption that because she had come to his flat and kissed him and crossed one line she would cross the next.

“Yes,” she said. “Unless you’ve changed your mind.”

“I haven’t.”

She undid the buttons one by one, and he stood still and let her. She had seen him in expensive suits and across conference tables and under the cold lights of his office, and this was a man letting her take her time. She pushed the shirt off his shoulders and laid her palms flat on his chest, and felt his heart going much faster than his face suggested. She unbuckled his watch and set it on the side table beside the untouched water.

“You don’t have to do everything yourself,” he said.

“I want to.”

So he let her, and she learned the small differences between the man at work and this one: how his breathing changed when she touched the side of his neck, how his hand came to her back whenever she leaned in, how he watched her face.

He undressed her in the bedroom, more slowly than she could stand. Her blouse first, button by button, as she had done to him, his knuckles brushing her skin all the way down; then the zip of her skirt, which he lowered. When she stood in front of him in nothing but the city light from the window, he looked at her long enough that her face went hot, and then he said, low, “You’re beautiful,” as if it were a fact he was entering into a record, and kissed her collarbone, her shoulder, the inside of her wrist.

She pushed him back onto the bed and climbed over him. He let her. His hands came to her hips and stayed there, steady, while she lowered herself onto him, and they both went still at once. She heard him breathe out through his teeth. She began to move, slowly, finding the angle she wanted, and he held her and watched her with that unbearable patience, his jaw tight, his thumbs pressing into the hollows of her hips, saying her name once when she leaned down and kissed him and changed the angle.

“You’re thinking,” she said against his mouth.

“Yes.”

“Stop.”

He laughed, a breath of it, and his hands tightened. She sat back up and moved faster, and he met her, and it was good, good, and still she could feel him holding something back, keeping himself in order the way he kept his desk.

So she leaned down until her lips were at his ear, and said, “Professor.”

He went still. It was barely anything, a pause in his hands, a catch in his breathing, but she felt it everywhere, and she smiled into his neck.

“Don’t,” he said.

“Why not? You never told me to stop.”

The name had followed him through a year of school lunches. She had used it whenever he fixed her maths, whenever he refused to answer, whenever she wanted him to look up from his book. He had never once asked her not to. Hearing it now, in his own bed, from her, broke something in his careful composure. He rolled them over in one movement and pinned her wrists lightly to the pillow and kissed her with an intensity that wiped the next joke clean out of her head, and when he moved in her again there was nothing measured in it at all.

“Say it again,” he said, his forehead against hers.

“Professor.”

He shut his eyes and drove into her, and she lost the thread of everything, his name and hers and the city behind the glass, until she came apart under him with her heels pressed into the backs of his thighs, and felt him follow her a moment later, her name in his mouth, his whole weight shaking over her before he caught himself on his forearms so as not to crush her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she lay with her head on his shoulder, listening to his breathing slow while his fingers moved through her hair. She traced the line of his collarbone with one finger.

“Can I ask you something? Why did you ask for me?”

“At Northlight? You know why.”

“I know you remember me. I know you kept the crane and learned my timetable.” She lifted her head. “I want to know why you wanted me on your account.”

He was quiet. “I wanted to see you again.”

“That sounds personal.”

“It was.”

“And the best way to do that was to become my client?”

“I thought it would give me a reason to speak to you.”

She sat up a little. “That isn’t fair, An Yu. You could have just called me.”

“I didn’t know whether you’d want to hear from me.”

“So you decided for me.” He didn’t answer, and she lay back and looked at the ceiling. “You’re very good at making decisions for other people.”

“I’ve been told.”

“By whom?”

“Everyone who works for me.”

“They’re right.” She turned her head on the pillow. “Do you regret it?”

“No.”

“Even knowing what it could do to my job?”

His face changed. “I didn’t think that through properly.”

It was the first answer that night that surprised her, not because it was reassuring but because it was honest. She found his hand. “Then think about it now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was dressing just after midnight when his phone lit up on the bedside table, and the preview was right there on the screen.

Legal (Never Sleeps): As requested, the review of Ms. Tang’s employment agreement and Northlight’s client-service provisions is complete. Relevant clauses below…

She looked away. It wasn’t her phone or her business. Then An Yu came back from the bathroom drying his hands, saw her face and followed her eyes to the screen.

“Was that work?” she asked. “At this hour?”

“Something I asked them to prepare.”

“What?”

“Your contract.” Her hands stopped on her blouse buttons. “Your employment agreement, and the relevant parts of Northlight’s agreement with us. I wanted to understand what restrictions applied to you. Confidentiality, conflicts, reassignment. What happens if a relationship with a client is declared.”

“You had your lawyers read my contract. Clause by clause.” He didn’t deny it, and she gave a small, incredulous laugh. “Did you ask me?” He was silent. “No. You didn’t.”

“I wasn’t trying to interfere with your job.”

“You were trying to find out how much you could interfere without causing a problem.”

“That’s not what I meant to do.”

“Maybe not.” She picked up her bag.

“Xi.”

She looked at him. He stood a few feet away and no longer looked like the man who’d been kissing her an hour before. He looked like the chairman again, the man who could have another person’s contract read before she knew he was thinking about it.

“Tell me what you want me to do,” he said.

“That’s exactly the problem, An Yu. You keep working out what should happen to me before you ask what I want.” She put her coat on. “I don’t need protecting from my own contract.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?”

He didn’t answer straight away. “I’m beginning to.”

He followed her to the door and didn’t touch her. With her hand on the latch she turned. “If your lawyers read anything about me again, you tell me first. And you don’t use what they find to make decisions for me.”

“I won’t.”

She opened the door, and he said, before she could go, “Will you come back?”

It was an unexpectedly naked question from a man who rarely asked for anything straight out.

“Yes,” she said. “But not because you arranged it. Because I choose to. Good night, An Yu.”

“Good night, Xi.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He stood alone in the flat for several minutes after the door closed. Then he went back to the bedroom and opened Legal’s review: confidentiality, conflicts and disclosure, the agency’s right to reassign an account manager where a personal relationship could compromise, or appear to compromise, her independence. He had asked for it because he wanted to know what could happen to her if they were found out. He’d believed that understanding the rules would let him keep her safe. He hadn’t seen that going through her contract without her was another way of taking control.

At the end, counsel had highlighted a note: any personal relationship between the client and the assigned account manager should be disclosed through the proper channels, and the client shouldn’t seek confidential employment information beyond what the commercial relationship requires. He closed it and opened her contact instead.

An Yu: I should have told you before I asked Legal to look at it.

This time he didn’t delete it. In the back of the taxi her phone buzzed in her lap.

Professor: I should have told you before I asked Legal to look at it.

Professor: I won’t do it again without talking to you.

Tang Xi looked out at the lights sliding across the glass for a while before she answered.

Tang Xi: Thank you.

Tang Xi: And I had a lovely evening.

His reply took a little longer.

Professor: So did I.

The declaration was still in Daniel’s office with her signature on it, and in the morning she would walk back into Northlight as the account manager with nothing to declare. She put her phone in her bag and kept her hand on it all the way home.

chapters.title: Forced Proximity
chapters.desc: A pitch in Singapore, a wrong number caught in front of the room, a cancelled flight and a hotel with one room left.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s a hotel room, An Yu. Not a marriage proposal.”
chapters.content:
The flight to Singapore left at ten past seven on Tuesday morning, and by ten past six Tang Xi had already decided that the chairman of An-Tech wasn’t going to distract her for three days. She was going to secure a regional partnership for An-Tech, write it up for Northlight, and come home.

He was standing by the departure gate reading something on his phone: charcoal suit, white shirt, no tie, his carry-on beside him and an expression that suggested the boarding schedule was the most interesting thing he’d seen all week.

“Good morning, Mr. Wang.”

“Good morning, Ms. Tang. Did you sleep?”

“Yes.”

“How long?”

“Are you going to ask for a sleep report every morning?”

“If necessary.”

“Then I’m charging you for it.”

His eyes stayed on her face. “Put it on the company account.”

She laughed, and covered it by adjusting her laptop strap. “Daniel sent the final deck last night. I changed the partner case study.”

“I saw. At twenty to midnight.”

“Do you ever sleep?”

“When you’re not sending me revised presentations.”

“That’s an extremely unfair way to make it my fault.”

His mouth curved. It was still new, seeing him smile this easily. At work he stayed measured and hard to read; with her the edges had begun to soften, not disappear. She liked that he wasn’t trying to be someone else. She liked it even more when he looked at her as if he had something to say and decided to wait until they were alone.

“After you,” he said, when boarding was called.

“Very gentlemanly.”

“I can be.”

“Debatable,” she said, and walked ahead of him onto the plane.

✦ ✦ ✦

Alder Vane, the Singapore group An-Tech wanted as a regional partner, had several floors of a glass tower near the financial district, and by two that afternoon its leadership team had filled the meeting room. It was a big opportunity for An-Tech: a regional profile, one coherent story, a stronger position before its next expansion. Northlight had built the strategy. An Yu was there to represent his company. Tang Xi was there to make sure it happened.

She took them through the regional opportunity, the research, the gaps in An-Tech’s communications and the rollout, and she was clear and unhurried and answered without notes. When Alder Vane’s communications director challenged the timeline, she walked him through the dependencies and resequenced the first two phases without losing the shape of the plan. From the far end of the table An Yu watched her. He had seen her present before. He had also seen her in the archive, laughing at him with her fingers in his hair, and he was beginning to understand how much of herself she had learned to keep behind a closed door.

“Mr. Wang,” said the finance director. “Perhaps you could take us through the projections.”

He stood and took the clicker. Tang Xi sat down and followed the numbers in her notebook. An-Tech’s finance team had built the projections, she had checked them twice, and the final figures had been updated that morning.

“Our regional investment is projected to deliver an incremental return of approximately—”

Her pen stopped. The figure on the slide was last quarter’s forecast. The revised regional costs were in the supporting workbook, but nobody had updated the summary slide, and if he carried on, the return would be overstated by more than three points in front of the one person in the room paid to write it down. She could wait until afterwards. She could pass him a note. The finance director’s pen was already moving.

She leaned towards her microphone. “May I clarify one figure before we go on?”

The room turned. She stood.

“This slide uses the previous cost assumption. We’ve since built in the revised regional allocation, so the figure to use is the one in the appendix. On current assumptions the incremental return is twelve point eight per cent, not sixteen point two. The difference is the extra activation costs and the revised media split.”

The finance director looked down at his copy. An Yu looked at the slide, and then at her.

“That’s correct,” he said. He didn’t defend the old number or call it rounding. “Please use the revised projection. We’ll send the corrected slide this afternoon.”

“Thank you for catching that,” the finance director said.

By the end of the meeting Alder Vane had agreed to move to a detailed scope discussion. It wasn’t a signed partnership, but it was a good start, and on his way out their regional director stopped by Tang Xi’s chair.

“Not everyone would correct their chairman in front of a room, Ms. Tang.”

“I’d rather fix a number in the meeting than let it turn into a problem afterwards.”

“Good. We need people who think that way.”
