When he’d gone, An Yu came over. “You could have waited.”

“And let you present the wrong figure? I’d have had to watch their finance director write it down.”

He considered that. “You’re right. Thank you.”

“You don’t have to thank me for doing my job.”

“I know. I wanted to.”

She forgot whatever she’d been about to say and pretended to check her laptop. “Let’s get lunch, Mr. Wang.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain started as they came back from their second meeting, a light shower that made the pavement shine under the streetlights, and by the time they reached the hotel it was a downpour pouring off the entrance canopy and running fast along the kerb.

“Did you bring an umbrella?” he asked.

“Do you see one?”

“No.”

“Then why ask?”

“To confirm.”

She laughed. A doorman came at them with umbrellas, and An Yu pointed out, politely, that they were already inside.

“Our flight’s tomorrow evening?” she said, checking the time.

“Twenty past eight. The follow-up with Alder Vane is at half past nine in the morning.”

They had checked in separately: two rooms, two keys, two reservations in their own names, one night each, because Tang Xi had made it clear she didn’t want the agency’s travel records to become something people talked about. He hadn’t argued. He had simply booked two rooms.

At the lifts he looked at her. “Are you going to your room?”

She held up her key card. “That’s generally what people do with hotel rooms.”

“Would you like to have dinner first?”

“Is that a professional invitation?”

“No.”

“Good,” she said, and stepped into the lift.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tang Xi woke to rain against an unfamiliar window and, for a moment, didn’t know where she was: strange curtains, a hotel desk, her laptop bag on the chair. Singapore. The pitch. An Yu.

There was a message on her phone, sent at six minutes to six.

Professor: Good morning. Breakfast is on its way. I ordered yours.

Tang Xi: You don’t know what I want for breakfast.

Professor: I think I do.

At half past six an attendant knocked with a trolley: a glass of strawberry milk, toast, a little plate of fruit, a warm egg sandwich. She stood in the doorway and didn’t move. It was exactly the kind of thing she used to bring to the library when she needed an excuse to sit opposite a certain boy.

“Who ordered this?” she asked.

“Mr. Wang, from the room next door.”

She thanked him, and instead of wheeling the trolley inside she wheeled it eight steps down the corridor and knocked on the next door with her foot. An Yu opened it in shirtsleeves, tie in his hand.

“You remembered,” she said.

“Yes.”

“The strawberry milk.”

“Most of all the strawberry milk.”

She pushed the trolley past him and sat down at his little table, and after a moment he sat opposite her, which made something in her chest turn over, because it was the right way round.

“Do you know what I used to think?” She picked up the glass. “That you only took it because you didn’t know how to say no to me.”

“I took it because you brought it.” He said it calmly, the way he said everything. “I liked that you came.”

There were times she wished he were less exact with his words, that he would say something ordinary she could laugh off. Instead he kept handing her things she would remember. She reached across the table, and he took her hand and held it until her egg sandwich was cold.

“You have twenty minutes,” he said eventually.

“You’re very bossy.”

“Nineteen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second meeting was harder. Alder Vane’s regional director liked the strategy, but finance wanted a line-by-line breakdown of spend, and legal had concerns about approval rights, data ownership and the use of An-Tech’s leadership material across regional channels. Tang Xi led. She separated the core retainer from project work and set out which deliverables needed An-Tech’s sign-off, which the communications matrix could handle and which would need separate approval. An Yu came in on corporate positioning and was precise, direct and unwilling to promise anything his company couldn’t deliver.

“Would An-Tech give us some flexibility on regional messaging?” the director asked.

“Within the brand framework, yes.”

“And if we wanted to adapt it for one market? Would that need review every time?”

“We could agree pre-approved messaging territories,” said Tang Xi. “You’d have freedom on local execution without touching the core positioning, and anything that moves outside the framework goes through An-Tech’s approval process. We’ll put the territories and the thresholds in the scope, so nobody has to interpret the rules differently once it starts.”

“That’s sensible,” said the finance director, and by noon they had agreed to draft a memorandum of understanding.

They checked out, ate lunch and took a car to Changi at four for the twenty-past-eight flight. At a quarter to five the departures board went red in three places at once. Weather. Cancelled. The terminal filled with stranded passengers, and Tang Xi stood in the rebooking queue with her laptop bag against her leg while An Yu talked to his office.

“The earliest confirmed flight is tomorrow afternoon,” he said, ending the call.

“Then we need somewhere to sleep.” She messaged Daniel about the cancellation and moved the internal debrief to Friday, and An Yu was already ringing the hotel.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hotel didn’t have two rooms. The receptionist apologised several times, checked the system again and offered a waiting list. “There is one room. A king bed. We can hold it for the extra night.”

Tang Xi looked at the receptionist and then at An Yu. The alternative was an evening hunting for a bed in a city where thousands of other passengers were doing the same.

“How much?” She heard the rate and nodded. “That’s fine.”

“Are you sure?” An Yu asked.

“It’s a hotel room, An Yu. Not a marriage proposal.”

“Understood.”

She collected the single key card. “Don’t look so pleased.”

“I’m not.”

“You’re a terrible liar,” she said, and he picked up her suitcase and followed her to the lift.

The room was bigger than she’d expected: a sitting area, a desk, one large bed and a wide window with rain running down it in long, uneven lines. He put her case by the wardrobe and loosened his watch.

“Would you like me to take the sofa?”

She looked at the sofa, which was wide enough and not comfortable. “We can share the bed. Don’t make it strange.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“Besides, it’s raining. That makes it less strange.”

“Does it?”

“No,” said Tang Xi, and they both laughed.

They ordered dinner and ate at the little table by the window, going through the revised travel plan and the follow-up documents, and it was almost ordinary, except that every time she looked up he was there, and every time he reached for something his hand brushed hers. Eventually she closed her laptop.

“Enough. You’re not going to ask me to review another spreadsheet?”

“No.”

“Promise?”

“I promise.”

“Good.” She tilted her head back to look at him. “Then stop working.”

He put his pen down and came round the table. She was still in her chair when he stopped in front of her, and she looked up at him and he bent his head and she kissed him. The first kiss was soft. The second wasn’t. His hand came to her jaw and she took hold of his shirt, and he kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine the rain got heavier, streaming down the glass and smearing the city into light. She stood at the window and he came up behind her and put his hand on her waist.

“You’re quiet,” she said.

“I’m listening. To the rain.”

“That’s terribly romantic.”

“Is it?”

“No. It’s terrible.”

He kissed the side of her neck, and her smile went away, not because she disliked it but because she liked it too much. She turned in his arms. “Do you remember what you said in the archive? That you were listening?”

“Yes.”

“Then listen now. I want you to kiss me.”

He did, and when she leaned into him, his hands moved down her back, careful at first and then sure. He drew her back against the glass, and she gasped at the cold of it through her blouse and he immediately started to move her away.

She caught his wrist. “I didn’t say stop. Stay.”

He stayed. He undid her blouse with the city blurred behind her and kissed his way down from her throat, and when he knelt to slide her skirt and underwear down her legs she put a hand flat on the window to steady herself, her palm leaving a print in the condensation. He looked up at her from there, with that maddening, careful attention.

“Tell me,” he said.

“Tell you what?”

“What you want.”

“Stop guessing, and stop looking at me as if you’re waiting for board approval.”

He laughed against her thigh, and then his mouth was on her and she stopped making jokes. He was patient in a way that made her impatient, slow until she said his name, then exactly as she asked, and when she was trembling against the cold glass with her fingers in his hair he stood and lifted her, and she wrapped her legs round him and felt him hard through his trousers.

“Say it,” he said against her mouth.

“You,” she said. “I want you. Now.”

He carried her to the bed and undressed without taking his eyes off her, and then he was over her and inside her, and slower than the first time, much slower, watching every change in her face, asking again whenever she was too far gone to tell him: harder, like that, don’t stop. She made him wait for the answers on purpose once, and he made her pay for it, holding still inside her until she was begging and laughing at the same time, and when he finally gave her what she wanted she came with her face pressed into his shoulder and the rain loud on the window. He followed her with a low, broken sound she had never heard from him before.

Later she lay against him with one leg over his under the sheet, tracing the line of his shoulder.

“That was different,” she said. “From your flat. Slower.”

“Was that a problem?”

“No.”

“You’re very pleased with yourself,” she said, after a moment.

“I’m not.”

“You’re smiling.”

He brushed her hair off her forehead and didn’t deny it, and outside the rain began to ease.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke before her alarm. The rain had stopped and left the window beaded, and the city looked pale in the early light. An Yu was awake on his side, watching her.

“How long have you been awake?”

“A while.”

“Why?”

“You were asleep.”

“That’s not a reason.”

“It was enough for me.”

Her stomach made a small, unmistakable noise, and she shut her eyes. “Don’t.”

“I didn’t say anything.” He reached for his phone and the room-service menu, and then he stopped and held the phone out to her instead. “What would you like this time?”

She looked at the phone and then at him, at the man who had ordered her breakfast from ten years ago without asking and was now, deliberately, asking.

“Look at you,” she said, taking the phone. “Asking.” She ordered rice porridge for both of them and a pot of jasmine tea, no sugar, and made him drink a cup.

At half past ten they waited in the lobby with their luggage with the concierge. He brought her a coffee.

“You had tea,” he said, when she looked at the cup.

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“I know,” he said, and she took it.

“About last night,” she said. “I liked it.”

“So did I.”

“But we should talk about what happens at home. Not just us. The account. I don’t want this trip turning into something that touches my work.”

“It won’t.” She looked at him, and he corrected himself. “I won’t let how I feel decide your professional position. And if we need to declare anything or change how the account works, we decide it together, with you in the room.”

“Better,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flight home was delayed forty minutes, but it was confirmed. At the gate at Changi she went through the partnership timeline and he read a report beside her, and her phone buzzed.

Rachel (Lunch Police): How was Singapore? Did they agree to the next stage?

Tang Xi: Yes. Draft MOU and a detailed scope. I’ll brief you tomorrow.

Rachel (Lunch Police): Excellent. And did you survive travelling with the chairman?

Tang Xi: Perfectly well.

Rachel (Lunch Police): You sound suspiciously calm.

She locked the screen.

“Rachel?” An Yu asked. “What did she want?”

“To know if I survived travelling with you. I said perfectly well.”

“Accurate.”

She laughed, and then she leaned over and rested her head on his shoulder and closed her eyes. “Don’t say anything.”

He didn’t. He went back to his report, but his free hand found hers between the seats, and she let him keep it. She knew it would be more complicated when they landed: there would be declarations, boundaries and decisions that couldn’t be made in a hotel room. For now, she stayed where she was and, for once, didn’t feel any need to fill the quiet.

chapters.title: Her Rules
chapters.desc: She writes three rules and they both sign. By Friday the café under her office opens at six.
chapters.epigraph: “I want to be your girlfriend, not one more thing you manage.”
chapters.content:
On Monday morning Tang Xi let herself into An Yu’s flat with a document in her hand. He was in the kitchen pouring coffee, sleeves rolled, phone beside the machine, and he looked up when she came in.

“Read this,” she said, and put it on the island.

At the top, in her neat handwriting, it said PERSONAL RELATIONSHIP — BOUNDARIES AND CONDITIONS. Underneath were three numbered clauses.

1. Nobody at work knows. No one at Northlight or An-Tech is told unless company policy makes it necessary. Neither of us uses colleagues, assistants or work channels to arrange anything personal.
2. Nothing on the account changes. Tang Xi stays primary account manager on her professional appointment. No preferential access, special treatment, private information or influence outside the client relationship. Work stays in the documented channels.
3. He doesn’t buy anything. No gifts, purchases or arrangements involving her workplace, home, transport or expenses without her explicit agreement. No solving a problem with money before asking her what she wants.

He read the last clause twice. “That’s very specific.”

“It needs to be.”

“Is this because of Singapore?”

“It’s because of you.” She took off her coat. “I know how you work. If something’s inconvenient, you remove the inconvenience. If someone’s difficult, you find a way round them. If you want something, you make arrangements. I’m not a business problem, An Yu. I don’t want to find out one morning that you’ve bought something or arranged something or talked to someone on my behalf because you thought it would make my life easier.”

“I understand.”

“Read the whole thing.”

He sat down opposite her and read it again from the top, and when he’d finished he picked up the pen beside it. “Where do I sign?”

She blinked. “You’re not going to negotiate?”

“There’s nothing to negotiate.” He signed under the third clause. She signed beside him, and he folded the page with great care.

“Do I get a copy?”

“You’re joking.”

“I’d like one.”

She shook her head, smiling despite herself. “Fine. I’ll scan it. And don’t make me regret this.”

He reached across the island and stopped just before his hand touched hers. “I won’t knowingly give you a reason to.”

She put her hand in his. “That’s not quite the same as a promise.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.” And he lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles, and she let him.

✦ ✦ ✦

By Tuesday the first two rules turned out to be easy. At Northlight she was Ms. Tang; at An-Tech she was the account manager. Their emails were professional, their calls were logged and their meetings had agendas, minutes and actions. He never asked her to stay behind after a meeting because he wanted to see her, and she never used her access to him to skip an approval. In every visible way they were exactly what they had been.

Except for the messages.

Professor: Have you eaten?

Tang Xi: It’s seven. You’re supposed to say good morning first.

Professor: Good morning. Have you eaten?

Tang Xi: The café downstairs was shut again. I had a biscuit out of my drawer.

Professor: That isn’t breakfast.

Tang Xi: You are not my nutritionist.

Professor: No. I’ll stop asking.

Professor: For today.

She bit the inside of her cheek to keep from smiling, and slid the phone under a folder when Rachel leaned over the partition.

“Who are you smiling at?”

“No one. A message.”

“From?”

“A person.”

“You’re getting very hard to interview.”

“Then stop interviewing me,” said Tang Xi, and Rachel laughed and went away.

Wednesday was long: a campaign review, a difficult client call, a last-minute change to An-Tech’s leadership calendar, and an afternoon in a meeting room reworking messages with Rachel and the creative team. It was half past six when she got back to her desk.

Professor: Still at the office?

Tang Xi: Yes. No idea how late.

Professor: I’ll wait.

Tang Xi: No. Rule two.

Professor: I wasn’t going to talk about work.

Tang Xi: Rule one, then. Go home, An Yu.

Professor: All right.

At a quarter past seven:

Professor: Home. Are you?

Tang Xi: Not yet.

Professor: I’ll leave the light on.

She read it twice. It was such a simple thing to say, and it felt more intimate than half of what he’d said in Singapore.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday she reached the café under Northlight’s building at ten past seven and found the shutters down and a handwritten sign: OPEN 8:00 A.M. – 5:00 P.M. Her first meeting was at half past. The café had been unreliable for weeks; the owner had cut hours for lack of staff and had been talking about closing since Christmas.

“Morning, Xi,” said Mr. Lei from the security desk. “No coffee today?”

“Not today.”

“They’re under new management, I heard. Changing the hours.”

“Good for them,” she said, and got in the lift and forgot about it.

On Friday she was at her desk by twenty past six, and at a quarter to seven she went down for air and stopped dead in the lobby. The café lights were on. The shutters were up, a young barista was laying out pastries, there was a new coffee machine, a new menu, and a printed card by the till. OPEN DAILY FROM 6:00 A.M. UNDER NEW OWNERSHIP.

“Since when are you open?” she asked.

“Since today. New owner. They wanted to keep the place and open earlier for people in the offices upstairs.”

“Who bought it?”

The barista shrugged. “A management company handled it.”

Tang Xi ordered a flat white, paid, took it, walked as far as the lifts and stopped with her phone already in her hand.

Tang Xi: Did you buy the café under my office?

The message showed as delivered. Three dots appeared and disappeared.

Professor: Good morning.

Tang Xi: An Yu.

Professor: Yes.

Tang Xi: So it would open at six?

Professor: Yes.

Tang Xi: We need to talk. Now.

Professor: I’m downstairs.

She turned round. He was by the glass doors of the building in dark trousers and a white shirt with his coat over his arm and a takeaway cup in his hand. He walked over.

“Good morning.”

She looked at the coffee. “Don’t.”

“All right.”

“You bought a café. Because I couldn’t get coffee before work.”

“You’re often in early, and you said on Tuesday it was shut again.”

“I said it once.”

“I remembered.”

“Of course you did.” Her voice softened for half a second and sharpened again. “That isn’t the same as asking me whether you should buy it. Did you read the document?”

“Yes.”

“Did you sign it?”

“Yes.”

“Did you understand the third rule?”

“Yes.”

“Then why?”

He didn’t answer. She looked past him at the café, the new sign, the raised shutters, the staff getting ready for the morning rush, and all of it looked enormous.

“You didn’t ask me. You didn’t even tell me you were thinking about it. You bought an entire business.”

“It’s a small café.”

“That is not the point. Do you know what this looks like? If anyone finds out the chairman of An-Tech bought the café under his account manager’s office, what do you think they’ll assume?”

His face tightened. “I didn’t think about how it would look.”

“That’s becoming a pattern.”

He took it without looking away. “Nobody knows why. The purchase went through a holding company, and no An-Tech money was used.”

“That isn’t reassuring.”

“I know.”

He didn’t try to touch her or explain the structure, or point out that it was small and sensible and entirely legal. He stood there and let her be angry, which was better than arguing and still infuriating.

“You’re unbelievable,” she said.

“I’ve heard.”

“Don’t.” She looked at him a moment longer and jerked her head at the lifts. “Come with me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The lift was empty. She pressed eighteen, he stood beside her at a respectful distance, and the doors closed.

“It wasn’t about the money,” she said. “The third rule. It was about the choice. I want to walk into a café and decide whether I want coffee without wondering whether you’ve bought the building. I want to complain about something without it turning into one of your projects. I want to be your girlfriend, not one more thing you manage.”

That one landed. He looked down, and when he looked up his face had changed.

“I don’t want you to feel like that.”

“Then stop acting as if you can fix everything by acquiring it.”

“I’ll have the café sold to an independent buyer,” he said. “The staff stay. And I won’t decide anything without talking to the owner it goes to.”

“And you’ll tell me before you do anything else. Even if you think it’s small. Even if you think I’ll say no.”

“Especially then.”

She went quiet. She had expected him to argue, explain, remind her he’d only been trying to help. He’d just agreed. It didn’t wash out the frustration, but it made her look at him differently, and she stepped closer.

“What are you doing?” he asked.

She took hold of the front of his coat. “Something very stupid.”

She kissed him hard, with all the anger and all the affection she’d been trying to keep in separate boxes knotted together, and he barely had time to catch her waist before she was pulling him in. He drew back a fraction, “Xi—”, and she kissed him again, and he made a low sound and put a hand to the back of her neck, and she reached past him and hit the emergency stop.

The lift jolted and stopped. An alarm chirped once overhead.

“You stopped the lift,” he said.

“I wanted to kiss you without it arriving anywhere.”

He looked at her, then reached past her and pressed the button again. Nothing happened. “That isn’t how it works.”

She laughed into his shirt. “Are you going to complain?”

“No. But someone is going to notice.”

“Always so practical,” she said, and this time he kissed her, slower than she had, his hand along her cheek and his arm round her, no less certain for being slower. She tasted the coffee he hadn’t been allowed to give her.

A speaker crackled above the panel. “Lift three, this is building control. Is everyone all right in there?”

Tang Xi pressed her face into his shoulder. An Yu leaned towards the grille. “We’re fine. The stop was pressed by mistake.”

“Resetting now. Please stand clear of the doors.”

The lift hummed and rose. They stepped apart before it opened on eighteen, onto an empty corridor and the silent glass doors of Northlight.

“You’re still in serious trouble,” she said, stepping out.

“I understand.”

“Good.” She looked back at him as the doors began to close. “The coffee’s annoyingly good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past nine Rachel arrived at her desk with a folder. “Have you been downstairs? The café’s open at six now. Somebody bought it and changed the hours. Strange, isn’t it? The old owner was talking about closing for months.”

Tang Xi kept her eyes on her spreadsheet. “Good for them.”

“You’re very interested in that spreadsheet. Coffee?”

“I’ve had one.”

“From the new place? How is it?”

Tang Xi took another sip. “Good.”

“Maybe I’ll try it tomorrow,” said Rachel, and went.

Tang Xi waited until she was alone.

Tang Xi: We need to talk about the café. And the sale. And the fact that you apparently can’t follow three simple rules.

Professor: I followed two.

Tang Xi: That is not a defence.

Professor: I’m sorry.

She knew he meant it. She also knew apologies stopped meaning anything if the same thing kept happening.

Tang Xi: Don’t make me write a fourth rule.

Professor: What would it say?

Tang Xi: No buying anything within five kilometres of me.

Professor: Understood.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening he got home before her, and she came in at eight with a paper bag and put it on the island. Two sandwiches and a box of pastries.

“From the café?” he said.

“I bought it. Myself.”

“How much?”

“Don’t.”

“I was asking.”

“And I’m not answering.” She put the pastries on a plate. “Did you speak to the management company?”

“They’re selling to an independent operator. The staff stay, and the hours are up to the new owner.”

“Good.” She held out a pastry, and he took it. “I’m still angry.”

“All right.”

“Less than this morning.”

They stood in the kitchen eating. After a while she said, “You know, you could just have bought me a coffee. That would have been allowed.”

“I’ll remember that.”

He brushed a crumb from the corner of her mouth, and she caught his wrist. “An Yu. Don’t buy the bakery either.”

He laughed, quietly, and promised, and she kissed him, not because she was angry this time or because she wanted to stop a lift, but because she wanted to.

“Are the rules still in force?” he asked against her mouth.

“Every one of them. The third more than the others.”

And this time he didn’t try to improve anything. He stayed exactly where she wanted him.

chapters.title: Everyone Can See It
chapters.desc: His assistant can see it, her team can see it, and a colleague says it out loud. He says nothing, and she watches him remember the name.
chapters.content:
By April Tang Xi had learned that keeping a secret wasn’t the same as keeping something invisible. For nearly four weeks they had followed her rules. Nobody at work knew. Nothing on the account had changed. After the café, he hadn’t bought anything. On paper they were doing very well. The trouble was that people had started to notice the things they weren’t doing.

Ding, An Yu’s assistant, noticed that the chairman no longer ended conversations with Ms. Tang as quickly as he ended everyone else’s, that he knew her meeting schedule without checking, and that he looked at the door when her name came up on the visitor list. Rachel noticed that Tang Xi smiled at her phone, left on time on certain evenings, and that the chairman’s eyes found her even when somebody else was talking. An-Tech’s legal team noticed that the chairman had become unusually insistent that every decision involving Northlight be documented, independently approved and filed. They didn’t know why. They were lawyers; noticing things was their job.

And then there was the shoot.

✦ ✦ ✦

The campaign was supposed to be straightforward: portraits, short interviews and behind-the-scenes footage of An-Tech’s leadership for regional channels, shot on the executive floor, in the innovation centre and in the main conference room on Thursday the tenth. Tang Xi had coordinated it for three weeks. She knew the call sheet by heart, which executives had approved their questions, which images needed clearance and which of the crew didn’t eat dairy. She also knew the chairman was booked for exactly forty minutes at ten.

So she was surprised to step out of the lift at twenty past eight and find him outside the conference room.

“Good morning, Mr. Wang. You’re early.”

“So are you.”

“I’m working.”

“So am I.”

Navy suit, white shirt, a watch she recognised, hair arranged for the cameras. “Your interview’s at ten.”

“I’m aware.”

“Then why are you on this floor at twenty past eight? Near the conference room?”

“I have work here.”

She smiled politely. “How convenient.”

“Ms. Tang, the photographer’s ready for the first setup,” someone called, and she excused herself and went, and An Yu watched her a second longer than he needed to before turning to Ding to ask whether ten o’clock was confirmed. It was. Ding glanced at Tang Xi, already deep in the lighting plan with the photographer, and back at his employer, and asked if there was anything else. There wasn’t. Ding had worked for Wang An Yu long enough to know when a conversation was over. He also knew when it wasn’t.

The photographer was friendly and professional and constitutionally unable to accept that some people didn’t enjoy having a camera pointed at them. “Mr. Wang, maybe a little more relaxed? A natural smile?”

An Yu looked at him, and the photographer’s own smile wobbled.

“Turn towards the window, Mr. Wang,” said Tang Xi from behind the monitor. “A little more. Now the camera.” She studied the first set. “We need another round. These are too formal. They’re fine for the corporate profile, but this campaign is about leadership people can approach, not an annual report. Try sitting.”

The second set was much better. At the break An Yu came round to the monitor, where she was going through the images with the creative director.

“These three,” she was saying. “The second has the strongest expression. The first is too distant, and the third looks as if he’s about to reject someone’s proposal.”

“Is that how I look?” he asked behind her.

For a second she forgot there were other people in the room, and then she recovered. “Only occasionally, Mr. Wang.”

The creative director laughed. An Yu looked at the screen. “Use the second.”

“I agree.”

When he’d gone, the photographer said, “He’s surprisingly easy to work with.”

“He’s very clear about what he wants.”

“That isn’t always the same thing.”

“No,” said Tang Xi. “It isn’t.”

He’d finished his interview by eleven, and he didn’t leave. He stayed in his office taking calls, and she passed his door twice, and both times he looked up. The third time she stopped and knocked on the frame. He was alone.

“The production team needs your approval on the interview transcript.”

“Leave it with Ding.”

She put it on the side table and lowered her voice. “Are you planning to stay here all day? You’ve been on this floor since eight.”

“I have an office here.”

She stared at him, and slightly, the corner of his mouth moved.

“You’re enjoying this,” she said.

“I’m working.”

She turned to go.

“Ms. Tang. Have you eaten?”

Her face changed. She glanced at the open door behind her. “Mr. Wang.”

He understood at once, and nodded, and she left. A few seconds later Ding put his head round the door to say the quarter-to-twelve call was ready, and then lingered.

“Would you like me to arrange lunch? You usually have it brought in on a day like this.”

An Yu looked towards the corridor. “Not today.”

Ding left. He had worked for the chairman for years, and in all that time he had never once heard him ask an account manager whether she had eaten.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday Rachel was the first to say something. She arrived at Tang Xi’s desk with two coffees and pulled a chair over.

“How was the shoot?”

“Good.”

“That’s all? Mr. Wang was there a long time for a forty-minute slot.”

“There were extra shots.”

“You’re very defensive.”

“I’m explaining the schedule.”

Rachel leaned in. “Does he always look at you like that? As if he knows what you’re thinking?”

Tang Xi’s fingers stopped on the keyboard. “He’s the client. He’s supposed to pay attention.”

“That’s not what I meant.” Rachel studied her a moment and stood up. “Never mind. I’m probably imagining things. Daniel wants the revised timeline before lunch.”

When she’d gone, Tang Xi looked at her phone.

Professor: Did you get the photographs?

Tang Xi: Yes. The second set’s much better.

Professor: I wanted to know what you thought, not what the photographer did.

Tang Xi: They’re good. Don’t get too pleased with yourself.

Professor: Have you eaten?

Tang Xi: An Yu. It’s nine in the morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

By the middle of the week it had become more noticeable, not because of any one thing but because the small things were piling up. Ding knew. Rachel suspected. An-Tech’s lawyers were asking questions about the strict paperwork on the Northlight account. And Fiona Siew had started watching her.

Fiona was a senior account executive at Northlight, competent and ambitious, and she had expected to run An-Tech herself before Daniel gave it to Tang Xi. She had never been subtle about it. At first it was small remarks. Must be nice to have the chairman asking for you. Some people really do get lucky. Tang Xi ignored them. She had learned long ago that not every unpleasant comment deserved an answer. Fiona was beginning to take that for permission.

On Wednesday afternoon she leaned on the partition while Tang Xi went through the campaign results. “Must be nice. Having a chairman who pays you that much attention.”

“Mr. Wang is the client.”

“Of course. He just seems unusually interested in your work.”

“He asked for me as account manager.”

“Exactly.” Fiona’s smile thinned. “Some of us have been here longer, you know. Some of us worked very hard for the accounts we deserve. Anyway. Congratulations.”

Tang Xi watched her walk away and went back to her report. She had no intention of letting Fiona make her feel guilty for being good at her job.

✦ ✦ ✦

The final campaign review was at six on Friday, at An-Tech. Daniel sent Fiona with Tang Xi to present the media numbers, and Ding and two people from An-Tech’s communications team sat in. Tang Xi took them through the results, the strongest formats and where the next phase needed a different approach. An Yu asked questions; she answered them. The communications director worried about the timing of the next leadership interview, and Tang Xi suggested moving it two weeks to clear the regional product launch, and An Yu agreed. Nothing in it could have been read as anything but professional.

When it was over, Fiona left first. The others followed, and Ding gathered the papers, glanced at the chairman and at Tang Xi, wished her a good evening and went. An Yu stayed in his seat.

“How was your day?”

“Busy.”

“Did you have lunch?”

She looked at him, and he stopped. “Sorry.”

“Are you going home?” he asked.

“Yes.”

“I’ll see you later?”

She glanced at the door. “Not here.” She picked up her bag. “Don’t stay too late.”

Fiona was waiting at the lifts on the forty-second floor, her handbag over her arm and her eyes on the numbers above the doors.

“Long day?” she said.

“Quite.”

“Must be tiring. Managing An-Tech.” Fiona looked at her. “You know people are talking. About you and Mr. Wang. He turns up to shoots he doesn’t need to be at. He asks for you by name. He seems to have an awful lot of time for you.” The lift chimed and the doors opened, and neither of them moved. “Some people are saying you’re sleeping your way to the account.”

For a moment Tang Xi heard nothing: not the lift, not the footsteps along the corridor, not the hum of the building. Fiona said it almost casually, as if she were passing on something she’d heard over coffee.

“Who said that?”

“People.”

“Which people?”

“I don’t know. It’s just what I’ve heard.”

“Then be more careful about repeating it.”

“Don’t be so sensitive. I’m only telling you what’s being said.”

“And I’m telling you not to repeat it,” said Tang Xi, and stepped into the lift. Fiona followed. They stood at opposite sides all the way down and said nothing, and when the doors opened on the lobby, Tang Xi walked out without looking back.

Behind them, at the corner of the corridor, Ding stood still with the meeting folders under his arm.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Mr. Wang. Ms. Tang has left.” Ding paused in the office doorway. “There’s something else. One of the Northlight team made a remark to Ms. Tang at the lifts. I heard it.”

“What remark?”

Ding told him, word for word. Sleeping her way to the account. The room went quiet.

“Who?”

“Fiona Siew. Senior account executive.”

An Yu said nothing. He picked up his phone, opened the account directory and went down Northlight’s staff list until he reached the name, and read it once, and then again.

“Shall I contact their managing director?” Ding asked.

“No. Don’t do anything.”

Ding’s face changed almost imperceptibly. “Understood.”

When he’d gone An Yu sat with the phone in his hand and the name on the screen, and memorised it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past eight Tang Xi was taking off her earrings when her phone rang.

“Are you home?” he said. “Can I come over?”

“Why?”

“I want to see you.”

She sat on the bed. “Did something happen?”

“Ding told me what was said to you.”

She closed her eyes. She had known it would reach him. “It’s fine.”

“It isn’t.”

“That’s easy for you to say. Please don’t do anything.”

“I haven’t.”

“Good.” She heard his breathing change and knew he was angry, not the way he was angry in meetings, at a careless decision or an unfinished report, but quieter and much more dangerous. “Did he tell you who?”

“Yes.”

“I thought that’s what would happen. I kept thinking about what you’d do if you heard. I thought you’d go quiet, and then you’d remember her name.” She waited. “I was right, wasn’t I?”

“Yes.”

“I don’t want you calling Daniel. I don’t want you threatening anyone. I don’t want Fiona finding herself off a project because the chairman didn’t like what she said.”

“I wouldn’t do that.”

“Wouldn’t you?”

He didn’t answer, and the silence told her more than she wanted to know.

“I know you’re angry,” she said. “I am too. But if you react, it becomes exactly what she said. Proof, to everyone, that you can protect me because I’m special to you.”

“I don’t want you to have to put up with it.”

“Then don’t make me put up with something else.” She looked at her hands. “I don’t need you to punish people for me, An Yu. I need you to stand next to me, where I can see you.”

There was a long pause. “I understand.”

“Do you still want to come over?”

“Yes.”

“Then come.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He arrived twenty minutes later in his suit, tie loosened, his face controlled. Too controlled.

“You’re angry,” she said, closing the door.

“Yes. Has she said things before?”

“Little things. How lucky I am. How you asked for me personally.”

His jaw tightened. “Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because I didn’t want it to become your problem.”

“It is my problem if someone’s undermining your work.”

“No.” She came towards him. “It’s my problem, because I work there. It’s mine to deal with through the right channels. I emailed Daniel from the taxi. You can support me. You can’t take it away from me.”

He looked at her, and nodded. “All right.”

“Can you do that? Without a phone call? Without asking Ding to look into her?” He hesitated, and she raised an eyebrow. “An Yu.”

“I won’t.”

She took his hand, and he held on at once. “I’m not asking you not to be angry. I’m asking you not to turn your anger into a decision about my life.”

She leaned against him and he held her carefully, and for a while neither of them spoke.

“You were supposed to say something,” she said eventually, into his shirt. “When Ding told you. You could have said it was unacceptable. You could have told him to report it properly. You could have said my work speaks for itself. And you said nothing.”

“You’re right.”

She could see how much he wanted to do something: in the set of his mouth, in the way his hand had closed round hers, in the stillness he used when he was trying not to give anything away. She also understood that his silence wasn’t neutral. It was a choice, and she was beginning to see that the same silence that had once felt safe to her in a school library could become a weapon in the hands of a man with power.

“Next time,” she said, “don’t make me wonder whether you’re protecting me or deciding what to do with someone.”

“I won’t.”

She believed he wanted to mean it. She wasn’t yet sure he knew how.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Saturday morning Ding brought the briefing in at twenty to nine. “Northlight sent the updated schedule. And Ms. Tang has asked that any concern about staff conduct go through Northlight’s management, not through us. Their managing director is aware of the remark.”

An Yu looked up. “She has?”

“Yes. Would you like a call with him?”

“No. Did you put it in the account record?”

“As a reported concern. No recommendation about personnel.”

“Good. Keep it there.”

Ding nodded, and this time he understood.

On Tuesday afternoon Daniel called Tang Xi into his office. “I’ve spoken to Fiona, and I’ve reminded the team about conduct and the proper way to raise concerns about who gets which account. Do you want to make a formal complaint?”

“Not yet. I want it on record, and I want it to stop.”

“Understood.” He sat back. “Let me be clear. You were put on An-Tech because the client asked for you and because your pitch earned it, and you’ve delivered. If anyone has a problem with that, they bring it to me. Are you comfortable carrying on?”

“Yes.”

“Then we’ll keep the focus on the work. And Xi? If anything else happens, tell me. Don’t feel you have to handle it quietly.”

She left his office feeling, for the first time in days, that someone had dealt with the problem without making her smaller.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday night she was on his sofa when he came out of the kitchen and handed her a glass of water and sat beside her.

“How was work? Fiona?”

“Quiet.”

“Good.” He didn’t ask for more.

“You’re not going to ask for details?”

“You’ll tell me if you want to.”

She leaned on his shoulder and his hand settled on her knee, and they watched the city for a while.

“Ding knows,” she said. “Rachel suspects. Your legal team probably knows. Everyone can see it.”

“Does that bother you?”

She thought about it. “Not that they can see I like you. That they might decide my work is worth less because of it.”

“I won’t interfere with your work,” he said, before she could turn round and look at him. “And I won’t let anyone at An-Tech treat your position as anything other than what it is.”

“That’s better.”

He looked at her. “Can I kiss you?”

“You’re asking? After all this?”

“It seemed worth asking.”

“Yes,” she said, and he kissed her slowly, her hand along his cheek, close enough afterwards to feel his breath. “Next time somebody says something like that, I want you to speak. Not because I’m your girlfriend. Because it’s wrong.”

“Because it’s wrong,” he agreed.

Later, after she had fallen asleep beside him, he lay awake with his phone in his hand and the directory open, and the name was still there. He could make a call. He could find out exactly who had repeated the rumour and how far it had gone. He could make the problem disappear before she heard another word of it. His thumb rested on the screen for a long time.

Then he locked it and put it face up on the table beside hers. Tang Xi shifted in her sleep, and her hand found his on the sheet, and he held it and tried, for once, not to decide what happened next.

chapters.title: The Old Nickname
chapters.desc: Dinner with his brother and sister-in-law, and the nickname from the library said across the table.
chapters.content:
Wang An Yu had neglected to mention that dinner was with his family.

Tang Xi found out at twenty to seven on Saturday evening, when the car turned through a pair of iron gates and stopped outside a restaurant she recognised from its discreet entrance and notoriously impossible bookings.

“An Yu. Who are we having dinner with?”

He looked up from his phone. “My brother and his wife.”

“You could have told me.”

“I did. This morning. I said I had dinner plans with family.”

“You said dinner plans. That could have meant your mother, your father, an aunt, a cousin, an entire family reunion. You didn’t say your brother and sister-in-law.”

“I didn’t think the distinction mattered.” He took in her expression. “Would you like me to cancel?”

“No.” She opened the little mirror in her bag. She had dressed for dinner, not for meeting his family: an ivory blouse under a dark jacket, a black skirt, hair pinned loosely, small earrings. She looked presentable. She wasn’t prepared to meet the people who had known him long before she had. “How long have they been married?”

“Almost two years.”

“And you didn’t think to mention that either?”

“I believe I did. Last month.”

“In what conversation?”

He paused. “I don’t remember.”

He reached over and straightened the collar of her jacket. “You look lovely.”

She caught his wrist. “Don’t try to distract me.”

“Would it help if I told you my brother is harmless?”

“Is he?”

“No. He’s a surgeon. He has a very low tolerance for nonsense.”

“And your sister-in-law?”

“Worse,” said An Yu, entirely serious, and opened his door.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wang Xing Yue was already at the table. At thirty-three he had the composure of a man who had spent years staying calm in rooms where other people were allowed to panic: gold-rimmed glasses, dark hair swept back, sleeves turned once at the wrist, and a tiredness round the eyes that looked less like exhaustion than a permanent occupational condition. Beside him sat Elara, twenty-five, delicate-faced, with an attentive gaze that took in Tang Xi in one sweep and seemed to like what it found. A star sapphire caught the light on her left hand when she lifted her glass.

“You’re late,” she told An Yu.

“Seven minutes.”

“Eight.”

Xing Yue stood to greet his brother and turned to Tang Xi. “You must be Tang Xi.”

“It’s lovely to meet you, Mr. Wang.”

“Mr. Wang is my brother. Apparently.” He shook her hand. “Xing Yue.”

“Then please call me Tang Xi.”

“This is my wife.”

“Hello,” said Elara, standing. “I’ve heard a little about you.”

Tang Xi glanced at An Yu. “I’ve heard very little about you. From him.”

“That sounds right,” said Elara.

An Yu sat down. “Have you two been discussing me?”

“No,” said Xing Yue.

“Not yet,” said Elara.

Tang Xi laughed, and something in Elara’s face warmed at once. She was easy to talk to, not loud or forward, but warm in a way that made it feel less like an interview than being let into a room where everyone already knew each other. Inside ten minutes she had asked about Northlight, how long Tang Xi had been there, whether she liked account management, and whether her hours were as bad as theirs.

“Sometimes,” Tang Xi admitted. “But I think every job has its own kind of terrible hours.”

“Some people think four hours’ sleep is a personality,” said Elara, looking at her husband.

“It isn’t,” said Xing Yue.

“You behave as if it is.”

“I have a schedule.”

“You have a problem.”

Tang Xi hid a smile in her glass. An Yu had said little, answering when he was spoken to and correcting his brother’s recollections now and then, but whenever she laughed his attention went to her. Xing Yue noticed. He had known his younger brother for twenty-six years.

“How long have you known each other?” he asked.

“Since school,” said Tang Xi. “Shanghai.”

Xing Yue turned to An Yu. “And I’ve never heard about her.”

“You never asked.”

“Convenient.”

“Wait,” said Elara. “Were you in the same class?”

“We studied in the same library. I talked to him every lunchtime for a year. He ignored me.”

“That sounds familiar,” said Xing Yue.

“Does it?” said An Yu.

“Very.”

Elara leaned forward. “What did you talk about?”

“Everything. Teachers, exams, the canteen, whatever came into my head. He hardly ever answered. Sometimes he looked at me.”

“For him that’s a conversation,” said Xing Yue.

An Yu put down his menu with the expression he saved for difficult meetings, composed, faintly displeased and fully aware that nobody intended to listen to him. Tang Xi found it unexpectedly endearing.

“He read maths textbooks at lunch,” she told Elara.

“He still does that,” said Xing Yue.

“I don’t.”

“You read financial reports over breakfast.”

“That’s work.”

“And you think that’s different?”

The food came before Tang Xi could tell them anything else. For the next hour the talk moved easily between work, the hospital and old school stories, and Elara asked about the An-Tech campaign with real interest, how you measure whether people trust a company’s leaders more than they did, and Tang Xi found herself explaining it in more detail than she’d meant to. When she mentioned how hard it was to separate a company’s reputation from its chairman’s, Xing Yue looked at his brother.

“He’s been talking about this campaign for weeks,” Elara said. “Not directly. He came to dinner one evening and complained about a presentation.”

“I didn’t complain.”

“You said the strategy was unnecessarily complicated. Then you explained the whole thing over the fish.”

An Yu gave Tang Xi a warning look. She smiled anyway.

“Do you know what he was like at school?” Elara asked her.

“Very quiet. Very particular. He had a favourite chair in the library.”

Xing Yue put his chopsticks down. “A favourite chair.”

“He always sat in the same place. I used to ask if he was in love with it.”

“Xi,” said An Yu, in the voice that meant stop.

So of course she didn’t. She leaned towards him and said, barely above a whisper, the way she had once said it across a library table when she wanted him to look up from his book, “Professor.”

His face went still. The name hadn’t changed in ten years, and neither had what it did to him.

✦ ✦ ✦

Xing Yue was telling a story about a patient who had taken him for a medical student, in his flat, dry way, which made it funnier, when Tang Xi felt An Yu’s hand settle on the back of her chair. He was listening to his brother, or appearing to. She could feel the restraint in the small pressure of his fingers.

“Are you all right?” she murmured, while Elara asked her husband something.

“Perfectly.”

“You’re very quiet.”

“I’m always quiet.”

“Not like this.”

He leaned in. “Don’t.”

“Don’t what?” she said innocently.

His eyes dropped to her mouth. “Xi.”

She knew it was a mistake. But she had spent a year talking to him when he wouldn’t answer, and months finding out what happened when that quiet man finally let himself be known, and she had never quite lost the pleasure of making him lose his composure.

“Professor,” she breathed.

His hand tightened on the chair. Across the table Xing Yue stopped mid-sentence. Elara looked at her husband, then at An Yu, then at Tang Xi, and a slow, delighted understanding spread over her face.

“Oh,” she said, into her glass.

An Yu put his napkin down. “Excuse me.” He stood, and Tang Xi followed him a moment later.

Elara watched them go and turned to her husband. “Your brother is in trouble.”

Xing Yue picked up his glass. “He’s been in trouble since 2014.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The corridor behind the private rooms was narrow and warmly lit, and he was waiting by a service door when she found him.

“Mr. Wang?”

“Don’t.”

“Are you angry?”

“No.”

“Embarrassed?”

He took her hand and drew her in. “You’re enjoying this.”

“A little. You looked so serious.”

“I was having dinner.”

“You were introducing me to your brother’s wife.”

“I’ve known her a year and a half.”

“And she liked me.”

“She did. I’m glad.”

“Why?”

“Because I like you.”

It was so simple that it took her next remark away. He pressed his mouth to her knuckles. “Don’t call me that in front of them again.”

She tipped her chin up at him. “Would you rather I called you Wang An Yu?”

“Not particularly.”

“Then what?”

“An Yu.”

“That’s very ordinary.”

His hand settled on her waist. “You’re making it very difficult to behave.”

“Are you supposed to be behaving?”

He kissed her before she could say anything else, and it wasn’t a careful kiss: his hand at the back of her neck, his mouth hot on hers, drawing her in so suddenly that her fingers caught on his jacket. Somewhere beyond the service door a trolley rattled past. She pulled back, breathless.

“Someone might come.”

“Then we should go.”

“Back to dinner?”

“No.”

“An Yu.”

He put his forehead against hers. “You’re going to be the end of my patience.”

“That’s dramatic.”

“You’ve had ten years to practise,” he said, and she laughed and kissed him again, and then they went back in long enough to say good night to his brother, who said nothing at all, and to Elara, who kissed Tang Xi’s cheek and said, “Tea. Soon. Without him,” in a voice that made it a plan.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had sent the driver home and drove himself. At the first red light she said, “Your brother is funny.”

“He thinks so.”

“Your sister-in-law is lovely. She likes me.”

“I noticed.”

“She’ll ask you about me.”

“She already did. Before you arrived. She asked whether I was serious about you.”

“And what did you say?”

“That I was.”

“Oh,” she said, and looked down at her hands, and when he reached across the console she wove her fingers through his. “Professor.”

His hand tightened. “Xi.”

“You’re very sensitive about that name.”

At the next red light he turned to her. “Do you know why I don’t want you saying it in public? Because when you say it, I remember exactly how it sounded when you were sixteen. As if you knew I’d listen, even when I didn’t answer.”

Her smile went. “I didn’t know that.”

“I know.”

The light changed. She watched him drive for a while, then lifted their joined hands and kissed his knuckles. “Do you still listen?”

“Always.”

She leaned across the console and kissed him, and he kissed her back at the next light with one hand still on the wheel and the other on her cheek, and drew away only when someone behind them sounded a horn.

In the car park under his building he switched the engine off, and neither of them moved to get out. The garage was concrete and fluorescent light and silence, and she climbed across the console into his lap with her skirt riding up her thighs, and he pushed the seat back to make room and kissed her as if they had all night and no flat upstairs. His hands slid up under her blouse to the small of her back. She rocked against him and felt him hard through his trousers, and he made a sound into her mouth and said, “Not here,” and didn’t stop.

“You’re the one who parked,” she said against his jaw.

“Upstairs,” he said. “Now. Before I forget there are cameras.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The door had barely closed when she turned and took hold of his tie.

“You’re still wearing your earrings,” he said.

“That’s what you’re thinking about?”

“They’ll fall.”

She took them out and put them on the console table. “Better?”

“Much.”

She tugged the tie. “Now you can stop pretending to be a reasonable person.”

He caught her hand, and something serious came into his face under the heat. “Are you sure?”

“Yes. I want you.”

“Tell me if you want me to stop.”

“I will.”

The first kiss was slow, almost restrained, and the second wasn’t. She worked his collar open and slid the tie free and let it hang across her hands, and he watched her look down at the dark silk and back up at him.

“May I?” she asked.

He understood. “Yes.”

“Both wrists?”

“If you want to.”

“I do. Sit down, Professor.”

He gave a short, disbelieving laugh. “You really aren’t going to let that go.”

“Not tonight.”

He sat on the edge of the sofa. She stood between his knees and looped the tie round his wrists in front of him, careful to leave it loose enough for him to move, and checked the knot.

“Comfortable?”

“Yes.”

“Can you get out?”

“Probably.”

“That’s not very romantic.”

“It’s an accurate assessment.”

He could have freed himself, and they both knew it, and he stayed exactly where he was and watched her with a look that made her own smile go soft.

“You’re trusting me,” she said.

“Yes.”

She undressed in front of him slowly, the jacket, the blouse, the skirt, letting each one fall on the floor by his feet, and his bound hands rested on his knees and didn’t move, though his breathing did. When she unbuttoned his shirt and opened his trousers he lifted his hips to help her and said her name like a warning, and she ignored it. She took him in her hand and then in her mouth, and his head went back against the sofa and his tied wrists strained once against the silk and then went still again, because she had told him to keep them still. She took her time. She made him say please. He said it. Then she climbed onto him and sank down, and the sound he made was nothing like the chairman of anything.

She rode him slowly with her hands on his shoulders, and he couldn’t touch her, and every time he tried she caught his bound wrists and put them back in his lap, laughing, and he kissed whatever part of her he could reach, her throat, her collarbone, her breast, his mouth hot and open. “Xi,” he said, and then, rougher, “Xi,” and she leaned down to his ear and said “Professor,” and felt him shudder under her.

“Untie me,” he said.

“Ask nicely.”

“Please.”

She pulled the knot loose. His hands were on her before the tie hit the floor, gripping her hips, holding her down on him, moving her the way he wanted, and she let him, gasping, until he turned them both and laid her back along the sofa and drove into her so deep and so steady that she stopped being able to tease him at all. She came with her nails in his back and his name in her mouth, and he followed her with his face in her neck, saying something she didn’t catch.

When he could speak again, he caught her hand and pressed it to his mouth. “Thank you. For trusting me with who you are when nobody’s watching.”

She brushed his hair back from his forehead. “You’re welcome. Although I think you liked being told what to do.”

“Don’t push your luck,” he said, and she laughed into his shoulder.

✦ ✦ ✦

After midnight she lay against his chest under the blanket, his tie folded on the bedside table, and was quiet for several minutes, which he found suspicious.

“What are you thinking about?”

“Your sister-in-law. I like her. She asked me about work properly, not to be polite.”

“Elara likes people who speak honestly.”

“Then she must find you very difficult.”

“She does.”

She shifted closer. “Do they know about the library?”

“They do now.”

“Not everything. Not that I brought you strawberry milk and you never said thank you. Or that I spent a whole lunch telling you to try the canteen’s new noodles.”

“You said they were terrible.”

“They were. You ate them anyway.”

“I was proving a point.”

She was quiet again. “Do you remember the last day? What I said?”

He didn’t answer straight away. “’Good luck, Wang An Yu.’”

Her fingers stopped on his chest.

“I should have asked you to stay,” he said.

“You were sixteen.”

“I still should have.”

“You didn’t know what you were losing.” She touched his cheek. “Neither did I.”

He turned his face into her palm, and for a while the room held nothing but the sound of the city beyond the glass.

“Your sister-in-law is going to ask me out,” Tang Xi said eventually. “Without you.”

“Probably.”

“Will you mind?”

“I trust you to survive an afternoon with her.”

“That’s not what I meant.”

He kissed her forehead. “I won’t mind.”

She settled back against him. “Good night, Professor.”

He closed his eyes. “Good night, Xi.”

chapters.title: Why She Stopped Coming
chapters.desc: He finally asks why she stopped coming. She came back once, on a Thursday, and his chair was empty.
chapters.content:
Elara’s message arrived on a Thursday, nearly four weeks after the dinner, which Tang Xi suspected was exactly as long as Elara had been able to make herself wait.

Elara (Tea, Soon): Afternoon tea, the Saturday after next? Just us. Xing Yue has offered to babysit his brother.

On Saturday afternoon Tang Xi sat at An Yu’s dining table with her laptop open on a campaign proposal while he went through a stack of documents beside her. The flat was quiet, the sun lay across the floor, and it caught the face of his watch every time he turned a page.

“Your sister-in-law invited me to tea.”

“I know.”

“You know?”

“She told me on Thursday.”

“Your entire family communicates independently of me.”

“Would you like me to coordinate it?”

“No.”

“Then I don’t see the problem.”

She threw a cushion at him. He caught it without looking up. “Violence,” he observed, and put it down beside him, and they went back to work.

“Xi,” he said, a while later. “Can I ask you something difficult?”

She stopped typing. “All right.”

He closed the document in front of him. “When we were at school. Why did you stop coming to the library?”

The question was simple, almost ordinary, and it changed the temperature of the room. She lowered the laptop screen.

“Why now?”

“Because I’ve wanted to ask for a long time.”

He waited. He had learned, slowly, that waiting for Tang Xi to speak was different from waiting for someone to finish a presentation: she needed room to decide what she was going to tell him. He didn’t fill it.

“My father’s company failed,” she said at last, looking at her hands. “That June. It had been struggling for a while, but I didn’t know how bad it was. My parents tried to keep everything normal. I had exams, school, the programme. They didn’t want me worrying about things I couldn’t change. Then one Saturday I came home and there were boxes in the living room.” She gave a small, almost apologetic smile. “He’d spent months trying to find investors. It didn’t work. The company couldn’t pay what it owed, and everything fell apart very fast. We left Shanghai a week later.”

“A week.”

“My mother’s sister had a restaurant here. She took us in, and my mother’s worked there ever since. There was a flat to give up, paperwork, school records. I remember thinking a week wasn’t long enough to say goodbye to anything.” She laughed under her breath. “I was more upset about leaving school than leaving the flat. That sounds ridiculous.”

“It doesn’t.”

“I didn’t tell anyone. Everyone was talking about universities and summer and what they’d do next year. I didn’t want to explain that my family was leaving because we couldn’t afford to stay. So I stopped talking about it.”

His hands had gone still on the table. “Did you tell your friends?”

“I didn’t have many I was close enough to tell.”

“And me?”

She turned to look at him, and smiled, a little. “You never asked me anything.”

It wasn’t an accusation, which made it worse. He looked down.

“I know you remember me talking,” she said. “But I don’t think you ever knew how much I was waiting for you to ask me something.” She pulled her feet up onto the chair and wrapped her arms round her knees. “That Monday I came to tell you, and I couldn’t. I folded you a crane instead and put it in your book while you were at the shelves, and I said good luck, as if it were the end of term. Then on Thursday I came back to tell you properly. Two days before we left. I was going to say I was leaving and ask for your number. Maybe say something ridiculous about how you had to remember me.” Her eyes drifted to the window. “You weren’t there.”

The room went quiet.

“I sat in my seat and waited. Your chair was empty. I thought you were late. Then I thought you’d gone somewhere else, and I checked all the other tables.” A small laugh. “I was very determined. I stayed until Mrs. Hua rang the bell. And then I left Shanghai.”

He could see it: the library, the afternoon light, the chair opposite his, and a girl who had spent a year filling the space between them with words, waiting for something back.

“Which day was it?” he asked. “Exactly.”

She frowned. “The Thursday. The eighteenth, I think.”

He lowered his eyes. He remembered the eighteenth.

✦ ✦ ✦

The hospital corridor smelled of disinfectant and old air conditioning. Nainai had come to Shanghai that week to see the end of his school year and was staying in his flat, because she always stayed with him, and that morning she had missed the bottom step in the hall. It wasn’t serious, the doctors said, but she was in her eighties, and the fall had frightened everyone more than anyone would admit. His father had gone to deal with the doctors and the papers. Xing Yue was on a flight from home. An Yu sat by the bed with a book he hadn’t read a word of for an hour, and his grandmother, who had refused to let the nurses touch her pillows, complained about the hospital food and sent him for the tea she kept in his kitchen, lay against her pillows with her polished stick hooked over the rail and watched him.

“You’re not reading,” she said.

“I am.”

“Then why have you been on the same page since lunch?”

He closed the book.

“At least you’re honest now. Are you waiting for someone? Then stop looking at the door.” She reached for her tea. “That girl from school?”

He turned. “What girl?”

“The one who talks. You told me about her.”

“I didn’t.”

“You said there was a girl who sat opposite you in the library.”

“That isn’t telling you about her.”

“Of course it is.” Nainai studied him over the rim of the cup. “Does she know you like her?”

He was sixteen. He looked down at his book. “I don’t know.”

His grandmother sighed. “Then perhaps you should tell her.”

He meant to, the next day. On Friday he went to the library at twelve. Her chair was empty. He read for twenty minutes, then thirty, and the bell went, and she didn’t come. He came back every day the next week, sat in the same chair at the same time and left when the library closed. On the Wednesday he asked Mrs. Hua whether she’d seen Tang Xi.

“The cheerful one? Not this week, dear. You could ask her classmates.”

He didn’t know who her classmates were. He knew her timetable, the teachers she complained about, the subjects she found hard, that she liked strawberry milk better than orange juice and always sat facing the window. He knew almost nothing about the life she went back to when she left the library. He had never asked.

✦ ✦ ✦

“An Yu?”

He had gone still. “I was at the hospital. That day. Nainai had fallen. I was with her.”

Her face changed. “Was she all right?”

“Yes. It frightened us, but she was fine.” He looked at his hands. “I went back on the Friday. I sat in the same place. I went back every day the week after. I asked Mrs. Hua if she’d seen you.”

“You asked about me? Then why didn’t you ever ask me?”

“I didn’t know how to.”

She gave a small, incredulous laugh. “You knew how to find the library. You knew how to ask the librarian. You could remember my entire timetable, but you couldn’t ask for my number? You could have written a note. You could have said literally anything.”

“Yes.”

Her face softened. “Why didn’t you?”

He took a long time to answer. “Because I thought there would be another day. I thought I could talk to you tomorrow, or next week. There was no hurry. You were always there.” His voice was quiet. “Then you weren’t.”

He reached across the table and stopped before he touched her hand. “Xi. I’m sorry.”

It was a simple apology: no explanation about being sixteen, no attempt to make it hurt less, no suggestion that she should have told him. She put her hand in his.

“I wish you’d been there that day.”

“So do I.”

“I really did wait. I’d planned what I was going to say. I was going to tell you I was leaving, and then ask if you’d miss me.”

“And what would I have said?”

“I don’t know.”

“I would have.”

She laughed. “You don’t know that.”

“I do. I knew it at sixteen.”

He lifted her hand and pressed his lips to her fingers. “I’d have asked you to stay in touch. I’d have given you my number.”

“Would you actually have called?”

He paused, and she looked up. “An Yu. You have to answer.”

“I would have.”

She laughed, and her eyes had gone wet. He got up and came round the table and crouched beside her chair so that his face was level with hers, and took both her hands.

“I can’t change that day. I can’t give you the goodbye you should have had. But I can tell you now. I missed you.”

Her mouth trembled. “I missed you too.”

He leaned his forehead against hers, and for a while they stayed like that.

“I thought you weren’t there because you didn’t care,” she whispered. “I was embarrassed. About how much I liked you. About how often I went to that library just to see you. I thought I’d made up the whole friendship in my head while you barely spoke to me.”

“You didn’t make it up. I came early because you came at a quarter past. I sat at the same table. I kept the chair opposite me empty.”

“You did?”

“I never told you.”

“You really were hopeless,” she said, and leaned in and kissed him, gently, with no teasing in it. He held her face between his hands, and when she drew back she stayed close.

“I used to think if you ever spoke to me properly I’d faint.”

“Did you?”

“No. Very disappointing.”

He kissed her again, and she smiled against his mouth and then pulled away far enough to look at him.

“There’s something else. My father was very ashamed. He’d spent years building that company. It wasn’t big, but it was his: people worked for him, suppliers trusted him. When it collapsed he took it personally. He didn’t want anyone in Shanghai to know, or to ask questions, or for me to explain why we’d gone. I think that’s why I disappeared so completely. I didn’t even tell some of my classmates.”

“Did you ever go back?”

“Once, years later, for work. I didn’t go near the school. I didn’t know what I’d feel.”

He brushed her hair off her cheek. “Would you like to go? With me?”

She looked at him. “Maybe.”

“No rush,” he said, and kissed her temple.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were getting ready for bed that night when she noticed the box on his bedside table, the one she’d seen before and never asked about.

“What’s in there?”

“Something from school. You can look.”

Inside were a few old papers, a photograph of a school sports day and a maths textbook with a worn cover. She knew the book at once. Between its pages was a sheet of wax paper, and inside it the crane, back where it had lived for ten years, its uneven wings and the one deep crease exactly as she’d made them.

“Even when you went to Zurich?” she said. “And London?”

“Yes. It was the only thing you left me.”

“I thought you’d have thrown it away.”

“I couldn’t. I knew you’d made it for me.” He reached past her and straightened one wing with a fingertip. “Do you remember what you wrote?”

“’For the person who never talks. I hope you find something interesting to do when I’m not here.’”

“I did.”

“What?”

He slid the crane back into the wax paper and closed the book. “Remembering you.”

She laughed. “That’s an awful line.”

“You’re smiling.”

“I know.” She put her arms round his waist from behind and pressed her face into his back. “Next time we’re in Shanghai, I want to see the library. I want to sit in my old seat.”

“I’ll sit opposite you.”

“Will you talk to me this time?”

“Yes.”

“Promise?”

“I promise.”

“Then I have a lot to tell you,” she said, and turned him round, and began with the chemistry teacher who had once poured a beaker of blue solution into his own shoe, and he got into bed beside her and listened to every word.

chapters.title: The Building on Her Street
chapters.desc: A laminated notice by the lift: her building has a new landlord, and it belongs to him. The fight ends in his chair.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t want you to find a more sophisticated way to own the things around me.”
chapters.content:
The notice was small: a laminated sheet beside the lift buttons in Northlight’s building, which Tang Xi only read on Monday morning because the lift was slow and she had nothing else to look at.

PROPERTY MANAGEMENT UPDATE
Effective 1 July 2025, ownership and management of this building have transferred to An-Tech Property Management.
For tenancy, maintenance and building enquiries, please contact the management office on Level 2.

She read it twice. The lift arrived, and she didn’t move until a woman with two coffees stepped round her and said, “Coming?”

On the way up she searched the name. An-Tech Property Management was a subsidiary of An-Tech Holdings. A short business notice the week before had announced it had bought a portfolio of commercial buildings, and listed the addresses. Hers was third. She rang him before the doors opened.

“Xi.”

“Did you buy my building?”

There was a pause. “Yes.”

The lift stopped on eighteen. She stepped out and hung up without saying goodbye.

✦ ✦ ✦

Daniel was on a call. He held up a finger, and when he’d finished he looked at her standing in his doorway. “Morning, Xi. Everything all right?”

“Did you know the building had been sold?”

“We had a notice last week. An-Tech Property, one of their subsidiaries. Our lease carries on unchanged, so there’s nothing for us to do.” He studied her face. “Is there a problem?”

“No. I just wanted to check.”

His phone rang again, and she went back to her desk and opened the announcement a third time. A portfolio acquisition, alongside several other office buildings, completed through An-Tech Property’s investment arm. A business decision. A transaction with commercial logic. Except that she knew Wang An Yu, and she knew he had a gift for finding a perfectly reasonable explanation for doing something nobody had asked him to do.

Professor: Can we talk?

Tang Xi: You can explain.

Professor: In person.

Tang Xi: After work. Your office. Don’t send a car.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was standing beside his desk at ten to seven with his jacket off, his sleeves folded to the forearm and a file open in front of him.

“Xi.”

She shut the door. “Don’t. You bought my building.”

“Yes.”

“Without telling me. After everything. Do you remember the rules?”

“Yes.”

“Say them.”

His face tightened. “Nobody at work knows. Nothing on the account changes. I don’t buy anything for you, or arrange anything involving you, without your agreement.”

She put both hands flat on the edge of his desk. “Then explain why you bought the building I work in.”

“It was part of a portfolio. It’s commercially sound. The existing leases are stable, and the location is strategically useful.”

“That sounds like a paragraph from an investment memo.”

“It is.”

“An Yu.”

He breathed out. “I knew Northlight was a tenant. Before the acquisition, not after. I didn’t go to the seller because of you; the investment team had been looking at the portfolio for months. But I knew, and I went ahead.”

“Why?”

He didn’t answer.

“Please don’t tell me you bought it to make my working life easier.”

“I didn’t.”

“Then why?”

“Because I wanted to own it.”

She stared at him. “Not the whole truth.”

He looked at the window and back. “I knew where you worked. I knew the building was being sold. I knew it was an opportunity. And I wanted it.”

“Because of me?”

He didn’t answer quickly enough, and she laughed under her breath. “Right. You promised.”

His expression changed. “I promised not to buy anything for you.”

She went still. He seemed to hear how it sounded a moment after he’d said it, and he didn’t take it back.

“You promised,” she said again.

“I didn’t buy it for you. I bought a commercial property.”

“Where I work.”

“That doesn’t make it yours.”

“Do you hear yourself?” She came round the corner of the desk. “This is worse than the café. The café was somewhere I liked, and you thought you were making something convenient for me. This is my workplace. My salary, my colleagues, my professional life, and now the building they sit in belongs to a company you control.”

“The lease is unchanged.”

“That’s not the point.”

“Northlight’s tenancy will be respected.”

“That isn’t the point either.” She hated that her voice was going unsteady. “You can tell me the lease is unchanged and the deal is sound and it’s one building in a big portfolio, and I will still walk into work every morning knowing that the chairman of my client owns the walls. I can’t complain about the lifts without wondering whether someone tells you.”

“You complain to the management office. I won’t see it.”

“But you could.”

“Yes.”

“And if I don’t like how they handle it?”

“You can escalate.”

“To whom?”

He stopped.

“Exactly,” she said. “Your power is there even when you don’t use it.”

For the first time he had nothing ready. He came round the desk. “Xi, I would never use the building to influence your work.”

“I know you don’t intend to. I shouldn’t have to rely on what you intend. I need the lines we draw to be real, not real when they’re convenient for you.”

His face had gone still. “You’re right. I should have told you before it closed. I should have thought about what it would mean for you. I didn’t. I’m sorry.”

She looked away. She had wanted him to say it. She had also wanted him not to have done it, and no apology could undo a property deal.

“Will you sell it?”

“I can put in an independent property manager.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

“I don’t think selling a sound asset because of our relationship is the right decision. But I can set up management with no reporting line to me on anything involving Northlight.”

She shook her head. “You still don’t understand. I don’t want you to find a more sophisticated way to own the things around me.”

That one went somewhere the others hadn’t; she saw it land. She picked up her bag. “I need some time.”

“Xi. Are you coming over tonight?”

“I don’t know.”

“All right.”

She opened the door and stopped. “And An Yu? Don’t send anyone to check I got home.”

“I won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ding came in after eight with the property team’s revised structure and found the chairman exactly where he’d been an hour earlier.

“Leave it,” said An Yu. “Send me Northlight’s lease, the full terms and the renewal provisions. And every tenant decision involving Northlight goes to an independent property director. No line to my office. Have Legal write it down.”

When Ding had gone, he sat alone with the file. The deal was sound. The building was valuable, the location good, the leases stable; the investment team had recommended it months before. He could defend every part of it. He could also remember the night she stood in his bedroom doorway in her coat and told him not to decide things about her life without asking. He had agreed, and then he had done it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday evening she brought the revised campaign report to his office herself. She could have sent it through the portal or asked Rachel to deliver it, but she was the account manager, and the report was hers.

“Ms. Tang.”

“Mr. Wang. Next quarter’s recommendations, with the data in the appendix.”

“Thank you.” He stood as she turned to go. “I’ve put independent management on the building. The property director reports through investment operations, not to me, and Northlight is handled like every other tenant. Legal has confirmed there’ll be no change to your lease or renewal outside the ordinary process.”

“That’s appropriate.”

“I know it doesn’t undo it. And I won’t ask you to accept an apology because I’ve made an arrangement afterwards.”

“Good,” she said. “Good evening, Mr. Wang.”

She didn’t go to his flat that night, or the next. He didn’t text to ask why.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday the final review ran late, and when the others had gone she stayed to pack her laptop while he stood at the window with the city behind him.

“Are you still angry?” she asked.

“With myself. I knew the rule and why you made it, and I still persuaded myself this was different.”

“Why?”

“Because I wanted to be close to your life.”

Her face softened a fraction. “You already are.”

“I know.”

“Then why do you keep trying to own the things around it?”

“I don’t have a good answer.”

She walked over to him. “I’m still angry, An Yu. Very. And I still want to kiss you.”

His eyes came up. He reached for her waist and stopped just short of it.

“You can,” she said.

The kiss started with more anger than tenderness. She caught his loosened tie and pulled him down to her, and he came, one hand at her waist and the other at her jaw, and she kissed him as if she could make him understand everything she hadn’t managed to say across his desk on Monday. He broke away first.

“We should talk.”

“We’ve talked.”

“Not enough.”

She put her palm flat on his chest. “Then listen. I don’t want you to stop taking care of me. I like that you remember things. I like that you notice when I’m tired, and that you know what I drank at sixteen. But I don’t want your care turning into a way of controlling the world around me. I can be angry with you and still love you. Both of those are true tonight.”
