He went still. She hadn’t said it before. Neither had he.

“Say that again,” he said.

“Which part?”

“The second.”

“I love you,” said Tang Xi, “and you’re still in trouble,” and she pushed him back until he hit the edge of the desk, and then further, round it, into his own chair.

He sat. She stood between his knees and pulled his tie free and dropped it on the report she’d delivered on Tuesday.

“You’re asking a lot of questions with your face,” she said.

“I want to be certain.”

“I want you. I’m angry with you. Both.”

She climbed onto him in the big leather chair with her skirt pushed up her thighs, and his hands came to her hips and held on. She kissed him hard and he kissed her back the same way, unbuttoning her blouse with fingers that weren’t quite steady, his mouth following them down. She worked his belt open. The city lights hung in the glass behind his head, and the office beyond the glass wall was dark and empty, and he said her name against her collarbone as if it were an apology and she said, “Not yet,” and took him in her hand and sank down onto him.

He swore, which she had never heard him do. She rode him slowly at first, holding the back of the chair on either side of his head, making him look at her, and every time his hands tried to set the pace she caught his wrists and put them back on her hips. “My turn,” she said, and he let her have it, his head tipped back and his jaw tight, until she was shaking and close and he finally gripped her and drove up into her, hard, and she came with her forehead pressed to his and her nails in his shoulders. He followed her a moment later, her name broken in half in his mouth.

They stayed like that, the chair creaking, both of them breathing hard, his hand moving slowly up and down her spine.

“You’re not forgiven,” she said into his neck.

“Not yet.”

“Not yet,” she agreed. She lifted her head. “Take me home. Mine.”

She found her earrings on his desk, among the papers, and put them back on. At the door she turned. “And don’t buy the block of flats I live in next. Or the street. Or the dumpling place across from my aunt’s restaurant.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

“That sounded suspiciously specific.”

He laughed, and she kissed him once more, and for once he let her walk out first and followed only when she held out her hand.

chapters.title: Promotion
chapters.desc: Senior Account Director at twenty-seven. She doesn’t know if she earned it, so he forwards her every email, in order.
chapters.epigraph: “Did you ask Daniel to promote me?”
chapters.content:
Tang Xi found out about her promotion on a Tuesday morning in August, between a client email and a reminder to approve a production budget. The subject line said Senior Account Director — Appointment, and she opened it expecting someone else’s name. It was hers. From the first of September she would be Senior Account Director, with several key accounts and continued leadership of An-Tech. At twenty-seven she would be one of the youngest people at Northlight to hold the title.

Her first reaction was happiness. Her second was disbelief. Her third was Wang An Yu.

She closed the email, opened it again and checked the sender. Daniel.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Congratulations,” Daniel said, standing up when she knocked. “Sit. The leadership team approved it yesterday; the agency hears on Thursday.” He slid a folder across the desk: the title, the new pay structure, the responsibilities. “You’ve earned it. An-Tech has been excellent, the Alder Vane partnership, the leadership campaign, the regional rollout. You’ve handled a demanding client without giving away our scope or our margins. Rachel says you lead well, and strategy keeps asking to bring you into pitches earlier.”

“Thank you.” She looked at the folder. Part of her wanted to be happy without a single reservation. She had worked for this: difficult clients, defended budgets, late revisions, decisions made under pressure. She had never expected anything to arrive without effort. But An-Tech was one of Northlight’s biggest accounts, An Yu was its chairman, and he had already shown that his idea of taking care of her could go a long way past anything she’d asked for.

“Daniel, was this discussed with the client?”

He frowned. “No. Why?”

“Did Mr. Wang make any kind of recommendation?”

“No. I started the review after the last quarterly assessment, and the leadership team approved it on your results.” He watched her. “Is there something I should know?”

“No. I wanted to be sure.”

“Your promotion isn’t a favour from a client, Xi. It’s recognition of your work. I don’t want you second-guessing that.”

She said she understood. She wasn’t sure she did.

✦ ✦ ✦

Rachel found her at the coffee machine after lunch, grinning. “I hear things. Senior Account Director at twenty-seven. That’s ridiculous. I was twenty-nine when I made Account Director and I thought I was extraordinary.”

“You were.”

“I know. That’s why I’m annoyed.” Rachel leaned on the counter and looked at her properly. “You’re not happy.”

“I am.”

“You’re thinking. Is it An-Tech?” Tang Xi didn’t answer, and Rachel sighed. “Xi, I don’t think he asked for this. Daniel’s been talking about your development for months. Strategy has been pushing to give you more. You know that.”

“I don’t want anyone thinking I got it for the wrong reasons.”

“Then don’t let them. People can say what they like, but they still have to explain why the campaigns worked, why the client renewed, why the regional team trusts you and why Daniel wants you on bigger accounts.” She nudged her. “Enjoy it.”

“I’ll try.”

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu knew something was wrong before she’d taken off her shoes on Wednesday night. She put her bag on the console and came into the living room, and he closed the document he was reading.

“How was your day?”

“Good.”

He looked at her.

“Don’t,” she said, taking off her jacket.

“I haven’t said anything.”

She sat beside him and stared at the coffee table. “Did you ask Daniel to promote me?”

He didn’t move. “No.”

“Did you ask anyone at Northlight? Did you speak to their leadership? Did you recommend me?”

“No. Xi, I didn’t.” He reached for her hand, and she let him take it without holding on. “Why would you think I had?”

“Because I’m being made Senior Account Director, and I don’t know if I earned it.”

His face changed. “You did.”

“You don’t know that. You know what I tell you about my work.”

“I’ve seen your presentations. I’ve read your recommendations. I’ve watched you run the account. I’m not on the agency’s leadership team, but I know how you work.”

She was quiet. “Did you ask for this?”

“No.”

She nodded, and didn’t look convinced.

“Would you like me to prove it?” he said.

“Can you?”

He picked up his phone, opened his email, searched for Northlight and sorted it by date. “Everything I’ve had from them since May. You asked whether I influenced it. I’d rather you saw than had to take my word.”

He didn’t summarise anything or pick the convenient ones. He opened them in order and forwarded each one as he went: the May quarterly review, with his reply about strategy; the renewal and scope confirmation from Northlight’s finance team; a June campaign review; a July note about the next phase; the extra approvals for Alder Vane; a note from Daniel about agency capacity. Her phone lit up again and again on the cushion beside her. Once he stopped. “There’s an internal one here that isn’t mine to forward. It was copied to me by mistake.” He showed her the sender and the date, and closed it.

Then a message from Daniel, dated the twenty-third of July.

We’re reviewing the senior account team for next year. Tang Xi has been taking on broader responsibility across An-Tech and Alder Vane, and I expect to formalise her expanded role internally.

And another, from the twenty-ninth.

As part of our succession planning we’re considering promoting Tang Xi to Senior Account Director from September, to recognise her responsibilities and formalise her leadership across several accounts.

Under it, his reply.

Thank you for letting us know. We will continue to assess Northlight’s work against the agreed service standards. Please make your staffing decisions independently of An-Tech.

She read it twice. “You knew. Since the end of July.”

“I knew Daniel was considering it.”

“And you didn’t tell me.”

“It wasn’t mine to tell.”

The last one was dated the fourth of August: the leadership team had approved the promotion, she would stay as An-Tech’s lead with Rachel supporting strategy, and An Yu had acknowledged it and asked for the responsibility matrix to be updated. Nothing else. He hadn’t called Daniel, hadn’t asked for anything, hadn’t recommended her or used the account as leverage. There was nothing there.

“You really didn’t,” she said.

“No.”

She let out a breath and leaned back into the sofa. “I’m sorry I asked you like that.”

“You were entitled to ask. If you ever think something in your life was decided by me, you should question it.”

“Even if it meant turning the promotion down?”

“If you thought I’d caused it, yes.” His hand found hers. “I hope you won’t.”

“Why?”

“Because you earned it. Your campaigns worked. Your recommendations were adopted. You ran the account without giving away the agency’s position, and you’ve told me I was wrong whenever you thought I was.” His mouth moved. “Sometimes quite forcefully.”

She laughed despite herself. “Only when necessary.”

“Frequently, then. Take the promotion, Xi. Not because I say so.”

“Because I earned it.”

“Yes.”

She leaned in and kissed him, and when she drew back she was smiling more freely than she had all day. “Senior Account Director.”

“Congratulations, Ms. Tang.”

“Thank you, Mr. Wang.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday morning Daniel announced it at the weekly agency meeting, and Tang Xi stood at the front of the room while they clapped. She thanked the leadership team and the people who had backed her, and spoke briefly about what she’d be taking on. She didn’t mention An-Tech. She didn’t need to.

Rachel hugged her first. “Senior Account Director.”

“Please stop saying it like that.”

“Never.”

“Bigger team now,” Daniel said. “Don’t try to do everything yourself.”

“I’ll delegate.”

Fiona stood a little behind the others. When Tang Xi turned, their eyes met, and Fiona offered a small, careful smile. “Congratulations.”

“Thank you,” said Tang Xi, and nothing more, because she had work to do.

✦ ✦ ✦

She rang her mother from the bus stop that evening, because her mother didn’t read emails and wouldn’t have forgiven hearing it second-hand. It took four rings. Behind her mother’s voice there was the extractor fan and somebody shouting for more rice, which meant she was still at the restaurant, which meant she had worked through lunch and dinner both.

“Senior what?”

“Senior Account Director, Mum. From September.”

“Is that more money?”

“Yes.”

“How much more?” Tang Xi told her, and there was a short silence on the line, and then the clatter of a ladle being put down. “That’s a lot of money for talking.”

“It’s not talking. It’s running accounts. Lots of them.”

“You’re twenty-seven.”

“I know how old I am.”

Another pause, longer. When her mother spoke again her voice had changed, and Tang Xi knew exactly which question was coming, because she had asked it herself two days before. “This isn’t because of him? The one with the company?”

Her mother had known about An Yu for a month, in the sense that she knew there was a man and knew his name and had refused to say anything about him except that she hoped he ate properly. She had never once said it kindly.

“No,” said Tang Xi. “It isn’t. I checked.”

“How did you check?”

“I asked him. And then I made him show me every email.”

On the other end of the line her mother made a sound that might have been a laugh. “Good. Then it’s yours.” The fan roared; someone called her name. “Come and eat on Sunday. I’ll make the dumplings. Bring yourself. Not him.”

“Not him,” Tang Xi agreed, and when she had hung up she stood at the bus stop for a while with the phone against her chest, smiling at nothing, while two buses came and went.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday night she sat cross-legged on his bed reading the formal letter, and he came in from a call and sat beside her.

“Still reading it?”

“It’s official.” She put it on the bedside table. “Daniel told me to stop trying to do everything myself.”

“Good advice.”

“Don’t agree with him. You’re supposed to be on my side.”

“I am on your side. That’s why I agree with him.”

She laughed and lay back against his shoulder. “Thank you for showing me the emails. I think I needed to see that you could let something happen in my life without arranging it.”

“I should have understood that sooner.”

She tipped her head back to look at him. “I’m proud of myself, you know. I worked hard. I earned it.”

“You did.”

She kissed him, and there was no anger behind it this time, only relief, and the happiness of having something she could claim without wondering whose hand had put it in hers.

“Senior Account Director Tang Xi,” he murmured.

“That sounds very serious. Do I have to start behaving differently?”

“No.”

“Good. I don’t intend to.”

The letter lay on the bedside table, and for once she didn’t feel the need to read it again.

chapters.title: His Grandmother’s Stick
chapters.desc: Nainai arrives unannounced with two suitcases and a polished stick, and remembers a girl from 2015 who talked.
chapters.content:
At a quarter past eight on Saturday morning, Wang An Yu’s phone rang with the sound of a car horn behind it, and the call ended with his grandmother telling him to come downstairs.

Tang Xi opened one eye. “Who is it?”

“Nainai. She’s downstairs.”

She sat up. “Your grandmother is outside your building? Why didn’t you tell me she was coming?”

“I didn’t know.” The phone rang again. “Nainai.”

“Are you deaf? Then why am I standing on the pavement? Bring a jacket. It’s cold.”

It was twenty-six degrees. “All right,” he said, and hung up, and looked at Tang Xi, who was already on the floor hunting for her slippers.

“Your grandmother,” she said, “is downstairs.”

“Yes. You should get dressed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nainai stood beside the car with a small leather handbag in one hand and her polished stick in the other, planted on the pavement like a gavel. She was in her eighties and small in everything but presence: silver hair pinned neatly, a dark green cardigan over a pale blouse, two suitcases in the driver’s hands. She came south every September for the Wang board meeting, and she stayed with An Yu every time, and nowhere else.

She looked him up and down. “You’re thin. Do you eat? Properly?”

“Yes.”

She pointed the stick at him. “Don’t lie to me before breakfast.”

“Why didn’t you tell me you were coming?”

“I told your father.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“Your father knows where you live.” She tapped her way towards the lift. “Which floor is it again?”

“Thirty-eight.”

“Too high. Everything breaks eventually.” In the lift she looked at him sideways. “You’re still not married.”

He watched the numbers. “Nainai. Good morning.”

She clicked her tongue. “Useless.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Tang Xi had changed into a cream knit top and dark trousers and tied her hair back, and she was standing straight by the kitchen counter when the door opened.

“Good morning, Nainai.”

The old woman stopped. She looked at Tang Xi, at An Yu, at Tang Xi again, and the stick came up. “Who is this?”

“Tang Xi,” said An Yu, setting down a suitcase.

“That tells me her name.”

“It’s lovely to meet you,” said Tang Xi.

Nainai pointed the stick at her grandson. “In August I asked you whether you were seeing someone. You said yes. I asked who. You said Tang Xi. I asked whether she’d be here. You said you didn’t know.”

“I didn’t.”

Nainai turned back. “And now you’re here. Good.” She lowered the stick and peered past them at the kitchen. “Have you two eaten?”

“We were waiting,” said Tang Xi.

“He’s a grown man. He can get ready and eat at the same time.” Tang Xi bit back a smile, and Nainai caught it. “You think that’s funny?”

“A little.”

Nainai considered her. “Good. At least one of you has a sense of humour.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Breakfast came up from the kitchen downstairs: congee, steamed buns, eggs, fruit. Nainai took the head of the table with her stick hooked over the chair beside her, put Tang Xi on her right and An Yu opposite, and inspected everything.

“Too much oil in the greens. Don’t tell them. Just don’t order it again.”

Tang Xi had made the tea herself while they were downstairs. She poured Nainai’s cup, and Nainai smelled it and sipped and sipped again.

“Jasmine. Who chose it?”

“I did. I thought something light in the morning.”

“Not too strong.” Nainai looked at her over the rim of the cup. “How long have you known him?”

“Since school. In Shanghai.”

The cup stopped halfway to the saucer. Nainai looked at her, and then at An Yu, and something sharpened in her face. “Shanghai. The library.”

An Yu put down his spoon.

Nainai set the cup down. “You’re the one who talks.”

Tang Xi went pink to the ears. “He told you about me?”

“He was sixteen. He told me there was a girl who sat opposite him and talked. That’s telling, for him.” She drank her tea. “I was in hospital. He sat by my bed and looked at the door all afternoon.”

Tang Xi looked at An Yu, who was studying the congee with great attention, and her eyes went bright.

“Did he speak to you?” Nainai asked. “At school?”

“Hardly ever.”

“How did you put up with him?”

“I talked enough for both of us.”

Nainai laughed, low and delighted. “Ah. That’s why he likes you.” And she said nothing else about it for the rest of the meal.

✦ ✦ ✦

By eleven Nainai had inspected the flat. She had opinions about the sofa, the curtains, the lighting and the books, which were arranged by subject and looked, she said, like a library after a storm.

“They’re organised,” said An Yu.

“You’re arguing with an old woman.”

“I’m explaining.”

“Same thing.”

Tang Xi sat on the sofa and watched. At work he was controlled to the point of being frightening; in private he could be teasing, stubborn, unexpectedly playful. With Nainai he was something else again. He let her interrupt him. He let her criticise his flat. He moved the footstool when she pointed at it and fetched a cushion before she’d finished asking. He didn’t seem to mind any of it.

Nainai settled into the armchair and patted the seat beside her. “Sit here. How old are you?”

“Twenty-seven.”

“Work?”

“Senior Account Director at an agency. I started this month.”

“Do you like it?”

“I do.”

“Good.” Her eyes slid towards An Yu. “Does he bother you?”

“Nainai,” said An Yu, looking up from his phone.

Tang Xi thought about it and answered honestly. “Sometimes. He’s a little too determined to solve things. He means well, but sometimes he decides what’s best before he asks me what I want.”

“That’s an incomplete description,” said An Yu.

Nainai tapped the stick on the floor. “Let her finish. Does he listen when you tell him?”

“He tries. He’s getting better.”

Nainai pointed the stick at her grandson. “Listen properly. Not with your ears. With your head.”

Tang Xi lowered her eyes to hide her smile, and An Yu looked at her and saw that she was enjoying herself enormously, and filed it away for later.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch Tang Xi made another pot, and Nainai came and stood in the kitchen doorway without her stick to watch her measure the leaves.

“Less than before?”

“The water’s hotter this time. The first pot was a little weak.”

“Who taught you?”

“My mother. She makes it better than I do.”

“Then learn from her.” Nainai took the cup Tang Xi handed her, drank, and drank again. “Good. Not bitter.”

Then she picked up her stick from the counter and went back to the living room, and that was all: one word. Tang Xi stood at the counter for a minute afterwards, unaccountably pleased.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three An Yu came off a call to find them on the sofa with a photo album from one of the suitcases.

“What are you showing her?”

“Your childhood. She should know what she’s dealing with.” Nainai pointed with the stick. “That one. He was eight.”

In the photograph a small An Yu stood next to his older brother, who had an arm round him and was looking at the camera with the same dry patience he still had at thirty-three, while An Yu looked thoroughly unimpressed. White shirt, a scratch on one cheek.

“You look exactly the same,” said Tang Xi.

“I do not.”

“He never smiled for photographs,” said Nainai. “His brother would at least stand still. This one stood still and frowned.” She turned a page. “He was always quiet. But he remembered everything.”

“That sounds familiar,” said Tang Xi, and An Yu met her eyes and shook his head slightly.

Nainai shut the album. “Enough. My eyes are tired.” She waved An Yu off when he moved to help her up. “I can stand. Don’t hover. Where’s my tea? Bring it.”

He went. Nainai watched him go.

“Good boy,” she said, and then, more quietly, “He was lonely when he was young. He had everything he needed, good schools, a family who cared for him. But he was always somewhere else in his head. He doesn’t know how to ask people to stay.”

Tang Xi looked at her hands. “I think he’s learning.”

Nainai studied her. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He suggested ordering dinner, and Nainai wanted something cooked properly, and when Tang Xi offered to help, An Yu objected, and Nainai pointed the stick at him. “She can decide for herself.”

So they made it together, steamed fish, greens, soup and rice, while Nainai sat at the counter giving instructions that weren’t always necessary. Not so much ginger. More water. Don’t rush. An Yu stood behind them watching until she asked why he was standing there and told him to sit, and he sat.

Over dinner Nainai asked about Tang Xi’s family, and Tang Xi told her what she wanted to: that her parents were well, that her mother worked in her aunt’s restaurant and her father did some consulting now, that they lived.

“Do they know about him?”

Tang Xi nearly choked on her soup. “They know I’m seeing someone. They know it’s him. They haven’t met him.”

“Then he should meet them. Not at some point. When?”

“We’ll arrange it,” said Tang Xi.

Nainai looked at her grandson. “Don’t make her do all the arranging.”

“I won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past ten Nainai had gone to bed in the guest room, having insisted she wasn’t tired, asked for a glass of water and reminded An Yu to shut the balcony door. Tang Xi stood out on the balcony anyway, a cardigan round her shoulders, the city bright below.

He came out and put his hands lightly on her waist from behind. “You’re smiling.”

“Your grandmother likes me.”

“She does.”

“She likes my tea.”

“She said one word about it. With Nainai that’s a speech.” He was quiet. “I didn’t know she remembered the library.”

“She remembered you looking at the door.” Tang Xi turned in his arms. “She told me you were lonely.”

He looked out at the city. “She shouldn’t have said that.”

“She loves you. She worries about you. And she thinks you’re a good boy.”

“She was talking about my childhood.”

“She said it today, about you fetching her tea.” Tang Xi stepped closer. “She approves, An Yu.”

“Of the tea?”

“Of me.”

He touched her cheek. “I think so.”

“Aren’t you going to say something romantic?”

He considered it. “She has good taste.”

“That’s terrible,” she said, laughing, and kissed him.

He kissed her back slowly, his hands at her waist, the balcony door a few inches open behind them and the flat dark and quiet. Then she slid her hands up under his jumper, flat against his back, and felt him draw a breath, and the kiss stopped being slow. He turned her so the railing was at her back and the whole lit city behind her, and kissed her as if they had been made to sit at opposite ends of a dinner table all evening, which they had: deep and unhurried and quiet, his thumb at the corner of her jaw tilting her face up to him, her fingers digging into the muscles either side of his spine. When she bit his lower lip he made a sound low in his throat, and she put her hand over his mouth, shaking with laughter.

“Shh,” she breathed. “Your grandmother.”

He kissed her palm. Then the inside of her wrist, where her pulse was going far too fast for a woman who had spent the day pouring tea. “Do you think she’s asleep?” she whispered.

“Probably. She’s been tired all day.”

“Probably isn’t good enough.” But she didn’t let go of his jumper, and he didn’t move his hands from her waist, and for a long time they stood pressed together against the cold rail, kissing in near silence, stopping every so often to listen to the flat and then not stopping.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the guest room Nainai lay with her eyes shut and her breathing even, and when she heard the balcony door slide closed, one corner of her mouth went up. She hadn’t raised a child who could fool her by being quiet, and she had certainly not raised a grandson who could.

A few minutes later the door opened. An Yu checked the lamp and straightened the blanket over her feet.

“An Yu.”

He stopped.

She opened one eye. “That girl makes good tea. Don’t let her go.”

He stood still. “I won’t.”

“Good. Now go to sleep.” She shut the eye again, and when the door had closed she reached for her stick and laid it beside the bed, where it would be ready in the morning to point at him again.

chapters.title: The Pitch She Loses
chapters.desc: A client pulls out of her pitch because of an umbrella in the rain, and an industry column wonders about her promotion.
chapters.epigraph: “Then don’t carry it for me. Stand next to me. That’s all.”
chapters.content:
The first sign that something was wrong was the silence. Tang Xi had just finished presenting the revised campaign direction when the man across the table stopped taking notes. It was a small change: a pen laid beside a notebook, a glance between two executives, and then none of the questions that had filled the room for forty minutes. She noticed, and carried on.

“To summarise, we’d position the new regional platform around three things: trust, access and long-term engagement. We don’t want the launch to be a one-off announcement. We want it to start a relationship with your audience that lasts.”

The client’s marketing director, Mr. Quek, nodded. “Thank you, Ms. Tang.”

Daniel took the commercial proposal and Rachel the measurement framework, and Tang Xi watched the room. Mr. Quek was no longer looking at the deck. He was looking at her, not quite directly, the way people look when they believe they’ve learned something about you that you didn’t mean to tell them. When the meeting ended he shook Daniel’s hand and said they’d discuss it internally. He shook hers. His smile was polite, and it was the last time he looked at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

The team came back to Northlight with the usual post-pitch energy, Rachel already arguing with herself about the budget. “They liked the platform. It’s the money. Their original brief was much more conservative.”

“We’ll wait for feedback,” said Daniel. “No speculating.”

“I’ll send the follow-up deck before lunch,” said Tang Xi, and she was halfway through the appendix when Daniel’s phone rang. She watched his face change in the first few seconds.

“Understood. May I ask if there’s a specific concern?” A long pause. “All right. Thank you for letting me know.”

Rachel looked up. “What happened?”

“That was Mr. Quek. They’re withdrawing us from the pitch. They’re appointing another agency.” Daniel hesitated, and then he turned to Tang Xi. “They raised a concern about a possible conflict of interest. He said he saw you leaving An-Tech with Mr. Wang last week. He was in their lobby for another meeting.”

For a moment the room seemed to lose its sound.

Tang Xi remembered. Thursday evening, a late review on the forty-second floor; An Yu waiting in the private lift lobby, the two of them walking out into the rain under one umbrella. Nothing more, and nothing that would have looked odd to anyone who knew she ran the An-Tech account. Except Mr. Quek hadn’t known that. Or perhaps he had.

“Did he say anything else?”

Daniel glanced at his notes. “That he wasn’t comfortable appointing an agency whose account director appeared to have a personal relationship with the chairman of another company.”

“That’s absurd,” said Rachel.

“Let’s be careful,” said Daniel.

“Did he say he believed I had a relationship with Mr. Wang?” Tang Xi asked.

“Not in those words.”

“But that’s what he meant.” Daniel didn’t disagree, and she looked down at the table. The pitch had taken six weeks: interviews, research, competitor analysis, workshops, financial modelling. She had rewritten the strategy herself when the client’s regional director changed the brief. They hadn’t been certain to win, but they’d been close enough for losing to matter, and now the work had vanished under a single observation. Two people leaving a building.

“All right,” she said. “We’ll record the reason for withdrawal. I’ll have the team close the proposal file.”

“Are you all right?”

“I’m disappointed. But I don’t want us spending the day persuading someone to work with us when they’ve already decided not to trust us. Shall I send the close-out note?”

“Please.”

She began typing. Her hands were steady, which was something.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past twelve Rachel forwarded her a link with no message at all. It was an industry gossip column, and the headline was carefully vague.

A Chairman, an Agency Darling and a Very Convenient Account

The writer didn’t name An Yu. They didn’t need to: a fast-growing technology group led by a young founder, an agency identified by its recent regional expansion. And then her. Not her full name; just enough.

A rising senior account director at the agency, already attached to the group’s lucrative account, has reportedly been seen leaving the chairman’s headquarters after hours. One wonders whether the agency’s latest success story is being measured by campaign performance alone.

The next paragraph was worse. It mentioned a recent promotion and wondered whether the agency’s internal advancement had been influenced by the client’s chairman. Her stomach tightened. They had taken the one thing she’d been so careful to make sure of and turned it into another insinuation.

She closed the page, opened it again and read it through from the top, looking this time for something she could use. No dates. No evidence. No named source. Only suggestions, arranged to look like information. She sent the link to Daniel and sat back, and her phone lit up.

Professor: Are you all right?

He’d seen it. Of course he had.

Tang Xi: Have you read it?

Professor: Yes.

Tang Xi: Don’t do anything. I mean it. Don’t contact the writer, don’t ask anyone to take it down, and don’t use An-Tech’s lawyers to make it disappear.

Professor: I understand.

She turned the phone over on the desk, and for the first time that day she felt tired.

✦ ✦ ✦

At An-Tech, An Yu read the column twice: once for facts and once for the source. There was almost nothing to work with. No quotation, no named witness, nothing that could be challenged without handing the writer exactly what they wanted.

“Legal has seen it,” said Ding, beside the desk. “They can review the publication and advise. It insinuates a conflict of interest, but it doesn’t make a direct factual allegation.”

“Have they contacted Northlight?”

“No.”

“Good.”

Ding hesitated. “It mentions Ms. Tang’s promotion. Would you like a statement confirming An-Tech had no part in her appointment?”

It was a reasonable suggestion. A statement would make An-Tech’s position clear. It would also push the story into a wider news cycle, invite questions about the relationship, and force Tang Xi to answer things she had never chosen to make public.

“Has she asked for a statement?”

“No.”

“Then don’t prepare one.”

Ding stayed where he was. “Would you like me to find out who gave them the information? Even if it came from inside the company?”

An Yu looked at him. “If there’s been a breach of confidentiality, Legal deals with it through the proper process. I don’t want anyone looking into her personal life. Don’t contact the publication. Don’t ask them to remove it. Don’t make a call on her behalf.”

When Ding had gone, he sat alone. He could make a dozen calls before the end of the afternoon. He knew how these columns worked, who supplied them and who decided what appeared and what didn’t. He could probably make the article vanish. She had told him not to, and this time he was going to have to let her decide what happened next.

✦ ✦ ✦

Northlight was quieter than usual all afternoon. Nobody stood over her desk or asked anything they shouldn’t; it was smaller than that. Conversations ended a little too fast when she walked up. Someone from finance glanced at a phone when the article came up. A junior executive who had never spoken to her became interested in the coffee machine. She kept working.

Just after four Daniel called her in. Rachel was already there, and he shut the door.

“We’ve had two calls asking whether the article means you. I told them we’re aware of it and don’t comment on unverified speculation. And we need to record the Quek withdrawal accurately.”

“I’ve drafted it.”

Rachel leaned forward. “Xi, you shouldn’t lose a client because someone saw you leave a building. This is exactly what Fiona was doing in April. People have a story ready. They don’t need evidence. They need a reason to repeat it.”

“I know.”

“Let me be very clear,” said Daniel. “Your position isn’t under review. Your promotion isn’t under review. The leadership team won’t treat a gossip column as evidence of anything. But I also have to protect the agency. If there is a personal relationship that could reasonably look like a conflict, we’d need to review our disclosure arrangements.” He said the next part, without accusation. “Would you like to make a disclosure now?”

She looked at the two of them. She had kept it private because she wanted her work to stay hers, but privacy was becoming a different thing from secrecy, and the difference was getting harder to hold on to.

“Can I have until tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

Rachel touched her hand across the table. “Whatever you decide, we’ll do it properly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came out of the kitchen when he heard the door, and he didn’t touch her straight away.

“How was your day?”

She laughed, small and tired, and took off her shoes. “Professional answer or honest one?”

“Both.”

“Professionally, we’ve recorded the withdrawal and Daniel has told me my promotion isn’t under review. Honestly, I feel humiliated.” His face tightened, and she put her bag down. “I know the article doesn’t say anything definite. I know there’s no evidence. But people are reading it, and now every decision I’ve made this year is going to be picked over as if there must have been something behind it. I lost a pitch today. Not because the work wasn’t good enough or the budget was wrong. Because someone saw us walk out of a building together.”

He came a step closer. “I’m sorry. I can—”

“No.”

He stopped.

“You were going to say you could fix it,” she said. “I know you can. You could call the publication. You could have your lawyers on it. You could find out who gave them the story and make sure nobody repeated it.” He didn’t deny any of it. “But I asked you not to. Please don’t make me wonder whether you’re doing it anyway.”

“I won’t.”

“Promise?”

“Yes.”

She stepped forward and rested her forehead against his chest, and his arms came round her. He didn’t tell her not to worry, or that it didn’t matter. He held her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She barely touched dinner, and he noticed and said nothing until she pushed the bowl away.

“Do you want to talk about it?”

“I don’t know what there is to say.”

“Then we don’t have to.”

She smiled faintly. “You’ve got very good at that. Not solving everything.” She leaned back in her chair. “Do you know what bothers me most? I can’t even be properly angry with you. You didn’t write it. You didn’t withdraw the pitch. You didn’t tell anyone. And I still feel as if I’m paying for being with you.”

“You shouldn’t have to.”

“No.” She looked at her hands. “I chose this. I don’t regret it. But I need to know I can keep choosing it without losing everything else.”

He reached across the table and she put her hand in his. “I can’t promise nothing will happen,” he said. “I can promise I won’t make decisions for you to stop it happening. And I won’t use my position to silence people because I don’t like what they say.” He paused. “Even though I want to. Very much.”

That made her look up. A small, sad smile touched her mouth. “I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she stood on the balcony with her cardigan wrapped round her, watching the lights move along the road far below, and he came out and stood beside her without speaking.

“You’re quiet.”

“I’m listening.”

“To what?”

“Nothing.”

“That’s not very useful,” she said, and after a while: “Do you remember what Nainai told me? That you don’t know how to ask people to stay. I think I understand it now.” She turned to him. “I don’t want to leave you because this is difficult. But I don’t want to become someone who has to keep proving she deserves to stand next to you. You don’t think that. I know. The world doesn’t know what you think. It sees your company and your name, and then it sees me.”

“I don’t want you carrying that alone.”

“Then don’t carry it for me. Stand next to me. That’s all.”

He brought her hand to his mouth. “I can do that.”

He kissed her slowly. There was no hurry in it, and no attempt to make the day disappear; his hand rested on her cheek and hers settled at the back of his neck.

“Tomorrow I might tell Daniel,” she said when they’d parted. “I haven’t decided. And if I do, I want it to be because it’s right, not because the article made me.”

“Then take your time.”

“You’re not going to tell me what to do?”

“No.”

“Good,” she said, and leaned into him, and neither of them mentioned the column again that night.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday morning he came out of the bedroom dressed for work and found her on the sofa reading it again.

“I hate this headline.”

“Which part?”

“All of it.”

“Then stop reading it.”

“I know.” She put the phone in her bag and stood up to straighten her jacket. “Thank you for not fixing it.”

“It doesn’t feel like something to be thanked for.”

“Maybe not. But I know it wasn’t easy.”

He stepped closer and straightened her collar. “Don’t mistake my silence for indifference.”

“I don’t.”

He kissed her once and let her go, and when the door had closed he stood where he was for a while. He had spent most of his adult life believing that if he had the means to stop something hurting someone he cared about, he should use them. He was finding out that sometimes the person he loved needed him to leave the decision with her, and that doing nothing could be harder than making a call.

✦ ✦ ✦

At Northlight the column was still online, the pitch was still lost, and the comments under it were still there. She closed the browser and opened the project tracker, where a new brief was waiting. She read it, made a note and assigned the research.

At eleven she knocked on Daniel’s door, and he waved her in and she shut it behind her.

“About yesterday. I don’t want to wait until the paperwork’s ready to tell you, so I’m telling you now, off the record until it’s on it. Mr. Wang and I are in a relationship. It started in February. We knew each other at school, years ago. When you asked me in February whether there was anything to declare, I should have said yes. Nothing about the account has been decided because of it, and I’ll put all of that in writing properly.”

Daniel looked at her, and then, unexpectedly, he smiled. “Thank you for telling me yourself.”

“You knew.”

“I suspected. Rachel suspected louder.” He picked up a pen. “Send me the written disclosure when you’re ready. We’ll set up the account so nobody can question it, and we’ll do it before anyone else tries to do it for us.”

She went back to her desk lighter than she’d been in a day. The column was still there whenever anyone refreshed the page. It wasn’t going to be the most important thing she did that week.

chapters.title: The Gossip
chapters.desc: The column names her, with a photograph. At two in the morning she finds a lawsuit and a list of advertisers on his desk.
chapters.epigraph: “Look at me. Not the article. Not the writer. Not whoever sent the picture. Me.”
chapters.content:
At sixteen minutes past seven on Thursday morning, Tang Xi’s photograph appeared beside her name.

She recognised the suit before the occasion: charcoal grey, worn to An-Tech’s regional partnership announcement in September, her hair behind one ear and a folder held against her waist. It had been taken from across the lobby. She remembered the press wall, and the photographers beside it, and An Yu arriving after the speeches to speak to the regional director before he turned to look for her. She hadn’t known that anyone had photographed them leaving. In the cropped picture he was beside her at the revolving doors with his hand resting at the small of her back. It looked intimate. It was.

THE CHAIRMAN’S FAVOURITE: WHO REALLY BENEFITS FROM THE AN-TECH ACCOUNT?

Her name was in the second paragraph. Not initials this time, not a description. Tang Xi, Senior Account Director at Northlight Agency. The piece went through her promotion, the lost pitch and the earlier column, and asked why Northlight still ran An-Tech’s account when its chairman appeared to be personally involved with the woman in charge of the work. Questions about governance. Questions about favouritism. Questions about whether the agency’s other clients knew. And then, almost in passing, a sentence about her.

For a young woman whose career has advanced remarkably quickly, the photograph raises questions her CV may not be able to answer.

She read that sentence twice and closed the page, and her phone rang.

“Have you seen it?” said Rachel. “Oh, Xi. They’ve named you. They’ve used your picture. Daniel’s on with Legal.”

“All right.”

“Don’t say all right like that. Say you’re furious.”

“I’m getting there.”

“Do you want me to come down and meet you?”

“No. I’m not going to hide in my flat because someone’s decided to write about me.”

When the call had ended she opened the article once more and looked at her own face in it. She had spent years learning to be taken seriously: to speak without rushing, to make a point without apologising for it, to sit at tables where people twice her age expected her to be grateful for the invitation. She had earned the promotion. She had earned her clients and every room she’d walked into. And now a photograph of a man’s hand on her back was being used to question all of it.

She shut the laptop and got dressed.

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu had read it in the car, again in the lift, and once more at his desk. The first time he had looked at the photograph, the second time at the words; the third time he had stopped reading.

“Legal’s initial view,” said Ding, “is that there may be grounds to challenge the use of the photograph and some of the implications. It seems to have been taken from the press area at the announcement. Someone who was there may have supplied it.”

An Yu looked at the printout. His hand on her back; her face turned a little towards him. She had been telling him something about the revised schedule and he had bent his head to hear her over the noise, and she had smiled at whatever he’d said, and he’d touched her as they walked out. He hadn’t thought about the cameras. He had simply wanted to touch her.

“Find out whether the photograph was obtained lawfully. If there’s been a breach of event access or image rights, deal with that on its own. Not her movements.” He kept his eyes on the page. “And prepare the legal options. Defamation, privacy, image rights. An assessment only. No filing, no contact with the publication.”

“Yes, Mr. Wang.”

“And a list of the column’s major advertisers.”

Ding looked at him. “Advertisers?”

“I want to know who pays for it. Two separate documents.”

Ding gathered the papers and went, and said nothing else, which was the most disapproving thing he knew how to do.

✦ ✦ ✦

Northlight had already heard. She could tell before she reached her desk: there was a particular quality to a room in which everybody knew something about you and nobody wanted to be caught knowing it. A conversation dipped as she passed. Someone looked away. Someone else looked a fraction too long.

Before she could sit down Fiona came over with a coffee in one hand and her phone in the other. “Have you seen it? That’s awful. I suppose it’s hard when people start making assumptions.” She glanced at the phone. “And there’s a photograph this time. Those are harder to explain away.”

“Fiona,” said Rachel, from beside the desk. “Not now.”

“I’m only saying.”

Tang Xi closed the document on her screen and looked at her directly, which she almost never did with anyone who was being unpleasant. “Then perhaps you should stop. I don’t think this is a conversation you need to have with me.”

“I wasn’t trying to offend you.”

“Then you haven’t managed to make it sound that way.”

Fiona left. Rachel looked at the carpet to hide her face. “Deserved. Come on. Daniel’s waiting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Daniel had the article on his monitor and didn’t ask whether she’d seen it. “Legal’s reviewing the piece and the photograph, and we’ve asked the publication to preserve all material connected with it. There are two separate questions. One is their conduct. The other is our own governance.”

“I know.” Tang Xi took an envelope from her notebook and put it on the desk. “I said I’d put it in writing. Here it is. I signed it on Friday and I’ve been sitting on it, waiting to find the right moment. There isn’t one.”

He opened it and read it in silence: the date the relationship began, the date she’d told him in person; that it hadn’t affected the management of the account; that An Yu had asked for no changes to staffing, scope or commercial terms because of it. And a paragraph she had rewritten four times.

There have been personal decisions by Mr. Wang that I considered inappropriate, including his company’s purchase of a business and a building connected to my working life and a legal review of my employment contract that I didn’t ask for. I challenged each of them. None changed the account’s commercial arrangements. I can provide full details if needed.

Daniel read that paragraph twice, and looked up. “Thank you. That’s more than most people would have written.”

“I didn’t want there to be anything you could find out later.”

“Then here’s what happens. Legal reviews whether we need an independent lead for any decision involving An-Tech. It doesn’t mean we’re taking you off the account today. It means we have a process that protects you as well as us.” He put the letter down. “And hear this clearly. The article doesn’t change my view of your work. Your promotion stands. Your responsibilities stand. We decide things on documented performance and proper governance, not on gossip.”

For the first time that morning her eyes stung, and she blinked until they stopped. “Thank you, Daniel.”

“Let’s get through it properly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past two she woke to a cold space beside her.

She lay and listened. Typing, from the study. She put on the cardigan hanging over the chair and went down the corridor. The study door was open, and he was at his desk with his glasses on and his sleeves rolled to the forearm, his tie folded beside the keyboard and printed pages spread round him, reading with the concentration of a man who had forgotten that anything else existed.

“An Yu.”

He looked up, and his face changed at once. “Why are you awake?”

“Why are you?”

“Couldn’t sleep.” He closed the file on the screen. “Something Legal prepared.”

She came to the desk. The first page was headed Preliminary Legal Assessment: Potential Claims Arising from Publication, with sections for identification, implication, damages and remedies. Under it was a second document.

Advertising and Commercial Relationships

Names. Corporate groups. Estimated annual spend, campaign partnerships, contact details.

She went still. “What is this?”

“A list of the publication’s advertisers.”

“Why?”

“I wanted to understand who funds them.”

“Why do you need to understand that?” He took his glasses off, and she held up the second document. “Did you ask someone to make this? At two in the morning?”

“Ding compiled it. Nothing’s been filed. I haven’t contacted anyone.”

“But you were going to.”

“I was considering the options.”

She looked down at the list. The companies whose budgets could be withdrawn, the people who could be called, the quiet pressure that could be applied without anyone ever having to say what it was for. She knew this man. She knew what he could do with a phone call, and she knew that the silence he used so carefully could be more frightening than anger.

“Did you mean to make them lose their advertisers?”

His jaw tightened. “I meant to find out how much influence the publication’s commercial partners had over it.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“No,” he said. “It isn’t.”

“Would you have told me?”

He didn’t answer, and the silence was enough.

She tore the list in half. The sound was small. His eyes went to her hands, and she tore the halves again, and again, and laid the pieces on the desk. Then she picked up the legal assessment, and he stepped forward and said her name, and she tore that too. It caught at the staple and she pulled harder until it split, and put it beside the other.

He didn’t move.

“Do you understand why I’m angry?”

“Yes.”

“I don’t think you do. Every time you hear someone has hurt me, your first instinct is to find the person responsible and make them regret it. You think protecting me means having enough power that people are afraid to hurt me.” Her voice cracked and she let it. “You sat here at two in the morning working out who you could squeeze. Do you know how frightening that is? You didn’t need to write the word threaten for me to know what that list was for.”

“I haven’t used it.”

“But you wanted to. You told me you wouldn’t fix it, and because I told you not to, you found a way to call it preparation.” She came round the desk. “I don’t need you to be powerless. I don’t want you pretending you have no influence. I need you to understand that my life isn’t another company you can restructure when something goes wrong.”

He was quiet. When he spoke, his voice was lower. “I see what they’re doing to you and I can’t stand it.”

“Neither can I. But I don’t get to make it go away by making somebody else afraid.” She touched the torn pages. “I want to be able to look at you and know that when I ask you not to use your power, you won’t spend the night looking for another way to use it.”

He stood still. “You’re right. I should have asked you. I should have left it alone. I’m sorry.”

She reached up and took his face in her hands. Not to kiss him; to hold it. “Look at me. Not the article. Not the writer. Not whoever sent the picture. Me. I’m here.”

He shut his eyes for a moment, and when he opened them something in his face had let go. “I see you.”

“Then stay with me.”

He covered her hands with his. “I will.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They stood by the desk with the torn paper between them.

“Are you still angry?” he asked.

“Yes. With you. And with everyone else much more.” She studied his face. There was nothing waiting behind his teeth now, no explanation, only a tired man working hard not to turn this into another problem he could solve. “I don’t want to spend the night fighting. I want you to hold me.”

He reached for her slowly, and she went. His chin came to rest on her hair and her hands settled on his chest, where she could feel his heart under the shirt, and for a while neither of them spoke.

“Kiss me,” she said.

“You’re still angry.”

“I’m not asking you to make me feel better. I’m asking you to kiss me.”

The first kiss was gentle, almost cautious. She held his face and kissed him again, longer, until he stopped holding himself at a distance, and then his hand came to the back of her neck and he kissed her with everything he’d kept behind his silence all evening. When she stepped back he followed her with his eyes. She took his hand.

In the bedroom the city beyond the windows was mostly dark. She undid the top button of his shirt and he watched her do it. She undid the second, and stopped.

“You’re thinking again.”

“I’m trying not to.”

“Tonight isn’t about the article. It isn’t about the people who wrote it. It isn’t about proving anything.” She laid her hand against his cheek. “Tonight I just want you.”

“Then you have me.”

She took the rest of his shirt off herself, slowly, one button at a time, and pushed it from his shoulders; he lifted the cardigan from hers and then the thin top she’d slept in, and stood looking at her in the half-light as if he had never seen her before. She drew him down onto the bed. He went where she put him, on his back, and she knelt over him and kept one hand along his jaw the whole time, through all of it: through his mouth on her breast and her hips settling over his; through the long, aching moment when she guided him into her and they both stopped breathing.

“Look at me,” she whispered.

He did. She didn’t let him look anywhere else. She moved slowly, much more slowly than either of them wanted, and every time his eyes began to close or slide away into whatever he was thinking about she said his name, and they came back to her. His hands were on her thighs, holding on. He had never been so quiet, or so undone, and she could see all of it in his face: the anger, the shame about the list, the want, and under everything a kind of fear she had never seen him let anyone look at.

“Not somewhere else,” she said against the corner of his mouth. “Here.”

“I’m here.”

She believed him. She rolled them over without letting go of his face so that he was above her, his weight on his forearms, and wrapped her legs round him and pulled him deeper, and he made a sound she felt in her own chest. They found the rhythm together, unhurried and deep, his forehead nearly touching hers, and she watched his eyes the whole time and he watched hers. When she came it was slow and long and she held his face through it so that he saw every second, and he said, low, almost as if it had been torn out of him, “I love you.” He had never said it aloud. He shuddered into her a moment later with the words still in his mouth.

Afterwards she lay with her head on his chest and his fingers moving slowly through her hair, and neither of them spoke for a long time.

“I hate that they used that photograph,” he said at last.

“So do I.”

“I hate that you have to go in tomorrow and face people who’ve read it. I hate that I can’t—”

She lifted her head, and he stopped.

“Don’t finish that sentence. You can hate it. You can be angry. You can tell me you want to do something. But you don’t decide what happens next without me. And no more lists. Not at two in the morning, not at any hour.”

A faint line appeared between his brows. “No more lists.”

“You said something just now.”

“I know what I said.”

“Say it again. Not because I asked. Because you mean it.”

He looked at her. “I love you, Xi.”

She smiled into his chest, and after a moment, unexpectedly, he laughed: quiet and tired, but real.

“I don’t want you to be afraid of me,” he said.

She propped herself up to look at him. “I’m not afraid of you. I’m afraid of what you might become if you think loving me gives you the right to decide what everyone else deserves. I don’t want to love someone I have to keep stopping.”

“Then I’ll learn to stop myself.”

“Don’t promise that because you’re afraid I’ll leave.”

“I’m not. I want to be someone you can stand beside without having to defend yourself from me.”

That silenced her, and she bent down and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke to the smell of coffee and found him in the kitchen in a clean shirt with his hair still damp: toast, eggs, fruit, a pot of jasmine.

“Did you sleep?”

“Some.”

“How much is some?”

“Three hours.”

“An Yu.”

“I’ll sleep earlier tonight.” He set a cup in front of her. “Both documents are in the bin. The electronic copies are deleted. Ding’s been told not to go ahead with either. I won’t contact the publication or its advertisers. If there’s a real legal issue with the photograph or a false statement, I’ll bring it to you first and we’ll decide together.”

She considered that. “That’s fair.”

Her phone buzzed. Daniel: Legal had reviewed the piece and wanted to send a formal response on the false implications about her promotion and the account. Nothing would go out without her approval. She held it out so he could read it, and he read it where she held it, without reaching for the phone.

“What do you want to do?”

“See the draft first. And it comes from Northlight. Not An-Tech.”

“That’s right.”

“You’re not going to argue?”

“No,” he said, and she looked at him over the rim of her cup and didn’t say anything, because she didn’t need to.

✦ ✦ ✦

The draft came at twenty past nine. It was short. Her promotion had followed Northlight’s internal review; An-Tech had played no part in it; the agency’s account management remained under its standard governance. There was nothing about her private life. She read it carefully and approved it, and opened the An-Tech tracker, where three items were waiting, and started on the first.

The article was still online. The photograph was still there. She didn’t open it.

When her phone lit up a little before ten, for once she didn’t angle the screen away from the room.

Professor: Is the morning easier?

Tang Xi: It is.

Professor: Good. I meant what I said.

Tang Xi: I know. Now go to work, Mr. Wang.

Professor: Yes, Ms. Tang.

chapters.title: Equal Footing
chapters.desc: She asks him to say no to her in a meeting if he means it. He does, in front of twelve people.
chapters.epigraph: “Say no to me in a meeting, An Yu. If you mean it.”
chapters.content:
On Tuesday night she put the deck on his coffee table, upside down, and sat on the floor beside it with her back against the sofa.

“I’m not going to show you that.”

“All right.”

“It’s tomorrow’s proposal. You’ll see it with everyone else.” She tipped her head back to look up at him. “I want to ask you for something, and I want you to think before you answer.”

He closed his laptop. That was how she knew he was listening.

“Two things. The first is that when I tell you no, you hear it. Not argue until I’m too tired to keep saying it, not agree and then find another way round. Hear it, and stop.” She waited until he nodded. “The second is harder. Tomorrow there’s a page in there you won’t like. If you disagree with it, I want you to say so. In the meeting. In front of everyone. Don’t nod it through because it’s mine, and don’t ring me afterwards to tell me what you really thought.”

He was quiet. “You want me to say no to you in front of your director.”

“I want you to treat me the way you treat anyone whose work you take seriously. Nobody in that room has ever heard you disagree with me. Do you know what that looks like, after October?”

“It looks as if I agree with everything you do.”

“It looks as if I’m the one person you can’t say no to. Say no to me in a meeting, An Yu. If you mean it.”

He looked at the face-down deck, and then at her. “Only if I mean it.”

“That’s the whole point.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday morning Tang Xi had been looking at the same paragraph for six minutes, not because it was difficult but because she was waiting for him to disagree with her.

He was reading the revised regional communications proposal across the conference table, one hand flat beside the printed deck and the other holding a pen, his face giving nothing away. There were twelve of them: six from An-Tech, four from Northlight, and two outside consultants brought in for the regional rollout. Daniel was at the head of the table and Rachel beside her with a laptop and a page of handwritten notes. The agenda was simple enough: the scope of the next phase, the regional approval structure, the extra production costs.

Except that Tang Xi had proposed something he would almost certainly dislike. Northlight would keep its own approval over creative work inside the agreed strategy and budget. An-Tech would keep final approval over corporate statements, regulatory claims and anything the executives said, but it would no longer be able to step into every individual creative decision. It was reasonable. It was also a direct challenge to the way he liked to work. He liked precision, and knowing what was going to happen before it happened, and when he wanted something changed he generally expected it changed. She had no intention of letting the account turn into a series of small permissions.

He turned a page and stopped. She knew that look. He’d found it.

“Before we go on, I’d like to take you through the approval structure on page seventeen.”

“Go ahead.”

She explained it: calm, exact, careful not to sound defensive. The communications director worried about brand consistency, and she answered him. One of the consultants asked whether the agency could be held to account if a piece of content performed badly, and she answered him too.

Then An Yu spoke. “I don’t agree with the proposed division.”

The room went still.

“Which part, Mr. Wang?”

“Creative execution should stay under client approval. I don’t see a reason to separate it from the wider communications process.”

“I understand the preference. But that would put routine production decisions through the same approvals as executive and regulatory communications. It would create delays we don’t need.”

“Delays can be managed.”

“Not when every small adjustment needs several senior signatures.”

“Then the agency should improve its internal review.”

“The agency’s internal review isn’t the problem.”

Rachel stopped typing. He put down his pen. “Then what is?”

“Who owns the decision.” She turned a page. “Northlight is accountable for delivering the campaign inside the agreed scope, budget and strategy. If we’re responsible for the result, we need the authority to make the routine decisions that deliver it.”

“You’re asking the client to give up control.”

“I’m asking the client to tell the difference between oversight and interference.”

The word sat in the room. She had chosen it on purpose, and she knew he knew why.

“That’s a strong word, Ms. Tang.”

“Then perhaps we should look carefully at the process that makes it necessary.”

The communications director cleared his throat. “Perhaps a tiered system of approvals—”

“I’ve proposed one,” said Tang Xi. “Page seventeen.”

He looked down. “Oh.”

An Yu sat back. “Let’s take ten minutes.”

People reached for water and checked their phones. Rachel raised her eyebrows at her, and Tang Xi gave the smallest shake of the head. Not now.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had expected him to refuse outright when they came back. Instead he asked them to go through the approval matrix line by line, which was much harder than a refusal. He questioned the definition of a routine adjustment, the escalation thresholds, unplanned media responses, what the regional teams could sign off. She had prepared for every one of those questions, and she answered them, and he listened to every answer through to the end. Twice he accepted a point and moved on without arguing it again. By the last page the structure was stronger than the one she’d brought in.

“That seems workable,” said Daniel, sounding relieved.

“With the thresholds written down,” said the communications director.

“We’ll add a decision log and a weekly summary of everything approved under delegated authority,” said Tang Xi.

An Yu looked at the page. “I don’t agree.”

Her pen stopped. This silence was different from the first. The chairman had just turned the proposal down, and he had done it to the face of the account director who wrote it.

“Which element, Mr. Wang?”

“Delegated authority in the new regional markets. Not the principle. The timing. Three of those markets have regulators we haven’t worked with, and their rules on product claims are stricter than ours. For the first six months I want every piece of creative in those markets approved on our side. After that we review it against your decision log, and if the log is clean, I’ll agree to your structure as written.”

She looked at him, and for a moment she wasn’t in the meeting at all. It was a good reason. It was a reason she would have given a client herself.

“Understood,” she said, and closed the deck. “Then Northlight will need to revise the commercial assumptions. The retainer and the delivery timeline assume the delegated structure. If An-Tech needs senior client approval on every piece of creative in those three markets, we’ll need to price the extra review time and the people it takes.”

“You’re saying the current fee doesn’t cover that process?”

“I’m saying the scope and the approvals have to be commercially consistent.”

“Then send a revised fee proposal.”

“We will.”

He turned to Daniel. “By Friday, please.”

The meeting moved on, but it never quite found its earlier rhythm. Tang Xi went on taking notes and confirming actions; her voice didn’t change and she didn’t look at him again until it ended. As everyone packed up he said, “Ms. Tang. Thank you for the presentation,” and she said, “You’re welcome, Mr. Wang,” and there was nothing personal in either.

Rachel waited until the door had shut. “Well. I’m trying to work out whether to congratulate you or ask if you need medical attention. You just told the chairman of our biggest account that his process was interference.”

“I said we should tell oversight from interference.”

“Oh, much more diplomatic.” Rachel watched her slide the deck into its folder. “Are you all right? That was quite something.”

Tang Xi looked at the door. “That was the point.”

Rachel’s face softened. “Ah,” she said, and understood, not everything, but enough.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found him in the stairwell between the forty-second and forty-first floors, by the landing window, reading something on his phone. He put it away when the door opened.

“Ms. Tang. Is something wrong?”

She let the door close behind her. “Do you know what just happened in there?”

“You presented a proposal. I disagreed with part of it. You defended it, I listened, and we agreed to revise the commercial terms.”

She stared at him. “Do you know how many people in that room have ever heard you say no to someone who wasn’t already on your side?”

“I don’t know.”

“None.” She stopped in front of him. “I asked you to do something.”

“I remember.”

“And you did. Why?”

He looked genuinely puzzled. “Because I disagreed.”

“Not to prove something? Not to show everyone you weren’t giving me special treatment?”

He thought about it, which she loved him for. “That may have been part of why I knew it mattered to do it properly. It wasn’t why I said no. I said no because the regional markets aren’t ready. You were right to expect me to say so.”

She smiled at him: a real smile, not the polished one she wore in meetings. “Thank you.”

His eyes went to her mouth. “You’re welcome.”

She reached up and straightened his tie, which was already perfectly straight. “I wanted to know you could disagree with me without making me feel I’d done something wrong by having an opinion. You did. And you listened when I pushed back. You gave in twice. Did you notice?”

“I noticed.”

“Will you do it again?”

“Yes.”

He caught her hand before she could take it away. “You’re pleased with me.”

“Don’t sound so surprised.”

“I’ve been told I have a difficult face to read.”

She laughed, a small sound that changed the whole landing. “Is this where I give you feedback? Your disagreement was clear. Your reasoning was sound. Your timing was terrible.”

“Terrible?”

“You could have disagreed before I spent six weeks on it.”

“I wanted to see the whole thing.”

“Of course you did.” She put both hands flat on his chest, and her face changed. “There’s one more thing.”

She walked him backwards the two steps to the wall and kissed him, and it wasn’t a tentative kiss. Her hands came up either side of his face and she held him there and kissed him with everything she had kept out of the conference room, and he made a low sound against her mouth and his hands closed on her waist and pulled her in until there was no space left between them. When she drew back his eyes had gone dark.

“That’s your proper thank you,” she said.

“For saying no.”

“For saying no and meaning it.” She kissed him again, and this time he smiled into it. “I don’t need you to agree with me, An Yu. I need to know that when you don’t, I can still stand here.”

“You can.”

“Good.” She stepped back and smoothed his lapel. “You go first. If we walk out together, someone will notice.”

“Understood, Ms. Tang.”

“Very professional, Mr. Wang.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The revised commercial proposal took less time than she’d expected. The extra reviews were clear, the fee adjustment was reasonable, and there was a defensible basis for every line.

“You’re sure about the additional resource?” Daniel asked.

“The new process adds two senior review stages and a longer approval window in three markets for six months. We should price the work for what it is.”

“An-Tech may push back,” said Rachel.

“They can. If they want client approval on everything in those markets, that’s their decision. But we shouldn’t pretend it costs the same.”

Daniel smiled faintly. “Send it.”

When it had gone, Rachel leaned across. “Can I ask? Did he really disagree with you? Properly? Without ringing you afterwards to say he actually agreed?”

“Properly.”

“Remarkable.”

It wasn’t remarkable, Tang Xi thought, looking at the sent email. It was what should have been happening from the start. A client should be able to disagree with its agency, and an agency with its client. A chairman should be able to tell an account director no, and an account director should be able to tell a chairman his process was wrong. None of it should have been extraordinary. For the two of them, it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got to his flat later than usual, and he looked up from a report on the sofa. “Did Daniel approve the revision?”

“We sent it.” She took off her jacket. “You’re not going to ask what I changed?”

“You’ll tell me if you want to.”

She sat down next to him. “Asking that question used to take you three attempts.”

“Should I be worried?”

“Possibly.” She leaned against his shoulder. “I’m still pleased about this morning.”

“Even though I turned down your proposal.”

“Because you turned it down for a reason, out loud, where everyone could hear. Because I know now that you can.” She looked up at him. “An Yu, you once bought a café because I mentioned it opened late.”

He considered that. “Fair.”

“You bought a building. You had lawyers read my contract without telling me. You made a list of a publication’s advertisers at two in the morning.”

“I’ve stopped making lists.”

She laughed. “Good.”

He brushed her hair behind her ear. “I don’t want you to have to keep teaching me the same thing.”

“Then remember it.” She was quiet. “Do you think we’re getting better at this?”

“Do you?”

“Yes. Today I disagreed with you, you disagreed with me, and neither of us had to leave.”

“That sounds like a low standard.”

“It is. It’s a good place to start.”

He kissed her hair, and she laced her fingers through his. There were still things they hadn’t worked out. Her career would always sit beside his, and in some rooms his influence would always be the larger. People would go on making assumptions. There would be times when he wanted to step in and times when she wanted to step back. They wouldn’t become equal just because they loved each other. They were going to have to keep choosing it.

She lifted their joined hands and kissed his knuckles. “Next time, disagree with me before the meeting.”

“I’ll consider it.”

She turned her head. “That wasn’t a yes.”

“No.”

She stared at him, and then she laughed, and he smiled, quiet and pleased with himself, and kissed her, and for once neither of them was trying to win.

chapters.title: Her Mother
chapters.desc: Her mother has never forgiven Shanghai. Lunch at the restaurant, chive and prawn dumplings, and a question he answers.
chapters.epigraph: “Men like that buy girls like you.”
chapters.content:
Tang Xi changed her blouse three times. The first was too formal. The second looked as if she’d made an effort. The third was the one she ended up in once she’d given up trying to dress for her mother’s opinion, and she stood at the mirror doing up the small pearl button at her wrist while An Yu fixed his cuff behind her.

“Is this all right?”

“Yes.”

“You didn’t even look.”

“I looked at your face. Your face is usually a reliable indication.”

She turned round. Navy jumper, charcoal coat, no tie, no watch that announced its price; he had even left his briefcase behind. He looked like a man who had made a conscious effort not to look like himself.

“You’ve dressed down.”

“I thought it was appropriate.”

“You’ve never dressed down in your life. Your idea of casual is a shirt without a jacket.”

He considered this. “That’s sometimes true.”

She laughed, and it faded too quickly, and he noticed. “Are you nervous?”

“No.” He waited. “Yes.”

“Would you like me to say something reassuring? Your mother invited me to lunch. I assume she means to feed me.”

“That’s your reassurance?”

“It seems a reasonable assumption.”

“She’s not like Nainai,” said Tang Xi. “She doesn’t care that you’re a chairman, or how many people work for you, or where you went to university. She doesn’t even particularly like people who speak politely. She might say something unpleasant. She might ask things you won’t like.”

“Then I’ll listen. And answer what I can.”

“And if she doesn’t like you?”

“Then I’ll have to accept it.”

She searched his face. He wasn’t pretending not to care, and that was what she valued; he understood that her mother’s opinion mattered even though he couldn’t decide what it would be. She straightened his jumper. “Don’t try too hard. Don’t call her Auntie unless she tells you to. And please don’t buy anything. Not flowers, not a present, not a restaurant, not the building next door.”

“I remember the rules.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The restaurant was her aunt’s, the ground floor of a narrow building on a street in the old town that had been there long before the new district went up on the other side of the river. The sign was faded. A row of red lanterns hung under the awning and the windows were fogged from the steam inside. A delivery rider was eating at the counter, two old men were arguing over a newspaper, and somebody in the kitchen was shouting for another plate of noodles.

“She works here every day?” An Yu asked.

“Six days a week. Seven if someone’s ill. She started as a kitchen hand when we first moved here, ten years ago. Now she runs the lunch service and does half the menu.”

He looked through the window, and she watched him take it in. Nothing about it was polished. The tables were old, the floor tiles uneven, the laminated menus wiped so often their corners were peeling. But she knew every inch of it. She had done her homework at the back table after school with the smell of garlic hitting hot oil and the roar of the extractor fan, and her mother had put a bowl of soup in front of her without stopping whatever she was doing. Once, at sixteen, she had been embarrassed by it, not because she disliked the place, but because her classmates in Shanghai had talked about their parents’ offices and holidays and houses and she had wanted to belong in that world. Her mother had never forgiven Shanghai for making her daughter ashamed of where she came from.

“Ready?” he said.

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother was behind the kitchen counter in a dark apron over a pale shirt, her hair tied back and a few strands loose at the temples, a faint line of flour along one wrist. Her eyes went first to her daughter and then to the man beside her, and for a second she didn’t move.

“You’re late.”

“By four minutes, Mum.”

“Four minutes is late.” She wiped her hands on the apron and looked at An Yu, and he stepped forward.

“Good afternoon. I’m Wang An Yu.”

“I know. You think I don’t know who my daughter’s seeing?” Tang Xi went pink, and her mother turned towards the back. “Come. The food’s getting cold.”

That, apparently, was the greeting.

The table at the back was already laid: steamed fish with ginger and spring onion, stir-fried greens, a clay pot of tofu with mushrooms, and a big bamboo steamer of dumplings. Tang Xi stopped.

“Are those chive and prawn?”

“What else would they be?”

“You made them?”

“I had time.” Her mother put a dish of vinegar on the table.

There were enough for six people, and Tang Xi knew what that meant. Her mother might be angry. She might be suspicious. She might already have decided the man at her table was trouble. But she had cooked, and she had made the dumplings Tang Xi loved most.

An Yu pulled out Tang Xi’s chair before he took his own, and her mother saw it and said nothing, and he waited until she had sat down before he served himself. He ate one dumpling slowly.

“Too salty?” her mother asked, pouring tea.

“No.”

“Too much chive?”

“No.”

“Then why are you looking at it like that?”

“I was thinking about the filling. It’s very good. Very well balanced. The prawn is fresh and the chive doesn’t overwhelm it, and it holds together without being dense.”

Tang Xi nearly choked on her tea. Her mother stared at him and then at her. “Does he always talk like that?”

“Only when he’s being polite.”

“I’m not being polite,” said An Yu.

“Then you’re strange.”

He looked down at his bowl. “I’ve been told.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first questions were about work. What did he do? He’d founded An-Tech and chaired it. How many people? He gave her the number. Was it profitable? He told her. Had he always been rich?

“Mum.”

“What? Have you?”

“No,” said An Yu, as if they were discussing the weather.

“Then your parents are rich.”

“Yes.”

“Very rich?”

“Yes.”

“How rich?”

He thought about it. “Comfortably.”

Her mother snorted. “That’s what rich people say.”

“I suppose it is.”

“You don’t have to pretend with me.”

“I won’t.”

“Good.” She pushed the greens towards her daughter. “Eat. How did you meet?”

“At school,” said Tang Xi quickly.

“Shanghai.” Her mother’s face changed, only slightly, and both of them saw it. “How long ago?”

“Ten years.”

“Ten years.” She said it as if the words had a particular taste. “You were in Shanghai when she was sixteen? You knew each other?”

“We were at the same school,” said An Yu. “She used to talk to me in the library.”

Her mother gave a short laugh. “She talked to everyone.”

“Not everyone. She talked to me. Almost every lunchtime, for a year.”

That got her attention. “And you talked back?”

“No.”

Her mother stared, and then she laughed properly, short and surprised. “That sounds like her. Talking to someone who doesn’t answer.”

“He was very difficult to talk to,” said Tang Xi.

“You were persistent.”

“I was friendly.”

“You were persistent.”

Her mother watched them, and the ease of it, and her smile went. “Then why did you leave?” Tang Xi’s fingers tightened on her chopsticks. “You were sixteen. We had to go in a week. You cried for weeks afterwards and wouldn’t tell me why. I thought it was school. Your friends. Being ashamed of what happened to your father.” She looked at An Yu. “Did you know what happened to us?”

“Not then. I found out this year.”
