“This year.” She nodded slowly and reached for the teapot. “Shanghai took a great deal from us.”

“Mum—”

“Don’t.” It wasn’t loud. It was worse than loud; it was tired. “I worked two jobs after we left. Your father was ashamed. You were angry. We started again with nothing, and every time anyone asked where we were from, I had to say Shanghai.” She poured. “I hated saying it.”

Tang Xi looked at the table. She remembered the first months: her mother coming home with swollen feet, the little rented flat, the way her mother never bought anything for herself. She remembered being sixteen and feeling that everything had got smaller.

“And now you bring a man from that world to my table.” Her mother put the teapot down. “Men like that buy girls like you.”

Tang Xi’s head came up. “Mum.”

Her mother’s eyes didn’t leave him. “Men with money and family names, who can give you things you never had. They know exactly how to make a girl feel lucky.”

“That’s enough.”

“Is it? I don’t want you thinking that because a man like this chose you, you have to be grateful. Your father and I worked for everything we had. I don’t want anyone coming into your life and making you think your place beside him is something he can hand you.” She turned to him. “Do you understand what I’m saying?”

“Yes.”

“Then tell me. What do you want from my daughter?”

He put his chopsticks down and didn’t look away. “I want to be with her. I want to build a life with her, if she wants the same. But I don’t believe she owes me anything for what I can offer.”

“Easy to say. Easier with money.”

“Yes,” he said. “It is. And I know I can make decisions that change her life without meaning to. I’ve done it. She’s told me each time I’ve crossed a line, and she’s been right each time. I can’t promise I’ll never make a mistake. I can promise I won’t ask her to accept something because I have more money or influence than she does. And I won’t ask her to be grateful for being with me.”

The table was quiet. Her mother picked up her chopsticks. “Eat your food before it’s cold.”

It wasn’t approval and it wasn’t forgiveness, but she had stopped. Tang Xi’s appetite had almost gone. Under the table An Yu’s hand found hers, and he didn’t squeeze it. He just rested his fingers against hers.

✦ ✦ ✦

By half past one the steamer was nearly empty. Tang Xi had eaten four. An Yu had eaten seven.

“You’re hungry,” said her mother.

“They’re very good.”

“You said that.”

“I meant it.” He looked at the steamer. “May I ask how you make the filling?”

Her mother stopped. “What?”

“I’d like to know how you make them.”

“Why? You can buy them here.”

“I’d rather learn how you make them.”

Tang Xi turned and stared at him. He was entirely serious. Her mother lifted the lid of the steamer. “There’s more. Some were left from this morning.” She put three more in his bowl, and he thanked her, and ate one, and asked a third time. “There’s nothing special,” she said, picking up her tea.

“I’d still like to know. Please.”

That was four. Her mother looked at him for a long moment over the cup, the way she might look at a fish she suspected of not being fresh, and then she put the cup down.

“Chives. Prawns. Egg, scrambled soft and cooled first, so it doesn’t make the filling wet.”

“How much chive?”

“Enough.”

“Chopped finely?”

“Not too fine. They let out water.” He listened, and she saw that he was listening the way he must listen to a proposal, and she sat back. “Why do you want to know?”

“Because I’d like to make them.”

“Yourself? Have you ever cooked?”

“Some things. Eggs. Noodles. Fish.”

“That’s not cooking.”

Tang Xi laughed. An Yu accepted the verdict without argument. “Then I have more to learn.”

Her mother shook her head. “Strange,” she said, and then, slowly, she began to explain. The chives washed and dried properly, or they’d weep. The prawns chopped by hand, never in a machine, so there was something to bite on. The egg broken up small. A spoon of sesame oil, white pepper, a little salt on the prawns on their own first. Everything stirred in one direction until the filling turned slightly sticky. He asked whether the chives went in first or last. She told him last. He asked whether they could be frozen, and she told him how to lay them on a tray so they didn’t stick. He asked how much prawn to egg, and she showed him with her hands.

Then she picked up a wrapper and folded it in five quick pleats, and he watched her fingers.

“May I try?”

She looked at him, and pushed the bowl of filling and the stack of wrappers across. “Go on.”

He washed his hands and sat back down. The first was too full. The second didn’t seal. The third looked like a folded envelope.

Her mother inspected it. “That’s ugly.”

Tang Xi burst out laughing.

“Understood,” said An Yu.

“Less filling. And your fingers are too dry.” She handed him a little bowl of water. The fourth was better. She nodded at it. “That one can be cooked.”

“You’re doing very well, Mr. Wang,” said Tang Xi.

“Thank you, Ms. Tang.”

“Don’t call each other those names at my table,” said her mother.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch ended slowly. Her mother packed a box of dumplings for Tang Xi to take home, since she’d never finish them otherwise. When An Yu stood to help clear, her mother told him to leave it.

“I can help.”

“You don’t know where anything goes.”

“Then you can tell me.”

She gave him a look and handed him the empty plates. “Kitchen. Sink. Not the dishwasher.”

He carried them through, and her mother lowered her voice. “You like him.”

“Mum.”

“Don’t pretend.”

Tang Xi folded a napkin. “Yes. Very much.”

Her mother looked towards the kitchen, where he stood at the sink while one of the cooks explained where the plates went. He was nodding. Actually nodding. “Does he treat you well?”

“He listens to me. Not always the first time, but he does.”

“Does he let you work?”

“Of course.”

“Does he make decisions for you?” Tang Xi hesitated, and her mother saw it. “Ah.”

“He used to. Now he asks.”

Her mother wiped a spot of water from the table. “Money makes people think they’re allowed to decide things. Your father thought that too, once.” She was quiet. “I don’t want you spending your life feeling you have to say thank you. I didn’t work all these years so you could become someone’s possession.”

“I know, Mum.”

Her mother reached out and straightened the collar of her blouse, a small, old gesture. “You look tired. Eat properly. You’re too thin. Take the dumplings.” She glanced at the kitchen again. “He’s polite. Too polite.” And then, as if it cost her something: “He asked about the filling properly. Most people just eat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Outside, the afternoon was mild and the old street was busy, people coming out of shops with bags, a van trying to back into a lane too narrow for it, the smell of roast chestnuts from a cart on the corner. He carried the box of dumplings.

“You asked her four times,” she said.

“I wanted to know.”

“You really want to make them? You can’t even fold them.”

“I can practise. Being a chairman doesn’t stop anyone making dumplings.”

She laughed, and then stopped at the corner, and he stopped with her. “Thank you for coming. And for not arguing with her.”

“Arguing wouldn’t have helped. She was trying to protect you.”

“She thinks men like you make girls like me forget where they came from. Do you think she’s wrong?”

“No.” She blinked. “I think she’s seen things that made her careful. I don’t know everything she went through after Shanghai. But I know she worked to give you a life that was yours. Your mother didn’t raise someone who needs rescuing. You built your own life, Xi. I don’t want credit for any of it.”

Something tightened in her chest, and she took his free hand. “She doesn’t dislike you as much as you think. She gave you the recipe.”

“She gave me instructions.”

“That’s practically an invitation into the family. If you get the filling wrong she’ll never forgive you.”

“Then I’ll take it seriously,” he said, and she pulled him down by the front of his coat and kissed him on the corner of the street, briefly, with the box of dumplings between them.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening she found him in his kitchen with his sleeves rolled up, a bag of prawns from the market, a bunch of chives drying on a tea towel and a page of handwritten notes propped against the kettle. There was flour on the counter. One dumpling was already finished. It looked remarkably like an envelope.

She picked it up. “It looks like a letter.”

“The edges were difficult to seal.”

“You really listened to everything she said.”

“Of course.” He looked at her. “It matters to you.”

She went quiet, and then she came round behind him and put her arms round his waist, and he covered her hands with one of his.

“You’re getting flour on your sleeve,” he said.

“I know.”

“Your mother would disapprove.”

“She’s not here.” She laughed against his back. “Can I help?”

“With the filling. Not the folding.”

“How romantic.”

So they made them together. He was meticulous, measuring each spoonful and checking every fold against the one he had drawn in his notes. She wasn’t. She pinched the edges carelessly and laughed when one split, and stole a piece of cooked egg out of the bowl when he wasn’t looking, and he caught her.

“That’s for the filling.”

“It’s delicious.”

“Xi.”

“You’ve become very strict.”

“I’m following the method.”

After a while he said, “I think I understand why you love these. She makes them by hand. She knows exactly how much belongs in each one. She doesn’t hurry the folding. And she makes enough for everyone before she sits down. She doesn’t measure the work by whether anyone notices it.”

“No,” said Tang Xi. “She doesn’t.”

He kissed the top of her head. “I’d like to learn properly. I’ll ask her again next time.”

“She’ll make you chop the chives. And peel the prawns. And wash up.”

“That seems reasonable.”

She leaned against his shoulder and watched a chairman who had negotiated across three continents make a small, determined adjustment to a dumpling wrapper so the filling didn’t escape. There was nothing to buy, nothing to arrange and nothing to fix: only something her mother had made with her hands, a method passed across a table, and a man who wanted to learn it properly. She thought that might be a good beginning.

chapters.title: Winter Without the Account
chapters.desc: The account renews, and page four has someone else’s name on it.
chapters.content:
The renewal reached An-Tech on Monday morning, and An Yu was reading the commercial schedule when he noticed the name. Not hers.

Northlight Agency · An-Tech annual communications retainer
Renewal term: February 2026 – January 2027
Account Director: Rachel Ji

He turned the page. The account team was listed underneath with the usual responsibilities, reporting lines and escalation steps, and Tang Xi’s name appeared nowhere in it. The commercial terms had barely moved: some changes to the regional allocation, revised service levels, a new reporting calendar. Nothing unusual, except page four.

He read page four again and called Ding in.

“Has Northlight changed its account team?”

Ding checked his tablet. “Yes, Mr. Wang. The renewal documents came in on Friday. Ms. Ji is the account director.”

“And Ms. Tang?”

A pause. “I understand she’s no longer assigned to An-Tech.”

“Since when?”

“I don’t have the date. Shall I ask Northlight?”

“No.” He closed the file. “Leave it.”

When Ding had gone he looked at the cover page for a long time. He had expected to see her name there. Not because he thought the account was hers, or that she ought to keep it for ever. Because for nearly a year every important conversation about the agency’s work had gone through her. He had got used to her name in the subject line. Ms. Tang’s revised proposal. Ms. Tang’s comments. Ms. Tang’s approval matrix. He knew the rhythm of her emails, short and exact, never a word more than they needed, and now and then one last sentence that made it impossible to misunderstand what she thought.

The account had renewed, and she wasn’t on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At Northlight, Rachel was standing by Tang Xi’s desk when the phone rang. An-Tech Executive Office.

“Good morning. Tang Xi speaking.”

“Good morning, Ms. Tang. It’s Ding, from Mr. Wang’s office. Mr. Wang has read the renewal and noticed the change in account leadership. He asked whether it was connected with the renewal itself.”

Tang Xi looked at Rachel. “No. It was an internal Northlight decision. Rachel Ji leads the account from the new term. She’s worked on it for months, and the handover finished last week. Please tell him the transition is complete and that Rachel has full sight of everything.”

“Of course. Thank you, Ms. Tang.”

She put the phone down. Rachel raised an eyebrow. “That was quick.”

“He’s noticed.”

“Of course he’s noticed. Do you want me to talk to him? He might think this is because of him.”

“He can ask me. And if he doesn’t, he can read the contract.”

Rachel laughed. “You’re terrible.”

“I’m being professional.”

“You’re being extremely professional.”

Tang Xi went back to the handover document. She had raised it with Daniel at the end of November, after the second column and the photograph, after the questions about her promotion and the pitch she’d lost, and after she had stood in Daniel’s office handing him a signed letter. It hadn’t been impulsive. She had read the agency’s conflict policy twice, written a transition plan and taken it to Daniel herself: Rachel to lead from the new term, Tang Xi available inside the agency for the handover, nothing changing for the client. Daniel had agreed in the first week of December. Rachel, who knew the account almost as well as she did, was more than ready for it.

She hadn’t been pushed off it. She had stepped away. There was a difference, and she meant to keep remembering it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven he rang her himself, and she looked at his name on the screen for a moment before she answered.

“Hello, Mr. Wang.”

“Ms. Tang.” She could almost see him at his desk with page four still open. “You’re no longer on the account.”

“That’s right.”

“Why?”

“Because I handed it over.”

“I can see that. Was it your decision?”

“Yes. I took it to Daniel at the end of November.”

There was a silence. Through the glass wall of her office she could see Rachel on a call, pointing at something on her screen.

“Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Because it was an internal staffing decision.”

“Xi.”

She shut her eyes. “An Yu.”

“I’d have liked to hear it from you.”

“I know.”

“Did you think I’d object?”

“No. I didn’t want my decision to turn into another conversation about what you wanted. I didn’t want you asking Northlight to keep me. I didn’t want you telling Daniel you were perfectly comfortable with me on the account, or reassuring anybody that there was no conflict.”

“I wouldn’t have—”

“You might not have meant to. But you’d have had an opinion, and people would have known you had one.” She looked down at her hands. “I wanted to make one decision about my career without having to think about what the chairman of An-Tech would make of it.”

He was quiet. “Are you unhappy with the work?”

“No.”

“With Rachel taking over?”

“Not at all. She’s good, and she’s earned it.”

“Then why leave?”

“Because I want my work to be mine.”

“I understand,” he said. “I won’t ask Northlight to change anything. I’ll work with Rachel.” And then, more quietly: “I hadn’t realised how used I’d got to seeing your name on everything.”

Her face softened. “That’s because I was on everything.”

“I know.”

“Don’t worry. Rachel will make very sure you know who’s in charge.”

“I expect she will.”

She laughed, and she heard him relax. “Will I see you tonight?”

“Yes.”

“Goodbye, Ms. Tang.”

“Goodbye, Mr. Wang.”

She sat for a while afterwards looking at the screen. It was strange how a name disappearing from a contract could feel like an ending and a beginning at once.

✦ ✦ ✦

He read the agreement a third time after lunch. He understood the commercial logic; the account had grown and the agency needed a broader leadership, Rachel had the experience, the handover was documented. There was no operational reason to object. But it meant something else to him. She had taken herself out of the one working relationship that had brought them back into each other’s lives, and she had done it without asking him, and he had no right to be asked.

Ding came in with the afternoon schedule. “Ms. Ji has confirmed Thursday’s transition meeting. Shall I include Ms. Tang for the first one?”

“No. Ms. Ji is the account director. We deal with her.”

“Should I take Ms. Tang off the recurring correspondence?”

“Yes. Unless Northlight copies her for a specific reason of their own.”

When Ding had gone, he sat back. A year ago he’d have found a way to keep her in it: an advisory role, a strategic review, an invitation to look over a proposal, anything that let him go on seeing her name. He could see that clearly now. He could also hear exactly what she would say, standing in this room in July with her bag on her shoulder: I don’t want you to find a more sophisticated way to own the things around me.

He closed the contract. For the first time since he’d asked for her by name, he would meet the account without her.

✦ ✦ ✦

She arrived at his flat with a paper bag. “Dinner. Noodles from the place near the office.”

He took it and helped her out of her coat. “You’re quiet.”

“I’m always quiet.”

“Not with me.” He hung the coat up. “Do you regret it?”

“No.” She studied his face. “You’re disappointed.”

“A little.”

“Because you won’t see me in meetings?”

“Partly. I liked working with you. You were difficult.”

She laughed. “Excuse me?”

“You challenged nearly every proposal I made.”

“Because nearly every proposal you made needed challenging.” She leaned on the counter. “Do you remember the first meeting? You asked about slide thirty-one while I was on slide twenty-eight.”

“You were taking too long.”

“I was explaining something.”

“You were repeating yourself.”

She stared at him and then laughed. “You were so annoying.”

“I remember.” He looked at her. “I’ll miss having you on the account.”

“I’ll miss some of it. The work. The people. Arguing with you most of all.” She caught his wrist when he reached for her cheek. “An Yu. Now nobody can say it.” He was still. “Nobody can say I got the account because I was with you. Nobody can say I kept it because you wanted me there, or that my work depended on being close to the chairman. People can still talk. They always can. But there’s no account left for them to use against me.”

Her voice was steady, and he could hear what it had cost her to get to the point where it was. He looked at her and nodded.

“I wish you hadn’t needed to do it,” he said. “I wish the world had made it easier for you to stay.”

“So do I.”

He bent his head until his forehead touched hers. “I’m proud of you. Not because you left the account. Because you made the decision yourself, and you didn’t let me make it for you.”

She shut her eyes, and then she put her arms round his waist, and he held her, and for a while neither of them said anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at the table, two cartons of noodles and a box of greens, an ordinary dinner they might have had on any Monday. But something about the evening was different. The account had been the reason they met again; then the reason they kept meeting; then the thing neither of them knew how to manage. Now it was somebody else’s job.

She raised her glass. “To Rachel.”

“To Rachel?”

“She’s going to need it.”

He smiled. “Then to Rachel.”

He cleared the plates while she rinsed the cartons. “Are you going to be difficult with her?”

“No. I’ll be reasonable.”

“That’s not the same thing.”

“Professionally reasonable.”

“Poor Rachel.”

“She’s competent. I’ll respect her decisions.” He dried his hands. “Including the ones I argue with. She’ll hear about those in the meeting, not from you.”

She turned round. “Good answer.”

“Would you like another? I’d like to have dinner with you without discussing An-Tech.”

“That’s ambitious.”

“I can try.”

She straightened his collar. “All right, Mr. Wang. No more work tonight.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was lying on her side reading when he came out of the bathroom and turned off the main light.

“You’re still thinking about it,” she said, putting the book down.

He considered denying it. “Yes. I hadn’t realised how much I’d tied to it. Not the account. Having you there. It was where I first saw you again. Where I learned how you work. Where I got to watch you challenge me in front of people who expected everyone to agree with me.”

“That last part was your favourite.”

“It was.” He took her hand. “But I didn’t want you there only because I wanted to see you. I wanted you there because you were good at it. You made the work better. And you never let me get away with anything.”

“Someone had to.”

“I’ll miss that.”

She moved closer. “You still have me. Outside the account.”

He kissed her, slowly, without the hurry of the first months, without needing to steal a minute between meetings or hide behind a professional goodbye. She laid her hand along his cheek.

“Do you know what I like about this? You don’t have to ask for me by name any more. You can just ask me to come over.”

“Would that work?”

“Depends whether you ask nicely.”

He kissed her again. “Would you come over tomorrow?”

“Yes.”

“And the day after?”

“Don’t push your luck.”

He laughed under his breath, and she settled against him. The renewal would start in February. Rachel would lead the account and An Yu would meet her on Thursday, and the work would go on without Tang Xi’s name attached to any of it: no special role, no private invitation to stay involved, no reason to be copied in. For the first time they would have to find each other without a meeting in the diary.

“An Yu? Do you miss me already?”

“Yes.”

“Good,” she said, and closed her eyes, and when he held her this time there was no contract between them.

chapters.title: A Date Without a Contract
chapters.desc: A bookshop, a bowl of noodles, rain, and her very small bed.
chapters.epigraph: “You hit your head on my shelf.”
chapters.content:
At twelve minutes past nine on Saturday morning, Tang Xi was sitting cross-legged on her bed trying to decide whether a cream jumper looked too much like work when her phone lit up.

Professor: What time should I pick you up?

Tang Xi: Where are we going?

Professor: I thought we could spend the day together.

Tang Xi: That’s not a place.

Professor: I haven’t decided.

Tang Xi: Chairman Wang, are you telling me there’s no agenda?

Professor: I’m trying very hard not to make one.

Tang Xi: How uncomfortable for you.

Professor: Very.

She laughed out loud in the empty room. Then:

Professor: Would you like to go to a bookshop?

She looked at the screen. Not a restaurant he’d booked out. Not an exhibition with a private viewing. Not somewhere chosen because someone had told him it was impressive. A bookshop.

Tang Xi: Yes. No driver.

Professor: All right.

Tang Xi: No assistant.

Professor: All right.

Tang Xi: And you don’t buy the bookshop.

There was a longer pause.

Professor: I wasn’t planning to buy a bookshop.

Tang Xi: I’m setting the boundary early.

Professor: Sensible.

She put the phone down, smiling. For the first time in a long while she was getting ready to go somewhere with him without thinking about how it would look in a diary.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was waiting outside when she got there, dark coat over a grey jumper, hands in his pockets. No driver hovering, no car at the kerb. He was simply standing on a pavement in the old book district on his own, which she wasn’t sure she had ever seen him do.

“You’re early.”

“By three minutes.”

“How long have you been waiting?”

“Not long.”

“An Yu.”

“Seven minutes.”

She smiled, and he held out his hand, and she took it.

The shop filled two floors of an old building. The front windows were crowded with handwritten recommendations and second-hand novels whose spines had faded in the sun, and a bell rang over the door when they went in. The smell reached her at once: paper, dust, wood, and something faintly sweet from the little coffee counter at the back.

“Oh,” she said.

“Good?”

“Very good.”

For the first quarter of an hour she forgot he was there. She went slowly along the shelves, pulling books out and reading the first page, and every so often turned round with one in her hand.

“Have you read this?”

“No.”

“This?”

“No.”

“Do you read fiction at all?”

“Sometimes. When I have time.”

“Do you enjoy it?”

He thought about it. “Some of it.”

“You’re making it very hard to recommend anything.”

“Then recommend something hard.”

He watched her browse. There was something familiar in the way she handled books: the tilt of her head over a blurb, her thumb along the edge of the pages, the way she sometimes mouthed a sentence before deciding whether she liked it. He remembered her at sixteen with a book open and a carton of strawberry milk by her elbow, explaining a story she hadn’t finished because she’d been too busy telling him the ending she’d imagined for it. She had once informed him that anyone who only read textbooks was missing half the world. He hadn’t answered her.

Now she was asking him whether he preferred hardbacks or paperbacks.

“Paperbacks. They’re easier to carry.”

“That’s practical.”

“Is there another reason to choose a book?”

She looked at him in genuine disbelief. “Sometimes people choose things because they like them.”

He took that in. “Then choose one for me.”

She held one out. “People who make terrible decisions and spend three hundred pages trying to understand themselves.”

“That sounds familiar. Is it good?”

“I haven’t read it.”

“Then how do you know?”

“The cover’s beautiful.”

He looked at the cover, and at her, and nodded with great seriousness. “Then I’ll consider it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Upstairs there was a reading corner by the window, and she sat on the bench with one leg folded under her while he went along the shelves and came back with a collection of essays.

“That’s what you picked?”

“Yes.”

“Very chairman of you.”

He sat down next to her, shoulder to shoulder, and for a while they read in silence. When she’d finished her first chapter she closed the book on her finger.

“Do you know what I remember about the library? You always sat in the same place. Same chair, same table, same side of the window.”

“It was quiet.”

“It was sunny. You never moved.”

“I did sometimes.”

“Only when the librarian made you.” She turned to him. “Did you really like that chair so much?”

He looked at the page in front of him. “No. After the first month I came at twelve instead of half past, so I’d be there before you. I didn’t want you to find the seat empty and sit somewhere else.”

She stared at him. “You changed your whole lunchtime. And you never said anything.”

“I didn’t know how to start.”

Her face softened, and she leaned her head on his shoulder. “You’re doing better now.”

“I hope so.”

She found his hand and kept it between them and picked her book up again. “Read your essays, Professor.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The noodle shop was small and loud, with a handwritten menu over the counter and the kitchen open behind a wide hatch in the wall. Tang Xi ordered for both of them, two bowls of braised beef noodles, a plate of smashed cucumber and some fried tofu, while he stood behind her holding the books.

“Do you always order for two?” he asked.

“Only when I’m hungry.”

“Then it’s lucky I came.”

The bowls arrived steaming, and she stirred hers and took a mouthful, and caught him watching her.

“Why aren’t you eating?”

“I wanted to know if it was good.”

“It’s good.”

He tried it. “It’s good.”

“Very articulate.”

“I’ve been told.”

They ate slowly and talked about nothing that mattered: the books, a film she wanted to see, a restaurant she kept meaning to try. At some point she asked what he would have done if he hadn’t started An-Tech.

“Research, perhaps. Mathematics. Economics. Something that needed more patience than people do.”

“You make people sound exhausting.”

“Sometimes they are.”

“Excuse me?”

“You’re very difficult to ignore. That isn’t the same thing.” He reached across and moved a loose strand of hair off her face. “You’re not exhausting.”

She looked down at her noodles. “Good answer. Are you enjoying today? Without a schedule?”

“More than I expected to. I keep reaching for my phone to check what’s next, and nothing is.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The rain started without warning as they came out of the noodle shop, the first drops dark on the pavement.

“We can wait inside till it passes,” he said.

“No. I want to walk.”

“It’s raining.”

“I noticed.”

He opened his umbrella and she stepped under it, laughing, and they walked slowly along the street while it grew heavier, drumming on the canopy and turning the road to glass. She held the books against her chest. He kept the umbrella tilted towards her, and she noticed.

“You’re getting wet.”

“It’s a coat.”

She stopped, and he stopped. Then she reached up, took a lapel in each fist and dragged him down to her. He barely had time to bend his head before she kissed him. The umbrella tipped sideways; a passing cyclist rang his bell; neither of them moved. She kissed him again, smiling against his mouth, and when she let go there was rain in his hair.

“You’re getting my coat wet,” he said.

“You were already getting it wet.”

“Holding the umbrella over you.”

“Then we’re even.”

He looked at her and bent and kissed her again, and this time he kept the umbrella straight.

“Come on,” she said. “My flat.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her flat was small. Not unpleasantly so, but unmistakably hers: a narrow hall opening into a living room with a compact sofa, a low bookcase and a table that was also her desk, plants along the windowsill, a blanket folded over the arm of the sofa and a stack of parcels she hadn’t opened by the door. He stood just inside while she took off her shoes.

“Don’t look so surprised.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

She watched him take it in, and it was nothing like his. No high ceilings, no glass walls, no furniture set at exact distances from other furniture. Through the bedroom door she could see her bed, small, in a room smaller still, with a narrow shelf fixed to the wall above one side of it. She was suddenly self-conscious. “It’s not very big.”

“It’s comfortable.”

“You haven’t sat down yet.”

“I can tell.”

He hung his coat on the hook next to hers. “Would you like me to make tea?”

“You’re in my flat and you want to make me tea?”

“It seemed polite.”

She laughed. “Sit down, Mr. Wang.”

She went into the kitchen and felt him watching her from the sofa, and didn’t mind. There was something intimate in having him here, not in any grand way but in the ordinary details. His shoes beside hers. His coat on her hook. His hands resting on her little table while the kettle boiled. When she came back he had picked up the book from her coffee table.

“How is it?”

“Good. A bit sad.”

She sat down next to him, knees touching, and they drank tea and listened to the rain.

“Do you know what this is?” she said. “Our first proper date. We’ve had dinners, hotel rooms, business trips, a lunch with my mother. Today’s the first time we went somewhere just because we wanted to, not because there was a meeting or somebody expected us.” She put her cup down. “I like having you here.”

His face softened. “I like being here.”

She leaned in and kissed him, warm and unhurried, and then moved closer, her hand at the back of his neck, and he put his cup down and pulled her in, and their knees banged the coffee table.

“Careful.”

“Your furniture is very close together.”

“It’s a small flat. Don’t complain.”

“I’m not complaining,” he said, and kissed her again.

She stood up and held out her hand. “My room.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The bed was much smaller than his. He sat on the edge of it while she moved a pile of books off the pillow and onto the shelf.

“Sorry. There’s not much room.”

He looked at the bed. “I can see that.”

“Don’t start.”

She came and stood between his knees and took hold of the hem of his jumper. “Can I?” He nodded, and she pulled it over his head and laughed when it caught on his hair, and he put it aside and his hands settled on her waist. She kissed him, and he kissed her back slowly, one hand coming up to the back of her neck, and she felt the familiar restraint in him, the care, the way he waited for her to decide how far she wanted to go. She liked it. She also liked that he was beginning to understand she didn’t always want him to wait.

She undid his shirt and pushed it off his shoulders, and he lifted her jumper over her head, and her skirt, and she stood in front of him in her underwear in the grey rainy light and watched his face change.

“Are you comfortable?” he said. “Tell me if—”

“An Yu. I’m comfortable.”

She pushed him back onto the bed and climbed after him, and they tried to arrange themselves in a space built for one person and failed. The mattress slid against the wall. Her elbow found his ribs. He rolled her under him with great care and his foot hit the end of the bed frame, and she was already giggling when he propped himself above her on one hand and lifted his head.

There was a dull knock. He froze. He shut his eyes.

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.”

“Did you just hit your head?”

“No.”

She looked at the shelf, and back at him. “An Yu.”

“It was the shelf.”

She pressed her lips together. He opened his eyes. “Don’t.”

That was all it took. She burst out laughing: not a small laugh, not the careful sound she used at work, but the kind that took over her whole body. She laughed so hard she had to turn her face into the pillow, her shoulders shaking, one hand flapping uselessly at the shelf.

He stayed where he was above her and looked at the shelf, and at her, and at the shelf. “I don’t see what’s funny.”

“You’re—” She couldn’t breathe. “You’re too tall for my flat.”

“That seems unlikely.”

“You hit your head on my shelf.”

“I noticed.”

Every time she looked at his face it started again. The chairman of An-Tech, who could silence a room with one sentence, kneeling in her tiny bed looking personally offended by a piece of furniture. She laughed until there were tears at the corners of her eyes, and then, to her astonishment, he began to laugh too, at first and then properly, his forehead dropping onto her shoulder.

“You’re laughing,” she said.

“Apparently.”

“I’ve never seen you look so defeated.”

“I’ve never been attacked by furniture before.”

He kissed her hair, and her cheek, and the corner of her mouth, still laughing, and she pulled him down by the back of the neck, and the laughter slowly turned into something else. He slid her underwear down her legs and she kicked it off the end of the bed, and he kissed his way down her body with his head carefully below the level of the shelf, which set her off again, until his mouth reached the inside of her thigh and she stopped laughing suddenly.

“Oh,” she said.

He didn’t say anything. He took his time. The rain ran down the window and her hand found his hair, and she talked to him the whole way through it because she couldn’t help it, there, yes, don’t you dare stop, and he answered her each time with his mouth and not with words, until she was arching off the narrow mattress with her heel against the wall.

When he came back up she was flushed and breathless and grinning. “Mind the shelf.”

“I’ll remember.”

He didn’t. He knocked it with his shoulder this time as she pulled him over her, and a paperback slid off the end and landed on his back, and she was laughing again when he pushed into her, and the laugh broke in the middle into a gasp. He went still, and looked down at her, his mouth twitching.

“Are you laughing at me or—”

“Both,” she said. “Don’t stop.”

He didn’t. He moved in her slowly, holding himself up on his forearms, with the book still lying on the blanket beside them, and every time she started to giggle he kissed her until she lost the thread of it, and she held on to his shoulders and wrapped her legs round him in the too-small bed, the frame creaking with them. She told him exactly what she wanted and he gave it to her. When she came, she was laughing, helplessly, her whole body shaking with both at once, and he looked at her as if he had never seen anything like it, and said her name, and followed her down a moment later with his face buried in her neck.

For a long time neither of them moved. The rain went on. The paperback was somewhere near her feet.

“You’re beautiful when you laugh,” he said into her hair.

“Even when I’m laughing at you?”

“That’s when I like it best.” He lifted his head and looked at the shelf with deep suspicion. “It’s mounted too low.”

“It’s mounted exactly right. You’re the wrong size.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At a little after seven he was trying to make tea in her kitchen in one of her spare T-shirts, which was too short in the sleeves, his trousers folded over the chair and his hair a mess, and she watched him from the bed through the open door.

“You’re staying?”

“Would you like me to leave?”

“No.”

“Then I’ll stay.” He came back with two cups and sat down, and she tucked herself into his side and tried the tea.

“Good.”

“I followed your instructions.”

“Very impressive.”

“You’re making fun of me.”

“A little.”

He took her hand. “Did you enjoy today?”

“Very much.”

“Even the shelf?”

She dissolved again, and he closed his eyes. “Xi.”

“I’m sorry.”

“No, you’re not.”

“Not really,” she said, and kissed him.

The rain had stopped. The streetlights were coming on one by one below her window and shining back off the wet road. He looked round the little room: the books, the plants, the narrow bed, the shelf that had nearly finished him. He had spent years building rooms big enough for anything he might want, and this one had none of that, and he couldn’t remember when he had last felt so at ease.

She traced a line across his palm. “You’re thinking.”

“Yes.”

“About the shelf?”

He laughed. “No. I’d like to do this again.”

“Have tea?”

“Go on a date. With you. If you’ll have me.”

She pretended to think about it. “Are you going to behave?”

“I’ll try.”

“Are you going to buy the bookshop?”

“No.”

“Are you going to bring an assistant?”

“No.”

“Are you going to hit your head on another shelf?”

“I can’t promise that.”

She laughed and kissed him. “Then I suppose I’ll have to keep you.”

He held her a little closer. There was no contract to renew, no title to protect, no reason to be careful about who had invited whom: only a bookshop, two bowls of noodles, rain on a pavement and a man who had been invited into a small flat and wanted to be invited back. And Tang Xi, who had spent so much of her life learning not to ask anyone to stay, found that she could do it at last without feeling foolish.

“An Yu? Next Saturday?”

“Next Saturday.”

chapters.title: The Library Again
chapters.desc: Back in Shanghai for the New Year holiday, the library is opened for an hour, and he talks.
chapters.epigraph: “I think you can kiss me now.”
chapters.content:
Tang Xi realised where they were going when the car turned into the road beside the old school.

The iron gates stood under the bare winter trees. The buildings had been repainted, the entrance rebuilt, and the old stone sign replaced with a new one, but the narrow road, the row of plane trees and the little shop across the street were all still there. She hadn’t been back in more than ten years.

“An Yu. Why are we here?”

He put his phone away. “I wanted to show you something.”

She couldn’t say anything for a moment. He reached across the seat and took her hand. “Do you want to go in?”

“Can we? It’s the holiday.”

“I asked the school. The library’s shut for New Year, but they agreed to open it for an hour or two.”

“You asked.” She looked at him sideways. “You didn’t buy it.”

“I asked. They said yes. I made a donation to the library fund afterwards, which they didn’t ask for, and which I’m telling you about now.”

She stared at him and then laughed, against the window. “You’re still very good at making ordinary things sound extraordinary.”

“I thought you might like to see it again.”

She looked down at their hands. “I would.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The woman who unlocked the library for them was older and smaller than Tang Xi remembered, in a dark cardigan with her reading glasses on a chain, and for a moment she looked at them with the polite uncertainty of someone meeting strangers. Then she looked at An Yu properly, and at Tang Xi, and her face opened.

“The boy by the window,” said Mrs. Hua. “And the cheerful one. You were the loudest girl I ever had in this room. I had to say your name every day.”

Tang Xi went pink to the ears. “I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be. It was much too quiet in here after you stopped coming.” She looked at An Yu, and then she asked exactly what she had asked eleven years before, over a sleeping girl’s head. “Your classmate?”

This time he didn’t look down at a book. “Yes. And more than that, now.”

Mrs. Hua smiled, as if he had finally handed in something long overdue, gave him the key and a few instructions about the lights, and left them alone.

The doors closed behind her, and there it was. The same long windows, the same wooden shelves, the same pale floor with fresh varnish on it, the same quiet. The tables had been replaced, but they stood almost exactly where the old ones had. The noticeboard by the door was gone. And the sun still came through the windows at the same angle, lying across the tables in long pale squares.

She walked slowly to the back, and he followed, and she stopped at a table by the window.

“This was it.”

“Yes.”

It probably wasn’t the same table. The wood was newer, the edges smoother. But it was in the same place. She touched it, and looked at the chair facing the window, and the one opposite.

“Your seat. And mine.” She pulled hers out and sat, and looked across at him. “Do you remember how I used to sit? Bag on the chair beside me, books everywhere, my strawberry milk at my elbow.”

“You put your bag on that chair so nobody else would sit there.”

“Nobody did.”

“People tried.”

“Not after I looked at them.”

He smiled. “You did that?”

“Of course.” She rested her chin on her hand. “Did I annoy you? Honestly.”

He sat down in his old place. “No. I was annoyed on the days you didn’t come.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They walked through the shelves. She stopped in the aisle where she used to stand when she wanted a book and didn’t know which one, and ran a finger along the spines.

“You used to take out three,” he said, “read the first page of each and put two back. And never the one you’d come for.”

“Sometimes I changed my mind.”

“Every day.”

“How do you remember all of this?”

He didn’t answer. He took a square of wax paper from the inside pocket of his coat, and she knew what it was before he’d unfolded it. The crane lay inside, its uneven wings a little softer than they had been in the box on his bedside table in June, the one deep crease exactly where she had folded too hard at sixteen.

“You brought it.”

“I wanted it here.” He put it in her palm, and she held it as if it might come apart, and opened one wing just far enough to see her own handwriting inside, the blue ink faded to grey.

For the person who never talks.

“Ten years in a maths book,” she said. Her throat had gone tight.

“Ten years in a maths book. Two weeks in my wallet, once, last February, because I wanted to have it on me the first time I was alone in a room with you.” He watched her fold the wing back down. “I used to think it was the only thing you’d ever given me that I didn’t have to pretend I hadn’t noticed. I had to pretend about all the milk.”

She laughed, and her eyes were wet. She gave it back, and he put it away, and looked at her. “There’s something I want to tell you. Can we sit?”

✦ ✦ ✦

They went back to the table. He sat in his seat and she sat in hers, and the sun lay between them.

“I’ve thought for a long time about what I should have said to you here,” he said. “I remember the first day you sat down. You asked if the seat was taken.”

“And you didn’t answer. You didn’t even look up.”

“I wanted you to stay.” Her fingers went still on the table, and he went on, slowly. “I didn’t know what to do with you at first. You came in every day and talked as if we’d known each other for years. You told me about teachers, exams, your friends, what you’d eaten, what you wanted to read. Sometimes you told me things that had happened to other people as if they’d happened to you.”

“I was a very involved listener.”

“You were. And I listened. I heard everything, even when I was reading, even when I didn’t look up. I knew when you were happy, and when you were angry, and when you were pretending not to mind about a test. I knew you were tired when you stopped in the middle of a sentence. I knew you hated the crusts on your sandwiches. I knew you turned to the last page of a book before you decided whether to read it.”

She smiled, a little helplessly. “That makes no sense.”

“I know.” He looked at the empty chair beside her, where her bag used to be. “And I knew you were waiting for me to say something. I thought that if I kept letting you come, if I never asked you to leave, you’d understand I wanted you there. I thought you knew. But we were sixteen. You shouldn’t have had to guess.”

She lowered her eyes.

“The Monday you said good luck, you were quieter than usual. I knew something had changed. I wanted to ask why. I wanted to ask whether you’d still come, whether you’d give me your number. And I didn’t, because I was afraid of making it obvious that I wanted you to stay.” He gave a small, humourless smile. “Ridiculous.”

“No,” she said. “It isn’t.”

“I thought there’d be another day. And then on the Thursday you came back, and I wasn’t here. I was at the hospital with Nainai. I came on the Friday, and the week after, and I asked Mrs. Hua, and I thought you were ill, and then I thought you’d gone on holiday. I didn’t know you’d left Shanghai.” He didn’t look away from her. “I’m sorry I let you think you were talking to someone who didn’t care. I’m sorry I let you go without knowing I’d miss you. And I’m sorry that when I finally saw you again, I still didn’t know how to talk to you.”

He was quiet. There was no calculation in it, only a man deciding to keep going.

“On the forty-second floor last February you walked in behind Daniel with a folder, and you looked at me as if I were a client you’d already decided to be careful with. I wanted to ask whether you still liked strawberry milk. Whether you still read the last page first. Whether you’d been happy. Whether you had anyone who listened to you, and whether anyone had ever made you feel you didn’t have to make yourself smaller.” Her smile had gone. “And I wanted to tell you I’d never forgotten you. I remembered your voice. How you said my name when you wanted my attention, and when you were annoyed with me, and the very last time. Good luck, Wang An Yu. I heard it every time I thought about you.”

Her eyes were shining. He didn’t reach across to wipe them, or stop, or ask her to make him feel better. He let her listen. For once he gave her every word she had waited eleven years to hear.

He told her about the first days after she’d gone, when he kept looking at the door. He told her about finding the crane in the last week of June, and opening the wing so carefully he was afraid he’d tear it, and laying it in wax paper. He told her about Zurich, his first winter, the snow that made the streets quiet in a way that reminded him of this room. He told her that sometimes, when something was funny, he’d thought about how she would have laughed. He told her about London, and the work, and the company, and the years in which he got good at talking when he had to and keeping silent when it suited him. And he told her that none of it had made him forget the girl who used to sit opposite him and talk.

He talked for almost an hour. She didn’t interrupt him. She didn’t tease him, or ask a single question. She listened.

When he stopped, the library was quiet, and the sun had moved across the table. His hands were resting together in front of him, and he looked almost uncertain.

“That’s everything,” he said.

She reached over and put her hand on his, and he turned his under it and held on.

“Thank you for telling me.” She was quiet for a while. “I used to think I’d made you up. That you were just a quiet boy who happened to sit in the same place every day, and I was a silly girl who couldn’t stop talking to him. Sometimes I’d hear someone mention Switzerland and wonder if you were still there. Whether you remembered the school at all. Whether you remembered me.”

“I never forgot.”

“I know that now.”

She got up and came round the table, and stood beside him, and then bent and put her arms round his shoulders and her cheek against his hair. His hands came to her waist.

“You finally talked,” she whispered.

“Yes.”

“A whole hour.”

“I had a lot to say.”

She laughed, and drew back enough to touch his face. “Professor.”

His eyes came up to hers.

“I think you can kiss me now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She led him to the back of the library, into the same narrow aisle between the same rows, and stopped where she used to stand choosing.

“This is where you used to disappear,” he said.

“I wasn’t disappearing. I was choosing a book.”

“You were reading the same paragraph over and over. For ten minutes.”

“How do you remember everything?”

“Because I was watching you.”

Her face softened, and she stepped closer. “Then look at me now.”

He did. She took hold of his coat and drew him down, and the kiss was gentle at first, two people who had found their way back to the place where they’d first learned the shape of each other’s company. Then he put his hand along her cheek and kissed her again, longer, and she backed into the shelves with a soft thud of spines, and held on to his coat, and he bent his head lower to her and she felt him smile against her mouth.

“What?”

“I like this place.”

“Because of the chair?”

“Because you were here.”

She kissed him again, and this time she didn’t let him be careful. She pulled him down by the collar until his back was to one shelf and hers to the other and there was no room in the aisle for anything but the two of them; his hand slid under her coat to the small of her back and spread there, and a row of paperbacks pressed into her shoulder blades, and somewhere at the end of the room the old radiator knocked twice the way it had in 2014. She laughed against his mouth at the sound, and he kissed the laugh away, slow and deep, with eleven years in it. Here, where she had once stood waiting for a boy to say something, he held her without holding anything back.

When they parted she rested her forehead against his. “I wish we could have had this then.”

“So do I.”

“We couldn’t. We were children.”

He brushed his thumb across her cheek. “Then let me have it now.”

“You have me now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Hua was waiting by the entrance when they brought the key back.

“Well? Was it the same?”

“Very nearly,” said Tang Xi. “Thank you for opening it.”

Mrs. Hua looked at the two of them, and at their hands, and nodded. Then she held out her hand for Tang Xi’s phone and made them stand by the window at their old table for a photograph. “Look at the camera,” she told An Yu, twice. He didn’t; in the picture he was looking at Tang Xi. “It’s nice when former students come back. It’s nicer when they come back together.” To An Yu she said, “You talk now.”

“I’m practising.”

“Good. She was always going to need someone who could answer.”

Outside the air was cold. Tang Xi put her hand into his coat pocket and found his already there, and they walked slowly to the gate. At the entrance she stopped and looked back. The library windows held the pale afternoon sky. For more than ten years she had carried that room with her as the place where she’d left something unfinished. She had come back, not to ask whether he remembered, or whether he had missed her. She knew.

“An Yu? Next time, tell me a story about Zurich.”

“All right.”

“And London. And something from when you were little.”

“That might take more than an hour.”

“Then we’ll need another date.”

“As many as you like.”

She leaned against his arm, and they went out through the gates together, and behind them, in a quiet library that had once held a year of unanswered conversation, the afternoon light went on falling across the same table.

chapters.title: Due Diligence
chapters.desc: An-Tech is buying her agency’s biggest rival, and she is the one who has to tell the regulator why that matters.
chapters.epigraph: “That’s the first time you’ve not told me something and been right.”
chapters.content:
The first time Tang Xi saw the name, it was at the top of a confidential notice that arrived in her inbox at ten to seven on a Monday evening, sent by Daniel to six people.

STRICTLY CONFIDENTIAL · PROJECT HERON
Notice under clause 14.3 of the Northlight–An-Tech agency agreement
An-Tech Holdings proposes to acquire a controlling interest in Corran Pike Communications Group. Pre-notification discussions with the competition authority are under way. This information isn’t public.

She read it twice. Her fingers stopped on the trackpad.

Corran Pike wasn’t a small agency with a handful of regional clients. It had offices in six markets, a large government affairs practice, a crisis division and a list of multinational clients, and for as long as she had worked at Northlight it had been the agency they lost to, or beat, or lost to again. It was Northlight’s biggest rival. And An-Tech was buying it.

She knew An Yu had been widening An-Tech’s investments. She hadn’t known about this. She hadn’t known he was even looking at her industry. Her phone lit up.

Professor: Are you home? I’ll come over after my meeting.

She looked at it before she answered.

Tang Xi: Yes. We need to talk.

Professor: I know.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at nine, still in his suit, and didn’t take his coat off until she told him to.

“How long?” she said.

“The board approved the approach in January. We’ve been talking to Corran Pike’s shareholders since December.”

“December.” She sat down on the arm of the sofa. “You were in my mother’s restaurant learning to fold dumplings, and you were buying my agency’s biggest competitor.”

“Yes.”

“And you didn’t tell me.”

“I couldn’t.” He stayed standing. “It was price-sensitive and it was confidential, and if I’d told you, you’d have known something about your own industry that nobody at Northlight knew. You’d have had to choose between telling Daniel and keeping my secret. Either way you’d have been in breach of something.” He paused. “You found out the same hour Daniel did. I asked our counsel to make sure of that. The clause says we notify Northlight before we sign. We notified Northlight. Not you.”

She looked at him. “That’s the first time you’ve not told me something and been right.”

“I know.”

“It doesn’t make it feel better.”

“No. It wouldn’t.”

“Why Corran Pike?”

He told her: An-Tech’s businesses needed communications at a scale they kept buying from outside; the group’s investment arm wanted a services business with regular income; Corran Pike’s founders wanted to sell. It was sound. It was also going to make her working life complicated, and they both knew it.

“From tonight,” she said, “we don’t talk about work here. Not yours, not mine. Not this.”

“Agreed.”

“I mean it.”

“So do I,” he said, and she believed him, mostly.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Tuesday morning Daniel stood at the head of the boardroom table with Northlight’s general counsel, the finance director, the head of strategy, two senior account leads, Rachel and Tang Xi.

“You’ve all seen the notice,” he said. “Before we go any further, Rachel, I’m sorry, but you need to leave.”

Rachel was already gathering her laptop. “I’m the An-Tech account director. I’m not allowed to know what we think about the people buying our rival.” She paused by Tang Xi’s chair. “You’re going to be busy.”

“Apparently.”

When the door had closed, the general counsel took over. The competition authority was in confidential talks with An-Tech before any formal filing. It would almost certainly come to Northlight as the main competitor, with questions about overlapping clients and markets, about how often clients switched agencies, and about one thing in particular: whether, once An-Tech owned Corran Pike, it would quietly move its own account there and leave Northlight without one of its largest clients.

“Then we need a wall,” said Tang Xi. “A hard one. An-Tech is our client. Corran Pike is our competitor, and soon it may be our client’s company. Nothing we know in one capacity can cross into the other. The account team stays out of anything to do with the deal. Anyone working on our response to the authority stays out of the account. A restricted group, named people only, separate storage, no forwarding, no informal requests through account staff. If An-Tech wants anything from us, it comes through Legal.”

The general counsel nodded. “That’s our preliminary view.”

“Good,” said Daniel. “Then I’d like you to lead our response to the authority, Xi. You’re off the account. You know the An-Tech contract history better than anyone in this building who isn’t Rachel, and Rachel can’t be in this room.”

She had expected it, and it still landed. “I have a conflict.”

“I know you do,” said Daniel. “That’s why we’re going to write it down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The protocol came on Friday at a quarter to nine. It had sections for the existing relationship with An-Tech, the competitive relationship with Corran Pike, the information barrier, the restricted personnel, requests from the authority and record-keeping, and a last section on personal interests that might reasonably affect professional judgement. Her name was highlighted in it.

“You disclosed the relationship last year under our client policy,” said Daniel, sitting down on the other side of her desk. “This is separate. A declaration for this deal only. Legal will look at what you can do and what you can’t, and our external counsel will tell the authority and An-Tech’s lawyers that you’ve made it. Nobody’s asking you to pretend it doesn’t exist. And you’re not being accused of anything.”

“I know.” She thought about it. “I’ll lead the submission. I won’t touch anything commercial. If the authority asks us about An-Tech’s fees or the terms of the contract, that goes to finance and Legal, and I don’t see it. And I don’t want to be shut out of everything just because I’m in a relationship with An Yu.”

“I wouldn’t expect you to accept that.” He stood up. “And Xi? Don’t try to prove you’re impartial by taking on more than you should. You’re allowed boundaries too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The data room opened the following Thursday on a separate secure platform. It wasn’t An-Tech’s; it had been set up by both sides’ lawyers at the authority’s request, so that a small clean team from Northlight could see the one thing the authority wanted it to comment on: An-Tech’s draft commitment about its existing agency contract. Every document was logged. Every page view was recorded. Each user had a profile of their own and a list of what they could open, and Tang Xi’s was short.

She sat in a glass room at Northlight’s lawyers with the general counsel and the finance director and read it.

An-Tech offered to keep Northlight on its account for two years after completion, on current terms.

“Two years,” said the finance director. “That’s generous.”

“It’s two years,” said Tang Xi. “Our retainer runs in twelve-month terms. After two years they can move the whole account to Corran Pike with one letter, and by then Corran Pike will have spent two years learning everything about An-Tech’s business from the inside.” She turned the page. “And look at this.”

It was a line in the description of the combined group’s plans: integration of client-facing capabilities across the group’s communications businesses.

“That describes the two companies as if they’re already one,” she said. “It talks about putting the client teams together. Before the authority has cleared anything. If that’s what they intend, the authority needs to know. If it isn’t, they’ve written it very badly.”

The general counsel leaned over and read it, and made a note, and for the first time that morning looked faintly pleased.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Monday the authority held its third-party meeting in a grey building with a long corridor of identical doors, and as Tang Xi came out of the lift with the general counsel, An Yu came out of the room at the end of it with his own lawyers and a man she knew from An-Tech’s organisation chart: Edmund Lung, deputy chief operating officer, nine years at the company, thinning hair and a careful face.

They met in the middle of the corridor.

“Ms. Tang,” said An Yu.

“Mr. Wang.”

That was all. His lawyers kept walking. Edmund Lung looked at her a second longer than was polite, and then at his chairman, and followed.

Inside, the case officer had her declaration on the table in front of him. “Before we start. You’ve told us you’re in a personal relationship with the chairman of the acquiring company.”

“Yes. Since February last year. It’s in writing, and Northlight’s counsel has told An-Tech’s counsel.”

“Thank you.” He turned a page, and that was that.

She spoke for twelve minutes. Corran Pike was stronger than Northlight in Singapore and Seoul, so a national market share figure would miss how concentrated those two cities would become. Crisis communications was its own market, not a slice of a bigger one, because clients in a crisis didn’t shop around. The two-year commitment was too short to protect anything, for reasons she set out in four sentences. And the description of the combined group’s plans read as though the two businesses meant to join their client teams before clearance, which she was sure the authority would want to ask An-Tech about.

The case officer wrote steadily. When she’d finished he looked up. “That’s very clear, Ms. Tang.”

On the way out the general counsel said, “Remind me never to be on the other side of you.”

“You’re on my side.”

“Exactly. That’s why I can enjoy it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Wednesday An Yu came to her flat at a quarter past nine with two paper bags. “Noodles. The place you like.”

“Good.”

For ten minutes they talked about nothing in particular: the rain, a book she’d finished, a colleague at Northlight who’d accidentally invited the entire agency to a dental appointment. He said his brother had rung. Elara had started teaching anatomy to the first-years while her hand mended, and Xing Yue said they were already frightened of her.

“I’ll text her,” said Tang Xi. “She’ll be dreadful at sitting still.”

“She is.”

Then he looked down at his bowl. “How was the—”

He stopped. She put her chopsticks down. “Sorry,” he said.

“We agreed.”

“We did. I was curious. That’s not a good enough reason.” He picked his chopsticks up again. “Can I ask you something that isn’t about work? Would you like to go somewhere at the weekend?”

“Where?”

“I haven’t decided.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re not very good at planning dates.”

“I thought you liked that.”

“I like bookshops. I don’t necessarily like your lack of preparation.”

“Noted,” he said, and they finished dinner without mentioning anything with a code name.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Saturday, on his sofa, she had picked a film, and twenty minutes in she noticed he wasn’t following it.

“What’s happening?”

He considered the screen. “She’s trying to find her brother.”

“That’s not what’s happening at all.”

“Then I don’t know.”

“You’re hopeless.” She settled against him. A few minutes later he said, “Do you think the authority will—” and she lifted her head, and he stopped, and smiled faintly. “Sorry.”

“You’re allowed to be worried.”

“I’m not worried.”

“You’re allowed to be concerned. You don’t have to bring it into this room.” She lay back down. “Go on. Say the thing you’re dying to say, and then we stop.”

He was quiet. “My counsel came out of the authority on Monday and said Northlight’s witness had taken our commitment apart in twelve minutes and he’d like to hire her.”

She laughed into his shoulder. “Tell him no.”

“I did.”

“Good. Now watch the film.”

He reached for the remote and turned the volume up, which was the nearest he came to an apology, and kissed her, and neither of them followed the next scene.

✦ ✦ ✦

The authority’s second set of questions came on the thirtieth and was harder. More on overlapping clients, on pricing, on internal emails about the deal, on exactly what integration of client-facing capabilities had meant. Outside counsel thought the review could take months. The timetable had stopped being realistic.

“Plan for a longer process,” An Yu said. “Keep the clean-team arrangements in place the whole way through. And rewrite that paragraph so it says what we actually intend, which is nothing until we’re cleared.”

Edmund Lung, at the far end of the table, folded his hands. “With respect, Mr. Wang. Northlight’s clean team includes Ms. Tang. The authority will notice that. Everybody will notice that.”

“Northlight chose its own team. The authority has her declaration. We have no say in who an independent agency puts in front of a regulator, and I won’t ask for one.”

“It looks bad.”

“Then we make sure it looks like what it is.” An Yu turned the page. “Next.”

Afterwards Ding brought in the folder for the day. The authority had sent its usual letter to both sides with the second set of questions: a request to preserve every record, and a list of everyone on every clean team, hers among them. It went into An-Tech’s restricted transaction folder, where seventeen named people could open it. Underneath that was the month’s ordinary account report from Northlight.

“Ms. Ji has sent the revised communications plan for the regional launch,” said Ding. “Ms. Tang isn’t copied.”

“She isn’t supposed to be.”

He read Rachel’s plan. It was thorough and careful and good, and at the end she had written a single line in her own voice: We’d like to keep this campaign completely separate from anything you may or may not be doing in our industry, and we’d like that in writing. He approved it, and didn’t send it to Tang Xi, and didn’t ask whether she’d seen it, and didn’t look for a reason to bring her back into the conversation. That evening he went home.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the last day of March he got to her flat after ten with two cups of tea from the stall on the corner, and she looked up from her book on the sofa.

“You’re late.”

“Long day.”

She took the tea and put her book open on her knee. “How’s the acquisition?”

He looked at her.

“That’s a work question,” she said. “I’m allowed to ask one if I want to.”

“Complicated. They want more. It’ll take longer.”

“Are you frustrated?”

“Yes. But it’s a proper review. We have to answer it properly.” He drank. “How’s Northlight?”

“Busy. Rachel’s changed the reporting structure on your account.”

“That’s her decision.”

She smiled. “Look at you, not asking me to explain it.”

She leaned against his shoulder, and he put his cup down and drew her in.

“It’s strange,” she said after a while. “We used to talk about work all the time. Even when we were together there was always the account. Now I can spend a whole evening with you and have no idea what’s happening in your office.”

“Is that bad?”

“No. It’s nice. Do you mind? Not knowing what I’m doing?”

“Less than I thought I would. I don’t need to know everything.”

“That’s a very important discovery for you.”

“I thought so.”

She kissed him, unhurried and warm, and rested her forehead against his. “Tomorrow, no work. No authority. No Corran Pike.”

“Agreed.”

She picked up her book again, and he settled beside her with his arm round her waist, and for the rest of the evening the only thing either of them read was the page she was on.

chapters.title: The Leak
chapters.desc: The deal leaks before breakfast with her name in it. His security team finds the source in one night.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t use her name to explain what you did.”
chapters.content:
The article went up at eighteen minutes past seven on Tuesday morning. By twenty-six past, Tang Xi’s phone had rung six times. By half past, Rachel was standing outside her office holding a printout, and at twenty to eight Daniel asked her to come down to the boardroom.

AN-TECH IN SECRET TALKS TO BUY CORRAN PIKE — AND THE REGULATOR’S FILE NAMES THE CHAIRMAN’S PARTNER

Under the headline was a photograph of An Yu leaving An-Tech, and under that a photograph of her walking into Northlight a few weeks before. The piece was written with care. It didn’t say she had leaked anything. It didn’t claim any evidence that she had. It simply laid things side by side. An-Tech’s confidential plan to buy Northlight’s biggest rival. The competition authority’s private review, quoted from its own letter. Northlight’s place in that review as the main competitor. Tang Xi’s old role on the An-Tech account. Her relationship with its chairman. And near the end, a line from the authority’s letter listing the members of Northlight’s clean team, with access to restricted material, and the first name on it was hers.

Her full name, spelled correctly. She put the phone on the desk. Rachel hadn’t moved from the doorway.

“Xi, I have to ask. Did you give anything to anyone?”

“No.”

“I know. I had to ask.”

“I know you did. Let’s go down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Daniel was at the head of the table with the general counsel and two of the directors; somebody had put a printout of the article in the middle of it. “Before we talk about a response, I want the facts,” he said. “The authority’s letter names you as one of our clean team.”

“Yes.”

“Did you receive the letter yourself?” asked the general counsel.

“No. You did. You sent me the paragraph about preservation and the list of names, because I was on it.”

“Did you see anything in the data room beyond your access list?”

“No. My access was logged. It’ll show everything I opened.”

“Did you forward anything outside the restricted group? Discuss any of it with anyone outside the process?”

“No.”

“Not even with Mr. Wang?”

She looked straight at him. “No.”

He wrote it down.

“Has anyone approached you about the deal? A journalist? Anyone at Corran Pike?”

“No. No. No.”

One of the directors cleared his throat. “The trouble is, it reads as if she had the access and a reason.”

Tang Xi turned to him. “I had access to one draft commitment and the authority’s questions about it. I had no access to most of what’s in that article. The talks themselves, the price, the shareholders’ names. Northlight never had any of that.”

“But your name’s in the regulator’s letter.”

“Because I’m on the clean team. Being on a list isn’t proof I gave the list to anyone.”

“Let’s be precise,” said Daniel. “Being named in a letter from the authority isn’t evidence of misconduct by anybody. Has the authority accused us of a leak?”

“No,” said the general counsel. “The letter asks for records to be preserved and names the people involved. It doesn’t accuse Ms. Tang or Northlight of anything. We should preserve every email, every log, every access record. Nobody deletes anything, even something they think is irrelevant.”

“I’ll keep everything,” said Tang Xi.

“You won’t handle the media yourself,” said Daniel. “And I want you to understand we’re treating this as a governance question. Not a disciplinary one.”

They talked for another half hour about a holding line and what to say if anyone rang. She answered every question she was asked and didn’t raise her voice once. But when it was over and the others were collecting their papers, she sat on. Her name had been on a page that existed for one narrow legal purpose. Someone had taken that page and given it to a journalist. And before anyone had found out how it got out, she had become the person everyone was looking at.

✦ ✦ ✦

At An-Tech, An Yu read the article once, and then again, and looked at the photograph of her for longer than he meant to. It had been cropped close, her face clear and her expression carefully blank. He disliked it more than he’d expected to. Not because it put her next to his building. Because someone had taken a document that existed for a specific legal purpose and made her name into an accusation.

“Who gave them the letter?” he said.

“We don’t know yet,” said Ding. “The communications team is drafting a holding statement.”

“Who can open it?”

“It’s in the restricted transaction folder. External counsel, our general counsel, the deal team, the clean team, a few senior executives. Seventeen named users.”

“Get me the access records. All of them. Opens, downloads, forwarding, printing, external sharing. Preserve the originals and don’t touch anything. Security does it under Legal, with outside counsel watching, and nobody questions anyone or guesses at anything. They work from the records.” He paused. “If they have to work through the night, they work through the night. A confidential file from a regulator has left this building. We have to tell the authority what happened before it tells us.”

“Yes, Mr. Wang.”

“And no one contacts Ms. Tang on An-Tech’s behalf. She answers to Northlight and to the authority. We do not make it more complicated for her.”

When Ding had gone he picked up his phone to call her, and put it down again. He knew the first question would be about the article, and the second would be whether she had eaten, and neither would change anything that had happened to her that morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter to eleven she was trying to work, and had read the same paragraph of a campaign report three times without taking any of it in, when her phone lit up.

Professor: I’ve seen it. I know you didn’t do it.

Tang Xi: Thank you.

Professor: Are you all right?

She wanted to say yes. It would have been easier.

Tang Xi: No. But I’m managing.

Professor: Do you want me to come?

She looked through her glass wall. Rachel was talking to someone by the printer; Daniel was on a call.

Tang Xi: Not now.

Professor: I won’t contact the press, or Northlight, or do anything that touches your position without talking to you first.

She noticed the careful shape of it, and she knew him well enough to know what he’d left out.

Tang Xi: What are you doing?

The answer took longer.

Professor: Finding out what happened inside An-Tech.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came to her flat that evening without dinner. He hung his coat beside hers, and neither of them kissed the other. The article was on her coffee table.

“Have you been reading it again?”

“I’ve been looking at it.” She sat down opposite him instead of beside him. “Tell me what you’re doing.”

He told her. The access records, every open and download and print of the file since it went into the folder. Security, under the general counsel, with an outside firm advising. No interviews, no confrontations, only logs. Working through the night if they had to.

“Because my name was in it?”

“Because a regulator’s confidential file was taken out of my company and given to a newspaper. We have a legal duty to find out how, and to tell the authority.”

“Would you be doing it tonight if my name hadn’t been in it?”

He didn’t answer straight away. “I don’t know.”

That was more honest than she’d expected, and it didn’t make it easier.

“I understand why you want to find who did it,” she said. “But I don’t want it to become a story about how fast the chairman of An-Tech hunted down the man who hurt his girlfriend. If you make it look like that, it stops being about the leak and becomes about your power again. Not what was done. Not the fact that I didn’t do anything.”

“It won’t be about you.”

“It already is about me.” She leaned forward. “I don’t need you to be quicker than everyone else, An Yu. I need you to be fair. Let Legal hold the evidence. Let the authority hear it properly. Let Northlight make its own response. No private punishment. No making an example of anyone because of me. No statement that says I’m innocent because you want people to stop talking.”

“I won’t.”

“Can you?”

“Yes.”

She let out a breath. “I’m angry. Not only with whoever it was. With the article. With every person who read it and decided I must have done something. With the fact that I was on a list, and somehow that was enough.”

He came round the table and sat beside her, and she didn’t move away. “I’m sorry,” he said.

“You didn’t leak it.”

“Someone in my company may have.”

“Then that’s theirs. You can be responsible for what happens in your company without being guilty of everything everyone in it does.” She found his hand. “But you’re responsible for what happens next.”

“I know.”

They sat without saying anything. Then she said, “Do you know what I hate most? When I saw it this morning, my first thought was whether you’d believe me.”

“Xi.”

“I know you do. I know. I still thought it.”

He turned and took her face in his hands. “I believed you before I’d finished the headline. I don’t need a security report to know you wouldn’t do it. I need the report to find out who did.”

She laughed, a small wet sound. “That’s a very An Yu answer.”

“I thought so.”

He stayed. She slept badly, and he barely slept at all, and at five he was sitting on the edge of her bed in the dark with his phone, reading.

✦ ✦ ✦

At ten past six on Wednesday the head of security stood in the chairman’s office with the general counsel and a report.

“Most of it was routine. Counsel downloaded it for the meeting with the authority. One copy printed for the deal team. One person opened it from an airport.” He put a page on the desk. “At eighteen minutes to seven on Monday evening it was opened from a terminal on the thirty-eighth floor. Six minutes later it was exported. At three minutes past seven that file was sent to a private address outside the company. The address has been used once. It belongs to a private mail service, but the outside firm has matched it to messages from the journalist who wrote the piece. The terminal and the login are both Edmund Lung’s. The building records show him coming in at half past six and leaving at ten past seven.”

An Yu looked at the page.

Edmund Lung had joined An-Tech in its second year, when it fitted on two floors and finance still reconciled spreadsheets by hand. He had built the operations division. He knew every system and every approval and every person who had been there from the start. He had been in the room for two funding rounds, three restructurings and the move into regional markets. He had never been a friend. He had been reliable, which An Yu had valued more.

“Could someone else have used his login?”

“We’re checking. Nothing unusual in the login history, and he was in the building.”

“Was there anyone else?”

“There were messages with the journalist for several days before Monday. We don’t know yet if anyone else was involved.”

“Then find out,” said An Yu. “Suspend his access. All of it, now, and preserve everything.”

“I’d like to arrange a formal interview,” said the general counsel.

“You will. First he hears it from me, with you in the room. And then he goes home and waits for your letter.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Edmund came up at half past eight expecting to talk about the timetable, and looked faintly surprised to find the chairman standing by the window and the general counsel at the end of the table.

“Sit down,” said An Yu, and put the access report in front of him.

Edmund read it, and his face didn’t change for a moment. Then it did. “That’s a serious allegation.”

“I know.”

“Then someone has used my account.”
