“There’s no sign of anyone else logging in. You were in the building.”

“There are people around me all the time.”

“Then explain why a confidential letter from the authority was sent from your terminal to a journalist at three minutes past seven on Monday.”

Edmund looked away. “We’re in the middle of a sensitive deal, Mr. Wang. There are people who’d love it to look like an inside leak. Northlight’s in the middle of it. Ms. Tang’s name is already—”

“Don’t.”

Edmund stopped.

An Yu said it quietly. “Don’t use her name to explain what you did.”

The silence went on. Then Edmund folded his hands. “I was worried about how the deal was being run. I raised it.”

“You raised concerns about the deal. You never said a word about a leak.”

“Because nobody would have listened.” For the first time his voice rose. “You have a relationship with a woman who sits on the other side’s clean team in front of a regulator. In front of a regulator, Mr. Wang. And everybody was expected to pretend that was normal. I wanted it looked at by someone outside this company.”

“By a journalist.”

“By someone you couldn’t overrule.”

“You could have gone to Legal. You could have gone to the board. You could have asked for an independent review.” An Yu didn’t raise his voice. “You sent a document with a named woman’s identity in it to someone with no right to see it, and you knew what the article would say about her.”

“I didn’t write it.”

“You gave them her name.”

Edmund looked down at his hands, and for the first time his composure went. “You weren’t listening,” he said. “To the people who built this company with you. You’ve spent a year running this deal with your own circle. I’ve been here nine years and you barely ask me anything any more.”

“And you decided that gave you the right to give away confidential information when you disagreed with me.” An Yu picked up the report. “Your access to every company system has been suspended. You’re relieved of your duties while there’s a formal investigation. Legal will write to you today with what happens next. Don’t contact anyone involved in the deal, and don’t contact anyone at Northlight.”

“You’re removing me? After nine years?”

“After nine years,” said An Yu, “you should have known better.”

Edmund stood up as if he were going to say something else, and didn’t, and left. The general counsel let out a breath. An Yu stayed by the table. He didn’t feel that he had won anything. He felt the weight of something that had been allowed to grow inside his own company while he was looking somewhere else.

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang her at ten.

“We know who sent it. Edmund Lung. My deputy.”

There was a long silence. “Edmund Lung. Nine years.”

“Yes. The records point to him. The investigation isn’t finished, and I won’t tell you anything we haven’t confirmed. He’s suspended, not dismissed. That’s for the investigation.”

“Did he mean to put me in it?”

“He knew your name was on the list.”

She closed her eyes. “So he knew.”

“Yes.”

“And you found him overnight.”

“The security team found him overnight. Under Legal. The authority will have a written account from us by this afternoon.”

She was quiet for so long that he thought the line had gone. Then she said, slowly, “Thank you for telling me first. Before anyone else.”

“Xi.”

“I’m not angry about that. I’m thinking.” He could hear her breathing. “Please don’t send your report to Northlight to clear me.”

“It’ll go to the authority. It won’t name you as anything but someone on a list.”

“Good. Because I don’t want your security team to be the reason anyone believes me. If people stop talking because the chairman of An-Tech proved I didn’t do it, that’s the same story with a happier ending.” He didn’t say anything, and she went on. “I’m going to clear my own name. With my own records. Every email I’ve sent since March, every time I opened that data room, every meeting, in order. Northlight’s logs, not yours.”

He shut his eyes, and he understood that she was right, and that it was going to be hard to watch.

“Will you let me help?”

“No,” she said. “You can bring me tea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The risk committee of An-Tech’s board met at nine on Thursday. The general counsel set out what they knew: Mr. Lung had taken and sent the authority’s letter to an outside address linked to the journalist; nothing in the copy had been altered; nothing else had gone with it as far as they could tell; the review of every message was continuing.

“What do you recommend?” one of the directors asked the chairman.

“That the independent investigation continues. That Mr. Lung stays away from our systems while it does. That we give the authority every fact we can establish and no guesses about why. And that we answer the press only on facts. We don’t threaten the publication or try to influence what it writes.”

“Even though it’s named someone at another company?”

“That’s the reason to be careful. Ms. Tang isn’t responsible for this. There’s no evidence she disclosed anything. I won’t let an article’s insinuations become the basis of anything we decide.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Northlight’s statement came out at six that evening. It was short: the agency had cooperated with the authority, kept its restricted materials restricted, and found no evidence of any disclosure by its people. It named nobody. Tang Xi read it twice and sent Daniel one line approving it. An Yu came later with a paper bag.

“Dinner?”

“Dumplings.”

She looked in. “Your own? My mother’s method?”

“I tried.”

“How badly?”

“One of them opened.”

“Only one?”

“Two.”

She laughed for the first time in two days. “That’s progress.”

They ate at her little table. She told him Daniel and the general counsel had agreed the agency’s line; he told her the authority had acknowledged An-Tech’s notification. Neither of them said Edmund’s name, not because they’d forgotten it but because there was nothing new to say.

Afterwards she sat beside him with her head on his shoulder. “Will he be dismissed?”

“Probably. It depends on what the investigation finds, and on the board.”

“Do you want him to stay?”

“No. The trust the job needs is gone. But that’s for the process to decide, not me while I’m angry.”

“You’re angry.”

“Very. I don’t want to mistake it for evidence.”

She sat up and kissed him. “That’s the best thing you’ve said all week.”

Later she cleared the table and took a new notebook out of her bag and put it on the coffee table, and opened it to the first page, and wrote the date at the top and a single line under it: 9 March, 6.50 p.m., notice from Daniel. Then she sat looking at it, pen in hand, already thinking about the second line.

He brought her a cup of tea and put it by her elbow, and went back to the sofa, and didn’t look at what she was writing.

chapters.title: She Clears Her Own Name
chapters.desc: She refuses his evidence and finds her own, down to a grey half-line at the bottom of a photograph. Then she kisses him in front of his board.
chapters.content:
The first thing Tang Xi did was refuse the evidence.

It arrived on the Friday through the proper channel: An-Tech’s general counsel to Northlight’s, a preliminary note of findings from the outside forensic firm. Mrs. Kho, Northlight’s general counsel, small and grey-haired and impossible to hurry, brought it to Tang Xi’s office in a sealed folder and put it on the desk.

“It’s thorough,” she said. “Access logs, the export, the transfer, the address. It says the letter left An-Tech through Mr. Lung’s account. If you want it, it’s yours to rely on.”

Tang Xi looked at the folder and didn’t open it. “It says what happened inside An-Tech. It doesn’t say anything about us. If I stand up anywhere and say I didn’t do this because An-Tech’s investigators say so, I’m the chairman’s girlfriend being cleared by the chairman’s company.” She pushed it back across the desk an inch. “I’ll quote it where it’s theirs to say. Everything about me comes from our own records.”

Mrs. Kho considered her over her glasses for a long moment, and then, for the first time since Tang Xi had known her, she smiled. “Then you’ll want IT on Monday.”

That evening An Yu asked, carefully, whether she’d seen the note. She said yes, and that she hadn’t read it, and why. There was a silence on the line.

“All right,” he said.

She had expected him to argue. He didn’t, and she was beginning to understand that this had become a different kind of difficulty for him. He had spent so many years being the person who made things happen that doing nothing, when she asked him to, took an effort she couldn’t always see.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning she had the small meeting room next to Legal. Two laptops, a printout of the authority’s letter, a folder of correspondence, and a sheet of A3 paper taped to the glass and covered in dates in her own handwriting. Mrs. Kho sat at one end with a young man from IT called Joel who had brought his own chair. Daniel stood by the window with his arms folded. Rachel, who was still the An-Tech account director and still on the wrong side of the wall, had left a coffee outside the door with a note on the lid that said I am not here.

“Scope first,” said Mrs. Kho. “We’re establishing Northlight’s records. Not investigating An-Tech. Nothing obtained outside our own systems.”

“Understood.”

“Then go.”

Tang Xi turned her laptop round. “Two weeks. From the thirtieth of March, when the authority sent its second set of questions and the letter with the clean-team names, to the evening of the thirteenth of April, when the letter left An-Tech. A hundred and eighty-six messages that touch the deal. I’ve sorted them four ways: access, circulation, communication, approval.” She brought up the spreadsheet. “Joel has pulled the original server records. These are read-only exports, with the message IDs and the attachment hashes, so nobody can say I’ve tidied anything.”

Joel nodded. “Nothing she’s using has been edited. I checked.”

“The letter reached our external counsel on the thirtieth. You got it on the thirty-first,” she said to Mrs. Kho, “and sent me two things: the paragraph asking us to preserve our records, and the list of names. I acknowledged at nine-forty that morning. I never had the full letter. It’s in your folder and nobody else’s.”

“Correct,” said Mrs. Kho.

“My data room access.” Another tab. “Eleven sessions between the nineteenth of March and the third of April, every one of them inside my access list. The platform logs every page I looked at. I didn’t download anything, because the platform doesn’t let the clean team download, and I didn’t print anything, because it doesn’t let us print. After the third of April I never logged in again.”

Daniel had come closer to the table without seeming to notice.

“Now the thirteenth.” She found the row she’d highlighted in yellow. “At sixteen minutes past five An-Tech’s legal team emailed our counsel, copied to me, asking us to confirm that the clean-team list was still accurate. I replied at twenty-nine minutes past. Two lines. Yes, it’s accurate; no changes.” She enlarged the header. “Message ID intact. Attachment field empty. Joel’s server record says no file left with it. And that was the last thing I sent that day about the deal. The letter left An-Tech’s building an hour and a half later.”

“So nothing went from your account,” said Daniel.

“Nothing went from my account, and nothing went from ours. Our copy of the list is in Mrs. Kho’s restricted folder. Four people have opened it, all of them authorised, and none of them forwarded it.” She looked at Joel.

“There are no external forwarding events on it at all,” he said.

Mrs. Kho wrote something down. “That’s useful. It isn’t everything.”

“No,” said Tang Xi. “It proves what I didn’t do. It doesn’t prove where the letter came from. That’s the next thing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found it on Tuesday in the article itself.

She had been looking at the photograph of the letter for two weeks without seeing it. The journalist had printed a picture of the page with the clean-team list, cropped tight, her own name in the first line. But the authority’s portal didn’t send identical documents to everyone. It stamped every copy along the bottom margin with a faint grey line of characters that identified the recipient: a forensic watermark, of the sort regulators had been using for years precisely so that when something leaked they could tell whose copy it was. Northlight’s copy, in Mrs. Kho’s folder, ended in NL-0331. In the newspaper’s photograph the bottom of the page had been cropped, but not quite far enough. Under magnification, at the very edge of the picture, the top half of a line of grey characters was still there.

AT-0330. She sat back in her chair and laughed out loud in the empty room, and then she took the magnified image and the explanation of the portal’s watermarking from the authority’s own published guidance down the corridor to Mrs. Kho.

Mrs. Kho looked at it. “That’s not our copy.”

“No. It’s the copy the authority sent to An-Tech on the thirtieth.”

“Can we prove that from our side?”

“We can prove it isn’t ours. Only An-Tech can confirm it’s theirs.” Tang Xi put the page down. “So we ask them. Through you. Not through me, and not through him.”

The request went from Mrs. Kho to An-Tech’s general counsel at four that afternoon. Tang Xi didn’t ring An Yu, or send him a message, or tell him it was coming. The reply came the following afternoon, signed by An-Tech’s general counsel and nobody else: the recipient code in the published image matched the copy issued to An-Tech’s restricted transaction folder.

She added one line to the timeline on the glass, and stood looking at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she sat at her little table with the laptop and the notebook and the A3 chronology, and he let himself in a little after nine and put a cup of jasmine tea beside her elbow without a word.

He didn’t ask whether she had finished. He didn’t ask what Mrs. Kho had said. He didn’t offer to have An-Tech’s lawyers check her timeline against theirs. He sat down on the sofa behind her with his own laptop and started to read.

After ten minutes she turned round. “You’re not going to ask?”

“No.”

“Not even one question?”

“You’ll tell me when you want to.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re being very disciplined.”

“It’s taking all of it.”

She tasted the tea. Hot, not scalding. No sugar. Exactly right. “Do you know what I’m doing?”

“A chronology for Northlight’s general counsel.”

“That’s the official answer. The unofficial one is that I’m making sure nobody can ever look at my name in that letter and wonder.” She turned her chair to face him properly. “I don’t want to be cleared because the chairman says he trusts me. I don’t want to be cleared because your company found your deputy. I want the record to show I did my job properly, and I want it to be my record.”

“Then that’s what you should do.”

“You’re not going to tell me your security team already has all of this?”

“No.”

“You’re not going to tell me what you think I’ve missed?”

He looked at her over the laptop. “You haven’t asked me to look.”

She stared at him, and then smiled, just a little, and turned back to the screen. For the next hour they sat in the same room without either of them touching the other’s work. It was an ordinary thing. She knew exactly how much it cost him, and when she reached back without looking, he put his hand in hers and left it there while she typed with the other.

✦ ✦ ✦

The last piece came on Thursday morning from an email she had nearly skipped.

It was dated the ninth of April, from An-Tech’s outside counsel to Northlight’s, an ordinary subject line: Clean team: access schedule. The schedule was attached: who on each side could open what. Her name was under communications review, with a list of everything she couldn’t see. No commercial diligence. No price. No client-level data. No valuation. The email had been copied, under the protocol, to An-Tech’s deal team so that they knew who on the other side could see what.

The fourth name on the deal team’s distribution was Edmund Lung.

She opened the header. Delivered. No bounce, no delay, no later correction. Five days before the leak, Edmund had been told in writing exactly how little she could see. And he had still sent a newspaper the one page that made it look as if she could see everything.

She didn’t feel triumphant. She felt calm. This was what she had wanted: not a confession, not an accusation, a dated record.

9 April · Clean-team access schedule sent to An-Tech’s deal team, E. Lung among the recipients. T. Xi’s access limited in writing to communications review.

✦ ✦ ✦

An-Tech’s board had its own duty to the authority, and its risk committee asked, through counsel, whether Northlight would set out its records directly. Daniel and Mrs. Kho agreed on one condition: Tang Xi presented them herself.

So at six on Thursday she walked into An-Tech’s boardroom on the forty-second floor with Mrs. Kho at her side and nothing in her hands but her laptop. Eight directors, the general counsel, a secretary taking the minutes. The chairman of the committee, a lean old man called Mr. Ashby, sat at the centre. An Yu was at the far end of the table, beside his general counsel, and when she came in he looked up.

“Ms. Tang.”

“Mr. Wang.”

That was all. He went back to his papers.

“We have An-Tech’s preliminary findings and Northlight’s chronology,” said Mr. Ashby. “Ms. Tang, we’d like to understand the sequence from your side. Please go ahead.”

She stood. She hadn’t brought the article. She’d brought the timeline.

“I’ll start with what I could see, because everything else depends on it.” The access schedule came up on the screen. “Northlight’s clean team was given limited access to one draft commitment and the authority’s questions about it. I could see none of the commercial diligence. No price, no client data, no valuation.”

A director at the end interrupted. “But you were named in the authority’s letter.”

“Yes. As a member of the clean team. Being named in a list of people with a narrow job isn’t evidence that anyone did anything wrong. I’d like to show you what I did do.”

She took them through it without hurrying. The thirty-first of March. The eleven sessions. The third of April. The email at twenty-nine minutes past five, its empty attachment field. Northlight’s copy of the list, four authorised readers, no forwarding. She didn’t make it more dramatic than the records were.

Then the photograph from the article, magnified, and the grey half-line at the bottom of it.

“The authority’s portal stamps every copy with its recipient. Northlight’s copy ends NL-0331. The copy in the newspaper ends AT-0330. An-Tech’s general counsel has confirmed in writing that this is the copy issued to An-Tech.” She let them read it. “I’m not relying on An-Tech’s investigation for that. I’m relying on the page the journalist printed.”

The director who had interrupted leaned forward. “And Mr. Lung?”

“Your preliminary findings say a transfer was made from his account at three minutes past seven on the thirteenth. That finding is yours; I’m not in a position to test it. What I can show you is this.” The ninth of April came up on the screen. “Five days before the transfer, the deal team, Mr. Lung included, was sent a schedule setting out in writing exactly how little I could see.”

“Are you saying he knew?”

“I’m saying he received a document that set out my limits. I can’t speak to why he did what he did. I can only show you what the records say.”

The room was quiet. Mr. Ashby looked at his notes. “Anything further, Ms. Tang?”

“One thing.” She went back to the first slide. “I understand why my name in that letter raised questions. But being named in a regulatory process is not the same as being responsible for a disclosure. I’ve given you every original record and the metadata behind it. If you need more from Northlight’s side, we’ll provide it through counsel.” She closed the laptop. “Thank you.”

She sat down. An Yu didn’t look at her. Under the table, out of everyone’s sight but hers, his hand had closed hard on the edge of his notebook.

✦ ✦ ✦

The committee went on talking while she and Mrs. Kho waited. An-Tech’s general counsel summarised: the evidence pointed to a transfer by Mr. Lung; the published copy was An-Tech’s; there was no evidence that Ms. Tang or anyone at Northlight had sent anything.

Then the director at the end of the table looked at her. “Ms. Tang, one last question. Given your relationship with our chairman, why should this board accept your account as independent?”

“You shouldn’t accept it because of my relationship with Mr. Wang,” said Tang Xi. “You should accept it as far as the records support it, and no further. You have the original messages, the server records, the watermark and the schedule. If any part of what I’ve said disagrees with them, challenge it. But if the records support me, my relationship with Mr. Wang doesn’t make them less reliable.”

The director sat back. Mr. Ashby turned to the general counsel. “Any objection to that?”

“None.”

“Then the minutes will record that there is no evidence implicating Ms. Tang or Northlight in the disclosure, subject to the continuing investigation into Mr. Lung.”

For the first time in two weeks, Tang Xi felt her shoulders come down. Not because the article had gone; it hadn’t. Not because everyone who had read it would change their mind; they wouldn’t. Because she had stood in front of the people whose opinion mattered to the investigation and shown them the facts herself. She hadn’t needed An Yu to speak for her or to tell them what kind of person she was. She had brought the records, and they had listened.

✦ ✦ ✦

The meeting broke up. The directors stood and gathered their papers, the secretary capped her pen, and Mrs. Kho was talking to An-Tech’s general counsel by the door. Tang Xi was unplugging her laptop from the screen when An Yu stood up at the far end and came down the length of the table.

“Ms. Tang. Thank you for attending.”

“You’re welcome.”

“Your presentation was thorough.”

She looked at him. “Only thorough?”

“Very thorough.”

“Better.”

His mouth almost moved. She put the laptop down on the table. He seemed to think she was going to say something about the meeting, and he was still thinking it when she took hold of his tie, close to the knot, and pulled him down to her and kissed him. In front of his board.

It wasn’t long, and it wasn’t polite. It was the kiss of somebody who had spent two weeks being careful and had just finished. For half a second his hand hovered at her waist as if he couldn’t believe what was happening, and then it settled there, warm and certain, and he kissed her back. Somewhere behind her a chair stopped scraping. Somebody’s pen hit the table.

When she let go of his tie she was smiling. His face had changed completely; the chairman who had sat through the whole meeting without moving seemed briefly unable to find anything to say. She smoothed his tie flat with two fingers.

“Thank you for the tea,” she said.

He blinked. “The tea.”

“Last night. You brought it and didn’t ask me a single question.”

Then the smile reached his eyes. “You’re welcome.”

“Good night, Mr. Wang.”

“Good night, Ms. Tang.”

She picked up her laptop and walked out with Mrs. Kho, who hadn’t said a word and whose face had gone extremely still. Behind them, the door closed on total silence.

Mr. Ashby was the first to speak. “Chairman,” he said, “Northlight’s representative is rather direct.”

An Yu was already back in his seat, squaring his papers. “She is,” he said, and didn’t try to hide what his face was doing.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the lift Mrs. Kho pressed the button for the lobby and looked at the doors.

“I’ll need to put a note on file,” she said.

“I know.”

“The note will say that after the formal business closed, our representative thanked the chairman of the client company in an unconventional manner.” She paused. “I’ll keep it short.”

Rachel rang before Tang Xi had reached the street. “Is it true? Joel says the whole forty-second floor’s talking about it and it’s been twenty minutes. You kissed him in front of his board?”

“After the meeting.”

“Oh, that makes it fine.” A shriek of laughter. “Professionally? Probably a disaster. Personally? About time. I’m coming over with wine. I’m not on the account any more by the time I’m at your door, I’ve decided.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at nine, after Rachel had gone, and she opened the door before he’d finished knocking.

“You’re smiling,” he said.

“So are you.”

“I was surprised.”

“I noticed. The whole board noticed.”

He came in and took off his shoes and stood looking at her. “Was it deliberate?”

“Of course it was.”

“Because you were relieved?”

“Partly.”

“Because you wanted them to know?”

“I don’t need your board to know anything about us.” She took his hand. “I spent two weeks proving I hadn’t done something wrong. When I’d finished, I wanted to do something just because I wanted to. Not to defend myself. Not to get anyone to believe me. I wanted to kiss you, so I did.”

His fingers tightened round hers. “I wanted to stand up in that meeting and tell every one of them who you were.”

“Why didn’t you?”

“Because it was your presentation.”

She put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his shirt. “You brought me tea and didn’t help. That was very hard for you, wasn’t it?”

He thought about lying. “Yes. I wanted to read every email. I wanted to check every timestamp. I wanted to find the missing piece before you did, so nobody could ever question you.”

“But you didn’t.”

“You didn’t need me to find your name in the evidence. You needed me to leave you room to clear it yourself.” He kissed her hair. “And you found the watermark. I didn’t know about the watermark.”

She lifted her head and grinned at him. “Nobody knew about the watermark.”

“Our general counsel is still embarrassed.”

“Good,” she said, and kissed him, and this time he was the one who walked her backwards, slowly, all the way to the sofa, and the A3 chronology slid off the table and lay on the floor until morning, with her name on it beside a record.

chapters.title: The Deputy
chapters.desc: He ends nine years in a room with no witnesses, and refuses to soften a single clause. That night she undresses him like something breakable.
chapters.content:
Edmund Lung came up to the forty-second floor at five to nine on Monday because a one-line email had told him to: a time and a room number, nothing else. He had assumed it was the end of the investigation. He wasn’t wrong.

There was nobody else in the room. No general counsel this time, no one from HR, no assistant by the door, no board member, no minute-taker. Two chairs, a glass table and a thin folder squared precisely in front of the empty one. An Yu was standing at the window.

“Sit down, Edmund.”

Edmund shut the door and looked at him, perhaps waiting for some sign of what this would be like: anger, disappointment, a lecture about loyalty. An Yu gave him none of it, and Edmund sat.

“The independent investigation has reported.” An Yu sat down opposite and opened the folder. “It confirms that you opened the authority’s letter in the restricted folder, exported it, and sent it to a journalist. It confirms that on the ninth of April you’d been sent the clean-team schedule, which set out in writing that Ms. Tang’s access was limited to a communications review.”

Edmund looked at the pages. “Yes.”

It was the first time he had said it plainly.

“I’ve already told you why.”

“You told me you disagreed with the deal. That isn’t a defence.”

“I didn’t make a cent from it.”

“That isn’t relevant to whether you broke your obligations.” An Yu turned a page. “You had the board. You had Legal. You could have asked for an independent review. You could have resigned. You chose to give a regulator’s confidential letter to the press, and you chose to make an accusation by implication against someone who had nothing to do with the decisions you disagreed with.”

“You think this is about Tang Xi.”

“No. It’s about what you were trusted with.” He closed the folder. “Your employment ends today, for gross misconduct, on the findings of the investigation and the disciplinary review. The letter’s in there.”

Edmund didn’t touch it. “Nine years.”

“Yes.”

“Do you have any idea how much of this company I built?”

“I know exactly what you built,” said An Yu. “That’s why I gave you the job.”

It landed harder than any accusation would have. Edmund looked away.

“Your unvested options lapse. The plan’s bad-leaver provisions apply, and the remuneration committee confirmed it on Friday. Your vested options can be exercised under the plan rules until the window closes in ninety days; we won’t change the rules for you in either direction.” He went on in the same level voice. “Your confidentiality obligations continue. And the restrictive covenants in your contract will be enforced as written.”

Edmund went still. “The non-compete.”

“Yes.”

“Two years.”

“It’s a two-year restraint. You were paid separately for it when you were promoted, and you signed the revised terms.”

“Two years out of the industry.” For the first time Edmund leaned forward. “You know what I’ve done my whole career. You know everyone I know. I’m fifty-one. I can’t start again somewhere else.”

“You can work outside the restricted sectors and territories. You can take advice and challenge the covenant if you think it’s unreasonable. That’s your right.” An Yu didn’t blink. “We won’t waive it.”

“My lawyer sent a proposal on Friday. I resign. We agree a reference. You let the restraint go, and I sign anything you like about confidentiality.”

“I’ve seen it. The answer is no.”

“To all of it?”

“There’s no agreed reference. HR will confirm your dates and your title in writing if they’re asked in writing. They won’t take calls, and nobody here will say anything about your work or your character.” An Yu stood. “You’ll leave with your personal belongings this morning. Security will walk you out after nine-thirty, when the lifts are quiet.”

“You’re very cold.”

An Yu looked at the man who had once been one of the few people inside the company he trusted without thinking about it. “Would you rather I pretended it hadn’t happened?”

“I’d rather you remembered who I was before.”

“I do. That’s why this is disappointing.”

He opened the door. The meeting was over. Edmund stayed in his chair for several seconds before he picked up the letter, and at the threshold he stopped.

“One day someone will do this to you.”

“Then I hope they have the evidence.”

The door closed. An Yu went back to the table and straightened the chair Edmund had left an inch out of line. He didn’t feel angry. He didn’t feel satisfied. He didn’t, as far as he could tell, feel anything at all. He sent the general counsel one line, Meeting concluded, proceed, and went back to work.

✦ ✦ ✦

It happened. HR issued the termination notice. IT removed the last of his access by ten. Legal sent a letter by courier and by email reminding him of his confidentiality obligations and the restraint, and of the dates on which they ran out. There was no announcement and no message thanking him for his service. When senior staff asked, they were told that Mr. Lung had left the company after an investigation into a serious breach of confidentiality, and that was all.

The first reference request came three days later, from a regional consultancy considering him for a senior operations role. HR sent back two lines: dates of employment; job title. The second, from a private investment firm, got the same two lines. A third came from an old industry friend of Edmund’s who rang the general counsel directly, and the general counsel said he couldn’t discuss it, and hung up. By Friday his name had gone from the internal directory, his office was being cleared for someone else, and his card no longer opened the door to the car park.

An Yu approved every step. He didn’t ask for anything harsher. He didn’t ask Legal to stretch the restraint or contact anyone who might hire him. He simply refused to soften a single consequence, and it was the refusing, done so calmly, that would have frightened anyone who saw it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tang Xi heard about it from Daniel, not from An Yu, at four that afternoon. He put his head round her door.

“An-Tech’s counsel has written to ours. Edmund Lung was dismissed this morning. Gross misconduct. Unvested options gone, the non-compete enforced, no reference.”

She closed the document she was reading. “Today?”

“This morning. In a room on his own with the chairman, I’m told.”

“Two years?”

“That’s the contract. Whether all of it would stand up if he challenged it is a separate question. But they’ve told him they mean to enforce it.”

He watched her. “Are you worried?”

“I don’t know.” She looked at the desk. “About how far it goes. And how fast.”

“He did something serious, Xi. They’re entitled to enforce what he signed, as long as they do it lawfully.”

“I know.” When he’d gone she sat for a while, and then picked up her phone.

Tang Xi: Can we talk tonight? About Edmund.

The answer came a minute later.

Professor: Yes. I’ll be home by eight.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in the kitchen when she let herself in, tie off, sleeves rolled, a pan of water just coming to the boil.

“You’re early,” he said. “Have you eaten? I made noodles.”

She looked into the pan. “These are instant noodles.”

“I added vegetables.”

“How impressive.”

They ate at the counter. For a while they talked about ordinary things: a campaign at Northlight, Rachel’s war with the creative director, a book Tang Xi had abandoned because its first chapter annoyed her. He listened and asked questions and didn’t mention the morning, and eventually she put her chopsticks down.

“Edmund’s gone.”

“Yes.”

“His options.”

“The unvested ones lapsed under the plan.”

“The non-compete.”

“Legal has told him we’ll enforce it.”

“His lawyer offered a deal. Resign, agreed reference, let the restraint go.”

“I said no.”

“Did you have to?”

He looked at her. “The agreement was signed. The breach was serious. There was no reason to waive anything.”

“That’s not what I asked.”

He put his chopsticks down. “No. I didn’t have to. I could have agreed a shorter restraint, or an agreed reference, or let him resign. I didn’t.”

“Why?”

“Because I didn’t think he deserved it.”

It was simple. Too simple. She leaned back.

“Did you think about what two years means for him? A man of fifty-one, at his level, who can’t work in the only industry he knows?”

“Yes.”

“And you still did it.”

“Yes.”

She looked at his face. There was no anger there, no pleasure, no satisfaction. He was describing a decision as if it were a set of accounts.

“What did you feel when you told him?”

He looked at his hands. “Nothing. I was disappointed. I wasn’t angry.”

“Then what were you?”

He thought about it. “Certain. He knew what he’d signed and what the document was. He made a choice, and the consequences are being applied.”

“You’re very good at making consequences sound clean.” She wasn’t smiling. “I know he did something wrong. I know what he did to me. I’m not asking you to forgive him or give him his job back. But when I listen to you talk about his life like a list of clauses, I don’t recognise the person I come home to.” She said the next part. “I know you don’t owe him kindness. I wanted to know if you still had any.”

For several seconds he didn’t answer. Then he said, “I don’t know,” and it was the first thing he’d said all evening that sounded uncertain.

She got up and took her bowl to the sink and rinsed it.

“Are you angry with me?”

She turned the tap off. “No. I’m trying to understand how you can be that certain about something that’ll shape somebody’s life for two years, and not feel anything until I ask you.”

He looked down, and that was when the question finally reached him. Not as a criticism of the decision. As a description of himself. He remembered Edmund leaning forward, saying I’m fifty-one, I can’t start again. He remembered answering. He had understood the restraint, the money, the professional consequences. He hadn’t thought about the man going home afterwards, to a wife, to a kitchen, to a phone that would ring less and less. He had thought about whether the decision was lawful, and justified, and consistent, and he had stopped there.

“I didn’t think about it like that,” he said.

“I know.”

“I should have.”

She came back to him. He was standing by the counter with his hands flat on its edge, and she put hers over them.

“You can be angry with him. You can decide he never works here again. You can enforce what he signed. I’m not asking you to pretend it was harmless. But I don’t want you to become someone who thinks being legally right means he doesn’t have to feel anything.”

For a moment his face looked almost lost. “I don’t know how to answer that.”

“You don’t have to.”

She put her arms round him. At first he stood quite still. Then his hands came up her back, slowly, and closed on her shirt, and she felt how tight his shoulders were. He bent his head until his forehead rested against hers.

“I don’t regret dismissing him,” he said.

“I know.”

“I don’t regret enforcing it.”

“I know.”

“But I should have felt the weight of it.”

“Yes.”

He shut his eyes, and something in him moved. Not regret for the decision. Something harder: seeing the person he’d been while he made it.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the bedroom she undressed him slowly. Not to seduce him. Because he seemed suddenly like a man who had been holding himself upright for far too long, and she wanted to take it off him one piece at a time.

She undid his shirt button by button, and he watched her hands.

“You’re quiet,” he said.

“So are you.”

“I’m always quiet.”

“Not with me.” She slid the shirt off his shoulders and laid it over the chair, not dropped, laid, and touched the crease between his eyebrows with her thumb. “Don’t think so hard.”

“I can’t help it.”

“I know.”

She kissed the corner of his mouth. He didn’t kiss her back straight away. Instead he took hold of her waist and rested his forehead on her shoulder and stayed like that, breathing, and she ran her fingers through his hair, over and over, the way you would for someone with a fever.

“Are you tired?”

“Yes.”

“Then let me look after you.”

She took his watch off and put it on the bedside table. His glasses, folded. She unbuckled his belt and he let her, and she knelt and took off his socks, one and then the other, which nobody had done for him since he was a child, and he made a sound she had never heard from him, half a laugh, half something else. She stood up and pushed him gently back onto the bed and undressed herself while he watched, not hurrying, letting him look.

When she climbed onto the bed beside him he reached for her. She lay along his side and kissed him: his mouth, his jaw, the hollow of his throat, the place on his chest over his heart where she could feel it going much too fast. She ran her hand down over his stomach and found him, and he was hard, and he shut his eyes and turned his face into her hair.

“Look at me,” she said.

He did. She kept her eyes on his and stroked him, unhurried, until his breathing changed and his hand closed on her hip. Then she moved over him and sank down onto him slowly, an inch at a time, and they both stopped breathing. She didn’t move. She just held him inside her and held his face between her hands.

“I’m here,” she said.

“I know.”

She rocked against him, gently, a slow, deep rhythm with no hurry in it at all, and every time he tried to take over she put her hand flat on his chest and he let her keep it. He touched her as if he were reminding himself she was there: her thighs, her waist, her breasts, the small of her back, all of it slowly. When she whispered his name, he answered. When she bent down and kissed him, he held the back of her head and didn’t let go. She came first, shuddering, her forehead against his, and he followed her a little after, with a long, broken breath that sounded almost like relief, his arms locked round her.

She stayed where she was, lying on him, until her own heart had slowed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Near midnight she woke because he was shaking. Not dramatically. Not enough that anyone across a room would have seen it. But she felt it under her palm on his chest: a fine tremor in him, his fingers trembling where they rested on her waist, his breath uneven. His eyes were open, fixed on somewhere above her shoulder.

She came up on one elbow. “An Yu?”

He blinked. “Yes.”

“Look at me.” He turned his head. She pushed the hair off his forehead. “What’s wrong?”

“Nothing.”

She gave him a look, and he shut his eyes. “I think I’m tired.”

“That’s allowed.”

He let out a breath that was nearly a laugh, and she wrapped herself round him, arms and legs, and held on until the shaking slowed.

“I used to think,” he said into the dark, “that if I made a decision correctly, everything after it was just the result. Contracts. Procedures. Consequences. That that was enough.”

“And now?”

“Now I’m wondering what happens when the correct decision still makes me someone I don’t want to be.”

“That depends on what you do once you’ve noticed.” She kissed his chest. “You don’t have to be gentle with everyone. You don’t have to forgive someone who betrayed you. But you have to know when you’re being cruel.”

“And if I am?”

“Then I expect you to notice. And to care.”

His arm tightened round her. For a long time he said nothing, and then, so quietly she nearly missed it: “I don’t want to lose that.”

“Then don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke first. He was asleep on his back, one arm stretched across the place where she’d been, and his face looked younger without the concentration round his eyes. She touched his cheek and he woke at once.

“Did you sleep?”

“Better than I expected.”

He got up to shower, and his phone lit on the bedside table.

Legal (Never Sleeps): Mr. Lung’s lawyers acknowledge the termination and the covenant letter. They indicate they may challenge the restraint. We’ll answer through the proper process.

When he came out with his hair wet she was tying hers back. “Edmund?”

“His lawyers may challenge the non-compete.”

“Then let them.”

“Yes.”

She straightened his collar for him. “Don’t turn it into another fight you have to win.”

“I won’t.”

“Breakfast? Something better than instant noodles?”

“I’ll arrange something.”

She narrowed her eyes. “Arrange?”

The corner of his mouth moved. “I’ll cook.”

“That sounds dangerous,” she said, and went to the kitchen laughing, and he stood by the bed for a while longer with the message in his hand. The company would defend its position. Edmund might challenge it, and the law would decide. That part was settled. But she had made him see something no contract had required of him. He could be right and still be cruel. If he wanted to stay someone she could love without being afraid of him, he was going to have to learn the difference.

chapters.title: The Agency Says Choose
chapters.desc: Head office flies in to sit in a glass room and make her choose. She doesn’t take the month they offer.
chapters.epigraph: “Your position at Northlight, or your relationship with Mr. Wang.”
chapters.content:
The invitation arrived at twelve minutes past eight on Thursday morning.

Confidential: employment and governance review
Daniel; Mrs. Kho; Laurence Pryor; Tang Xi
Executive meeting room, 10.00

No agenda. Tang Xi read it twice, accepted it, and went back to the campaign report she’d been reading. She knew what it was about. She’d known for weeks that something was coming. The article hadn’t gone away. The authority’s review of the Corran Pike deal was still open. Edmund Lung’s dismissal was being talked about at every industry breakfast. And a fortnight ago a newsletter that everyone in the business pretended not to read had run four lines about a senior agency director thanking a technology chairman in his own boardroom, in front of his board, in a manner the newsletter described as warm.

That one was hers. She had known it might cost something when she did it. She hadn’t known what.

Laurence Pryor’s name was the one that mattered. He ran the holding group that owned Northlight and four other agencies, and he flew in from head office about twice a year, and when he did, someone usually left.

A little after eight Rachel appeared at her door and shut it behind her.

“Did you get one?”

“Yes.”

“Pryor’s here. He’s been in with Daniel and Mrs. Kho since seven.” Rachel hesitated, which she almost never did. “Xi. Whatever happens in there, don’t let them make you feel you haven’t done your job.”

“I won’t.”

Rachel didn’t look convinced.

✦ ✦ ✦

The executive meeting room had glass on three sides. From her chair Tang Xi could see the whole floor: people crossing between desks, someone carrying a tray of coffees, two of the creative team arguing over a layout. The ordinary rhythm of the agency carried on outside. Inside, there was a folder on the table in front of Laurence Pryor, a tall, pleasant, silver-haired man who smiled at her as she sat down as if they had met many times, which they hadn’t. Daniel sat on his left and didn’t smile at all. Mrs. Kho sat on his right with her hands folded.

“Thank you for coming,” said Pryor. “I want to say first that this isn’t a disciplinary meeting.”

“Then what is it?”

“A conversation about whether your position here is still tenable.”

He said it gently, which almost made it worse.

Mrs. Kho opened the folder. “We’ve reviewed your disclosure in October, your handover of the An-Tech account, the communications review you did on the Corran Pike matter, and the findings about the leak. We’ve also reviewed the public coverage since April, including the newsletter.”

“I know about the newsletter.”

“We know you’ve kept to every restriction you were given,” said Mrs. Kho. “We’ve found no misconduct. I said so in writing, and I’d say it again in front of anyone.”

“Thank you.”

“The difficulty,” said Pryor, “isn’t whether you’ve broken a rule. It’s perception. Northlight has clients who compete directly with An-Tech. It holds their confidential information. And as long as the Corran Pike review is open, the authority keeps coming back to us as the main competitor, and every time it does, your name comes back with it. We have to ask whether we can keep you in a senior leadership role while your relationship with An-Tech’s chairman continues.”

“Have clients raised it?”

“Two have asked for reassurance about our governance,” said Daniel. His voice was flat. “One has asked that you not work on its account.”

“Has anyone complained formally? Taken any work away?”

“No.”

“Then what’s changed?”

“Head office has,” said Daniel, and Pryor gave him a look.

“We’ve considered alternatives,” said Pryor. “Another reassignment. Fewer client-facing responsibilities. A change in reporting line. None of them deals with the wider concern.”

The room was quiet. Then he said it.

“We need you to choose.”

“Choose what?”

“Your position at Northlight, or your relationship with Mr. Wang.”

For a moment she thought she had misheard. She looked at Mrs. Kho, who looked steadily back and didn’t look away, which Tang Xi would remember later as a kind of honesty.

“You’re asking me to end my relationship.”

“We’re asking you to consider whether the relationship is compatible with your continued employment,” said Pryor.

“Those are not the same sentence.”

“The practical outcome is the same.”

“You’re asking me to choose between my job and the person I’m with.”

He didn’t deny it. “We can’t carry on indefinitely as we are.”

“As we are? I have no access to anything of An-Tech’s. I haven’t been on its account since January. My work on the deal was limited, approved and recorded, and the only record anybody’s ever examined cleared me.”

“I know,” said Daniel.

“Then what’s the conflict?”

“That we can’t keep asking every client to trust a distinction they can’t see,” said Pryor, “when your name keeps appearing next to that company and that man. Including in his boardroom.”

She looked down at the folder. There were printed pages inside. The first article. The second. The newsletter. A summary of her declaration. Her name was in all of them.

“Have you considered that the association exists because the press keeps printing it? Not because I’ve done anything wrong?”

“Yes.”

“That nothing in the articles was ever substantiated? That I handed over the account myself, before anyone asked?”

“Yes. All of it.”

“Then why am I the one being asked to leave?”

Pryor spread his hands. “Because we can’t control what the market believes. We can only manage the risk to the agency.”

“So the risk is me.”

“The risk is the situation.”

“That’s a very convenient distinction.”

His smile thinned. “Please don’t make this personal.”

She gave a small, humourless laugh. “You’ve invited me into a glass room to ask me to end my relationship or resign. I’m afraid it’s already personal.”

Daniel leaned forward. “Xi, nobody here doubts your work. You’ve been one of the best account directors I’ve had. Your promotion was earned. Your reviews are excellent. Your team would walk through walls for you.”

“Then why can’t I stay?”

He opened his mouth, and looked at Pryor, and shut it again, and that was the answer.

She looked at Daniel. He had hired her when she was twenty-two and quieter than anyone in the building, and given her difficult clients and trusted her with them, and defended her when the first column printed her name. She knew he wasn’t enjoying this. It didn’t make it easier.

“Is there a third option? Unpaid leave until the review is over?”

“That defers the problem,” said Pryor.

“A role with no clients at all?”

“Not at your level.”

“So it’s final.”

“We’d like your decision by the end of the month.”

She looked down at her hands. Beyond the glass a colleague walked past with a laptop. Someone laughed by the kitchen. The printer made its familiar grinding noise. She had spent years in this building. She remembered the first time Daniel let her lead a client meeting without him; the first campaign she ran from start to finish; the night she stayed until two to rebuild a proposal because she wouldn’t send something she wasn’t proud of. She remembered opening her promotion letter at this same desk. And now the agency was making the man she loved the price of keeping all of it.

She looked up. “I’ll resign.”

Daniel’s face changed. “Xi.”

“I don’t need until the end of the month.”

“Don’t decide this because you’re upset.”

“I’m not upset. I’m clear.” She said it calmly, because she was. “You’re asking me to choose between two things that shouldn’t depend on each other. I’ve thought about the alternatives and I understand the agency’s position. I also understand that if I stayed, I’d be agreeing that Northlight can require me to hand over my private life in exchange for my job. I won’t do that.”

Pryor started to speak, and she went on over him without raising her voice.

“I’ll put it in writing today. I’d like to work a proper handover, unless you’d rather I didn’t. And I’d like it recorded that I wasn’t asked to leave for anything I did.”

Mrs. Kho wrote something down. “It will be,” she said.

Daniel rubbed his forehead. “We’ll talk to HR about the transition. Xi, I’m sorry.”

“I know.”

She stood. He stood too. “This isn’t how I wanted it to end.”

“Neither did I,” she said, and opened the glass door, and walked out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Rachel was waiting by the lifts. She took one look at Tang Xi’s face and stood up straight.

“What happened?”

“They asked me to choose. The job or An Yu.”

Rachel turned and stared through two walls of glass at the meeting room, where Pryor was putting his papers back in the folder. “You’re joking.”

“I resigned.”

“Did you think about it? Really think?”

“Rachel, I was never going to end my relationship because my employer found it inconvenient.”

Rachel’s eyes went soft. “Of course you weren’t.” She put her arms round Tang Xi in the middle of the lift lobby, and held on, and Tang Xi let her.

“I didn’t think I’d leave like this,” Tang Xi said into her shoulder. “I thought I’d leave when I was ready. When I’d found something. When I’d decided.”

“You still can.” Rachel pulled back and held her by both arms. “You’re not going to disappear. You’re going to have lunch with me. And you’re going to let me be furious on your behalf for at least twenty-four hours.”

“That’s a very specific request.”

“I’ve been told I’m good at account management.” Rachel let go of her, and something in her face settled. “And I’m coming with you.”

“You’re what?”

“Wherever you go next. I’m coming.”

“Rachel, you have a career here. You run An-Tech.”

“I run An-Tech because you gave it to me. And I’ve just watched this place make you pick between your job and your life in a fishbowl.” Rachel lifted her chin. “Pryor can have my letter on Monday. I want to enjoy writing it over the weekend.”

Tang Xi laughed, and her eyes were wet, and the laugh sounded more like herself than anything she’d said all morning.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wrote the letter herself before lunch. It was short and professional. No accusations, no explanations about her private life. She was resigning as Senior Account Director; she proposed a four-week handover; she thanked the agency for the opportunities she’d been given. She read it twice and sent it to Daniel and HR, and then she started a list of every live campaign, every client contact, every outstanding approval and deadline. She wasn’t going to leave anything unfinished.

Just after one Daniel wrote back.

Daniel: I’ve got your letter. Let’s talk about the handover tomorrow. I wish this were different.

Tang Xi: So do I. I’ll have a transition document ready.

Her phone rang. An Yu. She watched it ring and didn’t answer, not because she didn’t want to talk to him but because she needed a little time to know what she was going to say. It stopped.

Professor: Are you all right?

Tang Xi: Can I come over tonight?

Professor: Yes. Whenever you want.

✦ ✦ ✦

He hadn’t sent a car or come down to meet her. He’d left the door unlocked when she told him she was on her way, and she found him standing at the living-room window.

“Xi. What happened?”

She took off her coat. “Northlight asked me to choose. Work or you.”

He didn’t move. She watched it go into him.

“What did you say?”

“I resigned.”

His jaw tightened. “When?”

“This morning.”

“Did they give a reason? Did they say you’d breached a policy?”

“An Yu.”

He stopped.

“They said the relationship wasn’t compatible with my position. They talked about clients and the press and the deal and the authority. They said it wasn’t disciplinary. They had head office fly someone in to say it.”

He looked at the window. “They had no right to—”

“Don’t.”

“I wasn’t going to—”

“You were about to ring Daniel. Or Pryor. Or someone who knows Pryor.”

He let out a breath. “I was considering it.”

“Thank you for admitting it.” She sat down on the sofa, and after a moment he sat next to her. “Don’t turn this into something you need to handle.”

“Did you want to resign?”

“No.” Her voice was steady, but her fingers had started to twist together. “I wanted to stay. I wanted to keep doing the job I’d spent years building towards. I didn’t want to have to prove that loving you doesn’t make me worse at my work.” She swallowed. “I know I’ve made mistakes. I kissed you in your boardroom. I’d do it again. But I didn’t do anything that justified being asked to choose.”

He took her hand, and she let him.

“Did you think about staying?”

“Yes. I thought about what it would be like after a meeting like that. Wondering every day whether people were looking at my work or at you. Whether a client would ask for me to be moved. Whether my next promotion would become another question.” She looked at him. “I don’t want to work somewhere that makes me prove I’m independent by giving up something I want.”

“You shouldn’t have had to.”

“No.”

A long silence.

“What do you want to do now?”

“I don’t know. I’ll finish the handover. Then I’ll take some time.” She looked at him sideways. “You’re not going to suggest anything?”

“What kind of thing?”

“Anything.”

He thought about it. “I can listen.”

She smiled faintly. “That’s a good start.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He made tea, and she sat at the counter and watched him measure the leaves.

“You’re not going to ask whether I’d like to work at An-Tech?”

He stopped, and looked at her. “No.”

“Not even as a joke?”

“No.”

“Why?”

He poured the water. “Because you’d never forgive me. And because it would be the wrong thing to offer.”

“Even if you had a suitable position?”

“If I had a suitable position, it would be worse.” He brought her the cup. “You’d be leaving one company because it made your relationship a condition of the job, to go to another company because of the same relationship.”

“You’re not going to offer to make me independent inside the company? A separate division? A title that sounds impressive?”

“Do you want me to?”

“No.”

“Then no.” He sat down opposite her. “I’m not going to buy you an agency either. Before you ask.”

She laughed, and it caught in the middle. “I want to find something myself. I want to be hired because someone has seen my work. Not because they know who I sleep with.”

“I know. Take your time. Find somewhere you want to be, or decide to do something else. You don’t have to decide tonight.”

“You’re being very sensible.”

“I’m aware it’s out of character.”

“Don’t get used to it,” she said, and drank her tea, and some of the tightness went out of her shoulders.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later she was curled against him on the sofa with her head on his chest. They hadn’t talked about Northlight for nearly an hour. She’d chosen a film neither of them cared about, and halfway through she’d stopped watching and started undoing and redoing the third button of his shirt, and the film had finished some time ago without either of them noticing.

“Do you think I made the wrong decision?”

“No.”

“You’re supposed to think about it.”

“I have. I think you made a decision you can live with. You deserved to stay. And you shouldn’t have to give up your life to prove you deserve your job.”

“I worked so hard there.”

“I know.”

“I liked my team. I liked being good at something.”

He kissed her hair. “You’re still good at it.”

For a moment he thought she might cry. Instead she said, “I don’t want to be unemployed for long.”

“You won’t be.”

“How do you know?”

“Because you’re very good at what you do, and in about four weeks a great many people in this city are going to notice that you’re available.”

“That sounded suspiciously like confidence.”

“It was.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her last day was set for the seventeenth of July. By Friday morning the handover document was finished: every campaign, every contact, every approval, every deadline, cross-referenced and colour-coded and so complete that Rachel, reading it, said Tang Xi was going to make everybody left behind look bad.

“That’s the idea.”

Rachel sat down opposite her with two coffees. “How are you?”

Tang Xi thought about it. “Sad. Angry. Relieved, maybe.”

“All allowed.”

Tang Xi looked round her office: the shelves, the two campaign awards, the little plant Rachel had given her after the promotion, the photograph from the regional team’s weekend away. It had been a good place, once. Not perfect. Hers.

“Then leave properly,” said Rachel. “Don’t let the last thing they remember be that meeting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came to his flat late on the Friday with a small cardboard box: the photograph, two books, a ceramic cup, the plant.

He picked up the photograph. Tang Xi with Rachel and half her team at some agency party, laughing, her arm round a colleague’s neck. “You look happy.”

“I was.”

He put it down carefully and she took out the plant. “I’ll have to find somewhere for this.”

“There’s room by the window.”

“You’re not going to buy me a bigger window?”

“No.”

“Good.”

He helped her put it on the sill, and she stood back and looked at it, and then he came up behind her and his hands rested on her waist.

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.” She turned round in his arms. “I’m sad about leaving. I’m not sorry I chose you. Don’t make me regret it.”

“I won’t.”

She kissed him, gently at first, and then less gently when he drew her in, and when she pulled back she rested her forehead against his.

“I don’t need you to give me a job, An Yu. I don’t need you to buy me a company. I don’t need you to make the world easier because it’s got difficult.”

“What do you need?”

“Just be here.”

He kissed her again, and this time he didn’t try to turn the moment into a promise about what would come next. He simply held her. He couldn’t give her back her job. He couldn’t make Northlight change its mind, and he wouldn’t try to replace what she’d lost with something that had his name on it. For the first time he understood that loving her meant letting her walk out of a room he could have opened every door to keep her in. So he stood beside her with nothing in his hands, and she stayed close because she wanted to.

chapters.title: Her Own Shop
chapters.desc: Three desks over her aunt’s restaurant and five letters on a glass door. He sends flowers to the wrong address, on purpose.
chapters.epigraph: “For coming into my office and not trying to own it.”
chapters.content:
The office had three desks.

One was second-hand, with a long scratch down its left side. One had been lent by a friend who was moving abroad and would rather Tang Xi had it than pay for storage. The third was new, bought after a fortnight of arguing about whether they could manage with two. There was a kettle. There was a small fridge that made a noise like a cough every twenty minutes. There were two mismatched chairs in the corner they were calling the meeting area. And there was a glass door at the top of a narrow flight of stairs, with five new letters on it.

LEVEL

It was the room above her aunt’s restaurant in the old town. For twenty years her aunt had kept sacks of rice and broken chairs in it. In June she had looked at her niece across the kitchen and said she could have it for six months, rent-free, if she paid the electricity, cleared out the chairs and stopped arguing, and Tang Xi had stopped arguing. Underneath them, through the floorboards, came the clatter of the lunch service and the roar of the extractor fan and, now and then, her mother’s voice telling somebody they were slicing the ginger too thick.

On Monday morning she stood on the landing with a roll of masking tape and looked at the door.

“Is it crooked?”

Rachel, beside her with a cardboard box on her hip, tilted her head. “A little.”

“How little?”

“Enough that you’ll notice every morning for the rest of your life.”

“That isn’t helpful.”

“It’s honest.” Rachel watched her peel the E back off the glass and set it down again a millimetre lower. “You’re opening an agency with three desks and a kettle over a dumpling shop. The lettering will survive.”

“Rachel.”

“All right. I’ll shut up.”

She pressed the last letter flat and stepped back. It was straight. No logo, no gold, nothing commissioned from a design studio. Just five clean letters on a glass door. But she had chosen the name carefully. Not Northlight. Not a play on her own name. Nothing that hinted she was building a business on the clients she already knew. Level. A place where the work had to stand on its own; where she could decide what kind of business it would be. A place that was hers.

“Well?” said Rachel.

Three desks. A kettle. A room that smelled faintly of rice. Tang Xi smiled. “Let’s open.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Their first employee arrived ten minutes late with two paper bags of breakfast. Calvin Seah was twenty-nine and had been an account executive at Northlight for four years, three of them on Tang Xi’s team; he was excellent with clients, hopeless with charging cables, and had a habit of saying “one last thing” before adding five more items to any meeting. When Mrs. Kho had written to Tang Xi, politely, to remind her of the non-solicitation clause in her contract, Calvin and Rachel had each sent Northlight a letter of their own saying that they had gone to her, not she to them. Mrs. Kho had replied to all three of them with a single line: Noted. Good luck.

“Sorry,” said Calvin. “Traffic.”

“You live twelve minutes away.”

“Exactly. Terrible.” He looked round slowly. “So this is it.”

“This is it.”

“Three desks. Two chairs.”

“Three. One’s in the kitchen.”

“Is the kitchen the bit with the kettle?” He stared at the corner. “That’s not a kitchen.”

“It’s a kitchenette.”

“There’s no sink.”

“There’s a sink in the bathroom. And a whole restaurant downstairs.”

He looked at Rachel, who shrugged. “Don’t ask me. I just work here.”

Tang Xi took a small black notebook out of her bag. “Before we start, a few things.”

Calvin looked suspicious. “How many?”

“Not many.”

“That’s what you said before the Corran Pike submission.”

She opened the notebook. “One. We don’t take on work we can’t do properly. Two. Nobody gets special treatment because they know someone important. Three. We don’t promise things to win a pitch. Four. If something’s wrong, we say it, even when the client doesn’t want to hear it. Five.” She looked up. “We don’t take An-Tech as a client.”

Rachel’s eyebrows went up. “Even if they ask?”

“If they ask, the answer is no. Not until we’ve built something nobody can say he built for us.”

“She’s brought a list,” Calvin said to Rachel.

“Of course she has.”

“Can we put it on the wall?”

“We can,” said Tang Xi.

“Next to the crooked lettering?”

She gave him a look. He grinned and took a bite of his sandwich.

The morning went on in small practical jobs. They set up the email accounts and tested the website and argued about whether the printer belonged by the desks or by the kettle. Tang Xi wrote their first capability statement. Rachel rewrote the service descriptions. Calvin built a list of possible clients, almost none of whom they had ever worked for. They had no retainer, no portfolio of new work, no proper office. But by lunchtime they had sent their first introduction emails.

At fourteen minutes past one the printer jammed. At nineteen minutes past, the kettle stopped working. At twenty-six minutes past, Calvin discovered that the Wi-Fi password had been written down wrong in the welcome document, by Calvin. At twenty to two Tang Xi’s mother came up the stairs without knocking, put three bowls of noodles in broth on the nearest desk, looked at the door, looked at the room, said, “It’s crooked,” and went back down.

Rachel watched Tang Xi standing in the middle of the room with a bowl in her hands, looking at the three desks. “Regretting it?”

“No.”

“Even with the printer?”

“The printer least of all.”

For the first time in years, she had nobody else’s account to manage. Only her own.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flowers reached Northlight just after ten on Tuesday: white lilies and pale pink roses in a tall plain vase, no fuss, no ribbon. The card said For your first week. A. The receptionist checked the delivery slip, looked at the address, and rang the number on it.

“Mr. Wang? The flowers for Ms. Tang have arrived. I’m afraid she isn’t at this address any more.”

“I see.”

“Shall we send them on?”

“No.”

“Shall we return them?”

“No. Please leave them at reception.”

Across his office Ding looked up from his tablet. “Was that the delivery for Ms. Tang? At the old address?”

“Yes.”

“Would you like me to arrange another?”

“No.”

Ding looked at him a moment longer and went back to his screen without saying anything, which was the most eloquent thing he did all week. An Yu signed the document in front of him. He had known for three weeks exactly where Level was; he had read the company registration the morning it appeared. He had sent the flowers to the wrong address on purpose.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tang Xi found out from Rachel, who’d had a message from Northlight’s front desk.

“Flowers,” said Rachel, turning her phone round. “For you. At the old office. Lilies and roses. The card’s signed A.”

Tang Xi looked at the photograph. Then she rang Northlight’s reception herself and asked, and was told, and thanked them, and put the phone down.

“He sent them to the wrong address.”

“Maybe the florist made a mistake.”

“No. He knows where I work. He’s known since the day I registered the company.” She stood up and picked up her bag.

Rachel leaned back in her chair. “Where are you going?”

“To ask him why he sent them somewhere he knew I wouldn’t be.”

“That’s either very romantic or very irritating.”

“It’s both.”

Calvin looked up from his screen. “Are we expecting a client? Should I move a meeting?”

“There is no meeting.”

“Then where are you going?”

She paused at the glass door. “To have a conversation.”

“Bring the flowers back,” Rachel called after her.

“I might.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The receptionist at An-Tech recognised her at once. “Ms. Tang. Mr. Wang’s in a meeting until half past twelve. Shall I let his office know you’re here?”

“Please.”

She sat in the waiting area under the great glass atrium. She had been in this building more times than she could count; she knew the security gates and the private lifts and the quiet corridor on the forty-second floor. But today she wasn’t Northlight’s account director, or anybody’s representative. She wasn’t here about a deal or a campaign or a regulator. She was here because the man she was in love with had sent her flowers to an office where he knew she no longer worked, and she wanted an explanation.

A little after twelve the private lift opened and he came out of it himself, dark suit, white shirt, tie perfectly in place. His meeting had ended early. He crossed the lobby towards her, and she stood up.

“Ms. Tang.”

“Mr. Wang.”

He glanced at her empty hands. “No flowers?”

“They’re at Northlight.”

“I see.”

She stopped in front of him. “Why?”

“Why what?”

“Don’t.”

The corner of his mouth moved. “All right. I wanted to know whether you’d come looking for me.”

She stared at him. Then she laughed once, in disbelief. “You’re unbelievable.”

“I’ve been told.”

“You sent flowers to an office I left a week ago.”

“Yes.”

“Knowing they’d never reach me.”

“Yes.”

“And you thought I’d come here.”

“I hoped you would.”

“That’s ridiculous.”

“Possibly.”

“Did you think I’d be annoyed?”

“I considered it, and I did it anyway.” He looked at her. “Did it work?”

She tried to hold her face still, and failed. “Unfortunately.”

“There’s something else,” he said, before she could go on. “While you’re here. If Level ever wanted An-Tech as a—”

“No.”

“I hadn’t finished.”

“You didn’t need to. No. Not as a client, not as a referral, not as a friendly introduction to someone on your board.” She stepped closer. “When I’ve built something nobody can say you built for me, you can ask again.”

He looked at her, and nodded, and she saw that he had expected exactly that answer and had asked so that she could give it.

“You’re very pleased with yourself,” she said.

“Not particularly.”

“You are.”

“Would you like to come up to my office?”

“No. I came to ask you a question. I’ve asked it.” She took hold of the front of his jacket. “Now I want to do something else.”

She pulled him down and kissed him in the middle of his own lobby.

It wasn’t a quiet kiss. She hadn’t come to make a scene; but she had been annoyed with him the entire way across town, and by the time she reached him the annoyance had turned into something much warmer and much less patient, and she kissed him the way you kiss someone you have been arguing with in your head for forty minutes. His hand found her waist. His other hand came up to her cheek and held her there, and he kissed her back as if the lobby weren’t there at all. The receptionist looked hard at her monitor. A security guard turned to examine the revolving door. Two people coming out of the lifts slowed, looked at each other, and kept walking fast.

Tang Xi let go first. “You’re childish.”

“I know.”

“Manipulative.”

“That’s a strong word.”

“You sent flowers to the wrong address on purpose.”

“Yes.”

She shook her head, and kissed him again, and he smiled against her mouth. When she stepped back she straightened his tie. “You’re lucky I like you.”

“I’d gathered.”

“Don’t get smug. Come on.”

“Where?”

“To get my flowers. Unless you’d like to send them somewhere else.”

He held out his hand. “Let’s go.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Northlight’s receptionist looked delighted to see them. The vase was behind the desk.

“Would you like someone to help carry it, Ms. Tang?”

Tang Xi looked at An Yu. “He’s capable.”

He took the vase. “Congratulations on your agency,” said the receptionist. “Everybody’s heard. Good luck.”

In the lift he looked down at the lilies. “They’re quite large.”

“You sent them.”

“To the wrong place.”

“Do you intend to behave like this often?”

He considered it. “Would you come looking for me again?”

She laughed and leaned her head against his shoulder. “Next time, send them to Level. Don’t send anything expensive. And don’t buy the building.”

“I haven’t bought the building.”

“It belongs to my aunt. She’d eat you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Calvin noticed first when they came up the narrow stairs: Tang Xi, and behind her the chairman of An-Tech carrying a vase of lilies past a sack of rice someone had forgotten on the landing. Calvin stared at the flowers, and at An Yu, and at the flowers.

“Hello.”

“Good afternoon,” said An Yu.

Rachel came out of the kitchenette, and her eyes went straight to the vase. “Ah.”

“Don’t,” said Tang Xi.

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You don’t need to.”

“Where shall we put them?” said Calvin.

She looked round the room: three desks, two chairs, a kettle, barely enough space for the printer. “By the window.”

An Yu set them down beside the small plant Rachel had given her, and Tang Xi stepped back. The flowers looked almost absurdly grand in the plain little room.

“Very nice,” said Rachel.

“Improves the place,” said Calvin.

“Are you both just going to stand there?”

“Yes,” said Rachel.

An Yu turned to her. “Should I go?”

She could hear the question under the words. He had come into her office. He had carried flowers into the place she’d built. He hadn’t mentioned an investment, or asked again to be a client, or suggested she work with An-Tech. He had simply carried the flowers up the stairs.

“Yes,” she said, and caught his hand. “After lunch.”

“All right.”

“Downstairs. My mother’s cooking. You’ll be polite.”

“I’m always polite.”

“She’ll make you fold something.”

Rachel made a small noise. Calvin became intensely interested in his laptop.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to nine that evening the room was quiet. Calvin had gone at six, Rachel soon after, taking the last of the breakfast pastries with her. The restaurant downstairs had closed and the fan had stopped. Tang Xi was at her desk finishing the first proposal Level would ever send. The flowers stood by the window. She had moved them twice: once because the afternoon sun was too strong, and once because Calvin said they were blocking the printer.

Professor: Have you finished?

Tang Xi: Almost.

Professor: Dinner?

Tang Xi: Yes.

Professor: I’ll come by. I’ll use the stairs, not the restaurant. Your mother is still downstairs counting the takings and I’m not ready.

She laughed out loud in the empty room and went back to the proposal. Five letters on a glass door. Three desks. A borrowed room over a dumpling shop. A vase of flowers that had been sent to the wrong address. There was a client to win and a business to build, and in the morning she would get up and come back to work she had chosen. Not because someone had given her a position. Not because someone had made room for her. Because she had made the room herself.

When he came in, he stood in the doorway.

“You’re late,” she said.

“By four minutes.”

“Still late.”

He put a paper bag beside her laptop. Inside were chive and prawn dumplings in a box she recognised from the counter downstairs.

“My mother gave you those.”

“She was on the stairs. She looked at me for a long time. She handed me the box and said, ‘She hasn’t eaten.’”

Tang Xi shut the laptop and came round the desk and kissed him.

“Is that for the flowers?” he asked.

“No.”

“For dinner?”

“No. For coming into my office and not trying to own it.”

His face softened. “I wouldn’t.”

“I know,” she said, and kissed him again, and behind them, on the glass door, the five letters stayed perfectly straight.

chapters.title: Her First Client
chapters.desc: A tea company with no money, nineteen-hour days, and tomato and egg noodles at midnight. The kettle boils dry.
chapters.content:
The first client came through a referral, and not a grand one. No old executive friend, no one who’d read about the woman who left Northlight and decided to take a chance on her. A woman who bought tea from the same shop as Calvin’s mother had mentioned, at the counter, that the owner needed help with a launch and couldn’t afford an agency, and Calvin’s mother had said she knew somebody who couldn’t afford not to have a client.

The shop was called Second Steep. It had a narrow front in the old commercial district, a modest online store and six loose-leaf teas from small farms in the hills inland. The packaging was beautiful, the tea was good, and the marketing was almost non-existent. The owner, Grace Tham, had spent twelve years building it. She had never hired an agency. She had never run a proper launch. She had almost no money. Tang Xi liked her at once.

They met in the shop, at a long wooden table where Grace had laid out the six teas and made a pot of each herself. She did it properly: the cups warmed, the first infusion poured away to wake the leaves, the second poured into Tang Xi’s cup.

“That’s why we’re called Second Steep,” said Grace. “The first one opens the leaf. The second is the one you drink. Most people don’t know to wait.”

“What’s the new collection?”

“Three teas, out in September. A white tea from a farm where they still dry the leaves in the sun on bamboo trays, and when it rains they lose the batch. An oolong that’s roasted over charcoal four times and left to rest for a year between the second and third, so it doesn’t taste of fire. And a black tea from a family that’s grown it for three generations and still rolls the first flush by hand.” She put the lid on the pot. “I don’t want it to feel like another product launch.”

Tang Xi turned one of the tins over. Cream label, dark green lettering, a small drawing of a leaf. “What do you want people to feel?”

Grace thought about it. “I want them to slow down.”

“Not just buy tea?”

“Of course I want them to buy tea. I’m running a business.” Grace laughed. “But I want them to know why we made it. We don’t flavour anything. We don’t hurry the drying. When the white tea’s rained on, it’s gone and we don’t have it that year. I want people to know that.”

“Then we don’t start with the products,” said Tang Xi. “We start with the people. The farmers, the trays, the charcoal, the year of waiting. The collection is what the story produces. It isn’t the whole story.”

Grace was quiet, and then she smiled. “That’s what I’ve been trying to tell people for twelve years.”

By the time Tang Xi left she had a notebook full of observations, a rough idea for the campaign and a clear understanding of the budget. It wasn’t much. Not enough for a big production. Not enough for paid media at the scale Grace imagined. Nowhere near what Northlight would have recommended. But it was enough to start.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You’re taking it?” said Rachel, on Friday, after reading the brief twice. “With that budget? Xi, we have rent.”
