“We don’t have rent. My aunt has rice.”

“We have salaries. We have a printer that sounds like it’s dying.”

As if to make the point, the printer made a small grinding noise.

“We’ll manage.”

“You’re charging them almost nothing.”

“I’m charging them what they can pay.”

“That’s not the same.”

“I know.” Tang Xi closed her laptop. “I like the business. I like the tea. I think they have something worth telling people about. And I want Level’s first client to be one we can be proud of.”

Rachel looked at her, and then nodded.

Calvin turned round in his chair. “Are we celebrating?”

“We’re signing a client.”

“Then yes.”

They signed that afternoon. The scope was deliberately narrow: launch strategy, a campaign idea, a content plan, one small production day, social assets, and a report afterwards. No influencers, no venue, no event. Tang Xi had made the limits completely clear to Grace, and Grace had accepted them, and for the first time Level had a client.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week was hard. The second was worse. By the third, Tang Xi understood why people said starting a business was like having several full-time jobs and no promise that any of them would pay. She ran the client meetings, rewrote the campaign idea, negotiated production costs, checked copy, chased invoices, approved layouts and answered questions that arrived at every hour of the day and night. Rachel led strategy and content. Calvin ran production, suppliers and the schedule. There were three of them, which meant every problem eventually found its way to her.

The only photographer they could afford was free on Wednesdays. The shoot at the white tea farm had to be postponed twice for rain, which was, Grace said, the whole point. The first packaging proof came back in the wrong green. The venue they’d looked at for the launch quoted almost half the budget for an evening, and Tang Xi turned it down and moved the launch into the shop itself. They swapped a production crew for a photographer and one assistant. They shot the product films in natural light with a rented camera, and Calvin learned how to hold a reflector with his chin. And they built the whole campaign around the time it took to make the tea, instead of trying to look like the glossy lifestyle brands with ten times their money.

At a quarter past eight one evening Rachel found her sitting on the floor with three printed layouts round her knees.

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“What?”

A pause. “Something.”

“That isn’t food. That’s a category.”

“There’s a sandwich in the fridge.”

“From when?”

“Today.” Rachel looked at her. Tang Xi sighed. “Yesterday.”

“I’m ordering dinner,” said Rachel, and did.

Tang Xi looked back at the layouts. The headline on the first one said A GOOD CUP TAKES ITS TIME. She circled it. That was the one.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came up the stairs at twelve minutes to midnight on the Wednesday with a paper bag.

He had rung twice. The second time she’d answered, talked for less than a minute and told him she was working. He’d asked whether she’d eaten. She’d said yes. He’d asked what. She had said, “Something,” and he had recognised the answer.

The lights were still on above the shuttered restaurant. Through the glass he could see her at her desk, hair tied back, sleeves pushed above her elbows, a pen in one hand and a spreadsheet in front of her. Boxes stacked against the wall. A tripod leaning by the kitchenette. The printer open, its insides exposed, like a patient. He let himself in with the code she’d given him.

She looked up. “An Yu? It’s nearly midnight.”

He lifted the bag. “You haven’t eaten.”

“I have.”

He looked at her. She looked back. “All right. Not properly.”

She opened the bag. It wasn’t food. It was ingredients: a packet of noodles, four tomatoes, four eggs, spring onions, a knob of ginger.

“What is this?”

“I’m going to cook.”

“You? In my office?”

“There’s a kitchen.”

She looked at the corner: the kettle, a small induction hob, and a sink that had been put in after Rachel threatened to resign over the bathroom. “An Yu, you don’t have to cook.”

“I know. Tomato and egg noodles. Your mother says anyone can make them. I’d like to find out if that includes me.”

She laughed, and went back to her screen, and kept glancing at him. He was serious about it. He read the instructions on the packet twice. He washed the tomatoes and cut them into pieces of no two sizes alike. He cracked the eggs into a bowl and fished out a piece of shell with the grim concentration of a man defusing something. The first problem was the induction hob, which wouldn’t turn on until she told him which button. The second was that the pan was too small. The third was that he put in far too much water.

“Do you need help?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

A few minutes later a smell reached her desk. “An Yu. Is something burning?”

He looked at the pan. “No.” A pause. He turned the heat down. “Possibly.”

She laughed. He looked over his shoulder. “Don’t laugh.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

The result wasn’t beautiful. The noodles were overcooked. The tomatoes had collapsed into a sour red slick. The eggs, which were supposed to be soft yellow clouds, had caught on the bottom and come up in brown flakes. He put a bowl in front of her. “Eat.”

She took a mouthful. Chewed. Swallowed. Took another.

“Is it terrible?”

“No.”

“You’re lying.”

“A little.”

He sat down opposite her. She kept eating.

“You’re still eating,” he observed.

“I’m hungry. It isn’t terrible.”

“Too much salt. The noodles are overcooked. The eggs—”

“An Yu.” He stopped. “It’s good.”

He looked at her, and then down at the table. She ate all of it. The broth too, holding the bowl in both hands. When she’d finished she put down her chopsticks and leaned back, and he reached across and wiped a spot of tomato from the corner of her mouth with his thumb.

“Next time I’ll do better.”

“There’s a next time?”

“If you’ll let me.”

She looked round: the boxes, the layouts, a half-empty water bottle, the kettle. Then at him. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She got up to fill the kettle, because there were still the captions to check, and switched it on, and came back, and didn’t go to her desk.

“Are you going home?” she asked.

“In a while.”

“You’ve got work tomorrow.”

“So have you.”

“Mine’s more urgent. If this launch fails, we haven’t got another client.”

“That isn’t necessarily true.”

“It might be.”

“Then we’ll deal with it if it happens.”

“You make it sound simple.”

“It isn’t.”

She’d been thinking about the launch all day: the budget, the deadlines, the shoot that kept being rained off. About how much she needed this to work, and how much she wanted to prove that Level could survive without a big agency’s name behind it, and how much she hated that the fear followed her home at night.

He stood up and held out his hand. She looked at it, and took it, and he drew her in, his palm warm on her back.

“You’ve been working for nineteen hours.”

“Not quite.”

“Xi.”

“All right. Maybe.”

He pushed her hair back off her forehead. “You’re allowed to stop.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

“Not really,” she admitted, and he pressed a kiss into her hair, and her cheek, and the corner of her mouth, and she lifted her face. The first kiss was gentle, almost careful. The second wasn’t. She took hold of his shirt and pulled him closer, and he wrapped both arms round her, and she realised how much she’d missed him: not because it had been long, they’d seen each other two nights before, but because she’d missed being with him without a screen in between and a deadline behind it and one eye on the clock.

“Stay,” she said against his mouth.

“I’m here.”

“No. Stay with me. Here.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She switched off the overhead lights so that there was only the lamp by the kitchenette and the orange glow of the street through the window. She pushed the laptop away from the edge of the desk. He took his watch off and put it next to it, and then his glasses, and she reached up and started on the buttons of his shirt.

She had spent the whole day deciding things for other people. This one was hers.

She drew him down with her onto the strip of clean floor between her desk and the wall of boxes, and he stopped, propped on one arm above her, looking at her.

“Here? Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

His knee knocked an empty box and it fell over with a hollow sound, and she laughed. “Very elegant.”

“Your office has poor floor planning.”

“My office has three desks.”

“And a kettle.”

“And a very good agency,” she said, and he smiled against her mouth.

She pulled his shirt off his shoulders and he pulled her T-shirt over her head, and the floor was hard under her back and she didn’t care at all. He unbuttoned her jeans and she lifted her hips so he could pull them down, and then he was kissing his way along the inside of her thigh, slowly, watching her face in the half-light, and she had to put her hand over her own mouth, because the window was open to the street. He made her come like that, unhurried and thorough, his hands spread on her hips holding her to the floor while she shook, and when she could breathe again she pulled him up by the hair and kissed him, tasting herself on him, and reached down between them and undid his belt.

“Now,” she said.

He slid into her and she arched off the floorboards, and for a moment neither of them moved at all. Then he began to move, slow and deep, letting her set the pace with her heels against the backs of his thighs. She touched his face whenever he went too quiet and he answered every time with his mouth. A box of tins slid gently off the stack beside them and nobody stopped. The kettle had begun to roar in the kitchenette, then to rattle on its base, and she heard it and didn’t care, and he didn’t hear it at all. When she came again, holding his face between her hands, she said his name out loud and he went over with her, his forehead against hers, his breath breaking.

They lay in the warm dark afterwards on the office floor, her head on his folded jacket, his arm round her waist. She was looking at the ceiling. Then she began to laugh.

“What?”

“The kettle.”

He turned his head. In the kitchenette the kettle had boiled itself dry and clicked off, and the element was ticking as it cooled, and a faint smell of hot metal hung in the air.

He shut his eyes. “I forgot.”

“You nearly burned my agency down.”

“I didn’t switch it on.”

“You distracted the person who did. That’s worse.”

“You’re very ungrateful.”

She rolled over to face him, grinning. “I ate your terrible noodles.”

“All of them.”

“Every last one. And the broth.”

He brushed his thumb along her cheekbone. “Then we’re even.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Rachel arrived first in the morning, a little after eight. She opened the glass door, stepped inside, and stopped. Two bowls in the kitchenette. A paper bag by the sink. A kettle that smelled scorched. One of the campaign boxes on its side. And Tang Xi asleep on the office floor under a man’s suit jacket, next to a pair of expensive shoes that weren’t hers.

Rachel put her coffee down extremely carefully. “Xi.”

Tang Xi stirred. “Mm?”

“Did you sleep here?”

Tang Xi opened her eyes, looked confused, and then remembered. “Yes.”

“Comfortable?”

She sat up, trying to flatten her hair with both hands. “Not particularly.”

Rachel’s eyes went to the jacket. “Is that—”

“Yes.”

“Is he—”

“In the bathroom.”

Rachel stared at her, and then laughed helplessly into both hands. “Your mother’s been downstairs since six,” she said, when she could. “She sent up two bowls of congee with me and told me to give one to the tall one.”

Tang Xi put her face in her hands. “No.”

“She said, and I’m quoting, ‘He can’t cook. Tell him to stop trying in my sister’s building.’”

An Yu came out of the bathroom a moment later in his shirt, his hair damp, and took in the room, and Rachel, and the congee. “Good morning.”

“Good morning, Mr. Wang,” said Rachel. “I hope everyone had a productive evening. Professionally, of course.”

He picked up one of the bowls, looked at it, and said with great dignity, “Please thank her mother for me,” and Tang Xi lay back down on the floor and laughed until she cried.

✦ ✦ ✦

The launch was on the last Monday in August, and it went well. Not spectacularly. No celebrities, no installation, no queue round the block. But people came. They watched the short film about the farmers and the bamboo trays and the charcoal. They read the cards explaining the second steep and why you poured the first one away. They drank the new teas and asked Grace questions about the farms, and Grace answered every one. A food writer from a weekend paper stayed for nearly an hour and asked to come back to the farm in October. The online store took more orders on the first evening than Grace had expected in the first week.

It was small. The budget was small. It worked.

Tang Xi stood at the back of the shop watching Grace explain to an old man why the white tea from last year didn’t exist. Rachel came and stood beside her. “Look at that.”

“I know.”

Calvin appeared with a clipboard. “First numbers. Don’t get excited.”

The first day’s sales were modest, and comfortably over target, and the newsletter sign-ups had tripled. Tang Xi read them twice. “We did it.”

“LEVEL’s first successful launch,” said Calvin, lifting the clipboard.

Grace came over with three small tins. “I don’t know how to say this properly. You understood what I wanted to do. That’s why it worked.”

“Your tea made it work,” said Tang Xi.

“Then we’ll do the next collection together. The winter one. If you’d like.”

Tang Xi looked at Rachel, who was already smiling. “We’d like,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She got to his flat after eleven with a tin of the charcoal oolong. He opened the door.

“You look tired.”

“I am.”

“Did it go well?”

She held up the tin. “Very well. And we’ve got the next project.”

His face warmed. “Already?”

“Grace wants us for the winter collection.”

“Then congratulations on your second project.”

“Same client.”

“Different project.”

She laughed, and he took her coat. “Have you eaten?”

“Actual food.”

He looked relieved, and she narrowed her eyes. “Don’t look so proud.”

“I am.”

“Are you cooking tonight?”

“Would you like me to?”

She thought about it. “Maybe not.”

He laughed, and she kissed him, and when he held her she thought of three desks above a dumpling shop, a printer with its insides showing, and a small tea company that had trusted them with a launch it could barely afford. Level hadn’t become a success overnight. It had become something better. A beginning. And for the first time since she’d walked out of the glass room, she could look ahead without wondering whose name would be attached to her work. It would be hers.

chapters.title: The Pitch Against Him
chapters.desc: Her pitch against his own marketing team. She wins, his team hates her, and he congratulates her on his knees.
chapters.epigraph: “On behalf of An-Tech, I acknowledge that Level submitted the stronger proposal.”
chapters.content:
The first time Tang Xi saw An-Tech’s name on the list of competing agencies, she thought it was a mistake. The second time, she stopped reading. The third time she turned her laptop round on the desk.

“Tell me I’m reading this wrong.”

Rachel leaned across. “An-Tech? Is that the An-Tech?”

“How many are there?”

“Oh,” said Rachel.

The prospective client was Halloway Living, a regional hospitality group with four boutique hotels, a block of serviced apartments and two private members’ clubs, about to launch its first branded homes: forty-two residences above a new hotel, to be sold under the name Halloway House. It wanted a positioning, a launch strategy, regional communications, executive profiles, content and a twelve-month retainer. It wasn’t enormous by the standards of the big networks. It was large enough to change Level’s first year completely, and it was exactly the account Tang Xi wanted.

And An-Tech was pitching for it. Not as a client. As an agency. An-Tech had a marketing division, sixty people strong, that handled its own corporate brand and the launches of its own ventures, and in the last year it had started to pitch for outside work through a separate consultancy arm. The invitation listed three names.

Brightwater Collective
LEVEL
An-Tech Strategic Marketing

“Are we withdrawing?” Rachel asked.

“No.”

“Xi.”

“We’re not withdrawing.” Tang Xi opened the brief again. “Let’s read it properly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu learned about it at twenty past nine on Friday morning, from his head of marketing.

Felix Ong was forty-one, experienced, commercially confident and good, and his team had spent three weeks on the proposal and already had two conversations with Halloway’s executive committee. “It isn’t a property launch,” he said, clicking to the next slide. “It’s a repositioning. They’re known for hotels. They want to sell homes without losing the service identity.”

“Competitors?”

“Brightwater. And a new shop called Level. Founded this summer by a former Northlight senior account director.” Felix paused. “Tang Xi.”

The room went quiet. An Yu closed the deck. “Continue.”

Felix did. For twenty minutes An Yu asked about margins, staffing and the delivery model. He questioned the media split and asked whether the team really had the regional experience for a residential launch. He didn’t mention Tang Xi again. When the meeting ended, Felix stayed behind.

“Are you comfortable with us going ahead?”

“Why wouldn’t I be?”

“Because Ms. Tang is involved.”

“She is the founder of a competing agency. She’s entitled to compete.” An Yu put his pen down. “Don’t contact her. Don’t ask anyone about her and me. Don’t make it personal. Pitch your best work. If hers is better, the client will choose it. If yours is better, it’ll choose you.”

“Halloway’s chief executive has asked whether you’ll be at the strategy session. They’d like to hear from the chairman.”

An Yu was quiet. “Then I’ll come to the strategy session, and nothing else, and I’ll say so at the start. Go ahead.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Tang Xi didn’t tell him about the pitch. Not because she was hiding it, but because there was nothing to tell. He was a competitor. She was a founder. They didn’t talk about work at home, and now they had a reason not to that neither of them had to explain.

At Level they built the proposal around a single problem. Halloway wanted to go into a market where its reputation didn’t automatically mean trust. People knew its hotels. They didn’t yet know whether they could trust the company with their homes. People would pay a premium to have Halloway’s name on their front door; then they would read the service charge, and find out what the name actually bought them, and that was where branded residences went wrong. Tang Xi wanted the launch to answer that question before it tried to sell anyone a lifestyle.

Rachel built the audience research. Calvin built the delivery plan. Tang Xi wrote the argument. It wasn’t the most beautiful proposal anyone had ever seen; it didn’t have render after render of imaginary living rooms. It had three ideas.

Trust before aspiration.
Service you can see, not a promise you have to believe.
A local voice, not a borrowed one.

A phased launch: first, find out what the market actually thought of Halloway. Then a run of stories about the people and systems behind the hotels: the night manager, the head of housekeeping who’d been there for nineteen years, the engineer who could hear a lift going wrong from two floors away. Then the residences, with private previews and careful press. And a way to measure all of it that didn’t stop at reach and likes: qualified enquiries, conversions from previews, the shift in how people talked about the brand, and whether awareness turned into anyone actually considering a purchase.

On Monday evening Rachel put the first complete deck on the table. “Forty-two slides.”

“Too many.”

“Thirty-eight without the appendix.”

“Good.”

Calvin leaned over. “Can we win this?”

Tang Xi looked at the proposal and then at the two of them. “Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The pitches were on the Wednesday afternoon, in a conference room high above the city at Halloway’s head office. Tang Xi arrived with Rachel and Calvin a quarter of an hour early and they were shown to a waiting area with water. At two o’clock the client came in: the chief executive, Richard Fenwick, his chief operating officer, the marketing director, the head of residential, the finance director and an outside adviser to the board. Tang Xi greeted each of them.

The last person through the door was An Yu.

He wasn’t there as anybody’s chairman today. He was there for a competing bidder, and he said so before he sat down. “I’m here at Mr. Fenwick’s invitation for the strategy discussion. I’ll leave the room for everything else.” Dark grey suit, white shirt, a plain watch. He looked across at her.

“Ms. Tang.”

“Mr. Wang.”

That was all. No smile, no flicker of recognition, nothing to suggest that they’d stood in a kitchen at midnight or that he knew how she took her tea. He sat down next to Felix Ong, and she sat opposite.

“Ms. Tang,” said Richard Fenwick. “Would you like to begin?”

She stood and connected her laptop.

HALLOWAY HOUSE · TRUST BEFORE DESIRE

“Halloway has spent fifteen years earning a reputation in hospitality. When your guests walk into one of your hotels, they know what to expect. They know the standards and the detail and the people.” She paused. “But buying a home isn’t booking a stay. Your buyers aren’t choosing where to spend a weekend. They’re choosing where to live, where to put their money, in some cases where to raise children. The trust is different, the questions are different, and the communication has to be different too.”

She clicked. “So we wouldn’t launch Halloway House as another luxury property. We’d introduce it as homes backed by a hospitality company that already knows how to look after people. And then we’d prove it.”

Fenwick nodded slowly.

She took them through it without hurrying. Aspiration against credibility; making service something you could see; why each of their three markets needed its own proof even if the brand stayed the same. When the head of residential asked if they could use one message everywhere, she explained where it would work and where it would fail. When the finance director challenged the research budget, she showed him how it would stop them wasting media money in the wrong neighbourhoods. When the board adviser asked about reputation, she said something no one else in the building had said to them yet.

“Don’t promise anything about the service in the residences that isn’t in a signed operating agreement. Not a doorman, not a concierge app, not housekeeping. Buyers in branded residences read the service charge schedule line by line, and if the launch promised them something the schedule doesn’t deliver, you won’t be dealing with a marketing problem. You’ll be dealing with their lawyers.”

Rachel took the measurement section. Calvin took delivery. Then Tang Xi came back to the front.

“One last thing. We’re a small agency. I won’t pretend otherwise. We don’t have a production department or offices in six cities. But you won’t be passed from a senior pitch team to a junior account team the day you sign. The three people in front of you are the three people who will do the work. If you appoint Level, you’ll have us. All of us.”

Fenwick looked at her. “Thank you, Ms. Tang.”

✦ ✦ ✦

An-Tech presented next. Felix led it, with two of his people. It was polished, detailed and commercially ambitious. A bigger team, a much stronger regional network, far more money for media and production. It was also considerably more expensive. An Yu spoke only in the strategy discussion. He talked about what An-Tech had learned from launching its own ventures in new markets, about the value of integrated planning and of being able to move a great many people quickly. He was composed and persuasive, and Tang Xi listened to every word and didn’t underestimate him for a second.

When the client asked about staffing, Felix described the senior oversight structure. When they asked about continuity, he promised them direct access to the senior team. Tang Xi glanced at Rachel. Rachel gave her a look so small that nobody else in the room could have seen it. They’d both noticed the same thing. The names on An-Tech’s delivery team weren’t the names of the people in the room.

At twenty to five it was over. The client thanked everyone and said they’d decide after an internal discussion. Tang Xi packed her laptop. Outside the room, when Rachel and Calvin had gone on ahead to the lifts, An Yu caught up with her.

“Ms. Tang. Good presentation.”

“Thank you.”

“You made a strong case for senior involvement.”

“Because it’s what we’re offering.”

“Yes.” A pause. “Good luck.”

“Thank you. You too.”

She walked away, and he watched her go, and Felix came to stand beside him. “She was good.”

“Yes.”

“Very good,” said Felix, and An Yu didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

Richard Fenwick rang her himself at eighteen minutes past ten on Friday.

“Ms. Tang. We’d like to appoint Level for Halloway House.”

For a moment she didn’t say anything at all. Then she smiled. “Thank you. We’re delighted.”

“The board thought your proposal was right for where we are. That point about the service charge schedule went round the table twice. And we believed you that the three of you would do the work.” He paused. “We’ll send the contract on Monday. Congratulations.”

She put the phone down and looked at Rachel, who’d been watching her face. “Well?”

“We got it.”

Rachel stood up so fast her chair rolled backwards across the floor. “You’re joking.”

“We got it.”

Calvin spun round. “What?”

“Halloway House. They chose Level.”

Calvin let out a breath like a man surfacing. Rachel came round the desk and hugged her, and Tang Xi laughed into her shoulder. Their first big competitive pitch. A real twelve-month retainer, a client with real ambition and a real budget, the kind of project that would make other clients take them seriously. When Rachel finally let go, Tang Xi looked at the three desks: the same desks, the same printer, the same kettle. But something had changed. They weren’t an agency looking for its first client any more. They were an agency that won.

✦ ✦ ✦

At An-Tech, Felix came into the chairman’s office without his usual confidence.

“Level won.”

An Yu put his pen down. “Why?”

“The client preferred their strategy. They thought ours was too ambitious for where the residential business is. And they questioned the staffing model.”

“Was the staffing model accurate?”

Felix hesitated. “We’d planned to bring more people in after appointment.”

“Then it wasn’t accurate.”

“We could have adjusted.”

“Before the pitch?”

“Yes.”

“What else?”

Felix was quiet. “Ms. Tang’s proposal was more specific. They liked the phases. They liked that she tied everything to sales. And she told them something about service charges that none of us had thought of.”

“Was she better?”

It was a direct question. Felix could have talked about budgets or scale or the client’s preferences. Instead he said, “Yes. On this brief, she was.”

“Then we lost to the better proposal.”

Felix’s jaw tightened. “With respect, the team feels we were put in an awkward position.”

“Because she was competing?”

“Because of the relationship.”

“Did she get any information from us?”

“No.”

“Did we give her any? Did she see our proposal?”

“No.”

“Then what exactly was awkward?”

Felix didn’t answer.

“She was invited to pitch. We were invited to pitch. She presented her work, we presented ours, and the client chose,” said An Yu. “We don’t own a client because we want it. We don’t own the market because we’re bigger. And we certainly don’t own the right to win every pitch. Write me a review of what we should have done better by Tuesday.”

At the door Felix stopped. “Congratulations to her, I suppose.”

“She earned it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His team didn’t feel that way, and it reached her on the Monday.

She was at an industry breakfast at a hotel by the harbour, one of the ones she’d gone to for years at Northlight, standing by the coffee urns with a plate she wasn’t eating from, when two of Felix’s people came up to the table. A woman in her thirties she half recognised, and a younger man with an An-Tech lanyard still round his neck.

“Congratulations on Halloway,” said the woman, pleasantly, and loud enough for the next table. “It must help. Knowing what the other side’s going to say before they say it.”

The young man laughed. Two people at the next table stopped talking.

Tang Xi put her coffee down. “I’m sorry,” she said, as pleasantly. “I didn’t catch what you meant. Would you say it again, slowly, so everyone can hear it properly?”

The woman’s smile faltered.

“Because if you mean I had any information from An-Tech, you’re accusing your own chairman of leaking your own proposal,” said Tang Xi, “and you might want to think about whether you’d like to do that at a breakfast. If you mean something else, I’d be interested to hear what.” She waited. Nobody said anything. “No? Then thank you for the congratulations. Your proposal was very polished. The client just didn’t believe your staffing.”

She picked up her coffee and walked away, and her hand didn’t shake until she was outside on the terrace, where nobody could see it.

At An-Tech, the post-pitch review on Tuesday took forty minutes. At the thirty-fifth, the young man with the lanyard said, to the table in general, that it was hard to compete against the chairman’s girlfriend. An Yu looked up from Felix’s report.

“Say that again.”

The young man went red.

“Ms. Tang beat this team on a brief because her proposal was better and her staffing was honest. That is in Mr. Ong’s own report, on page three. If anyone in this company believes she won for any other reason, put it in writing to the general counsel with your evidence and I’ll make sure it’s investigated properly.” He turned the page. “Otherwise, page four.”

Nobody wrote anything to the general counsel. But they didn’t like her any better, and when she heard about it from Ding, who wasn’t supposed to tell anyone and told Rachel, who told everybody, Tang Xi found that she minded more than she’d expected. A room full of people who had decided she was a cheat, and nothing she could do about it except keep winning.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday night he sent one message.

Professor: Congratulations. You deserved it.

Tang Xi: I know.

Professor: Dinner?

Tang Xi: I’m working.

Professor: Of course you are.

Tang Xi: Don’t sound disappointed.

Professor: I’m not.

Tang Xi: Liar.

Professor: Very disappointed.

She laughed out loud, and Rachel looked up from her screen. “Congratulations from the chairman? Very professional?”

“Very.”

At a quarter to eleven that night she sent him a photograph of the signed letter of intent on her desk: LEVEL × HALLOWAY HOUSE. Underneath it she wrote, Our second proper client. He looked at it.

Professor: Best sentence I’ve read all year.

Tang Xi: Come over tomorrow. After the restaurant shuts.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came up the narrow stairs at ten on Saturday night, when the shutters were down and the fan had stopped and the only light in the building was the one over her desk.

“You’re late,” she said, opening the glass door.

“By six minutes.”

“You’re getting worse.”

He came in. There were new boxes against the wall marked HALLOWAY, the proposal had been printed and bound, and a whiteboard by the desks was covered in dates and names in three different colours.

“How do you feel?”

“Happy. Tired. Relieved. A bit frightened.” She leaned back against her desk. “Your team hates me.”

“Some of them.”

“Felix?”

“Felix is disappointed. Felix wrote on page three that your proposal was better.”

“Does he think I took something from him?”

“He may think the circumstances were unfair.”

“Were they?”

“No.”

“Good. I wanted to hear you say it.”

“Your proposal was better.”

“Say it again.”

“Your proposal was better.”

She smiled. He put his hand on her waist. “You’re enjoying this.”

“Very much.”

“Should I be offended?”

“Absolutely.” She reached up and loosened his tie. “Did you only come to congratulate me?”

“Yes.”

“Nothing else?”

“I thought you might want dinner.”

“There’s no food. There’s tea. And a printer that doesn’t work.”

“I’ve met the printer.”

She took his hand and drew him towards the desk and kissed him, and it began, but she was smiling too much to keep it that way. He touched her cheek, and then her waist, and pulled her closer.

She drew back. “Lock the door.”

“It’s locked.”

“Good.”

He looked at her. “Here?”

“It’s my office. My company. My decision.”

“Always,” he said, and then he did something she hadn’t expected at all. He went down on his knees in front of her, on the bare boards of her office, in his good suit, with his hands resting lightly on her hips, and looked up at her.

She went still. “An Yu?”

“Congratulations, Ms. Tang.” His face was perfectly serious. “On behalf of An-Tech, I acknowledge that Level submitted the stronger proposal.”

She laughed and touched his face. “That’s not enough.”

“No?”

“No.”

He kissed her hand. Then the inside of her wrist. The humour went out of his face and something much more intimate replaced it. “You did something I couldn’t have done, Xi. Not because you beat my team. Because you built something out of almost nothing, and you made people believe in it.”

“You did that,” she whispered. “You just did that.”

He slid his hands up under her skirt, slowly, watching her face the whole way, and drew her underwear down her legs, and she stepped out of it with one hand braced on his shoulder. He lifted her left knee over his shoulder and kissed the inside of it, and then higher, and then he put his mouth on her, and she had to grab the edge of the desk behind her with both hands.

He took his time. He always did, but this was different: devoted, unhurried, his hands spread on her thighs holding her up when her knees started to go. She looked down at him, at the chairman of An-Tech kneeling on the floor of an office above a dumpling shop with his tie hanging loose and his eyes closed, and the sight of it undid her faster than anything he was doing with his tongue. She said his name, and then she said “Professor,” the old word, and felt him groan against her. She came with her head thrown back and her fingers in his hair and the empty building ringing with it.

He didn’t stop until she pushed him away, laughing and shaking. Then he stood up, and she pulled him down onto her desk by his loosened tie, the bound Halloway proposal sliding off onto the floor, and it was a long time before either of them said anything else.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards she lay against him on the sofa she’d bought second-hand for the meeting corner, too small for both of them, her legs across his lap, smiling at the ceiling.

“Do you know what the best part was?”

“Tell me.”

“When Fenwick rang. I didn’t think about you. I didn’t wonder if you’d be proud. I didn’t wonder whether your team would be angry. I just thought: we did it.”

He looked at her. “Good.”

“Are you hurt? That we beat you?”

He thought about it. “I’m disappointed we lost. I’m not disappointed you won.”

“Good answer.”

“I’ve had a week to prepare it.”

She laughed, and he pulled her closer, and outside in the dark street a moped went by, and downstairs the restaurant’s fridges hummed, and the letters on the glass door caught the light from the street, perfectly straight.

✦ ✦ ✦

The kick-off with Halloway was at nine on Monday. Rachel had the agenda. Calvin had the contacts. Tang Xi had written the first thirty days. A little after nine her phone lit up.

Professor: How’s the new account?

Tang Xi: Difficult already.

Professor: I expected nothing less.

Tang Xi: We have a lot to do.

Professor: Then I’ll leave you to it. For the record, I’d have congratulated you if you’d lost.

She read it twice. Then she wrote back, I know, and put the phone in her bag, and went to the glass door, where Rachel and Calvin were waiting.

“Ready?”

“Yes,” said Tang Xi. “Let’s begin.”

chapters.title: His Father
chapters.desc: Dinner behind his father’s stone screen. A file on her family, a verdict, and a man at a window who says nothing.
chapters.epigraph: “I wasn’t asking you to choose me.”
chapters.content:
The invitation came on a Thursday, and it wasn’t sent to her. It was sent to An Yu, by his father’s office, on the family’s cream card: dinner at the house on Saturday at seven. His father wished to meet the woman he was seeing. There was no question about whether she was free. Only a date, a time, and the chairman’s seal at the bottom.

Tang Xi read it twice on his phone at his kitchen counter and looked up. “Your father.”

“Yes.”

“Why now?”

“He’s heard about you.”

“From whom?”

“Several people, I imagine. Nainai. His secretary. The newsletter.”

“Does he know about Level?”

“He knows you founded an agency.”

“Does he know I beat An-Tech for Halloway?”

An Yu looked at her. “He knows.”

She gave a small laugh. “That’s probably why.”

He didn’t smile. “Xi, you don’t have to go.”

“Do you want me to?”

“I want you to decide for yourself.”

It was a familiar answer now, one he had learned slowly and sometimes painfully to give her. She looked at the card again. “I’ll go. Is there anything I should know?”

“My father is formal.”

“I’d gathered.”

“He’ll ask questions.”

“I can answer questions.”

“I know.”

She watched his face. “Does he dislike me already?”

He took a moment. “I don’t know.”

She accepted that. She noticed that he hadn’t said no.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house didn’t need to show off, and didn’t. It stood on the hill above the harbour behind a high grey wall, at the end of a long drive through camphor trees, with a garden kept by people who had clearly been keeping it for decades. Inside the gate, before you could see the house at all, there was a screen wall of carved stone, the old kind built so that nothing could walk straight in. You had to go round it. Tang Xi thought that was probably the point.

He came round to open her door. She was in dark green, a plain neckline and a fitted jacket, almost no jewellery, her hair pinned back with a few strands loose. He looked at her.

“You look beautiful.”

“Thank you. I’m nervous.”

“About my father?”

“About what he might say.”

“You don’t have to prove anything to him.”

“I know.” At the foot of the steps she stopped. “An Yu. If he doesn’t like me, I want to know. And I don’t want you making excuses for him afterwards.”

“I won’t.”

His father was waiting in the drawing room and didn’t stand up when they came in. He was a little over sixty, grey at the temples, in a dark suit of the kind that is never noticed and costs more than a car; he had the stillness of a man who had never once needed to raise his voice to be obeyed. He chaired the group that owned fourteen hospitals, a medical school and a port. He looked first at his son.

“An Yu.”

“Father.”

Then at her. “Ms. Tang.”

“Mr. Wang.”

“Please sit.”

A housekeeper brought tea. Jasmine. Tang Xi knew it by the scent before the cup was in front of her, and she glanced at An Yu, and saw that he’d noticed too, and that it hadn’t come from him. Someone in this house had been told how she took her tea, and wanted her to know it.

His father lifted his cup. “You’ve recently started an agency.”

“Yes.”

“Level.”

“That’s right.”

“How many people?”

“Two, and me.”

“Clients?”

“Two active, and a third in discussion.”

“Small.”

“At present.”

“Ambitious,” he said, as if it were a diagnosis. “I hear your agency won a pitch against An-Tech.”

She put her cup down. “Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because we understood the client’s immediate problem, and proposed a team and a plan that matched what they actually had ready.”

“An-Tech has a larger team. More experience. Considerably more resources.”

“Those are advantages. They weren’t the only things that mattered on that brief.”

He looked at her, and then at his son. “Did you see the proposals?”

“I saw ours,” said An Yu. “Our own review says Level’s was stronger.”

“Then your team needs to improve.”

“Yes.”

The answer came at once, and Tang Xi looked down at her tea. She hadn’t expected him to be that plain about it.

“How did you meet my son?”

“At school. In Shanghai.”

“Close?”

She smiled slightly. “I talked to him in the library every lunchtime.”

His father turned to An Yu. “For how long?”

“Almost a year.”

“And you spoke to her?”

“Not much.”

“Not at all,” said Tang Xi.

“Yet you remembered him.”

“Yes.”

“And he remembered you.”

She glanced at An Yu. “Apparently.”

His father put his cup down. “That’s an unusual beginning.”

She didn’t know what to say to that. A housekeeper came in to say that dinner was ready.

✦ ✦ ✦

The dining table would have seated twelve; there were three places laid at one end. Steamed garoupa with ginger, greens, a clear soup, braised duck, a delicate dish of silken tofu with crab. It came in careful succession, and his father ate little and watched a great deal.

“Your family,” he said.

She told him simply. Her mother cooked at her aunt’s restaurant in the old town. Her father did some consulting now. They lived modestly, and well enough.

“Your father had a business in Shanghai. A small logistics firm. It owed a little under eight million when the bank called in its loans in June 2015, and your family left the city in a week.”

Tang Xi went still. An Yu looked up from his plate.

“You had us looked into,” she said.

“I have everyone looked into.” He didn’t apologise, and didn’t explain. “What happened?”

“You’ve just told me what happened.”

“I told you what’s in the file. I’m asking what happened.”

She looked at him. Then she answered, because she wasn’t ashamed of it and she wouldn’t let him think she was. “My father spent a year trying to save a company that couldn’t be saved, and borrowed against everything we had to do it. The investors he was waiting for never came. The bank did. My mother worked two jobs for three years so that I could finish school. My father paid back every creditor who’d talk to him, which took him eight years. I was sixteen.”

“That must have been difficult.”

“It was.”

He turned to An Yu. “You knew?”

“Yes. She told me.”

“And you intend to keep running your agency,” his father said to her. “Even when it becomes difficult.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She put down her chopsticks. “Because I chose to build it.”

“Your relationship with my son will attract attention. His position, his family and his interests are not ordinary. You understand that?”

“Yes.”

“People will question your work. Your decisions. Your independence. They’ll assume your success comes from him.”

“They already have. I resigned from my last job over it.”

“And you mean to go on.”

“Yes. Because I don’t think I should have to give up my life to make other people comfortable with who I’m with.”

For the first time something sharpened in his eyes. He looked at her for several seconds. “You speak confidently.”

“I try to speak clearly.”

An Yu said nothing. She glanced at him. He was listening, his face composed. She looked back at his father.

“May I ask you something, Mr. Wang? Why did you invite me?”

“I wanted to meet you.”

“Because I’m with your son, or because I beat his company?”

A pause. “Both.”

“Then I hope you’ve found what you were looking for.”

He didn’t answer, and dinner went on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards the tea was renewed in the drawing room. An Yu stood by the long window looking out at the dark garden. Tang Xi sat on the sofa opposite his father.

“Ms. Tang,” he said. “I’ll be plain. You’re not suitable.”

It wasn’t said with any emphasis. No anger, no contempt, no raised voice. He might have been turning down a proposal that hadn’t met its criteria.

Tang Xi looked at him. Then she nodded. “I know.”

For a moment nobody moved.

“You know?”

“Yes. By every measure you’re using, I’m not. My family lost everything. I have three desks and two employees above a dumpling restaurant. I’m loud, I argue, and I’ve kissed your son in front of his board.” She held his gaze. “I wasn’t asking you to choose me.”

“Marriage is not simply two people choosing each other.”

“I know that.”

“Do you? What happens when his responsibilities become inconvenient? When his family needs something of him? When your ambitions and his collide?”

“Then we’ll have to decide what to do.”

“You speak as if it will be simple.”

“I don’t think it will be.”

He leaned back. “Your circumstances and ours are very different. You’ve built a small agency. My son runs a company with considerable interests, and this family has responsibilities beyond any one person’s preferences. Your lives are not naturally compatible.”

“Perhaps not. But I don’t think you can decide whether two people are compatible by comparing the size of their companies and the families they come from.”

His eyes went briefly to his son. An Yu hadn’t spoken. Not once.

Tang Xi felt something move in her. She hadn’t expected him to argue with his father on her behalf; she had told him she wanted to answer for herself. But she had expected him to say something when the conversation stopped being about her and became a verdict on them. Anything. Instead he stood at the window, silent.

“My son,” said his father, “has spent most of his life making decisions that affect other people. He cannot afford to let his private life become a source of instability.”

“I don’t want to be a source of instability.”

“Intentions are not always relevant.”

“No,” she said. “They aren’t.”

“Then I would prefer that you reconsider this before it becomes more difficult for everyone.”

There was nothing to argue with. He had made his position perfectly clear. She turned her head and looked at An Yu.

He was still by the window. His face was calm. His hands hung loosely at his sides. He looked at her, and said nothing.

She waited. One second. Two. Three. She could almost hear the words he could have said. She isn’t a problem. She hasn’t done anything wrong. I chose her. None came.

She looked away first, and put her cup down on its saucer without a sound. “Thank you for dinner, Mr. Wang.”

His father inclined his head. “You’re welcome.”

She stood up. An Yu turned from the window. “Xi. I’ll get your coat.”

“No. I can manage.”

He hesitated, and then he followed her out.

✦ ✦ ✦

He caught up with her by the screen wall. The housekeeper had already brought her coat, and she put it on herself.

“Let me take you home.”

“Is that all you want to say?”

His face tightened. “No.”

“Then say it.”

He glanced back at the lit windows of the house. “Not here.”

“Why not?”

“Because my father—”

“Your father has already said what he wanted to say.”

He stopped. She could see him looking for the right words, and it made her want to scream, because the right words weren’t difficult. Not tonight. She didn’t need him to defend her. She didn’t need him to tell his father that she was intelligent or capable or that she’d earned her place at that table. She needed him to stand next to her. And he hadn’t.

“You didn’t say anything,” she said. “Not when he said I wasn’t suitable. Not when he told me he’d had my father investigated. Not when he asked me to reconsider us.”

“I wanted you to speak for yourself.”

“I did.”

“I know.”

“Then why were you silent?”

He was quiet. “I didn’t want it to become an argument between my father and me.”

“So you let it become an argument about me?”

He didn’t answer.

“I don’t need you to fight your father every time he disapproves of me. I don’t need a scene. But when someone reduces me to an unsuitable choice, I need to know you won’t stand at a window and let me carry the whole conversation on my own.”

“I understand.”

“Do you?”

“Yes.”

She wanted to believe him. But understanding afterwards wasn’t the same as choosing differently at the time.

“Good night, An Yu.”

He reached for her hand and stopped just before he touched it. “Let me take you home.”

She looked at his hand, and at him. “No.”

He lowered it. She walked round the screen wall and down the drive to the gate, where she had already called a car, and she didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t cry in the car. She didn’t cry in the lift. She didn’t cry when she took off her shoes and hung up her coat. She made tea, and stood in her tiny kitchen looking at the steam coming off the cup.

Professor: Are you home?

Tang Xi: Yes.

A minute went by.

Professor: I should have spoken. I’m sorry.

She sat down on the kitchen floor with her back against the cupboard. She had known his father wouldn’t like her. She hadn’t expected a warm welcome or an easy evening. She hadn’t expected to feel so completely alone while she was sitting in the same room as him. She typed. Deleted it. Typed again.

Tang Xi: I didn’t need you to make him approve of me. I needed to know you wouldn’t let me stand there alone.

It was a long time before he answered.

Professor: I know.

She looked at the two words, and turned the phone off, and sat on the floor until the tea went cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t go home. He went to his office, and stood at the window in the suit he’d worn to dinner. His father had been predictable. The tone, the file, the verdict, even the jasmine had been predictable. What he hadn’t foreseen was Tang Xi’s back walking away from him round a stone wall, not turning.

He had told himself he was letting her speak for herself. He’d told himself that if he intervened the evening would become a quarrel between father and son, and that she wanted to be judged on her own merits. She had been judged anyway, and he had left her to answer alone. He read her message again.

I needed to know you wouldn’t let me stand there alone.

He sat down. For years silence had been the easiest thing. At school he’d used it because he didn’t know how to ask anyone to stay. At work he used it because people told you more when you didn’t speak. With his father he used it because arguing had never once changed anything. He had mistaken the absence of a fight for being in control. And tonight he had let his father pass judgement on the woman he loved while he stood at a window and said nothing. It hadn’t been restraint. It had been a choice, and she had watched him make it.

He picked up his phone to call her, and didn’t.

Professor: I won’t ask you to make this easier for me. I should have stood beside you. I was wrong.

He sent it, and then sat at his desk looking at the city until it began to get light, and she didn’t answer.

chapters.title: The Silence
chapters.desc: She asks why. He has no answer. Two weeks, four handwritten pages and a crooked stamp later, she is at his door.
chapters.content:
She answered him on Sunday afternoon, eighteen hours after his last message.

Tang Xi: Tonight. Your flat. I want to ask you something.

He was at the door when the lift opened, and he didn’t reach for her, and she was grateful for that. They sat at either end of his sofa with the city going dark behind the glass. He had made tea and neither of them touched it.

“Why did you say nothing?”

He knew at once what she meant. His face didn’t change, but something in his attention went sharp. “I told you. I didn’t want it to become an argument.”

“That’s part of it. What’s the rest?”

He could have told her that his father had always been impossible to confront. That arguments in that house had never been loud; they had been long and deliberate and exhausting, and his father had a way of making disagreement feel like a waste of everyone’s time. He could have explained that he’d spent his whole childhood learning not to react. None of it answered her question.

“When he said I wasn’t suitable,” she said, “what were you thinking?”

“That he was wrong.”

“Then why didn’t you say so?”

“I should have.”

“That isn’t what I’m asking.” She wasn’t angry the way she’d been at the house. Her voice was quieter, which made the question harder. “I want to understand what happened inside your head. How you could hear him say that about me and stand there and not say a word.”

He had answers for most things. Sometimes too many. He could explain why a deal had been done, why a negotiation had failed, why someone had behaved as they had. He couldn’t find a single explanation for this that didn’t sound like an excuse.

“I don’t know,” he said.

“You don’t know?”

“No. I knew he was wrong. I knew I disagreed. I knew I should speak.” He looked at his hands. “I don’t know what stopped me.”

She was quiet. He thought she might go on asking. Instead she stood up and picked up her bag.

“Xi.”

“I’m going home.”

He stood too. “Can we finish?”

“We have finished. I don’t need you to have the perfect answer. I don’t need you to say something beautiful. I need you to understand why it hurt, and you don’t yet.”

“I do understand.”

“Do you?” She waited for him to say something more. He didn’t, and something in her face went not disappointed, exactly, but tired. “Good night, An Yu.”

He followed her to the door. “Let me drive you.”

“Please don’t make this about how I get home.”

He stopped. She put her shoes on. At the door she turned round once.

“I love you. That hasn’t changed. But I don’t want to keep explaining why I need you next to me.” She opened the door. “Good night.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He rang on Monday morning. She answered.

“Did you sleep?”

“Yes.”

“Are you free tonight?”

“I have a client dinner.”

“Tomorrow?”

“I’ll let you know.”

He waited, and she didn’t add anything.

“An Yu. I don’t want to pretend last night didn’t happen. So don’t keep ringing as if we’re both waiting for the right moment to go back to normal.”

He closed his eyes. “Understood.”

At eleven he chaired a meeting. At one he went through a regional investment proposal. At four he took his finance director apart over a discrepancy in the quarterly forecast. He did everything he was supposed to do, and every time he went back to his office he found himself looking at his phone, and there was nothing on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her days were full, and she made sure of it. Halloway had seen the first research findings and wanted the launch brought forward a fortnight. Rachel rebuilt the strategy. Calvin rebuilt the schedule. Tang Xi renegotiated the scope and the fees and fought the finance director to a draw. She had no time to sit and think about An Yu. Or rather, she had a hundred small moments a day in which she thought about him, and refused to let any of them become the middle of her day.

On the Friday, at eighteen minutes past nine at night, as she came off a call with Halloway, her phone lit.

Professor: Have you eaten?

Tang Xi: Yes.

Professor: Good. I hope the call went well.

Tang Xi: It did. Thank you.

She put the phone down. Across the room Rachel looked up and opened her mouth, and looked at Tang Xi’s face, and closed it again, and went back to her screen without asking anything at all, which was how Tang Xi knew how bad she looked.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stopped calling after that. Not because he’d stopped wanting to hear her voice. Because he had begun to understand that every time he reached for her without knowing what he was going to say, he was asking her to make the distance easier for him, and he didn’t want to do that any more.

He thought about the drawing room constantly. His father’s even voice. Tang Xi on the sofa with her hands round a cup. Her answer: I know. She had said it without hesitating. She hadn’t asked his father to like her. She hadn’t pleaded. She had simply accepted that he thought her unsuitable, and refused to let it decide anything. And he had watched.

He’d thought his restraint was neutral. It hadn’t been. His silence had put the whole weight of the room on her. He understood that now. What he still couldn’t understand was why, in the moment, he’d been unable to say the simplest thing in the world: I chose her.

He couldn’t explain it away with his childhood, or his father, or the habits of thirty years. Those things might have made him. They didn’t excuse him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She saw him for the first time in eleven days, on the Thursday, in a hotel lobby. Level had a workshop for Halloway on the fifth floor and An-Tech had a meeting on the same floor, and she was standing by the reception desk with Rachel when he came in through the revolving door. He saw her immediately. For a moment neither of them moved. Then he came over.

“Ms. Tang.”

“Mr. Wang.”

“Good afternoon,” said Rachel, looking from one to the other.

“Good afternoon.”

“Are you here for a meeting?” Tang Xi asked.

“Yes.”

“Then we won’t keep you.”

“How’s Halloway?”

“On schedule.”

“Good.” A pause. “I hope you’re well.”

“Thank you. You too.”

“Our room’s ready,” said Rachel.

Tang Xi looked back at him once as she turned. “Good afternoon.”

He watched her walk to the lift, and didn’t follow, and stood in the middle of the lobby for some time after the doors had closed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first page took him forty minutes that night, and he threw it away.

He’d bought the paper years ago, heavy cream sheets for correspondence that had never seemed important enough to deserve them. His first attempt began, Xi, I have been thinking about what happened. It was a poor beginning, and he crossed it out. The second began, I am sorry for what I did at my father’s house. It sounded like a statement prepared for a board. He put the pen down and sat for a long time looking at the blank sheet.

He had written thousands of emails. He had signed contracts, board papers, formal letters. He had never once written to Tang Xi. Not at school. Not when she left Shanghai. Not in all the years he’d remembered her. She had written to him: one line inside a paper crane. He had kept it for eleven years. And the first time he had something important to say to her face, he had said nothing.

He took another sheet, and this time he didn’t try to sound composed.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wrote four pages over two nights, by hand, with no computer, and showed it to nobody. Nobody corrected the grammar or suggested a better opening. The handwriting was neat at the top of the first page. By the third it had started to come apart.

He wrote about his father, and the house behind the stone screen, and what he had learned there: that silence could end a conversation without ever settling it. He wrote that he had spent years believing that refusing to argue was a kind of strength, and that he had confused not reacting with not being affected. And then he wrote the part that took him longest.

You asked me why I said nothing.
I have no answer that makes me look better. When he said you were unsuitable, I wasn’t looking for words. I was waiting for the conversation to end. I was afraid of the argument, of what it would cost, of the old familiar misery of disagreeing with him, and I let you carry it so I wouldn’t have to. I knew what I thought. I knew what I should say. I chose not to say it.
I can’t ask you to see that as something harmless. It wasn’t harmless to you.
I’m not going to promise I’ll never be silent again. There will be times I need to think, times I won’t know what to say, times I get it wrong. But I don’t want to use silence to avoid choosing. You should never have to stand alone while I decide whether speaking is worth the trouble.

On the fourth page he wrote about the library. About a boy who had listened to her talk every lunchtime for a year and never once told her that he came at twelve instead of half past so that he’d be there before her. About a man who had found her again and thought that wanting her was enough. It wasn’t. He had to be someone she could rely on when wanting her was the easy part and everything else was hard.

I love you. I have loved you for longer than I knew how to say it. But I understand now that how long I have felt something doesn’t make the way I treat you matter any less.
I’m not asking you to come back because I wrote this. I only wanted you to know what I should have said while you were standing in that room.
I should have stood beside you.
From the person who never talks,
An Yu

He put the pen down. Four pages. His first letter to her. He folded them, put them in an envelope, and wrote her name and the address of her flat on the front from memory.

In the morning he asked Ding what a stamp cost.

Ding looked at the envelope in his hand for a long moment. “I can have it couriered to Ms. Tang within the hour, Mr. Wang.”

“No. I want it to go in the post. With everything else. She can open it when she likes, or not at all.”

Ding went and bought him a stamp, and came back, and watched his employer stick it on himself, slightly crooked, and walk to the postbox at the corner of the street in the rain without an umbrella.

✦ ✦ ✦

It came on Saturday, among a gas bill and a flyer for a gym. She knew the handwriting before she’d picked it up off the mat, though she had almost never seen it: the same careful hand she remembered from the margins of a maths textbook across a library table.

She didn’t open it straight away. She put it on the coffee table and went to the market and bought vegetables she didn’t need, and came back and spent an hour rearranging the little bookshelf in her living room, which didn’t need it either. Behind a row of paperbacks she found the photograph from the library, printed from her phone in February: the old table by the window, the winter sun, her own hand on the wood, smiling. An Yu not looking at the camera, though Mrs. Hua had told him to twice. Looking at her.

She sat on the floor with it in one hand, and with the other she opened the envelope.

She read all four pages. Then she read the third one again, where the writing came apart. When she got to the last line she put the pages in her lap and sat with her back against the bookshelf, and cried, properly, for the first time in two weeks, and then she laughed, wetly, at From the person who never talks.

She missed him. That was the most inconvenient part of it. She missed the way he listened when she talked about work, and the way he looked at her when she teased him, and his quiet flat and his terrible noodles and the careful way he remembered small things. She missed him without wanting to forget what had happened. She had wondered all week whether he was waiting for her to make the first move, and told herself she’d made the first move often enough.

But he hadn’t sent a car, or flowers, or a courier. He had put a stamp on it and let the post decide.

✦ ✦ ✦

At twenty to nine on Sunday evening his doorbell rang.

He hadn’t been expecting anyone. He put down the report he hadn’t been reading and went to the door, and opened it, and she was standing there in a dark coat with her hair loose round her shoulders. Her face was composed. Her eyes weren’t.

“Xi.”

“Hello.”

He stepped back at once. “Come in.”

She didn’t move. “You wrote to me.”

“Yes.”

“By post.”

“Yes.”

“Why not a courier? Why not leave it on my desk?”

“I didn’t want to decide how you’d get it. Or when.”

She considered that. “I read it. Twice. The third page three times.” She held his eyes. “I don’t know if I’m ready to go back to how it was. And I don’t want you to think everything’s mended because I’m standing here.”

“I don’t.”

“Then what do you think?”

“I think I’m glad you’re here.”

Something in her face gave. He didn’t reach for her. He didn’t assume she’d come to be kissed. He stood in his own doorway and left it to her.

“I missed you,” she said, quietly.

“Xi.”

“I missed you, and I was angry with you. Both of those are true.”

“Yes.”

She looked at his mouth, and back at his eyes. “Are you going to ask me in?”

A faint, almost disbelieving smile. “You can come in.”

She stepped over the threshold, and he closed the distance before the door had swung shut behind her. His hand came to her cheek and the other to her waist and he kissed her, and it was nothing like the measured way he usually kissed her. There was two weeks in it. There was the drawing room in it, and a stamp stuck on crooked in the rain, and everything he had been holding back since he was sixteen years old. She took hold of his lapels and kissed him back just as hard, and he walked her backwards a step and her shoulders met the half-open door, and it swung and clicked shut behind her with the two of them pressed against it, and neither of them heard it close.

When they finally came apart his forehead was against hers and his breath was ragged. She put her face against his chest and he wrapped both arms round her and held on.

“I missed you,” he said into her hair.

“I know.”

After a while she looked up. “Four pages.”

“Yes.”

“You’ve never written me a letter before. Not even at school.”

“No.”

“From the person who never talks.” Her mouth shook. “That was mean.”

“It was true.”

“I’m keeping the letter. You kept my crane for eleven years. I’m keeping this for longer.”

“It’s yours.”

“I haven’t forgiven all of it yet.”

He brushed his thumb across her knuckles. “I’ll give you time.”

“Don’t just give me time. Be here.”

He turned his hand and held hers properly. “I will.”

She kissed him once. Then again. The third time she didn’t stop, and she unbuttoned his shirt with fingers that weren’t quite steady and he lifted her off her feet against the door and carried her down the corridor, and for the first time in two weeks they went to bed together, slowly and then not slowly at all, without either of them pretending that nothing had happened.

Much later, in the dark, with her head on his chest, she said, “Next time, try saying it before I have to leave.”

“I will.”

“Out loud.”

“Out loud,” he said, and to prove it, he said it: everything on the third page, in the dark, in his own voice, while she listened.

chapters.title: His Family’s Table
chapters.desc: New Year in the north hills: sixty Wangs, a coin in a dumpling, Nainai’s red envelope, and a toast that leaves her out.
chapters.content:
By the time their car came up through the bare trees on the second day of the New Year, the courtyard of Nainai’s house was already full.

It had been cold in the north since the first week of January. Frost still lay along the shaded edges of the stone path, and the old trees reached their black branches over the courtyard walls. Red lanterns hung under the eaves, bright against the grey afternoon, and new couplets in black and gold had been pasted either side of the gate, and the character for luck on the door had been hung upside down, the way it always was, so that luck would pour in. Somewhere beyond the main house somebody was letting off firecrackers, and the cracks came back off the hills a second later like an echo of an argument.

Tang Xi got out and pulled her coat tight. “How many people?”

“About sixty.”

“About?”

“My father said sixty.”

“Did he count them?”

“I didn’t ask.”

“You brought me to a house with sixty of your relatives on the second day of New Year, which is the day married daughters go home to their families, which means every aunt in the clan is here, and you said family dinner.”

“It is family dinner.”

“Sixty people is a small conference.”

He nearly smiled. “Would you prefer family gathering?”

“No. That’s worse.”

The smile came then, brief and real. She took his hand and he put both of their hands into his coat pocket. “All right. Let’s go.”

They hadn’t reached the steps when a voice came from the top of them. “You’re late.”

Nainai stood in the doorway in a deep red quilted jacket and a dark scarf, her polished stick planted on the stone beside her, wearing the face of someone who had been waiting long enough to have found fault with the entire household.

“We’re four minutes early, Nainai.”

“Then why have I been standing here?” Her eyes went past him. “Tang Xi. Let me look at you.”

Tang Xi went up the steps. “Happy New Year, Nainai.”

“Happy New Year.” The old woman took her hand in both of hers and frowned at it. “Your hands are cold.”

“I’m fine.”

“That’s what people say when they’re cold.” She turned towards the house without letting go. “Come. I’ve saved you a place.”

“Where?” said An Yu, following.

“Next to me. Where else?”

“Nainai, the seating—”

“I did the seating.”

He stopped. She turned her head. “You have a problem with where I’ve put her?”

“No.”

“Then don’t ask questions.”

Tang Xi glanced back at him. He gave her a small, resigned look. It was going to be a long evening.

✦ ✦ ✦

Inside it was much louder. Relatives had filled every room. Children ran between the chairs with red envelopes already sticking out of their pockets; older people sat in knots by the stoves talking about the weather and the hospitals and who had married whom; staff moved through all of it carrying tea and sunflower seeds and plates of candied lotus root. A woman in her fifties in a fur collar came up to greet Nainai almost before Tang Xi had her coat off.

“Auntie! You’ve come down early this year.”

“I came when I wanted.”

The woman laughed politely, and her eyes moved to Tang Xi. “And this is…?”

“Tang Xi,” said Nainai, as if the name should be enough. The woman waited. The stick came up an inch. “My grandson’s future wife, if the two of them would stop taking so long about it.”

Tang Xi nearly choked on the tea someone had just put in her hand.

“Nainai,” said An Yu.

“What?”

“Please.”

“Don’t please me. You should have brought her ten years ago.”

The woman’s eyebrows had gone up and stayed there. “Ah. So this is the young lady. I’ve heard about you.”

Tang Xi wondered from whom, and decided she didn’t want to know.

“Go and greet the others,” said Nainai, tapping the floor once. “Don’t stand there staring.” The woman retreated, and Nainai took Tang Xi’s arm. “Come. I’ll show you.”

“You don’t have to announce things like that,” Tang Xi said under her breath.

“Why not?”

“Because people will talk.”

“They talk anyway. At least now they’ll have the facts.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The dining hall had been opened end to end: one long table down the middle, two more at either end, white porcelain and red paper and branches of plum blossom in tall jars between the place settings. There were chairs enough for the whole family, and more than enough family to fill them.

Nainai went straight to the middle of the central table and pointed with her stick at the chair beside her own. Not at the end. Not at the side table where girlfriends and new cousins-in-law could be put without anyone having to decide anything. At her right hand, at the centre of the table, in the seat Tang Xi was fairly sure had been someone else’s for twenty years.

“Here.”

“Are you sure? There must be people who usually sit here.”

“Such as?”

Tang Xi had no answer.

“Then sit.”

She sat. An Yu moved towards the chair on her other side, and the stick came up.

“Not there. Opposite me.”

“Why?”

“So I can see whether you eat.”

He looked at Tang Xi, who was trying hard not to laugh. “Go on,” she whispered, and he went round the table and sat down facing them, and Nainai looked satisfied.

It held for about four minutes. Then an elderly uncle stopped beside Tang Xi’s chair and looked at the place card and then at her. “Isn’t this seat usually kept for—”

The stick rose. “Kept for whom?”

“Nothing, Auntie.”

“Then sit down.”

He sat. A teenage cousin wandered over and stood staring at Tang Xi with open curiosity, and Nainai tapped the floor. “Do you want something?”

“No, Nainai.”

“Then why are you standing there?”

The cousin fled. Tang Xi leaned in. “You’re frightening everyone.”

“Good. They should be frightened of their elders. It’s New Year.”

“She’s been doing this since we arrived,” An Yu said, reaching for his tea.

The stick swung round at him. “And you should be grateful I haven’t started on you.”

Tang Xi laughed out loud, and across the table An Yu went still and looked at her. Not the careful laugh she used in meeting rooms. The bright, unguarded one from the library. He watched her a moment longer than he needed to, and she caught him.

“That’s your answer to everything.”

“Not everything.”

“Most things.”

“Stop whispering,” said Nainai. “You’re at a family table.” Tang Xi sat up straight. An Yu looked into his tea. Nainai looked extremely pleased with herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wang Xing Yue and Elara came in as the first dishes arrived. He was in a dark wool coat over a plain jumper, calm as always, but with something under the calm that Tang Xi hadn’t seen in him before: he had been on leave from his hospital since the eighth of December, for reasons the table had collectively agreed not to mention, and he had the look of a man who hadn’t slept properly since. Elara walked beside him looking round the hall with undisguised interest. It was her first New Year in the north.

“Xing Yue,” said Nainai.

“Nainai.” He bent and kissed her cheek.

“You’re late.”

“I know.”

“And you.” Nainai looked Elara up and down. “First time here at New Year.”

“Yes, Nainai. Happy New Year.”

“Cold?”

“A little.”

“Then sit. Don’t stand about. Both of you, there.” The stick pointed at the two chairs on either side of An Yu.

Xing Yue looked at the arrangement. “You’re running the whole table?”

“Someone has to.” Nainai sniffed. “Yu Chen and his girl have gone to her family’s for New Year. Very correct. Very modern. I’ll have words with him in March.”

Xing Yue sat down next to his brother. “How are you?”

“Fine.”

“Still answering like that?”

“Yes.”

Xing Yue shook his head and poured tea for his wife. Elara reached across the table and squeezed Tang Xi’s hand. “Happy New Year. I’m so glad you’re here. I was afraid I’d be the only new face.”

“Me too.”

“Wait until tomorrow morning,” said Xing Yue. “You’ll both understand why the whole north complains about the cold.”

“You said it would be romantic,” Elara said.

“I said the snow would be romantic.”

“There isn’t any snow.”

“That’s not my fault.”

Nainai looked from one to the other. “Three years married and you still argue like that.”

“We’re having a conversation.”

“That’s what people call arguing when they want to sound polite,” said Nainai, and Elara hid her smile in her cup.

Tang Xi looked across at An Yu. He was watching his brother with faint amusement, and it was strange to see him here. At home he was the man who remembered how she took her tea, who made terrible noodles, who had written four pages by hand because he’d finally understood that some things couldn’t be left unsaid. Here he was also a grandson and a younger brother, a member of a family whose habits had been set long before she came into his life. She wondered how many versions of him she hadn’t met yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

Sixty people at one long table made conversation difficult, but the family had its own rhythm. Stories travelled from one end to the other and back again. Someone laughed too loudly. A child was told to sit properly. An uncle complained that the fish had too many bones and somebody told him he’d grown too fussy in his old age.

The dumplings came in great steaming platters: lamb and carrot, the northern way, and egg and chive for the ones who didn’t eat lamb. Somewhere in one of them, Nainai announced, there was a coin, and whoever bit on it would have the luckiest year, and there was a general rush of chopsticks. Tang Xi bit into her third dumpling and stopped, and took the coin out of her mouth, a small, old, worn thing, and held it up in dismay.

The table erupted.

“Of course,” said Nainai, not even looking. “Eat. Don’t swallow it.”

Tang Xi stared at her. “Did you—”

“I don’t know what you’re talking about,” said Nainai, and put a piece of fish in her bowl. The fish itself, a whole steamed carp, sat in the middle of the table and was carefully not finished, because you always left some, so that there would be more than enough in the year to come. Nainai ate little. She was more interested in watching everyone else.

“Why aren’t you giving her food?” she demanded of An Yu.

“I can help myself,” said Tang Xi.

“He’s sitting there with two hands.”

An Yu picked up his chopsticks and put the best piece of lamb on the table into Tang Xi’s bowl, across the whole width of it, in front of everyone. Nainai nodded. “Better.”

“You’re very busy tonight, Nainai,” said Xing Yue.

“Someone has to look after people.”

Elara leaned towards Tang Xi. “She hasn’t changed since September.”

“Does she always point the stick at people?”

“Only the ones she likes.”

“I can hear you,” said Nainai.

“Of course, Nainai,” said Elara.

Then Nainai reached into her jacket and took out a red envelope, plump and sealed, and put it on the table beside Tang Xi’s bowl, without a word. The conversation around them faltered. The aunt in the fur collar, two places down, stopped with her chopsticks in the air. An elder giving a young woman a red envelope at the family table, the first time she came home with a grandson, wasn’t a small thing, and every adult at that table knew exactly what it was.

“Nainai,” Tang Xi said, low. “I can’t—”

“You can. You will. Put it in your pocket and don’t open it at the table, it’s rude.” Nainai picked up her tea. “And don’t argue with me on New Year.”

Tang Xi put it in her pocket. Her hand wasn’t quite steady.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the far end of the central table, An Yu’s father stood up with a glass of wine, and the room went quiet.

“Another year has gone. I hope everyone has come safely, and that the year ahead brings health and stability to the family.”

He spoke for several minutes, calmly, without ever raising his voice. He talked about the hospitals and the medical school and the port. He thanked the senior members of the family for their work and the younger ones for carrying on their responsibilities. He didn’t need to be loud. People listened. Tang Xi kept her hands folded beside her bowl. She had sat in his drawing room. She knew the precision of him, the way he could make a room feel like a board meeting without changing his tone.

He raised his glass. “To the family. To those who have carried our name with dignity, and to those who will carry it on.”

The room lifted its glasses. Tang Xi lifted hers too.

But the toast had gone over her head. Not by accident. He had spoken about family, and the name, and the people who carried it, and he hadn’t acknowledged that she was in the room. Every person at that table had just watched Nainai give her a red envelope, and every person at that table had just watched the chairman decline to see her. She took a small sip.

Across the table An Yu hadn’t moved. His glass was still on the cloth. He was looking at his father. For one brief moment she wondered whether he’d do what he hadn’t done in October, and let the silence settle over her like snow. Then he pushed his chair back.

The sound was quiet. At the central table, everyone heard it. He stood up.

“An Yu?” said his father.

An Yu picked up his glass. “Father. I’d like to add something.”

The room was entirely still. His father gave the smallest nod. “Go ahead.”

An Yu looked down the length of the table, at sixty people and three generations of his family, and then he turned to Tang Xi.

“To Tang Xi.”

She went still.

“This year she built her own company,” he said, and his voice was perfectly steady. “She has worked for everything she has, and she did it without asking anyone to make room for her. She’s at this table because I asked her to come. More than that, she’s here because I want her here, next to me, now and in every year I’m allowed.” He lifted his glass a little higher. “I’m glad she’s here. I hope she’ll sit at this table for a great many New Years.”

For a moment the room was completely silent.

Then Nainai lifted her glass. “Good.” The stick came up and swept the length of the table. “Now drink. Why is everyone staring?”

Laughter broke out, ragged at first and then spreading. Xing Yue raised his glass. “To Tang Xi.”
