“To Tang Xi,” said Elara.

One by one, then in clusters, then all down the long table, the others lifted their glasses. The uncle who had asked about the seat. The aunt in the fur collar. The teenage cousin, red. Tang Xi’s fingers had tightened round the stem of her glass, and she didn’t look away from An Yu once. He hadn’t raised his voice. He hadn’t challenged his father or turned the evening into a scene. He had simply stood up and said her name. And this time he hadn’t left her to say it alone.

At the far end of the table his father sat down, and drank, and said nothing at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu sat. Nainai leaned across the table towards him.

“That was better.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. You should have done it the first time.” The stick tapped his chair leg. “Do you understand?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” She turned to Tang Xi. “Eat. The fish is getting cold.”

Across the table Xing Yue poured more tea for his wife and sat back and looked at his younger brother for a long moment without saying anything. Then he lifted his cup a fraction of an inch. It wasn’t quite a toast. An Yu understood it perfectly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, while the older relatives drifted to the drawing room and the children were let loose on the courtyard with sparklers, Tang Xi slipped outside into the cold, and An Yu followed her a minute later and put his coat round her shoulders.

“You’ll freeze.”

“I’ve been out here less than a minute.”

“Still.”

They stood under the lanterns. From the house came laughter and the clatter of dishes being cleared and a child shrieking with joy.

“You stood up,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You didn’t hesitate.”

He looked at the house. “I hesitated. I had to decide whether I was going to let it happen again.” He turned to her. “I kept thinking about what I wrote. That you shouldn’t have to stand alone while I decide whether speaking is worth the trouble.”

“I remember.”

He took her hand. “I don’t want you ever to wonder where I’m standing.”

“Your father won’t be pleased.”

“He doesn’t have to be.”

“An Yu.”

“I know what you’re going to say. I can’t make everything about whether I can disagree with him. But I can decide what I’ll let him say about you while I’m standing beside you.”

She looked at him, and smiled. “That sounded rehearsed.”

“It wasn’t.”

“Good. It was a little too polished.”

The corner of his mouth moved. She took the red envelope out of the pocket of his coat, where she’d moved it for safety, and turned it over in her fingers without opening it.

“Do you know what this means?”

“Yes.”

“Does everyone in there know what it means?”

“Everyone over the age of twelve.”

“She did it on purpose. Before your father’s toast.”

“Nainai has never done anything by accident in her life.”

“She told me she’d saved me a place.”

“She did.”

“And you were across the table so you could see me.”

“So she could see me.”

“Did you know?”

“I suspected.”

“You could have warned me.”

“You’d have argued with her.”

“Obviously.”

“That’s why I didn’t.”

She laughed and hit his arm lightly, and he caught her hand and kissed her. It was a quiet kiss under the red lanterns, the cold all round them and the warm house at their backs, and when it ended she kept her forehead against his.

“Happy New Year, An Yu.”

“Happy New Year, Xi.”

From the doorway a stick rapped sharply on stone. They sprang apart. Nainai was standing on the step.

“Are you two staying out here all night?”

“No, Nainai.”

“Then come in.” The stick swung to An Yu. “And you. Stop making her stand in the cold.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The family had started taking photographs. Nainai insisted on the centre of the sofa. Xing Yue stood behind her with Elara beside him; aunts and uncles arranged themselves round the arms; cousins crammed in wherever there was room. Tang Xi hovered at the edge.

“Tang Xi. Here.” The stick pointed at the cushion beside her.

Tang Xi sat. An Yu moved to stand behind her, and Nainai looked up at him. “Not there. Beside her.”

He came round and stood at Tang Xi’s shoulder, and Nainai examined the arrangement and nodded.

“Everyone, look here,” said the photographer.

“Wait,” said Nainai, and the photographer waited. She looked round the whole crowded group. “Nobody blink.”

“Nainai, that’s impossible,” said a cousin.

“Then try harder.”

The camera flashed. Tang Xi smiled. An Yu looked at her instead of the camera, the way he had in a library in Shanghai a year before, and this time she noticed, and didn’t turn away, and let the photograph catch him at it. When Nainai demanded another, she stayed exactly where she was. Beside him. At the family’s table. Not because everyone had agreed she belonged there, but because he had stood up and said her name.

chapters.title: He Says No to His Father
chapters.desc: Red dog day, when everyone quarrels. His father asks her to move. He picks up his bowl and moves with her.
chapters.content:
The snow came before breakfast on the third day of the New Year.

It started, fine white flakes settling along the courtyard walls and the dark tiles of the roof. By nine the garden had gone pale, every branch carried a thin white line, and the stone path outside the main hall was slick. Tang Xi stood at the window of the guest room with a cup of tea in both hands and her breath misting the glass.

“Does it snow like this every year?”

“Not every year.” An Yu came in from the corridor, sleeves rolled to the forearm, hair still damp. “I’ve never seen it at New Year since I was a child.”

“I’ve never seen snow at New Year in my life.”

“Then enjoy it.”

“I am.” She leaned against his arm. Last night had gone better than she’d let herself expect: Nainai’s chair, Xing Yue and Elara, the coin in the dumpling, the red envelope she still hadn’t opened, and An Yu standing up in front of sixty people to add her name to his father’s toast. She’d thought, falling asleep, that it might be enough for one visit. But the family was gathering again for the midday meal, and his father hadn’t said a word to either of them since the toast, and she didn’t think that kind of silence was the end of anything.

“Are you worried?” she asked.

“About my father? No.”

“Not even a little?”

He thought about it. “I know what he thinks.”

“That isn’t the same as knowing what he’ll do.”

“He may say something.”

“And?”

“And I’ll answer.”

She looked up at him. It wasn’t a promise made to calm her down. It was a decision. She put her tea on the sill and took his hand.

“All right.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nainai was already at the table when they came in, the stick hooked over the back of her chair.

“Do you know what day it is?” she said, before anyone could greet her.

“The third day, Nainai.”

“Chi gou. Red dog day. The day everyone quarrels. In my mother’s house nobody went visiting on the third day; you stayed at home and swept and kept your mouth shut, so you didn’t fight with anyone.” She looked down the long table, which was almost full again, with a dozen more relatives who’d come in late the night before. “And your father has invited half the family to lunch.”

“Perhaps he’s not superstitious,” said Tang Xi.

“He’s not anything. That’s his trouble.” Nainai patted the chair beside her own. “Sit.”

An Yu pulled it out for her and went round to sit opposite again, next to his brother. Elara, on Xing Yue’s other side, was gazing out of the windows at the snow with her chin on her hand.

“It’s beautiful.”

“You’re enjoying it now,” said Xing Yue. “Wait until you have to walk through it.”

“Are you going to carry me?”

“If necessary.”

Tang Xi smiled into her tea, and Nainai noticed. “What are you smiling at?”

“Nothing.”

“Then eat.”

Across the table Xing Yue leaned towards An Yu and said, quietly, so that only his brother could hear, “Father hasn’t finished.”

“I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The meal began with the usual greetings. Children collected more red envelopes, old people talked about the year ahead, and the conversation moved between family matters and the hospitals and the snow. Tang Xi listened more than she talked. She was starting to learn the shape of the Wang family: who interrupted whom, who was allowed to tease the elders, which cousins were always late, which aunts knew every piece of news before it happened.

She was reaching for a dish when a voice came from the head of the table.

“Ms. Tang.”

An Yu’s father was looking at her. She put her chopsticks down. “Yes, Mr. Wang?”

“How long are you staying in the north?”

“Until tomorrow afternoon.”

“Your agency has no work over the holiday?”

“Some carries on. Rachel’s covering anything urgent.”

“Your business is still very small. Three people.”

“Including me.”

“Do you intend to grow?”

“If the work needs it.”

“A cautious answer.”

“I’d rather grow at the pace we can deliver.”

A relative halfway down murmured that that was sensible. His father didn’t acknowledge it.

“My son tells me you won a contract against An-Tech. And that you intend to keep competing with agencies far larger than yours.”

“Yes.”

“Confidence is useful. It becomes an obstacle when someone doesn’t understand the size of what they’re challenging.”

“I agree,” said Tang Xi. He seemed to wait for more, and she gave it to him. “That’s why I try to understand the work before I decide whether to take it on.”

The silence that followed was short, and it was broken by the stick hitting the floor.

“Enough business,” said Nainai. “It’s New Year.”

“I’m only asking.”

“And she’s answered. Let her eat.”

A few people smiled. Tang Xi looked down at her bowl, grateful. Across the table An Yu caught his grandmother’s eye, and she gave him a small nod, as if to say she’d done her part, and the rest was his.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next part began over a chair. It was a small thing at first. One of the older men of the family, a cousin of An Yu’s father who sat on the board of the medical school, came along the central table holding his cup and stopped behind Tang Xi.

“Ms. Tang, would you mind changing places? We usually keep this end for the senior members. My brother-in-law would like to sit nearer the chairman.”

It was said quite politely. Tang Xi looked at Nainai, and before she could answer the stick had lifted.

“What end?”

The man smiled. “Nothing serious, Auntie. We just thought it would be more appropriate for—”

“More appropriate for whom?”

He hesitated. “For the family.”

Nainai’s face hardened. “She is sitting with the family.”

The man glanced towards the head of the table. “Chairman, perhaps—”

An Yu’s father put down his cup. “Mother, your seating isn’t necessarily what suits the whole table.”

Nainai turned her head slowly. “What did you say?”

“I said we should think about the seating properly.”

“Then think about it. She’s staying where she is.”

His father looked at Tang Xi then, directly, for the first time since the toast. “Ms. Tang. I believe you understand that some seats in this family carry a particular meaning.”

She understood. He wasn’t asking her to move because the table was crowded. He was asking her to agree, in front of sixty people, that she had no right to sit where Nainai had put her.

She laid her napkin beside her plate. She wouldn’t make Nainai fight for her in front of all these people. “I don’t mind moving, if it’s necessary.”

Nainai rounded on her. “It isn’t.”

“Nainai—”

“No. I put you there.”

His father’s eyes went to his son. “An Yu.”

An Yu had said nothing through any of it. Now he put down his chopsticks. “Yes, Father?”

“Ask Ms. Tang to move.”

The room seemed to get smaller. The neighbouring tables went quiet. A few relatives looked down at their plates; more watched openly. Tang Xi felt An Yu’s eyes on her before she saw him look up. He didn’t look angry. He looked entirely calm. And then he stood up.

“No.”

It wasn’t loud. It wasn’t hostile. It carried perfectly down the length of the table.

His father looked at him. “What?”

“I said no.” An Yu rested one hand on the back of his chair. “She sits where I sit.”

Silence.

Then he picked up his bowl and his chopsticks, and walked round the end of the table, past three uncles and a great-aunt, to the chair on Tang Xi’s other side, where a cousin of nineteen was sitting with his mouth open. The boy scrambled up and fled with his plate. An Yu set his bowl down beside hers and sat, so that the two of them were side by side at Nainai’s right hand, and laid his chopsticks straight.

“If she moves,” he said to his father across the table, “I move with her. She’s here with me. I asked her to come. I want her next to me. And I won’t ask her to get up because somebody has decided she doesn’t belong at this table.”

His father’s eyes narrowed slightly. “Don’t make this more difficult than it needs to be.”

“I’m not.”

“You are contradicting me in front of the whole family.”

“Yes.”

Somewhere at the far end a man shifted in his chair. His father looked at him. “You think this is an appropriate way to behave?”

“I think asking her to give up her seat was inappropriate.”

“That’s enough.”

“No, Father.”

It was the first time Tang Xi had ever heard him speak to his father like that. Not loudly. Not angrily. But without stepping back an inch.

His father’s face went perfectly still. “You seem to have forgotten where you are.”

An Yu’s reply was quiet. “I know exactly where I am.”

A long pause. Then his father pushed back his chair, and the sound of its legs on the floor was sharp in the silence. He stood up, laid his napkin beside his plate, and looked at the table.

“Carry on.”

He didn’t look at Tang Xi. He didn’t look at An Yu again. He walked out of the dining hall, and nobody spoke until the doors had closed behind him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It lasted several seconds. Then someone at the far end cleared his throat, and a small child asked loudly whether the grown-ups were still eating, and Nainai lifted her stick.

“Of course we’re eating. Why wouldn’t we be?” She turned to the staff. “Bring the soup.” They moved at once. Nainai turned to the cousin from the medical school board, who was still standing behind Tang Xi’s chair with his cup. “And you. Sit down. You’re blocking the dish.”

He sat down quickly. A few people tried to start talking again. It was awkward at first, and then it wasn’t, quite; the room slowly found its noise.

Under the table, An Yu’s knee was against hers. “Are you all right?”

“Yes.”

“Are you sure?”

“Yes.”

Nainai reached across and put a piece of fish in Tang Xi’s bowl. “Eat.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. You’re too thin.”

“She’s fine,” said An Yu.

The stick came round. “Did I ask you?”

Tang Xi laughed. It came out a little shakier than she meant it to, and he looked at her, and the tension went out of his shoulders, and his hand found hers under the table and held on, and she held on back. Red dog day, she thought. Everyone quarrels.

✦ ✦ ✦

The meal ended slowly. Some of the family went through to the drawing room. Some went out to take photographs in the snow. The children had been let into the courtyard, where they were already throwing it at each other in fistfuls and shrieking.

An Yu took her coat from the girl by the door and helped her into it, and they went out into the white courtyard. It had snowed all through lunch. It lay along the stone railings and the edges of the garden and on the lanterns, which glowed through it red and soft. The air was cold enough to make her cheeks ache, and she hardly noticed.

They walked without speaking to the far end, under the old persimmon tree, where nobody from the house could see them. Then she stopped.

“You said no.”

“Yes.”

“In front of everybody. Knowing he’d walk out.”

“I knew he might.”

“Why didn’t you wait? Say it to him later, in his study?”

“Because he asked you to move in front of everyone. I didn’t want you to sit there for one second wondering whether I agreed with him.” He took her hand. “I should have said it in October. I should never have let you wonder.”

She looked down at their hands, gloved and bare. “Do you know what I liked most?”

“What?”

“You didn’t tell him I was suitable.”

“You don’t need me to certify you.”

“Exactly. You just said I sit where you sit. And then you got up and did it.” She was laughing a little. “You walked round the whole table with your bowl. That poor boy.”

He brushed snow off her shoulder. “Because you do.”

“Even if your father hates it?”

“Even then.”

“Even if the whole family thinks I’m in the wrong chair?”

“Then the whole family is wrong.”

She looked at him, with the snow coming down between them and catching in his hair and on his eyelashes. Then she took hold of the front of his coat with her gloved fist and pulled him down to her, and kissed him first.

It was hers, all of it. She kissed him under the falling snow with one hand twisted in his lapel and the other, bare and cold, against his cheek, and he made a sound against her mouth and his hand came to her waist and pulled her in hard, and she felt his heart going under all the layers of wool. The cold air was sharp in her lungs and his mouth was warm and the snow was landing on her face and melting there, and she didn’t stop. She pushed him back against the trunk of the persimmon tree, and a whole branch-load of snow came down on both of them, and she laughed into the kiss and kept kissing him through it, snow down the back of her collar, snow in his hair, snow everywhere. When she finally drew back his eyes stayed closed for a second, and there were flakes caught in his lashes.

“Happy New Year,” she said.

He opened his eyes. “Happy New Year.”

She brushed the snow out of his hair with her bare hand. “That was for standing up.”

“Only for that?”

“Don’t get greedy,” she said, and he bent his head and kissed her again, and this time he was smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were coming back along the covered walkway, shaking snow off their coats, when Xing Yue appeared at the far end with a cup of tea in his hand. His eyes went from his brother to Tang Xi, and briefly towards the main house.

“Father’s gone to the study.”

“I know.”

Xing Yue took a sip of tea. For a moment he didn’t say anything. Then he looked straight at his younger brother.

“Good.”

One word. No lecture. No explanation. An Yu held his gaze, and Xing Yue nodded once and walked on past them towards the courtyard, where Elara was waiting for him in the snow with her arms full of it.

Tang Xi watched him go. “Does he approve?”

“He doesn’t usually say much.”

“Neither do you.”

“That’s different.”

“Is it?”

He thought about it, and smiled faintly. “Perhaps not.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nainai was in her chair by the stove when they came in.

“You’re back. Good. Your father’s gone to sulk.”

“Nainai.”

“What? He has. He’s done it since he was six.” She held out her hand to Tang Xi. “Did you get cold?”

“A little.”

“Then drink something hot.”

An Yu poured a cup and put it in front of Tang Xi, and Nainai watched him do it. “Good.”

For a while the three of them sat, listening to the house: the clatter in the kitchens, a child sobbing over a lost glove, someone laughing on the stairs.

“Your father has always believed,” said Nainai, “that a family table belongs to whoever decides who sits at it.”

An Yu looked at her. “And you?”

She lifted her tea. “I believe a table is for eating.” She looked at Tang Xi over the cup. “And you still haven’t opened my envelope. That’s also rude. Open it now.”

Tang Xi took it out of her pocket. Inside, folded round the notes, was a slip of red paper with four characters on it in an old woman’s careful brush hand, and Tang Xi read them and went still and looked up.

“Don’t cry at my stove,” said Nainai. “It’s bad luck on the third day.”

Outside the snow went on falling. The family would talk about what had happened at lunch for weeks. Some of them would say An Yu was right; others would say he’d shamed his father in front of everyone. One sentence wasn’t going to mend him and his father, and the family wasn’t going to become simple. But Tang Xi sat next to Nainai at the stove with An Yu across from her, and when he reached over to fill her cup again she let her hand rest on his for a moment. He hadn’t asked her to earn her place, or defend it. He had told the room where she belonged.

That afternoon, it was enough.

chapters.title: Equal
chapters.desc: She asks what he wants. He says: to be asked. Nine new rules, and a night where every answer is yes.
chapters.content:
The question came on a Sunday evening in March.

They were in his kitchen with the windows open an inch to let in the first soft spring air. Tang Xi was sitting on the counter eating slices of pear off a small plate while he washed up. He had insisted on cooking. It had been a simple meal, mostly because she had learned that letting him try more than three ingredients at once was a risk to public health, but he had improved: the greens were cut evenly, the rice was properly done, and the soup was salted like soup instead of the sea. She thought progress ought to be acknowledged.

“You’re getting better.”

He put the last bowl on the rack. “At cooking?”

“At being useful in a kitchen.”

“That’s generous.”

“I’m a generous person.”

He dried his hands and came and stood in front of her, between her knees, and she held out a piece of pear. He took it from her fingers with his teeth. She watched him eat it.

“An Yu? What do you want?”

“From dinner?”

“From me.” She slid off the counter and put the plate aside. “Not what you think I want. Not what you think we should do next. What do you want?”

He didn’t answer. Then he said, “To be asked.”

She blinked. “Asked?”

“About what I want. What I think. Whether I’m all right. Whether I need something.” He looked at the floor, and then back at her. “I’ve spent so long trying to work out what you need before you need it that sometimes I forget you might want to know what I need too. And I don’t always know how to say it unless someone asks.”

Her face went soft. “Then I’ll ask. And you have to answer.”

“I don’t always know how.”

“Neither do I. Perhaps we should stop pretending we’re supposed to.” She took his hand. “Do you know what I think we need?”

“Tell me.”

“Rules.”

“Again?”

“Again. The first ones were mine. Three of them, and you signed them in a café you’d secretly bought.” She smiled. “Some of them are out of date. This time we write them together.”

“Together,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat on the floor by the coffee table. She fetched one of the small black notebooks she used for Level, and he looked at it with interest.

“Are we having a meeting?”

“Yes.”

“Should I have prepared a presentation?”

“Don’t be difficult.”

“I’m asking about the agenda.”

She gave him a look, and he smiled and held out his hand for the pen. “Go ahead, Ms. Tang.”

She kept the pen. At the top of a clean page she wrote EQUAL, and the date, and looked at him. “Nine.”

“Why nine?”

“Because ten sounds like a commandment.”

“That isn’t a convincing reason.”

“It’s my notebook.”

He inclined his head. “Please continue.”

1. We ask before we assume.

“Neither of us gets to decide what the other one wants because we think we know,” she said.

“And if the answer isn’t clear, we ask again. We don’t take silence for yes.”

She wrote it underneath.

2. Either of us can say no.

“With nothing taken away afterwards,” said An Yu.

“Without sulking.”

“I don’t sulk.”

She stared at him. He considered it. “Not on purpose.”

She laughed and wrote, without sulking, in brackets.

3. We say when something hurts. Even when it’s small.

“I don’t want you to wait until you’re tired enough to leave before you tell me something’s wrong,” he said.

Her pen stopped. “Then you have to do the same.”

“I will.”

4. We can disagree and still be close.

“It means you can argue with me and still kiss me afterwards,” she said. “And you can be angry without making me guess whether you still love me.”

“Agreed.”

5. We never use power to settle anything between us.

He looked at that one. “That should have been the first rule two years ago.”

“Yes.”

He took the pen from her, and she let him, and he wrote underneath it in his own careful hand: No company, no money, no lawyers, no influence, no Ding.

She laughed out loud. “Ding?”

“He would want to be named.”

6. Your work is yours. Mine is mine.

“Neither of us makes decisions about the other’s career,” he said.

“Or becomes the other one’s client because we’re together.”

“I wasn’t planning to.”

“Good. Not until a panel says so,” she said, and didn’t know yet how much that would matter.

7. We make time for ordinary things.

“Such as?”

“Breakfast. Going to the market. Bad films. Your cooking.”

“My cooking has improved.”

“That’s debatable.” He reached for the notebook and she pulled it away. “Don’t edit my rule.”

8. We don’t use silence to get out of hard conversations.

Neither of them said anything for a moment.

“This one matters,” she said. “Sometimes you need to think. That’s fine. But you have to tell me you’re thinking. You can’t vanish into your head and expect me to know where you’ve gone.”

“And you don’t have to answer straight away either. If you need time, say so.”

“Agreed.” She wrote it slowly.

“Last one,” he said. “What should it be?”

She thought about it. “Something about choosing each other.”

He took the pen and the notebook from her, and she let him, and he wrote slowly.

9. We choose each other freely, every day.
Not because we owe each other. Not because we’re afraid to leave. Because we want to stay.

She read it twice, and her eyes stayed on the last words. “That’s good.”

“Do you agree?”

“Yes.”

She signed at the bottom. Tang Xi. She passed it to him, and he signed under her name, Wang An Yu, and dated it, and she closed the notebook.

“Nine rules. Will we keep them?”

“Not perfectly.”

“At least you’re realistic.”

He put the notebook on the table and turned back to her. “Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Will you stay tonight?”

“Do you want me to?”

“Yes. Very much.”

“Then yes.”

His hand came to rest lightly at her waist, and stayed there, not moving. “Can I kiss you?”

“Yes,” she said, and he did.

✦ ✦ ✦

It went on much longer than either of them meant it to. Her hands found his shoulders, and the familiar line of his collar under her fingers, and the small pause he always took before he let himself forget everything else. When he drew back he kept his forehead against hers.

“Are you all right?”

“Yes.”

“Do you want to go on?”

“Yes.”

“Tell me if anything changes.”

“I will. Can I take your glasses off?”

“Yes.”

She took them off and folded them and put them on the arm of the sofa. Without them his face looked less guarded; she could see the small crease between his eyebrows that came when he concentrated too hard, and she touched it with one finger.

“You’re thinking.”

“Yes.”

“About what?”

“Whether I’m doing this properly.”

She laughed. “You don’t have to get everything right. Stop looking like you’re sitting an exam.”

“Old habit.”

“I know a better one,” she said. “Rule one. I’m going to ask you what you want, and you’re going to tell me. Out loud. All of it.”

He went still, and she watched him understand that she meant it, and that it was the hardest thing she could have asked him.

“An Yu. What do you want?”

He swallowed. “I want to take you to bed.”

“And?”

“I want to undress you myself. Slowly.”

“Yes,” she said. “What else?”

He looked at her, and the colour came up under his skin, and he said it, low and steady, one thing at a time: where he wanted his hands, where he wanted his mouth, what he wanted to hear her say. She listened to every word of it without looking away, and when he’d finished he looked as if he’d run a long way.

“Was that so terrible?”

“Yes.”

“You’re very good at it.” She stood up and held out her hand. “Yes to all of it. Now ask me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the bedroom he asked before every single thing, and every time she said yes, and it was the slowest and most intimate night of her life.

He asked before he pulled her closer, and she said yes. He asked before he kissed her neck, and she said yes, and he kissed it, under her ear and then lower, and she shut her eyes. When she reached for his shirt buttons he caught her hand.

“May I first?”

“Yes.”

He waited.

“Please,” she said, and he smiled.

He undid her blouse one button at a time and didn’t hurry any of them. There was no impatience in him at all, no sense of getting past this towards something else; his attention stayed on her face. When the blouse fell open he looked at her.

“Is this all right?”

“Yes.”

She put her palm flat on his chest. “Can I?”

“Yes.”

She undid his shirt and pushed it back off his shoulders and laid her hands on his skin, and felt his breath change under her palms.

“That feels good,” he said, and she nearly laughed, because he had never once in his life said anything like that out loud.

“Good. Say more of that.”

He kissed her, and she felt the last of the day go out of his shoulders. They moved towards the bed, and she stopped once and caught his hand.

“Wait.”

He stopped at once. Not a second’s delay.

“I want something first,” she said. “Hold me. For a minute. That’s all.”

His face changed. He gathered her into his arms, and they stood like that beside the bed, her bare cheek against his bare chest, his fingers moving slowly through her hair. There was something almost unbearably intimate in being held like that, with neither of them needing it to lead anywhere at all.

After a while she lifted her head. “Do you want me?”

“Yes.”

“Not because you think I expect you to?”

“No.”

“Not because we’ve been apart, or because of your father, or because you want to make up for anything?”

“No.” He touched her cheek. “Because you’re here. Because I love you. Because I want to be as close to you tonight as it’s possible to be.”

“Then ask me.”

“May I?”

“Yes, An Yu.”

He knelt and drew her skirt down, and then her underwear, and asked with his eyes before he put his mouth to her hip, and she said yes out loud anyway, because she liked hearing herself say it. He laid her down on the bed. He asked before each new place he touched her: the inside of her knee, the soft skin of her stomach, her breast, and she answered each time, sometimes with yes and sometimes with please and once, when his tongue found her, with nothing at all but a sound. She asked him things too. Whether he liked her hand there. Whether he wanted her to go slower. Whether he wanted her to say his name. Yes, he said, to all of it, yes, and his voice had gone rough.

Once, she caught him being too careful, holding back. “Rule two. I’m allowed to say no. I haven’t. Stop waiting for it.”

He laughed against her throat, and something in him let go.

When at last he moved over her, he stopped, and looked at her, and waited.

“Ask,” she said.

“May I come inside you?”

“Yes.”

He slid into her slowly, all the way, and she held his face in both hands and watched his eyes close and open again. They moved together in no hurry at all, a long, deep, rocking rhythm, and he kept asking, in a whisper now, like this? and more? and she kept answering, yes, and yes, and there, and don’t stop, and then she stopped being able to answer in words and answered him with her hands and her hips and her mouth, and he understood every single one. Neither of them treated the other’s wanting as something to be assumed. She came with her heels locked behind his back, saying yes over and over against his shoulder as if it were the only word she knew, and he followed her, saying her name, and then, for the first time ever in that bed, the thing he wanted: “Stay. Stay. Don’t go anywhere.”

“I’m not going anywhere,” she said.

There was no performance in any of it. Nothing to prove. Only two people who had learned, some of it painfully, that being loved didn’t mean being understood automatically, and that asking wasn’t a lack of confidence. It was a way of paying attention.

✦ ✦ ✦

Past midnight she lay with her head on his shoulder, half asleep, his fingers moving slowly up and down her back.

“An Yu? Are you happy?”

“Yes.”

“Which is your favourite rule?”

He thought about it. “Eight.”

“Because of the silence.”

“Because I don’t want you ever to have to guess what I’m thinking.”

She traced a line on his chest. “Mine’s nine.”

“Why?”

“Because I like choosing you. I choose you when you’re difficult.”

“That’s unfortunate.”

“When you’re stubborn.”

“Also unfortunate.”

“When you cook terrible noodles.”

“That was one time.”

“Several times.” She lifted her head and kissed him and settled down again. After a moment he spoke into her hair.

“Xi. Would you tell me if you ever stopped feeling equal with me?”

She came up on her elbow to look at him. “Yes.”

“Even if it hurt?”

“If it hurt, that’s when you’d most need to hear it.” She touched his cheek. “And you?”

“I’ll tell you.”

“Even if you don’t know what to say?”

“I’ll tell you I don’t know what to say.”

“Good,” she said, and he reached over and switched off the lamp.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning the notebook was still on the coffee table. She found it while she was looking for her phone, and opened it at the page with their names.

He came out of the bedroom dressed for work. “Looking for something?”

“Our rules. I think we need to add something.” She picked up the pen and wrote underneath the ninth.

We’re allowed to ask again.

“Because sometimes we forget. Sometimes we get it wrong. Sometimes we need to hear the answer twice.”

He read it, and took the pen. “And we’re allowed to change our minds.” He wrote it below hers.

“That isn’t a tenth rule.”

“No?”

“It’s an amendment.”

“Then we should both sign it.”

She signed first, and he signed under her, and closed the notebook, and picked up his keys. At the door he paused.

“Can I kiss you before we go?”

“Yes.”

He kissed her gently. When he drew back she caught his hand.

“Thank you for asking.”

“Thank you for answering.”

They left together, with the notebook on the coffee table behind them: nine rules, an amendment, two signatures, and a promise neither of them had to keep alone.

chapters.title: The Business Proposal
chapters.desc: An-Tech tenders blind, and he asks Level to pitch. He isn’t in the room. She tells him afterwards, in a stopped lift.
chapters.content:
He asked her on a Sunday, at the market, between the fish stall and the man who sold nothing but chillies.

“An-Tech is going to tender its corporate communications,” he said. “The brand, the executive work, the regional reputation programme. Twelve months to start. Procurement’s sending the request out on Tuesday to six agencies.” He picked up a bag of dried chillies, looked at it, and put it down. “I’d like Level to be one of them.”

Tang Xi stopped walking. “No.”

“I haven’t finished.”

“You don’t need to. Rule five. Rule six. And the fifth thing on my list on the first day, which you’ve seen, because it’s on the wall.”

“I know what’s on the wall.” He turned to face her in the middle of the aisle while an old woman with a trolley went round them, muttering. “I’m not asking you to take An-Tech as a client because of me. I’m asking you to pitch, properly, against five agencies that are all bigger than you, to a panel I’m not on. The written submissions will be scored blind, with the agencies’ names taken off. I won’t see the submissions, the scores, the shortlist or the presentations. I won’t be in the room. I won’t know who’s winning until the procurement committee has decided, and then I’ll find out the same way the finance director does: from a memo.” He paused. “You told me you’d take An-Tech when you’d built something nobody could say I built for you. I think you have. I’d like a panel that has never met you to decide whether I’m right.”

She looked at him. The chilli man was openly listening.

“Who chairs the panel?”

“Ms. Harlow, from Corporate Affairs. She’s never met you. She thinks I’m overrated.”

“And if we lose?”

“Then you lose to a better proposal, and I’ll be sorry, and I’ll take you to dinner, and we’ll never mention it again.” He held her gaze. “And if you win, everybody who ever said you got anything because of me will have to read the scoring.”

She thought of a column with her photograph in it, and a glass room, and a breakfast by the harbour. “I’ll read the brief,” she said. “That’s all I’m promising.”

“That’s all I’m asking.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The request arrived on Tuesday morning from An-Tech’s procurement office, not from him, not from Ding.

AN-TECH · REQUEST FOR PROPOSAL
Corporate brand and strategic communications · initial term twelve months
Two-envelope tender: technical proposal (70%) scored blind; commercial proposal (30%) opened only after technical scoring is complete
Bidders must declare all conflicts of interest with directors or officers of An-Tech in the declarations schedule

Tang Xi read it twice and rang Rachel, who was already standing in her doorway with her own laptop.

“You’ve seen it.”

“I’ve seen it.”

“Are we pitching?”

“Why wouldn’t we?”

“Because it’s An-Tech.”

“That isn’t a business reason.”

“No. It’s a personal complication.”

“Which we declare, and manage, and then we beat five agencies.” Tang Xi turned the brief round. “Read it properly. Then tell me if you think we can.”

Her phone lit.

Professor: Have you read it?

Tang Xi: Yes.

Professor: And?

Tang Xi: We’re pitching. You’re not allowed to help me.

Professor: I know.

Tang Xi: I mean it.

Professor: So do I. I’ve already put it in writing to procurement, and copied the general counsel. Good luck, Ms. Tang.

Rachel was watching her. “What did he say?”

“That he’s recused himself in writing and copied Legal.”

“Of course he has.” Rachel grinned. “Let’s make him regret saying good luck.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The first internal meeting lasted two hours, round the three desks, with the brief taped to the wall next to the list.

An-Tech wanted an agency that could carry it into its next stage. It had outgrown its first business years ago; it had investments and partnerships now in half a dozen sectors, a services group that included Corran Pike, and no single story that held all of it together.

“They want a regional team,” said Calvin.

“They want regional capability,” said Rachel. “It’s not the same.”

“Exactly,” said Tang Xi. “We don’t pretend to have offices in six countries. We show them how we’d deliver in six countries.”

“With three people?”

“With three people and the right specialist partners in each market, every one of them named and costed.”

“If we under-cost it,” said Rachel, “we’ll win something we can’t deliver.”

“Then we don’t under-cost it.” Tang Xi got up and went to the whiteboard. “First. What’s the real problem?”

Calvin read from the brief. “Fragmented corporate messaging. Inconsistent executive visibility. Limited regional alignment.”

“Those are symptoms. The problem is that An-Tech has grown faster than its public identity. It’s six businesses with six audiences and six stories, and the market still sees all of it through one man’s face.”

“So the chairman’s become the brand,” said Calvin slowly.

“Yes. And that’s a dependency. If he walks under a bus, what does An-Tech stand for?”

“Please don’t say that in the room,” said Rachel.

“I’m going to say exactly that in the room. Politely.” Tang Xi wrote on the board.

FROM A FOUNDER’S NAME TO AN INSTITUTION PEOPLE TRUST

Calvin leaned back. “That’s strong.”

“It’s also uncomfortable. They may want more of the chairman, not less.”

“Then we tell them why those aren’t opposites,” said Rachel. “You can have him visible without the whole company hanging off him.”

“The company has to be able to explain what it does, why it matters and how it behaves when the chairman isn’t in the room,” said Tang Xi. “And on this tender, he won’t be. Which is the first thing they’ll notice about our proposal, and the last thing they’ll forget.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At An-Tech, the procurement director sent the chairman a note on the Monday: Level had registered its intention to bid.

He read it once and forwarded it to the general counsel and the procurement director with one instruction.

Please record the declared personal relationship and confirm in writing that I have no part in the procurement, evaluation, negotiation or award.

The reply came within the hour. The tender would run under the standard competitive framework. The chairman wouldn’t receive any submission, attend any presentation, see any score or join any discussion of the preferred supplier. The panel would be Ms. Harlow of Corporate Affairs, the finance director, the general counsel and two independent regional advisers from outside the company. Technical submissions would be stripped of agency names and scored separately by each evaluator against the published criteria before anyone compared notes. Identities would be revealed only after the technical scores were locked and the shortlist confirmed. The commercial envelopes would be opened after that.

“And the final approval?” he asked.

“The procurement committee,” said Ding. “You’re excluded.”

“Good.”

Ding hesitated. “Would you like to know whether Level makes the shortlist?”

“No.”

“Even after the first round?”

“No. Send me the final recommendation once the committee has approved it, and not a minute before.” He looked up. “And Ding. Make sure nobody reads my recusal as a hint that Level should be marked down to make a point. I don’t want them disadvantaged either.”

“I’ll make that clear.”

“Evaluate the work,” said An Yu. “That’s all.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The proposal was finished at seventeen minutes past two in the morning on a Thursday. Rachel had gone home an hour before. Calvin was asleep on the second-hand sofa with an arm over his face. Tang Xi was at her desk reading the commercial appendix for the third time, and when she reached the staffing section she stopped.

It was ambitious and it was honest. Level would lead the strategy, the executive work and the account itself, all three of them, directly. For delivery in the three priority markets they had found three specialist partners, each with their responsibilities written down and costed separately. No invented offices. No inflated headcount. No promise of round-the-clock regional coverage from three people above a dumpling shop. The fees weren’t the lowest. They weren’t meant to be. They paid for the senior time and the research and the partners the brief actually needed.

Her last page said:

Our recommendation is to build An-Tech’s reputation as an institution: clear about its purpose, credible in its leadership and consistent in how it behaves in every market. Visibility should follow trust. It should never stand in for it.

A little after two she pressed send. Calvin lifted his arm off his face.

“Did we win?”

“We haven’t presented yet.”

“Just checking,” he said, and went back to sleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

The shortlist came on a Wednesday at the end of May. Level was one of three. The other two were far bigger: one had offices in eight markets and a corporate affairs team the size of a small ministry; the other had twenty years of multinational clients and a reputation for handling the kind of crises that never reached the papers.

“Well,” said Rachel.

“You keep saying that,” said Calvin.

“I’m processing.”

“We’ve made the shortlist,” said Tang Xi. “Blind. They scored our proposal without knowing whose it was, and it came top three out of six.”

“Against those two.”

“Against those two.” Tang Xi looked at the schedule. Seventy-five minutes. Fifteen for questions. Strategy, delivery, team, regional execution, value, measurement. She would lead. Rachel would take measurement. Calvin would take delivery. And at the start, they’d been told, each agency would make its declarations aloud.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room on the first Tuesday in June was smaller than she’d expected. Six people round the table: Ms. Harlow in the middle, sharp and fifty and unsmiling; the finance director; the general counsel, whom Tang Xi had last seen in a boardroom watching her kiss his chairman; two regional advisers; the procurement director with a folder. No observers. No chairman. No assistant at the door. No An Yu. She felt a small, unexpected loosening in her chest. She was here to pitch. Nothing else.

“Before we begin,” said Ms. Harlow, “please confirm your team, and make any declarations.”

“I’m Tang Xi, founder and managing director of Level. Rachel Ji leads strategy and measurement. Calvin Seah leads delivery.” Tang Xi folded her hands on the table. “We’ve declared in writing that I’m in a personal relationship with An-Tech’s chairman, Wang An Yu. We understand he has recused himself from every stage of this process, and we’re happy to answer any question about our governance.”

“Thank you. The panel has the declaration. Mr. Wang has no part in this. We’ll proceed on the published criteria.”

Tang Xi didn’t mention him again.

She began with where An-Tech stood. It had built a strong reputation on its founder, its results and its speed. But as it grew, those same strengths were turning into problems. Its businesses weren’t understood as parts of one institution. Its public story leaned too heavily on one man. Its regional audiences didn’t share the same idea of what it was for. And its communications were becoming a list of announcements and partnerships and appearances, with nothing holding them together.

“We don’t think An-Tech needs to be louder,” she said, and clicked. “We think it needs to be clearer.”

She set out a structure: the group’s purpose, the stories of each business, and where the chairman fitted. A first phase of research among the people who actually mattered to each business, so that everyone knew where they were starting from. A framework for each market. A rule that nothing would be announced that the company wasn’t already doing. Rachel took them through measurement: whether the right people understood the messages, the quality of executive engagement, consistency across markets, and how credibly the company answered when it was challenged. Calvin took them through the partners, the quality checks, the approvals, the escalation routes, and the plan for hiring if they won, which made the finance director look up.

Then the general counsel asked the question she’d known was coming.

“How would you manage the relationship between the company’s reputation and the chairman’s personal profile?”

“As connected but separate. Mr. Wang’s profile helps people recognise An-Tech. The company shouldn’t need it to be believed.”

“And if the chairman disagrees with your recommended positioning?”

“Then we explain our reasoning, we record the disagreement, and we set out what each option would mean. You’d be appointing us to advise the company. Not to agree with whoever’s most senior in the room.”

Ms. Harlow looked up from her notes. “Would you be comfortable telling the chairman that to his face?”

“Yes.”

“Given your personal relationship?”

“More so because of it. If I couldn’t keep the two apart, I’d tell you so, and you shouldn’t appoint us.” Tang Xi held her gaze. “I’ve told him he’s wrong in front of twelve people before, Ms. Harlow. He survived. So did the account.”

There was a pause. One of the regional advisers coughed into his hand, possibly to hide something. Ms. Harlow made a note, and for the first time something at the corner of her mouth moved.

The questions went on for a quarter of an hour: the first ninety days, the research method, a crisis on a Saturday, the regional partners, how many senior hours a week. Tang Xi answered what she could. When she didn’t know, she said so. When the answer depended on data only An-Tech had, she said what they’d need to find out first.

“Your team is three people,” said the finance director. “How can you guarantee senior involvement for twelve months?”

“By not taking on anything that would stop us. If we win this, we’ll limit the other work we accept until we’ve hired. We’d rather grow slowly than promise something we can’t keep.”

“That limits your growth.”

“Yes.”

“You’re comfortable with that?”

“Completely.”

At half past eleven the procurement director closed his folder. “Thank you. You’ll hear through procurement.”

In the lift Rachel let out a long breath. “Well.”

“That went well,” said Calvin.

“You’re not going to ask what I think?” said Rachel.

“I know what you think,” said Tang Xi. “You think we did well, and you won’t say so because you’re afraid I’ll become unbearable.”

“Exactly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The decision came on Friday a little before five. Calvin was standing in her doorway with his phone held out at arm’s length as if it might go off. Rachel was behind him.

AN-TECH · PROCUREMENT OUTCOME
Level has been selected as preferred supplier.

Tang Xi took the phone and read the whole thing. The panel had scored every proposal against the published criteria. Level had come first overall, and first on strategy, on senior commitment, on governance and on value. The procurement committee had approved it. The award was subject to contract.

“We won,” said Calvin, unnecessarily, and his voice cracked.

For a second nobody moved. Then Rachel came round the desk and hugged her, and Calvin joined in and nearly knocked the laptop off the desk, and Tang Xi laughed with her face against Rachel’s shoulder. She had won one of the biggest corporate accounts in the city. Not a favour. Not an arrangement. Not something handed to her by a man who loved her. A panel that had scored her work without her name on it had put it above two agencies a hundred times their size.

She stepped back and wiped the corner of one eye. “All right.”

“All right?” said Rachel.

“We need to read the contract. And we need to hire about nine people by October.”

Calvin went slightly grey. Rachel laughed until she had to hold on to the desk.

✦ ✦ ✦

Just before six Ding put the approved recommendation on the chairman’s desk. An Yu read it. Preferred supplier: Level. First overall. The panel cited the clarity of its strategy, the honesty of its delivery model, the strength of its governance, and its confidence in the people who would do the work. He read it again, and closed it.

“Congratulations, Mr. Wang,” said Ding.

“For what?”

Ding’s face didn’t move. “Your company has chosen a good agency.”

An Yu’s mouth curved. When Ding had gone he picked up his phone to call her, and to tell her he’d read it, and that he was proud of her. Then he put it down. She hadn’t told him yet. It was hers to tell.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tang Xi: Are you still at the office?

Professor: Yes.

Tang Xi: Don’t leave.

She came into his office a little after seven, after most of the floor had gone home, and shut the door behind her. He was standing.

“Hello.”

“Hello.”

She put her bag on the sofa. “How was your day?”

“Quiet. Yours?”

She tried hard to keep her face still. “Something happened.”

He waited.

“An-Tech has chosen Level.”

His face changed. For a moment he looked almost surprised, and then his eyes went soft. “You won.”

“We won.”

He came round the desk. “Congratulations.”

She folded her arms. “Did you know?”

“I got the approved recommendation an hour and a half ago.”

“Did you read the scores?”

“The final ones. In the memo.”

“Did you look at the other proposals?”

“No.”

“Did you ask anyone why we won?”

“No.”

“Did you interfere? Even once?”

“Not once.”

Her face softened. “Good. I wanted to tell you myself. I wanted to see your face.”

“And?”

“You’re trying very hard not to look too pleased.”

“I’m very pleased.”

“Come with me,” she said, and took his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

He pressed the button for the ground floor. She stood beside him watching the numbers go down. Forty. Thirty-nine. Thirty-eight. Then she reached past him and pressed the red stop button, and the lift jolted gently and hung still between floors, and a small calm voice from the panel said that the lift had been stopped and assistance could be called with the button below.

He looked at her. “Xi.”

“Yes?”

“Is there a reason we’ve stopped?”

“Yes. I have something to do.” She stepped in close. “I haven’t congratulated you.”

“You’ve congratulated yourself. I’ve congratulated you.”

“Not properly,” she said, and took hold of his tie and pulled him down to her.

The first time she’d done this, two years ago, she had been furious with him over a café. This time she was laughing. She kissed him hard against the brushed steel wall, and he made a low sound and his hand spread on the small of her back and pulled her in until she could feel his heart going through his shirt, and she kissed him the way she’d wanted to in that room with six people round the table, the way you kiss someone when you have finally, completely, earned the right to stand next to them. Her hands went into his hair. His went to her jaw, tilting her face up, and he kissed her back slow and deep and thoroughly, as if they had all the time in the world and nobody in the building was ever going to need the lift again. The little calm voice repeated itself. Neither of them listened.

When she finally let him go, his tie was ruined and his forehead was against hers.

“You’re happy,” he said.

“Very.” She touched his cheek. “I wanted to win this one. Not because it’s your company. Because I wanted to prove that Level could stand in a room with agencies a hundred times our size and still be the better choice.”

“You did.”

“Say it again.”

“You’re the better choice.”

“Not me.”

He understood. “Level was the better choice.”

She nodded, satisfied, and kissed him again, and then reached past him and let the lift go.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the way down she straightened his tie, which was hopeless. “Are you going to be a difficult client?”

He thought about it honestly. “Probably.”

“Wonderful.”

“I’ll try to be reasonable.”

“That’s what difficult clients always say.”

“Will you tell me when I’m not?”

“Professionally? Absolutely. Personally? Even more.”

The doors opened onto the empty lobby. Before she walked away he caught her hand.

“Xi. Thank you for pitching.”

“Thank you for keeping out of it.”

“I didn’t keep out of it as a favour. It was supposed to be fair.”

She thought about that, and nodded. “You’re right. Good night, Mr. Wang.”

“Congratulations, Ms. Tang.”

They left the building separately, through different doors. Procurement would negotiate the contract. The scope would be agreed between the teams. The account would have its own reporting line, its own approval matrix and a governance structure Mrs. Kho at Northlight would have framed. He would be the chairman of the client. She would be the founder of the agency it had chosen. And for the first time, the two of them could be in the same room for work without either of them wondering what the other had given up to make it possible.

chapters.title: Her Mother Comes Round
chapters.desc: A box of forty dumplings arrives at his office with no note. He eats every one, and writes to a restaurant.
chapters.epigraph: “Next time come before they are cold.”
chapters.content:
The box reached An-Tech’s front desk at sixteen minutes past ten on a Thursday morning in June: plain cardboard, tied with brown string, brought in by a courier with no company name on his shirt and no interest in explaining anything.

Reception rang upstairs. “There’s a delivery for Mr. Wang. No sender. The courier says it’s food.”

Ding went down himself. The box was the size of a small printer carton, heavier than it looked, and still faintly warm through the cardboard; when he picked it up he caught the smell of sesame oil and ginger. There was no card. No letter. No logo. Only a strip of masking tape across the lid with a single character on it in black marker, the character for Wang, written by somebody who had been writing characters with a brush long before she ever used a pen.

He brought it up and put it on the chairman’s desk. “This came for you, Mr. Wang. We don’t know who from. Would you like it checked?”

An Yu looked at the tape. He knew the hand. He had seen it once before, on a paper bag of dumplings handed to him on a narrow staircase with the words she hasn’t eaten.

“It’s food, Ding.”

“We don’t know who sent it.”

“I do.” He untied the string and lifted the lid.

Inside, in two neat layers, each wrapped in its own square of greaseproof paper so they wouldn’t stick, were dumplings. Twenty on top. Twenty underneath. Forty. Chive and prawn: he could smell it, the ginger and the white pepper and the sesame oil, and he could see the pleats, five on every one, quick and even, except for one near the corner that had a little more flour on it than the others, as if someone had been interrupted.

“Could you ask the kitchen to steam these, please?”

Ding looked at the box. “All of them?”

“All of them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The kitchen did them in batches. He ate the first ten in his office, standing at the window. He ate the second ten after a meeting with the finance director, who looked at the steamer basket on the chairman’s desk and decided not to ask. When Ding came back from a call with Legal he found him reading a contract with one hand and eating with the other.

“Are they good, Mr. Wang?”

He considered it. “Very.”

“There are ten left. Shall I keep some for lunch?”

“No.”

A little after twelve he ate the last ten. He didn’t hurry. He ate them over the revised procurement schedule, stopping now and then to drink water, and once to check that the last one hadn’t split in the steamer. When he’d finished he sat back and looked into the empty box. The greaseproof squares lay stacked in one corner. There was a little flour in the bottom.

He took out his phone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tang Xi was going through a contract with Rachel in the new room they’d taken on the second floor above the restaurant, now that there were five of them, two more were starting on Monday, and the kettle had been joined by a coffee machine nobody understood, when her phone lit.

Professor: Did you send me something?

Tang Xi: No.

Professor: Forty dumplings.

Rachel saw her eyebrows go up. “What?”

Tang Xi held up a finger.

Tang Xi: What forty dumplings?

Professor: In a box. No note. Your mother’s.

Tang Xi: How do you know?

Professor: I recognise the folding.

Her mouth fell open. She rang the restaurant phone, which was nine metres below her, and her mother answered on the second ring with the extractor fan going behind her.

“What’s wrong?”

“Ma. Did you send something to An-Tech?”

A pause. “What?”

“A box. Forty dumplings.”

Her mother made a small sound. “Ah.”

“Ah?”

“They were left over.”

“Forty of them?”

“I made too many.”

“Ma, nobody makes forty extra dumplings by accident.”

Her mother said nothing. Tang Xi lowered her voice. “Why didn’t you tell me?”

“Why should I tell you?”

“Because you sent food to my boyfriend’s office.”

“Is that not allowed?”

Tang Xi shut her eyes. “It’s allowed.”

“Then what’s the problem?” A clatter of a ladle. “Did he eat them?”

“He says so.”

“All of them?”

“Yes.”

A longer pause. Then: “Good.”

Tang Xi smiled in spite of herself. “When did you make them?”

“Last night.”

“Why?”

“I had prawns.”

“Ma.”

“And chives.”

“Ma.”

Her mother sighed. “What do you want me to say? Go back to work. And tell him to chew. Forty is too many to eat quickly. He’ll make himself ill.”

“He ate forty dumplings, Ma. I don’t think chewing was the priority.”

“Then that’s his problem,” said her mother, and hung up.

Tang Xi put the phone down. Rachel was watching her with enormous interest.

“Your mother?”

“She sent An Yu forty dumplings and didn’t tell me.”

Rachel leaned back slowly in her chair. “Well.”

“Don’t.”

“Your mother,” said Rachel, with great relish, “has sent your boyfriend a box of dumplings with no note, and he has eaten all of it at his desk, and she has asked whether he chewed.” She put her hand on her heart. “That’s a proposal of marriage, Xi. From your mother. To him.”

“Please let me work.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He looked at the empty box for some time after lunch. Then he took a photograph of it: the lid folded back, the greaseproof squares stacked to one side, the flour in the corner. He thought about whether that was enough.

Professor: Your mother rang you?

Tang Xi: Yes. She asked if you ate them. She says you should have chewed.

Professor: I’ll remember.

Tang Xi: You could have saved some.

Professor: I didn’t know if there would be another box.

She sent a row of laughing faces. He didn’t send her the photograph. He went to his desk drawer instead and took out a paper takeaway menu he had kept there for eleven months, from a box of dumplings handed to him on a staircase, with the restaurant’s number printed on it in red. He sent the photograph to that number, and under it he wrote, carefully, and read it four times before he sent it:

Thank you for the dumplings. I ate all forty. I chewed most of them. They were the best I have ever eaten.

Nothing came back. He put the phone face up beside his keyboard and went back to work, and every few minutes, without meaning to, he looked at it.

✦ ✦ ✦

A little after one Tang Xi sent him a photograph: a bowl of dumpling filling on a steel counter, and beside it a list of ingredients in her mother’s hand.

Tang Xi: She’s seen your photograph. She showed it to my aunt and then to the delivery man. She says the next ones will be better if you come and eat them hot.

He read it twice, and smiled at his desk in a way that made Ding, coming in with a folder, turn round and go out again.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came at half past seven, out of his suit, in a dark shirt with the sleeves rolled to the forearm. Tang Xi was at the back table where she’d done her homework at sixteen, and her mother was behind the counter checking off a delivery of greens, and she looked up when he came in.

“You’re here.”

“Good evening.”

Her mother pointed her chin at the back table. “Sit.”

He sat. Tang Xi looked at him across the table. “You came.”

“You said there might be more.”

“I said no such thing.”

He glanced towards the counter. “She did.”

“Ma? Did you invite him?”

“He’s here, isn’t he?” said her mother, and went through to the kitchen.

Tang Xi turned back. “You ate all forty.”

“Yes.”

“Without offering anyone any.”

“They were addressed to me.”

“That’s your defence?”

“It’s accurate.”

She laughed. Her mother came out with two cups of tea and a small plate of smashed cucumber and put them down. He half stood, and she waved him back into his chair.

“Sit. You’re eating later.”

When she’d gone, Tang Xi said, “She’s never done that. Asked you to eat without me arranging it.”

“Perhaps she had too many dumplings.”

“Don’t get confident.”

“I won’t.” He looked at her across the table, and his voice changed. “She remembered how I fold them.”

“What?”

“The one in the corner, with too much flour on it. It had six pleats, not five. She put one in that looked like mine.” He turned his cup on the table. “She remembered that I was trying.”

Tang Xi stared at him. She thought of December, and a table at the back of this room, and her mother telling the chairman of An-Tech that his dumpling was ugly. She hadn’t praised him that day. She hadn’t welcomed him into anything. But she had remembered, and eighteen months later she had folded one of his clumsy six-pleated dumplings into a box of forty and sent it to his office without a word.

Tang Xi reached across and held his hand properly. “She liked that you listened.”

“I liked listening.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past eight he found her mother in the kitchen wrapping the evening’s leftovers, and stood in the doorway.

“Do you need anything?”

“No.”

He looked at the tray of dumplings waiting on the counter for the next morning. “May I ask something? Would you show me again? Properly?”

She looked at him. “I already showed you.”

“You did. I still press too hard.”

“You do. And your hands are too stiff, and you put in too much.” She wiped her own hands on her apron, and considered him, and then moved a bowl of filling a few inches along the counter towards the empty space beside her. “Wash your hands.”

He washed them. Tang Xi, who was listening from the dining room with a napkin she’d been folding for two minutes, came and stood in the doorway.

Her mother showed him once. The wrapper lay in her palm. The filling went in the middle, not too much, not too little. Her thumbs moved five times, quick and even, and it was closed. She pushed the bowl at him. “Try.”

His first was uneven. She looked at it. “Better.” The second was neater. The third held its shape. Nobody praised him unnecessarily. Nobody made a ceremony of it. When he pressed too hard she put two fingers on the back of his hand and he eased off. When the edges went messy she showed him once more and he tried again.

Eventually she picked one up and turned it over. “That one can be cooked.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. Make another.” She looked past him at the doorway. “Why are you laughing? You can help.”

Tang Xi picked up a wrapper at once. He glanced at her hands. “Are you sure?”

“Excuse me?”

“Nothing.”

Her mother snorted. “Both of you are slow.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards he walked Tang Xi to the end of the street while her mother pulled the shutters down. The evening had gone cool. She put her hand in his.

“You’re pleased with yourself.”

“Is that what it means?”

She thought about it. “No. It means she trusts you enough to feed you without asking me first. She hasn’t said she approves. She still thinks you’re too rich. Too quiet. Too serious.”

“That last one seems unfair.”

She laughed, and then stopped under the streetlight. “Thank you for eating them.”

“Why are you thanking me?”

“Because you understood what it meant.”

He was quiet. “I didn’t want her to think I took it lightly.”

Her eyes went soft. She straightened his collar. “She won’t.”

“May I kiss you?”

“Yes.”

He kissed her under the streetlight, quiet and warm and unhurried, with the smell of the old town round them, ginger and wet stone and somebody’s frying garlic. When they came apart she rested her forehead against his.

“Next time, don’t eat all forty.”

“I’ll ask you to share.”

“That’s better.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On Friday morning Ding came in with the post and stopped. The chairman’s phone was propped against his keyboard showing a photograph of an empty cardboard box.

“Is that from yesterday, Mr. Wang? Did you send it to Ms. Tang?”

“No.” An Yu turned the phone round so Ding could see the thread. A photograph of an empty box, sent to a restaurant’s number. His message under it. And under that, sent at ten to six that morning, which was when the restaurant’s prep began, a reply:

Next time come before they are cold.

“Ah,” said Ding.

“Could you ask the kitchen,” said An Yu, “to throw away the recipe card they made yesterday? I won’t be needing it. I’ll be going to the source.”

“Yes, Mr. Wang,” said Ding, and went out, and could be heard in the corridor telling someone that the chairman was in a good mood and nobody was to ruin it.

An Yu wrote back slowly.

Yes. Thank you. I’d like that very much.

He put the phone down and went back to work. Forty dumplings. No note. No explanation. And now an invitation to come and eat them hot.

chapters.title: Nainai’s Ring
chapters.desc: Nainai puts her mother’s jade on Tang Xi’s hand and tells him to hurry. Tang Xi tells him not to, yet.
chapters.content:
Tang Xi had been told to come for lunch. She hadn’t been told she was expected to leave wearing a ring. The difference, she decided afterwards, mattered.

The courtyard in the north hills was hot with late-summer sun. The persimmon tree she had kissed him under in the snow was thick and green now, its fruit still small and hard, and the cicadas in it were so loud they seemed to be part of the light. The kitchen windows stood open and the gardener was clipping the hedge somewhere beyond the wall. Nainai sat in the shade of the veranda in a cane chair with her stick against the arm of it, looking extremely pleased with herself, which Tang Xi had learned was usually a warning.

“Your tea, Nainai.”

“Put it down. Sit.” Nainai looked her up and down. “Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“Properly?”

“Yes.”

“Don’t lie to me. You’re thin.”

“I’ve been busy. We’ve hired nine people since June.”

“Being busy is not a reason to eat badly.”

“I’ll remember.”

“You say that every time.” Nainai drank her tea. Tang Xi waited. She knew Nainai’s silences by now. They were nothing like An Yu’s. Nainai could sit without speaking for five minutes and leave you feeling as though you’d been thoroughly cross-examined. Today, though, she seemed to be waiting for something.

“Where’s An Yu?”

“Late.”

“Work?”

“An excuse. That boy has been slow since the day he was born.”

Tang Xi laughed. “He isn’t that slow.”

“You’re defending him? Don’t. He needs someone to tell him the truth.” Nainai reached down beside her chair for a small wooden box Tang Xi hadn’t noticed: dark wood, polished smooth by years of hands, its corners worn. She opened the brass clasp.

On a piece of faded silk inside was a jade ring.

Tang Xi went still. It was a deep, translucent green, not bright or glassy, but full of the quiet colour of old leaves after rain, worn so smooth that it seemed to be lit from inside. A darker vein ran through one side of it like a thread.

“Do you know what this is?” said Nainai.

“A jade ring.”

Nainai gave her a look. “I can see that.”

“It’s very beautiful.”

“It was mine. I wore it when I was young, before I became old and difficult.”

“You’re still difficult.”

“Good. You have eyes.” Nainai turned it in her fingers. “My mother gave it to me the morning I married. She had it from hers. It’s been on a woman’s hand in this family for a hundred and ten years, and it has been in this box for nine, because my hands got too thin for it.” She held it out. “Give me your hand.”

“Nainai—”

“Do you think I brought it out to look at?”

Tang Xi slowly held out her left hand. Nainai’s fingers were thinner than she remembered and the skin like paper, but her grip was firm, and she turned Tang Xi’s hand and slid the ring onto the fourth finger. It fitted. Not perfectly, but well enough to stay.

Tang Xi couldn’t say anything for a moment. Nainai settled it with her thumb. “Good.”

“I can’t take this. It’s yours.”

“It was my mother’s. Then mine. Now I’m giving it to you.”

“But—”

“Do you dislike it?”

“No. Of course not.”

“Then why are you arguing?”

“Because it matters.”

Nainai looked at her. “Yes. That’s why it’s yours.” She shut the empty box. “Did you read what I wrote you at New Year?”

Tang Xi’s hand went, without her meaning it to, to her bag, where the slip of red paper from the envelope had lived since February. Four characters in an old woman’s brush hand that meant, more or less, come through our door soon.

“Yes.”

“Six months ago. Nobody in this family listens.” Nainai picked up her stick and rapped it once on the stone. “That boy is too slow.”

“Which boy?”

“How many grandsons have I got? Xing Yue has married the same girl twice, once in an office and once in a garden at six in the morning, which is ridiculous, but at least he did it. Yu Chen is marrying in October. That leaves one.” She leaned forward. “I’ve waited long enough. He’s had you for two and a half years, and he knew he wanted you for ten before that, and he still hasn’t done the proper thing.”

Tang Xi’s face went hot. “Nainai. Please don’t pressure him.”

“Pressure him?” Nainai looked genuinely offended. “I’m not pressuring him. I’m telling him to hurry up. There’s a difference.” The stick swung round at her. “And you. Stop making excuses for him.”

“I don’t.”

“You do. Keep the ring on. Now drink your tea.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came through the gate forty minutes late with a paper bag from a bakery in the city that Tang Xi liked, his sleeves rolled up, wearing the face of a man who had received a great many messages from his grandmother on the drive.

“Late,” said Nainai.

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t apologise to me. Apologise to the person who’s been waiting.”

He looked at Tang Xi. “Sorry.”

“It’s all right.”

“See?” Nainai said. “She says it’s all right. That’s why you’re spoiled.”

“I had a meeting.”

“Then finish your meetings on time.”

“That isn’t always possible.”

“Everything is possible if you hurry.”

Tang Xi ducked her head to hide her face, and he came closer to see what was funny, and then his eyes fell on her left hand and he stopped completely. The jade caught the sun.

“What’s this?”

“My ring,” said Nainai.

“Your ring?”

“I have several. Be more specific.”

“The jade one. Your mother’s.”

“I know whose ring it is. I was there.”

Tang Xi laughed out loud. He looked at her, and at the ring, and at his grandmother. “You gave it to her.”

“Are you deaf?”

“Nainai.”

“Don’t stand there looking confused. Sit.” He sat down beside Tang Xi. Nainai studied him and then said, with perfect calm, “Hurry up.”

“With what?”

Nainai stared at him. Tang Xi put her hand over her mouth.

“How long do you think I have?” said Nainai.

His face changed. “Nainai.”

“I’m not asking you to build a hospital. I’m asking you to stop taking so long. I gave her the ring. It’s a family ring. I want to see it on her hand while I’m still here to see it.” The stick tapped his knee. “Then?”

He looked at Tang Xi. “Do you like it?”

“I love it.”

“Does it fit?”

“Nearly.”

He touched the edge of the stone with one fingertip, carefully, without moving it. “It’s beautiful.”

“Then?” said Nainai again.

“Then what?”

“Hopeless,” said Nainai, and Tang Xi gave up and laughed until her eyes watered.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was in the courtyard under the persimmon tree: steamed fish, greens, braised tofu, and a winter-melon soup that Nainai said was good for people who worked too much, which she ladled into Tang Xi’s bowl three times. Nainai put Tang Xi beside her and An Yu opposite, and he didn’t argue.

He kept looking at her hand. She caught him the third time. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at the ring.”

“Yes.”

“Then stop looking as if you’re trying to work out what it means.”

He put his chopsticks down. “I know what it means.”

“Then say it,” said Nainai.

“Can we eat first?”

“No.” Nainai pointed her chopsticks at him. “You’re always asking people to wait. Your father waits. Your brother waited a year to speak to his girl. Everybody in this family waits too long to say the things that ought to be said.”

He looked down at his bowl. Then he looked up at Tang Xi, and she saw it coming, the whole thing, in his face; she saw him about to say it, here, at his grandmother’s table, because his grandmother had told him to. And before he could, she put her hand flat on the table between them.

“Don’t.”

He stopped. Nainai’s eyebrows went up into her hair.

“Not like this,” Tang Xi said, and only to him. “Not because Nainai told you to hurry. Not at lunch with a stick pointed at you. When you ask me, I want it to be yours. Your words. Your time. Something you decided.” She smiled a little. “Rule one. Ask. Don’t be told to.”

He looked at her, and she watched him understand, and then something in his face settled, like a man putting down a heavy box he’d been carrying the wrong way.

“Then I’ll hurry,” he said. “In my own way.”

“Good.”

Nainai looked from one to the other, and made a sound that might have been disgust and might have been something else entirely. “Young people,” she said. “In my day we were married in a fortnight and argued for fifty years.”

“You argued for fifty years, Nainai?”

“I won for fifty years. Eat your soup.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch Nainai went in to rest, taking the empty wooden box with her. An Yu excused himself to make a phone call. He walked to the far end of the courtyard by the gate and stood with his back to them in the hot shade, and Tang Xi watched him from the bench under the persimmon tree, turning the jade round and round her finger. He talked for a long time. Once he laughed, which surprised her. Once he wrote something on the back of his hand with a pen from his pocket. When he came back he looked like a man who’d just closed a difficult deal and wasn’t going to tell anyone the terms.

“Who was that?”

“Shanghai.”

“Who in Shanghai?”

“Someone I needed to ask a favour of.”

She narrowed her eyes. “You’re being secretive.”

“Only about this.” He stood in front of her. “You stopped me.”

“Yes.”

“I was going to say it.”

“I know. I could see it on your face from across the table.” She looked up at him. “Were you going to ask today anyway?”

“I was going to ask this autumn. I’ve been planning to since before New Year.” He looked at the ring on her hand. “I wanted to speak to you first. Not have it be a family announcement. Not let anyone else decide when.”

“And then your grandmother put her mother’s ring on me before you’d got through the gate.”

“Nainai has never done anything by accident in her life.”

“She did it so you’d hurry.”

“She did it so you’d know you were wanted,” he said, “whatever I did or didn’t do. That’s a different thing.”

Tang Xi went quiet. She looked down at the green stone, at the dark vein running through it, a hundred and ten years of women’s hands, and her throat went tight.

“An Yu.”

“Yes?”

She stood up. They were close under the tree, in the green shade, with the cicadas roaring above them and the courtyard empty and white with sun.

“You said you’d hurry.”

“In my own way.”

“Then hurry,” she said, and took his face in both her hands and kissed him.

It was nothing like the snow. It was slow and hot and certain, the jade cool against his jaw where her fingers were, and she kissed him. His hands came to her waist and drew her in against him. She pressed closer and he bent his head to her, and she felt him smile against her mouth and then stop smiling, and the kiss deepened until she had to hold on to his shirt. A persimmon leaf came loose above them and slid down her back and she didn’t notice. When she finally let him go, his forehead dropped to hers and his breath wasn’t steady.

“I’m hurrying,” he said.

“Not fast enough.”

“Seven weeks.”

She pulled back to look at him. “What’s in seven weeks?”

“Something I’ve just arranged with a favour I can’t tell you about.” He took her left hand and kissed the jade, lightly. “You’ll be wearing this. And you’ll have to wait.”

“I hate waiting.”

“I know. You were very bad at it at sixteen.”

“You never once made me wait at sixteen. You were always there first.”

“I know,” he said. “This time it’s your turn.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nainai wasn’t asleep. She was sitting by the open window of her room with the stick across her knees when they came in, and she looked at their faces and then at their joined hands.

“Well?”

“Nothing’s happened, Nainai,” said Tang Xi.

Nainai looked at her grandson. “Nothing?”

“Something will,” said An Yu. “When I’ve arranged it. Properly.”

“Properly.” Nainai sniffed. “Another excuse.” But she looked at Tang Xi’s hand on his arm, with the jade on it, and something in her old face moved. “Wear it. Don’t take it off to wash dishes. Jade likes skin.”

“I won’t.”

“And you.” The stick lifted at him. “Don’t take seven weeks.”

“Six and a half, Nainai.”

“Hmph. Go. I want to rest.”

They went out into the courtyard. The jade caught the afternoon light.

“Does it feel strange?” he asked.

“A little. Not uncomfortable. Unfamiliar.”

“Then we’ll get used to it.”

“We?”

“Yes.”

From the open window behind them came Nainai’s voice, loud. “An Yu!”

He stopped. “Yes, Nainai?”

“Ring your brother! And tell him he can’t come to whatever it is either!”

He closed his eyes. Tang Xi laughed until she had to sit down on the edge of the stone trough by the gate.

“She was listening,” he said.

“Of course she was listening. She’s always listening.”

He took his phone out. “I appear to have a schedule.”
