“Of course you do.” She looked up at him from the edge of the trough with the jade on her hand and the light in her eyes, and for the first time in his life, he didn’t mind being hurried at all. Not when he knew exactly where he was going, and she was coming with him.

chapters.title: The Library at Night
chapters.desc: The school library, at night, on National Day. He has brought an answer to every question she asked him at sixteen.
chapters.content:
The first of October was a holiday in Shanghai, and the city had poured itself out onto the river. From the car Tang Xi could see the crowds on the waterfront, the flags on every lamp post, the boats strung with lights; and then the car turned off into the quiet road beside the old school, under the plane trees, and stopped at the iron gates, and the noise of the holiday fell away behind them.

There was one light on in the building. The library.

She turned to him. “This is the favour. On the phone. In Nainai’s courtyard.”

“Yes.”

“You rang the school from your grandmother’s garden and asked them to open the library at night on National Day.”

“I asked Mrs. Hua. She asked the school. The school said yes to her. They wouldn’t have said yes to me.”

“Did you tell her why?”

“I told her it was important.”

“That’s all?”

“That’s all. She didn’t ask anything else. She said she’d been expecting me to ring for about eleven years.”

Tang Xi laughed and looked through the windscreen at the lit windows, and her eyes stung. “You’re getting better at asking for things.”

He took her hand, the one with the jade on it. “I had a good teacher.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Hua was waiting inside the door in a cardigan, with her glasses on their chain, and her hair had gone almost entirely white since February of last year. She looked at them over the top of the glasses for a long moment.

“The cheerful one. And the boy by the window.”

“Good evening, Mrs. Hua,” said An Yu.

“He speaks,” said Mrs. Hua, to Tang Xi, with great satisfaction.

Tang Xi had to hold his arm.

“You have an hour. I’ll be at the desk.” Mrs. Hua turned away, and turned back. “Don’t keep her waiting, young man. You did that enough the first time.”

“I won’t.”

She went to her desk at the far end and switched on a lamp and opened a book, and didn’t look at them again.

The library at night was a different room. The overhead lights were off. Someone had left on only the reading lamps along the window tables, so that the long room lay in pools of warm yellow light with the dark between them, and the shelves rose up into shadow. Through the tall windows she could see the black shapes of the plane trees and, far off, the glow of the river. Their table was by the third window. The lamp above it was on.

She walked to it slowly. Her shoes sounded loud on the floor. She stopped beside her old chair and put her hand on its back.

“Here.”

“Yes.”

“And you, there.”

“Yes.”

He pulled out her chair for her, and she sat, and he went round and sat in his, and for a while they simply looked at each other across the table, in the lamplight, eleven years after she’d first asked him if the seat was taken.

“Do you remember,” she said, “the first thing I ever said to you?”

“You asked if the seat was taken.”

“And you didn’t answer.”

“I’ve brought the answer.” He took a cream envelope out of his inside pocket and laid it on the table between them. It was thick. “I’ve brought all of them.”

She looked at it. “All of what?”

“You asked me a great many questions that year. I didn’t answer one of them. I thought it was time.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She opened it. It was several sheets of the heavy cream paper from his desk, written in his careful hand, the same hand as the four pages she kept in her bedside drawer. At the top he’d written her name. Under it was a list.

Is this seat taken?
No. It was yours from the second day. I never let anyone else sit in it.

She looked up. He was watching her.

“Keep reading.”

Maths. Of course. What else would someone like you be doing at lunch?
Waiting for you to come in. The maths was so you wouldn’t notice.

I got eighty-seven on my chemistry test. You’re supposed to congratulate me.
Congratulations. Eighty-seven was good. You’d been worried about it for two weeks, and you were right to be pleased.

Wang An Yu. Are you listening?
Yes. Every day. Always.

Why do you always sit here? Is it the window? The way the sun lands on this table?
Because it was where you knew to find me.

Or are you secretly in love with this chair?
No. Not with the chair.

She laughed out loud, and it came out wet, and down at the far end of the room Mrs. Hua turned a page.

Did I fall asleep? How long?
Twelve minutes. I moved my chair so Mrs. Hua would have to go round me to wake you. She didn’t.

You’re not even going to tell me?
I was going to tell you everything. On the Friday. I had it written in the back of my maths book.

If you could go to any university at all, where would it be?
Zurich. You said it would be somewhere quiet with good libraries, where nobody bothered me. Somewhere without people like you. You were right. There was nobody like you in Zurich. That was the worst thing about it.

Her hand had started to shake. She put the page down on the table and flattened it with her palm and kept reading.

That’s fine. I’ll visit anyway. Even if you go to Switzerland, I’ll find the library.
I went to every library in Zurich in my first winter. I didn’t know I was looking for you until about the fifth one. You weren’t in any of them. I kept going anyway.

You really don’t like telling people things about yourself, do you?
No. But I’ve wanted to tell you every one of them since I was sixteen.

Good luck, Wang An Yu.
Thank you. I’ve had it. It came back.

And at the bottom of the last page, after a space, one line on its own.

Will you miss me?
You never asked me this. I wish you had. Yes. Every day for ten years. I’d like never to have to again.

She couldn’t see the page any more. She put it down. Across the table he didn’t say anything, and didn’t reach for her, and let her cry for as long as she needed to, the way he had let her listen for an hour in February of the year before. It was a different thing this time. Then, he had told her what he’d been feeling. This was something else. This was the boy at sixteen, finally answering.

“When did you write this?” she said at last.

“Over the summer. I kept a list. Every question you asked that I could remember. Some I wasn’t sure of, so I left them out. I didn’t want to give you a wrong answer.”

“How many times did you write it?”

He hesitated. “Enough.”

She laughed and wiped her face with the heel of her hand. “You’re still terrible at saying things.”

“I know.”

“You’ve got much better at writing them.” She reached across the table and laid her hand on the paper, and then on his. “I used to wonder what you were thinking, sitting there.”

“I was thinking about you.”

“That boy,” she said, and shook her head, and her mouth trembled.

“Yes.”

“I wish you’d told me.”

“So do I.”

“Not because I needed you to be someone different. I only wanted to know I wasn’t talking to myself.”

“You never were,” he said, and she leaned across the table, across all the pages, and kissed him in the lamplight, holding his face between her hands as if she had been waiting eleven years to do it in exactly this place, which she had.

When she drew back he kept his forehead against hers.

“Xi. There’s one more.”

“One more question?”

“One I haven’t asked yet.”

He reached into his jacket again, and this time she understood.

✦ ✦ ✦

The box was dark blue. He put it on the table between the pages and opened it.

Inside was a ring: a plain gold band with a single clear stone set low, so it wouldn’t catch on anything she touched. It was beautiful and it wasn’t showy at all, and she knew at once that he had chosen it himself, that he hadn’t let anyone choose it for him, and that it had been made to sit beside the jade.

“I wanted something that could be next to Nainai’s,” he said. “Not instead of it.”

“Did you ask her?”

“Yes. She said it was about time, and that if I made it bigger than hers she’d throw it in the pond.”

Tang Xi laughed through her tears. He took the ring out of its box, and stood, and came round the table, and stopped in front of her chair, and for a moment seemed to lose every word he’d prepared.

“You’re nervous,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You’re Wang An Yu. You run a company.”

“I know.”

“You’ve negotiated with people much more frightening than me.”

“None of them mattered.”

He went down on one knee on the library floor, beside her old chair, under the lamp. The room seemed to go quiet. There was only the yellow light on their table, and the dark windows, and at the far end Mrs. Hua’s lamp, and Mrs. Hua not turning a page.

“Tang Xi.”

She held her breath.

“I can’t give you back the year we lost, or the ten after it. I can’t sit opposite you at sixteen again and answer you while you’re asking. I can’t change the Thursday you waited for me.” He looked up at her steadily. “But I can give you every answer I owed you, and I just have. And I can promise to ask you every question I was too frightened to ask. I can listen when you talk, and talk when you need me to. I don’t want you to make yourself smaller to fit into my life. I don’t want you to give up your work, or your voice, or one single opinion. I want to build a life with you that has room for all of it, and for me, and for your mother’s dumplings, and Nainai’s stick, and the arguments about dinner.” His voice dropped. “I want the ordinary days and the hard days and the days when neither of us has anything important to say at all. I want every one of them with you. Not because I waited for you. Because I love the woman sitting in that chair.”

He held up the ring.

“Will you marry me?”

She looked at him: at the boy she’d once thought didn’t care, and the man who had finally learned how to answer.

“Yes.”

He let out a breath. “Yes?”

“Yes, An Yu. I’ll marry you.”

He slid the ring onto her finger, next to the jade, and the two of them sat together on her hand under the lamp. For a moment he only looked at them. Then he looked up, and she leaned down and kissed him, and he rose and she rose with him, out of the chair, into his arms, and he held her so tightly she couldn’t breathe and didn’t want to.

“You’re engaged,” he murmured into her hair.

“So are you.”

From the far end of the room came the sound of a book being closed, firmly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Mrs. Hua was standing at her desk when they came back with their hands joined. She looked at Tang Xi’s hand, and then at An Yu.

“Finally.”

“Everyone keeps saying that,” said Tang Xi.

“Because everyone’s been waiting. I’ve been waiting since the day you fell asleep on that table and he moved his chair.” Mrs. Hua took off her glasses and let them drop on their chain. “Now you can talk as much as you like. Nobody will tell you to lower your voice.”

“That’s very generous.”

“It’s not generosity. It’s retirement. I finish in December.” She looked at An Yu. “Take care of her.”

“I will.”

“And talk to her.”

“Every day.”

“Good.” Mrs. Hua turned off her lamp. “Out. I want my dinner.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The hotel was on the river, high up, and from the window of the room the whole of Shanghai lay spread out below in light: the old buildings along the Bund lit gold, the towers across the water blazing, boats sliding along the black river trailing colour, fireworks going up somewhere downstream for the holiday and blooming silently on the other side of the thick glass.

Tang Xi stood at the window in her stockinged feet with her coat over a chair, holding her left hand up so the two rings caught the lights.

“Still looking?” he said, behind her.

“I’m checking they’re real.”

“They’re real.” He stood close enough that she could feel the warmth of him against her back, and touched the jade, and then the new ring. “Does it feel uncomfortable?”

“No.”

“Too tight?”

“No.”

“Are you sure?”

She turned round. “You’ve asked me about the ring four times.”

“I want to be sure.”

“It’s perfect.” She reached up and took hold of his tie. “May I?”

“Yes.”

She loosened the knot slowly and drew it out of his collar and dropped it on the floor. Then his jacket, off his shoulders. Then his shirt, one button at a time, the way he had once undone hers on the first night, and she watched his face while she did it, and he watched hers, and nobody hurried anything. When she had his shirt open she laid her left hand flat on his chest, over his heart, and looked at it there: the jade, the gold, the clear stone, against his skin.

“Look,” she said.

He looked. His heart was going hard under her palm. He covered her hand with his own and held it there, and kissed her.

They had all night, and they used all of it.

He undressed her by the window with the river behind her. Her dress, the zip drawn down so slowly she started to laugh; her bra, which he unhooked with one hand and a kind of absolute concentration that made her laugh harder; the rest. He knelt in front of her on the hotel carpet and kissed her stomach and her hip bones and the inside of her thighs while the fireworks went up behind her, and when his mouth found her she put her ringed hand on the cold glass to hold herself up and left a print there. He made her come standing up, with her other hand in his hair and her head against the window and the whole lit city at her back, and she said his name loud enough that someone in the next room might have heard, and didn’t care.

Afterwards he carried her to the bed. She pulled him down over her and wrapped her legs round him and took him inside her slowly, watching his eyes, and they moved together a long time without hurrying, the way they had learned to, asking without needing to ask now, and every time her left hand came up to his face or his chest or the back of his neck he turned his head and kissed the rings on it. She came again, slowly this time, shuddering under him with her ringed hand pressed flat over his heart, and he followed her with a long low sound and her name in his mouth.

They didn’t sleep. They lay and talked and ate the room-service noodles at two in the morning sitting cross-legged on the bed in the hotel robes, and she told him the ring was too beautiful and he told her the jade was older than his whole family’s company, and she laughed and kissed him with sesame on her mouth, and then it started again, unhurried, her on top of him this time, riding him slowly in the blue light from the river with her hands braced on his chest and the two rings shining there. He held her hips and watched her and didn’t look away once. When she came she bent down and put her forehead to his, and he said, against her mouth, the thing he’d written at the bottom of the last page: “Every day. I don’t want to miss you ever again.”

“You won’t have to,” she said.

Near dawn she lay with her head on his shoulder and her left hand on his chest, where he’d put it, and the river had gone from black to grey to silver below them. He lifted her hand and kissed the two rings, the old one and the new one.

“Your hand,” he said.

“What about it?”

“Leave it there.”

“Here?”

“On my chest. For the rest of my life, if possible.”

“That will make shaking hands with your board quite difficult.”

“They’ll adapt,” he said, and she laughed into his neck, and fell asleep that way, her hand over his heart, the rings against his skin.

✦ ✦ ✦

He woke first. The curtains were half open and the morning was coming up off the river into the room. She was asleep beside him with her hair everywhere and one hand tucked under her cheek, the rings showing. There were messages on his phone from his brother, from Nainai, and two from Ding. He ignored all of them, and looked instead at a photograph he’d taken in the night while she slept: her hand on his chest, the jade, the gold.

She stirred. “An Yu?”

“I’m here.”

“What time is it?”

“After eight.”

“Are we really engaged?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” She lifted her hand into the light and looked at it, and then at him. “Can I ask you something? If you could go back to that library at sixteen, what would you say first?”

He thought about it properly. Then he touched her cheek.

“I’d say, good afternoon, Tang Xi.”

“That’s all?”

“Then I’d ask if you’d eaten.”

She laughed. “An Yu.”

“And then I’d ask whether I could sit with you.”

“You’d ask? Even though you knew I’d say yes?”

“That’s why I’d ask,” he said. “So I could hear you say it.”

She leaned over and kissed him, and outside the river carried the morning light down through Shanghai, and inside she lay beside the boy who had been too quiet to answer her, who had answered her now, all of it, every question; and she had all the time in the world to hear whatever came next.

chapters.title: Two Agencies, One Wedding
chapters.desc: Three hundred guests cut to forty, an empty chair with white flowers, and his father, who comes and sits and stays.
chapters.epigraph: “One reminds me you asked. The other reminds me I answered.”
chapters.content:
The first wedding proposal arrived in a leather folder. The second arrived as a presentation. Tang Xi looked at the two of them lying side by side on his dining table on a Sunday evening in February and decided, with complete certainty, that she was going to marry Wang An Yu without letting either of them organise it.

The leather folder was from the Wang family office, which managed everything for the family that wasn’t a hospital or a port, and had been managing weddings for three generations. The presentation was from An-Tech’s own corporate events team, sent over with a warm note from Felix Ong, who had evidently decided that the best way to make peace with the woman who had beaten him for Halloway was to offer to stage her wedding.

“Three hundred and twelve guests,” she said.

He looked up from his tablet. “That’s the family office.”

“I know.”

“An-Tech’s has three hundred and forty.”

She closed the folder. “Absolutely not.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“You’re looking at me as if you’re trying to work out whether three hundred and twelve is a reasonable number.”

“I was considering whether the difference of twenty-eight was significant.”

“It’s twenty-eight more people I don’t know. Your father’s business friends are not people I know. They’re people who’ll ask me whether Level is expanding into Seoul while I’m trying to eat my wedding lunch.” She pushed the presentation across the table. “The family office suggests a ceremony, a tea ceremony, a lunch, a banquet for the family, and a separate evening reception for your father’s friends.”

“That’s quite a standard arrangement.”

“It’s five weddings.”

“Four.”

“An Yu.” She folded her arms. “I want to marry you. I don’t want to be the centrepiece of a regional hospitality programme.”

He thought about that. Then he opened the leather folder at the guest list and picked up a pen. “What number would you like?”

“Forty.”

His eyes came up. “Forty?”

“Forty people. Including us.”

“That’s a significant reduction.”

“I’m glad you can count.”

There was no irritation in his face, and no attempt to persuade her that a man of his family ought to be married in front of three hundred people. He simply turned to a clean page. At the top, in his precise hand, he wrote: Forty people. No corporate guests. No business obligations.

She took the pen out of his fingers and added underneath: No speech longer than three minutes.

“Whose speech?”

“Anyone’s.”

“That may be difficult to enforce.”

“Then enforce it.”

So they sat at the dining table and went through names. Not titles. Not positions. Not people whose presence would be useful to somebody. Just names.

Nainai, who had already told three separate relatives that she had been waiting long enough and would be sitting at the front. Wang Xing Yue and Elara, who had sent them a photograph from their own garden wedding last May, at six in the morning under the hospital’s old trees, with a note in Elara’s handwriting that said: the bride chooses the flowers, not a planner. Wang Yu Chen and Eliana, who had been married since October and had already started giving advice as if marriage were an exam they’d passed with distinction. Tang Xi’s mother. Her father, who had sent her a long letter when she told him, the first in years, in which he said little and meant all of it. Her aunt, who owned the restaurant and had lent her a storeroom. Rachel. Calvin. Grace Tham. Mrs. Hua, retired since Christmas, who had written back from Shanghai in a single line: I’ll come if he talks. Ding, who had asked in a small voice whether he might be allowed to stand at the back. Daniel from Northlight, who had once made her choose and then, last autumn, had sent the first big referral Level ever received. A handful of old friends. A few relatives on both sides who had been kind to her when they hadn’t had to be.

The list grew slowly. When it reached thirty-eight, he put the pen down.

“Two more.”

“Your parents,” she said.

“My mother died when I was nine.”

She looked at him. He didn’t say it sadly; it was simply a fact, one of the things in his life he had learned to mention without expecting anybody to ask about it. She had known, vaguely, since the first dinner with Xing Yue that there was no mother at the family table. She had never asked. She reached across now and touched his hand.

“I’m sorry.”

He turned his palm up and caught her fingers. “I’d have liked you to meet her. She’d have liked you.”

“You can’t know that.”

“No,” he said. “But I’d have told her about the girl in the library. I nearly did, once. She was very ill by then. She asked me if I had any friends at school, and I said there was a girl who talked.” He looked at their hands. “She laughed. It was the last time I remember her laughing.”

Tang Xi couldn’t speak for a moment. She held his hand tightly, and after a while she said, “Then she’ll have a chair. An empty one. With flowers.”

He looked at her. “Yes.”

“And your father.”

His eyes went to the last empty line. “Yes. I want him there.”

“Not because Nainai will be angry if he isn’t?”

“Nainai will be angry whatever he does.”

That made her laugh. He wrote his father’s name on the fortieth line, and the empty chair beside it, and then he folded both proposals and put them away.

“Should I tell them?”

“I’ll tell them,” she said. “Both.”

She stood and came round the table and put her hands on his shoulders and kissed his hair. “Good fiancé.”

He tipped his head back to look at her upside down. “Is that the standard now?”

“It’s a very high standard.”

“Do I get a reward for following instructions?”

“You haven’t followed them yet.”

“Then I’ll wait,” he said, and she bent down and kissed him properly, upside down, and he laughed into it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The family office rang the next morning, and she answered.

“Good morning, Ms. Tang. About the initial proposal. We have several options for something more intimate, though given the family’s profile we’d strongly recommend no fewer than one hundred and fifty—”

“Forty.”

A pause. “I’m sorry?”

“Forty guests. That’s the final number.”

“Of course, we can explore something smaller. But perhaps we should discuss the family’s requirements first. Mr. Wang’s father may have a number of important—”

“Then he can invite them to dinner on another day.” She kept her voice perfectly pleasant. “It’s our wedding. We’re not hosting a corporate event, and we’re not using it to strengthen anybody’s relationships. Thank you for your work. We won’t be going ahead with your proposal.”

Felix Ong, when she rang him, laughed for a full ten seconds before he said, “I told my team you’d say that. I bet them lunch. Congratulations, Ms. Tang.”

An Yu was at the kitchen counter pouring coffee. “Finished?”

“Finished.”

“Did you fire them?”

“I declined their proposals.”

“That’s a polite way of putting it.”

“I’m a polite person.” She took his coffee out of his hand.

“That was mine.”

“I’m your fiancée.”

“I wasn’t aware that extended to coffee.”

“It does,” she said, and drank it, and he let her.

He rang his father’s office himself. He listened for almost three minutes before he said, “No.” Then: “No additional guests.” Then: “I’m not asking you to negotiate the number with my father. I’m telling you what’s been decided. Please don’t contact the venue, or any of our guests, on the family’s behalf.” He put the phone down.

“Very chairman,” she said from the sofa.

“I’ll try to be less chairman at the wedding.”

“Please do. I don’t want to marry a man who issues procurement instructions during the vows.”

“What should I say during the vows?”

She leaned her head on his shoulder. “The right things. Tell me you love me.”

“I love you.”

“See? Not difficult.”

“I’ve had practice.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They were married at the registry office on a Saturday in April, at eleven in the morning, in a plain room with white walls and a window onto a camphor tree. There was no ballroom, no orchestra, no wall of flowers and no logo anywhere. Lunch afterwards would be at her aunt’s restaurant in the old town, closed for the day for the first time in thirty years, the tables pushed into one long one, the extractor fan switched off for once.

She chose her dress herself: ivory, simple, a clean neckline and a fitted waist, sleeves that were delicate without being fussy. She didn’t want anything that made her feel she’d borrowed someone else’s idea of a bride. He saw it for the first time that morning, waiting outside the little side room at the registry, and when she stepped out he didn’t move at all.

She looked down at herself. “Is something wrong?”

“No.”

“Is it too plain?”

“No.”

“Then why are you staring?”

He looked at her face. “You’re beautiful.”

He’d said it before: at home, on ordinary evenings, when she was in an old T-shirt with her hair still wet. But this time he said it with a kind of helpless sincerity that made her suddenly shy, and she looked away. “Thank you.”

He reached for her hand and stopped before he touched it. “May I?”

She gave it to him. He lifted it and kissed the jade, and then the engagement ring.

“You’re really marrying me,” he said.

“We’ve discussed this.”

“I know.”

“You nearly proposed at Nainai’s table and I stopped you. Then you got down on one knee in a school library. I said yes.”

“I remember.”

“Then why do you sound surprised?”

He looked at her. “Because I still haven’t got used to being this lucky.”

She straightened the front of his jacket. “You’re not lucky because I said yes. You’re lucky because I’m an excellent choice.”

He laughed. “That’s true.”

“And because you’re occasionally a good choice too.”

“Occasionally?”

“Don’t get arrogant on your wedding day.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nainai arrived before anyone else, in dark red silk, and directed the seating with her stick, though there were forty chairs in two short rows and they had already been arranged according to a plan.

“Too far apart,” she said, pointing at two of them.

“They’re next to each other, Nainai,” said Xing Yue.

“Not close enough.”

“They’re touching.”

“Then move them properly.”

Elara, beside her husband, was trying hard not to laugh. “I think the chairs are fine, Nainai.”

The stick swung towards her. “You’re a surgeon. You should know when something needs adjusting.” Elara looked at Xing Yue, who gave her the expression of a man who had long ago stopped trying to win an argument with this woman.

Yu Chen and Eliana came in together with a small gift wrapped in cream paper, which Yu Chen had insisted on carrying and Eliana kept retying because he’d done the ribbon badly.

“You’re late,” said Nainai.

“By three minutes,” said Yu Chen.

“Three minutes is late.”

“Happy wedding day, Nainai,” said Eliana, bending to kiss her, and Nainai’s face softened and she held Eliana’s face in both hands and looked at her, and then told them both to sit down before they made the room untidy.

Tang Xi’s mother came in with her father and her aunt, all three of them in their best and looking at the white room. Her mother walked straight up to An Yu, looked him over from his shoes to his hair, straightened his tie with two sharp tugs, and went to sit down without saying a word. Her father shook his hand for a long time.

Xing Yue came and stood beside Tang Xi in the doorway. “You look lovely.”

“Thank you.”

“He’s been checking the time every five minutes since eight. I think he’s been nervous since the day he bought the ring.”

“Which ring?”

Xing Yue looked at her left hand. “Both, I think.”

Across the room An Yu looked up from where he was talking to the registrar, and their eyes met. He didn’t smile straight away. He simply looked at her, with the same complete attention he had once given her from the other side of a library table when he was too young and too frightened to say anything. Then he crossed the room.

“Ready?”

“Are you?”

“Yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

His father came eleven minutes before the ceremony. He came alone, without a secretary or a driver at his elbow, in a dark suit, carrying nothing, his face as controlled as it had been in his drawing room when he’d told her she wasn’t suitable. The room went a little quieter. An Yu saw him, and looked at Tang Xi first.

“Go.”

He went. “Father. Thank you for coming.”

His father looked at him, and then past him at Tang Xi, at the rings on her hand. “Congratulations.”

She inclined her head. “Thank you for coming, Mr. Wang.”

He nodded, slightly. “Where should I sit?”

“Here.” An Yu took him to the front, next to Nainai, across the narrow aisle from his brother. Beside Nainai, on the other side, there was an empty chair with a bunch of white chrysanthemums on it, and his father looked at it and then sat down next to it without a word.

Nainai looked at him. “You came.”

“I said I would.”

“You’ve said many things.”

“Mother.”

“Don’t mother me. Sit up straight.” He did. Nainai turned to Tang Xi with deep satisfaction. “See? He can follow instructions.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The room was small enough that nobody could hide in it. There were no rows of strangers, no tables of people who had come because they had to. Everyone there had known them long enough to understand what the morning meant.

The registrar went through the formalities. Names. Identity cards. Did they each come freely. Tang Xi answered clearly. An Yu answered just as clearly. Then they were asked to say their vows, and he turned to her, and his eyes went for a second to her hands, and then to her face.

“Xi.”

“An Yu.”

“I have spent a long time remembering the things I didn’t say to you. The library. The first day you sat down opposite me, and every day after. The last time you came, and how I let you go without asking you to stay.” His voice was steady, but his eyes had changed. “I can’t give you those days back. I can’t promise I’ll always know what to say. But I can promise I won’t make my silence your job. I’ll ask. I’ll listen. I’ll tell you when I’m afraid, and when I’m wrong, and when I need you. And I’ll keep choosing you. Not because we’ve known each other so long. Because I love the person standing in front of me now.”

She hadn’t expected to cry. She had thought she’d be too happy, or too busy trying not to laugh at the sight of him in a registry office with his hands not quite steady. But the words went somewhere she hadn’t thought to guard.

“When I was sixteen,” she said, “I thought you didn’t like me.”

“I know.”

“I thought I was the only one who remembered that library. The only one who went home and wondered what you were thinking.”

“I was thinking about you.”

“I know that now.” She held his hands tighter. “You used to let me talk enough for both of us. Now I want you to keep talking, even when it’s hard. Most of all when it’s hard. And I want to keep being myself. I want to build Level. I want to make mistakes and be proud of things and be unreasonable about dinner. I want to disagree with you and still come home to you.”

“I want all of that.”

“Then that’s what I’m promising.” Her voice went soft. “I choose you, An Yu. Every day. Not because you waited for me, or because I came back, or because it all started a long time ago. I choose you because I know you now, and I still want you.”

For one brief second he looked almost overwhelmed.

The registrar asked for the rings. He put the plain gold band on her finger beside the jade and the engagement ring, and his hands were steady but she felt his thumb press hard against her knuckle. She put his on him. It looked different on his hand: not unfamiliar, but the first thing she had ever seen him wear that belonged to a promise between the two of them.

The registrar pronounced them married. There was a moment of silence. Then applause, ragged and loud in the small white room, and Nainai was first on her feet, rapping her stick on the floor.

“Finally.”

Xing Yue laughed. Elara wiped her eyes. Yu Chen clapped with both hands while Eliana leaned over and whispered something that made him grin. Rachel was crying openly, and so, Tang Xi saw, was Ding, at the back. Her mother sat perfectly upright with her hands in her lap and her mouth pressed tight, and her father had his arm round her.

Tang Xi hardly heard any of it. He was still looking at her.

“You may kiss,” said the registrar, smiling.

He didn’t move straight away. He looked at her, asking without a word.

“Yes,” she whispered.

He kissed her. It wasn’t a performance for the room, or a long theatrical kiss for photographs. His hand came up to her cheek, his thumb just under her ear, and he kissed her slowly and surely, like a man who had finally arrived somewhere he’d been trying to reach for years and intended to stay. She held the front of his jacket in both fists and kissed him back, and the room went on clapping, and for a few seconds neither of them could hear it at all.

When they came apart his forehead stayed against hers.

“Hello, husband,” she whispered.

His eyes went soft. “Hello, wife.”

She laughed, and he kissed her again, quickly, before the room could remind them that there were thirty-eight other people in it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was at the long table in her aunt’s restaurant. There were flowers she’d chosen herself on every table, and the kitchen had been running since five that morning, and nobody’s speech went over three minutes.

Nainai’s lasted two minutes and forty-seven seconds, most of the first minute spent complaining about how long it had all taken. Xing Yue’s was exactly three minutes. He talked about his little brother, about growing up in the same house, about the rare occasions on which An Yu had actually asked him for advice.

“Most of the time,” Xing Yue said, lifting his glass, “he believed he could solve everything by thinking quietly in a corner. Today I think he’s found the one person who won’t let him.”

Everyone laughed. An Yu looked at his brother. “Thank you.”

“That’s all?”

“That’s enough.”

Yu Chen’s was shorter. He thanked Tang Xi for joining the family and hoped An Yu would become slightly more approachable now that he had someone to talk to at breakfast.

“I’m approachable,” said An Yu.

“Of course,” said Yu Chen, and Eliana patted his arm.

Her mother spoke last. Tang Xi had been afraid she’d refuse. She had only agreed to the wedding at all after being promised there would be no grand family ceremony. But she stood up at the end of the long table, in the room where she had made a hundred thousand dumplings, with a small glass of tea in her hand, and everybody went quiet.

“I don’t have much to say. My daughter has worked very hard to become who she is. She can look after herself. She has always been stubborn.” A few people laughed. “Sometimes too stubborn.”

“Mum,” Tang Xi murmured.

Her mother ignored her and looked down the table at An Yu. “I only hope the two of you remember that being married isn’t one person looking after the other all the time. You look after each other. And you let each other stay yourselves.” She lifted the glass. “Eat properly. Come home safely. Don’t make each other unhappy for no reason.”

It wasn’t a conventional toast. Tang Xi loved it more than any speech she’d ever heard. An Yu stood and raised his own glass. “I’ll remember.”

Her mother looked at him. “Good.” And when she sat down she reached over with her chopsticks and put a dumpling on his plate. Chive and prawn. Five pleats. Tang Xi saw it, and so did he.

“Thank you.”

“Eat it before it’s cold.”

“Yes,” said An Yu, and ate it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards everyone spilled out into the street and the little square at the end of it for photographs. Xing Yue and Elara stood under a plane tree, his arm round her waist, her ring catching the afternoon sun as she straightened his collar. Yu Chen and Eliana were arguing quietly about whether they needed another picture.

“You blinked,” said Eliana.

“I didn’t.”

“You did.”

“I was looking at the camera.”

“You were looking at the photographer.”

“He was standing next to the camera.”

“Six months married,” said Tang Xi to An Yu, “and still arguing about photographs.”

“Some things don’t change.”

Nainai demanded one with all three couples and then told Tang Xi to stand next to her instead of next to her grandson. “Closer.” An Yu moved closer, and the stick came up. “Not you. Her.”

Then one with Tang Xi’s parents. Then one with his father. His father stood beside An Yu, with a small but definite space between himself and Tang Xi. The photographer asked them to move in. His father looked at the gap. For a moment nobody said anything. Then he stepped closer. Not much. Just enough. Tang Xi glanced at him. He didn’t look at her, but he stayed where he was, and the photograph was taken.

It wasn’t a reconciliation. It wasn’t an apology for the drawing room, or the file on her father, or the toast, or the chair, or the years An Yu had stood alone between them. But he had come, and he had sat, and he had stayed, and Tang Xi understood that it wasn’t nothing.

The last guests left a little after five. Nainai was driven home by Xing Yue and Elara. Yu Chen and Eliana promised to come the next weekend. Her mother left last of her family, after reminding them to take the leftover food and not waste it, and pressed a heavy plastic bag of boxed dumplings into An Yu’s hands.

His father was the very last. He stood by the restaurant door speaking to his son, and Tang Xi waited a few steps away and heard only part of it.

“Look after your responsibilities.”

“I will.”

“Not only the company.”

“I know.”

A pause. Then his father looked past him at her. “Goodbye, Ms. Tang.”

“Goodbye, Mr. Wang.”

He went. An Yu watched the car until it had gone round the corner, and turned back to her. “Are you all right?”

“Are you?”

“Yes. I wanted him here.”

“I’m glad he came.”

“So am I.”

He took her hand, and the two wedding bands touched. She looked down at her hand: the jade, the engagement ring, the plain gold.

“Three rings,” she said.

“Three promises?”

“Something like that.”

He lifted her hand and kissed her knuckles. “Which is your favourite?”

“The jade. Because Nainai wore it when she married, and her mother before that. It has a whole life behind it.”

“And the other two?”

She smiled up at him. “One reminds me you asked. The other reminds me I answered.”

“Then keep answering.”

“I will.” She put both her arms round his waist in the quiet street, where the flowers in the restaurant window were beginning to droop and the last of the sun lay on the shutters. For years their story had been measured in things left unsaid. A library seat. A paper crane. A goodbye neither of them had understood. Now there were forty names on a list, an empty chair with white flowers on it, two gold bands, and a home they were going to go back to together.

She tipped her face up. “An Yu? I’m hungry.”

“We’ve just had lunch.”

“Your grandmother made me eat three helpings of soup and I didn’t get to enjoy a single dumpling.”

He held up the plastic bag. “Your mother anticipated this.”

“Then let’s go home.”

“Let’s go, Mrs. Wang.”

She stopped dead. “Say it again.”

His face went soft. “Mrs. Wang.”

“Hmm. I’m keeping Tang Xi for work.”

“I’d expect nothing else.”

“Come on, husband,” she said, and took his hand, and this time when they left together neither of them had to wonder whether the other would stay.

chapters.title: The Chairman’s Wife
chapters.desc: A badge that says GUEST, and a programme that gets her name right. He watches from the back of the room.
chapters.epigraph: “Tang Xi, founder, Level. That’s why I’m here.”
chapters.content:
The first time anyone called her the chairman’s wife, Tang Xi was holding a paper cup of coffee and looking for the registration desk.

It was a Tuesday at the end of April, ten days after the wedding. The forum took up two floors of a hotel on the harbour, all glass and polished stone, with a screen in the lobby the height of a house announcing the Regional Forum on Corporate Reputation and Leadership. Level had been invited to sit on a panel about independent agencies. She had spent the evening before going through her notes with Rachel and Calvin, the questions and the other speakers’ biographies and the timings, and had reminded Calvin twice that the agency was called Level, not Level Communications, and Rachel once that she wasn’t allowed to change the opening slide at midnight.

She was there as the founder of an agency. Nothing else.

“Good morning. Name, please?”

“Tang Xi. Level.”

The young woman at the desk looked at her tablet and her face lit up. “Oh! Of course, Ms. Tang.” She reached for a badge and hesitated. “Are you here with Mr. Wang? Chairman Wang? I’m sorry, I should have realised. You’re the chairman’s wife.”

Tang Xi looked at the badge in her hand.

TANG XI · GUEST

She took it gently. “I’m here as the founder of Level.”

The young woman blinked. “Of course. I only meant—”

“I understand.” Tang Xi smiled. “Could you change the designation? Tang Xi, founder, Level. That’s why I’m here.”

There was no edge in her voice. She didn’t embarrass the girl or make a scene. She simply waited.

“Of course, Ms. Tang. I’ll have it reprinted.”

“Thank you.”

She’d gone three steps when her phone lit.

Professor: Have you arrived?

Tang Xi: Yes. Apparently today I’m your wife.

Professor: You are.

Tang Xi: That’s not my job title.

Professor: I know. What did they call you?

Tang Xi: The chairman’s wife. On a badge that said GUEST.

Professor: I’ll speak to the organiser.

She could hear exactly how he’d say it, low and level, already working out whose job the badges had been.

Tang Xi: No. I’ve corrected it. Myself.

A pause.

Professor: All right. Good luck on your panel, Ms. Tang.

Tang Xi: Thank you, Mr. Wang.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was speaking in the ballroom when she went in, on the stage under a screen with An-Tech’s name on it, in a dark suit, answering questions about leadership and the difference between a company’s reputation and its chairman’s. She stopped at the back. She had heard him speak a hundred times by now, in boardrooms and at dinners and across his family’s table, and she knew his public manner. He never hurried to fill a silence. He let a question finish and waited a second longer than anybody else would have, and then answered so precisely that people leaned forward.

The moderator asked whether founders and chairmen had become so prominent that companies depended too much on their personalities.

“Visibility has its uses,” said An Yu. “But it mustn’t stand in for the institution’s own credibility. A company should be able to explain what it’s for, and how it behaves, even when its chairman isn’t in the room.”

Tang Xi smiled into her coffee. She had said almost exactly that, eleven months ago, to a panel of six people in a room he hadn’t been allowed into. He had read it afterwards in a procurement report. And he had remembered it, word for word.

He stepped away from the lectern, and his eyes went out over the room, and found her. His face hardly changed. It rarely did in public. But she saw the small pause before he turned to the next speaker, and his hand tighten on the edge of the lectern.

She took a seat by the aisle. A few minutes later a man in a navy suit stopped beside her, fifties, a lanyard from one of the sponsoring companies.

“Mrs. Wang? I think we met at the An-Tech dinner in December. You’re Chairman Wang’s wife, aren’t you?”

She stood up. “I’m Tang Xi. I run Level.”

He looked at her badge, freshly reprinted. “Ah. Level. I didn’t know you were in the agency business.”

“I founded it.”

“How interesting.” A polite laugh. “Well, congratulations. It must be very convenient, having a chairman at home.”

Her smile didn’t move. “Not especially. We have different companies.”

He wasn’t sure whether she was joking. “Still. You must understand the corporate world.”

“I’ve worked in it for eight years.”

“Of course, of course,” he said, and moved on.

She sat down. She wasn’t angry, exactly. She had expected something like this. His name was known across the region, and since the wedding hers had been attached to it in photographs and on business pages. People would make assumptions. But there was a difference between being known as someone’s wife and being introduced as if that was the only useful thing about her.

Professor: I saw you.

Tang Xi: I saw you too.

Professor: You look beautiful.

She glanced at the stage. He was talking to another chairman, his face entirely composed.

Tang Xi: You’re supposed to be networking.

Professor: I am. Briefly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her panel was at eleven.

Independent agencies in an age of consolidation: trust, scale and the value of staying small

She sat between the managing partner of a regional network with offices in nine cities and the corporate affairs director of a listed shipping company. The moderator read out each of their biographies, and when he came to hers she listened.

“Tang Xi founded Level, an independent strategic communications agency, in 2026, after several years in agency leadership. Under her, Level has grown to twelve people and now advises clients in corporate reputation, brand strategy and executive communications across three markets.”

That was better. She had spent two years making those sentences true.

“Ms. Tang,” said the moderator, “can a twelve-person agency really compete with firms that have offices across the region and hundreds of staff?”

She moved the microphone an inch. “I think the first question is whether we’re competing for the same thing. A bigger agency can offer scale: more offices, more specialists, more people to run six markets at once. Those are real advantages. But scale doesn’t automatically mean a better understanding of the client’s problem, and it doesn’t guarantee the people who pitch are the people who’ll do the work.” She looked out at the room. “Our model is deliberately small. We don’t pretend to have what we haven’t. We bring in specialists where a project needs them, and we’re selective. That means we sometimes say no to work we could probably win and couldn’t deliver properly.”

The shipping director leaned into her microphone. “Doesn’t that limit your growth?”

“Yes.”

A few people laughed.

“Of course it does. But not every limit is a problem. Capacity is real. If we take on more than we can manage, the quality goes, sooner or later. Our clients don’t pay us to look busy. They pay us to do the work.”

“And does independence make it harder to be trusted by large corporations?” asked the moderator.

“Sometimes. Above all when procurement’s used to judging agencies by headcount and office count and last year’s revenue.” “So we show them who’ll actually do the work. We show them the scope and the capacity and the partners and the limits of what we can promise. If a client needs fifty people, we’re not the right agency. If they need twelve experienced people who understand their business and will still be in the room in month eleven, we might be.” She paused. “Being small isn’t a weakness we have to disguise. It’s a way of working we have to manage responsibly.”

At the back of the ballroom An Yu had come in and sat down. He wasn’t on the panel. His own session was long over, and there was a private room for senior speakers on the floor above with better coffee and nobody to talk to. He sat in the audience instead with his hands folded loosely on his knee and listened.

He knew what she’d put into Level. He remembered the room over the restaurant and the three desks and the kettle that boiled itself dry. He remembered the tea company that could barely pay. He remembered her on her office floor at one in the morning, and the night she’d called him after her first client meeting to ask, casually, whether she’d sounded convincing. He had watched her build it one decision at a time. And now she was on a stage explaining to people who’d never seen that little room why she had chosen to keep it small.

Something moved in his chest. It wasn’t the pride he felt when a deal closed or a hard negotiation went his way. It was different, and it took him a moment to understand why. There was no part of this that belonged to him. He hadn’t given her the opportunity. He hadn’t introduced the client, arranged the contract, funded the company or put her name on a programme. He had only watched her do it. And he was so proud of her that he found he was sitting perfectly still.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards people queued to talk to her. One wanted to know about Level’s executive work. One had a regional rebrand she might be interested in. One asked whether Level would join a consortium for a government tender in the autumn.

Rachel appeared with two glasses of water. “You were good. Not just good. You made the regional network man look slightly ill when you said headcount wasn’t a measure of quality.”

“I didn’t mean to.”

“I know. That’s why it worked.” Rachel looked across the room. “Your husband’s watching you. He’s been doing it for twenty minutes.”

“He’s at a conference. He has people to talk to.”

“Apparently.”

“He came to a corporate forum.”

“Of course.”

“And I came to represent Level.”

“Of course.” Rachel grinned. “I’ll leave you to your separate professional identities.”

He came over a minute later. “Ms. Tang.”

“Mr. Wang.”

“I listened.”

“I noticed.”

“You were excellent.”

She raised an eyebrow. “You sound surprised.”

“I’m not.”

“Then why do you look so pleased?”

He was quiet. “Because you did it. Everything you said up there. You built it. You decided what Level would be and what it wouldn’t, and how it would grow. You didn’t borrow anyone’s name to make them listen.” His voice dropped. “You stood up and talked about your company, and they listened.”

“An Yu.”

“I know you don’t need me to tell you.”

“Then what are you telling me?”

“That watching you up there was the best hour I’ve spent all year. Better than any deal I’ve ever closed.”

Her throat went tight. He looked down at the badge on her jacket. TANG XI · FOUNDER · LEVEL. His eyes stayed there.

“I like seeing your name there.”

“So do I.”

He reached for her hand, and stopped; they were in the middle of a crowded room and he knew she didn’t like being made a show of. She held it out to him herself.

“Congratulations, Ms. Tang.”

“Thank you, Mr. Wang.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a lunch for speakers. The seating plan had put him at the head of one table and her two places down, between Rachel and the managing partner of another agency, which was sensible, and was also the first thing she noticed when she sat down.

For twenty minutes everyone behaved exactly as they should. Then an executive across the table, a cheerful man from a property group, turned to her.

“Ms. Tang. Does your husband advise you on running Level?”

She put down her fork. “Sometimes he gives me advice.”

“That must be useful. Having someone of his experience.”

“A different point of view can be useful.”

“Do you take it?”

“When I agree with it.”

A few people smiled. The man laughed. “And when you don’t?”

“Then I don’t.”

He turned to the head of the table. “Chairman Wang, I imagine you must have some influence at home.”

An Yu put his glass down. “I imagine my wife has rather more influence over her company than I do. Level is her business. I don’t run it. She doesn’t run An-Tech. We talk about work sometimes, as married people do. She makes her decisions.” He glanced down the table at Tang Xi. “And usually disagrees with mine.”

“Only when you’re wrong.”

“Which is often, apparently.”

“Not often.”

“More often than you admit.”

Rachel laughed into her water, and the conversation moved on. Tang Xi looked down at her plate, smiling. She hadn’t needed him to explain her independence to anyone; she had done it herself, that morning, at a registration desk. But she liked that he didn’t treat her work as a small extension of his life. He hadn’t said she was lucky to have him. He hadn’t said he supported her. He’d simply made it clear that Level belonged to her, and she knew exactly how much it had cost him to learn to say that sentence and mean it.

✦ ✦ ✦

They left separately. She had a prospective client in the hotel lounge, and he had a call with his regional team. At half past six her phone lit.

Professor: Finished?

Tang Xi: Almost.

Professor: I’ll wait.

Tang Xi: You don’t have to.

Professor: I know.

He was by the hotel doors when she came down, tie loosened, jacket over his arm, looking tired until he saw her.

“How did it go?”

“Promising. They want a proposal next week.”

“Good.”

“You’re very pleased with yourself today. You’ve been looking at me all afternoon.”

“I was listening.”

“That’s worse.” She stopped in front of him. “Were you really proud? More than usual?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He thought about it. “Because I’ve seen what it took. I saw you walk out of Northlight. I saw you start with three desks and a kettle. I saw you worry about whether the first client would pay on time. I saw you work all night because you wouldn’t hand over something you weren’t happy with. And today you stood in front of a room of people and talked about the company you built as if it had always been there.”

She looked down. “It hasn’t.”

“I know.”

“Sometimes I still feel as if I’m pretending.”

“You always have. It’s never once been true.”

“How?”

“Because after your first client meeting you rang me and asked whether you’d sounded convincing.”

“I did not.”

“You did.”

“I asked if the proposal was clear.”

“You asked whether they’d think Level was too small.”

She pressed her lips together. He took her hand.

“They didn’t. They listened. And they’ll remember you.”

“I wanted that,” she said. “Not to prove anything to your family. Not for the people who think I’m only your wife. I wanted people to know my name.”

He lifted her hand and kissed the gold band on it. “They do.”

She smiled. “Do you know what the programme said?”

“Tang Xi, founder, Level.”

“You memorised it?”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

“Because I like it.”

“You’re ridiculous.”

“Possibly.”

He opened the car door for her, and before she got in she turned round. “An Yu. Today, when they called me your wife, I didn’t mind being your wife. I only didn’t want it to be the only thing they knew.”

“It won’t be.”

He touched her cheek. “And for the record, I like being your husband. Even when you disagree with me.”

“Even when I refuse your advice?”

“I’ve accepted that as part of the arrangement.”

“Even when I tell you your tie’s terrible?”

He looked down at it. “Is it?”

“Not today.”

She laughed and kissed him, briefly, warm, under the hotel’s lights with people passing on both sides, and when she pulled back he was looking at her with the same expression she’d seen from the back of the ballroom. Proud. Not possessive. Not triumphant. Just proud.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night she found the programme on the coffee table, where it had fallen open at the speakers’ biographies when she took out her badge. Her name was halfway down the page in black.

TANG XI · FOUNDER, LEVEL

She ran her fingers over it. He came out of the kitchen with two cups of tea and put one by her elbow.

“What are you looking at?”

“My biography.”

“It’s accurate. They could have written more.”

“Such as?”

“That you built a good company.”

“That isn’t a biography.”

“It could be.” He sat down beside her.

“Do you think people will remember me?”

“Yes.”

“Not because I’m married to you?”

“Some will know you that way first,” he said honestly. “Then they’ll remember the work. And if they don’t, they’ll have to meet you again.”

She laughed. “That’s a very confident answer.”

“I know you.”

She took his hand. “Today I liked being your wife. But I liked being Tang Xi, founder of Level, more.”

“Good.”

“Good?”

“That’s how it should be. I didn’t marry you so you’d turn into someone else. I married you because I wanted to spend my life next to you. Not with you behind me.”

She leaned her head on his shoulder. “Then tomorrow at work you’re Chairman Wang and I’m Ms. Tang.”

“Founder Tang.”

“That’s right.”

“And when we get home?”

She lifted her head. “Then you can call me whatever you like.”

He thought about it. “Xi.”

“That’s my favourite,” she said, and on the coffee table the programme lay open with her name on it, printed clearly in black, and for once she didn’t feel the need to correct anybody. They’d got it right.

chapters.title: Opposite Again
chapters.desc: Epilogue. A library table in their own house. She talks; he listens; then he talks.
chapters.content:
The library was Tang Xi’s idea.

At first An Yu thought she meant a proper one: shelves built to measure, a reading room with controlled light, a ladder on a rail, a separate corner for his papers. He’d had an architect send references. She had looked at the photographs, put the tablet down on the sofa, and said, “I want a room where we can read.”

“That’s what these are.”

“No. These are rooms where you can display books and make visitors feel undereducated.”

He had looked at the photographs again. “Then what would you like?”

“Shelves. A table. Two chairs. A window.” She thought. “And a lamp.”

“That’s all?”

“An Yu, I am not building a national archive.”

So they made a room at the quiet end of the house, where the afternoon came through a wide window and lay along the wooden floor. Shelves along two walls. Some held his books, arranged by subject with the precision she’d expected; some held hers, in no order at all: novels, battered paperbacks, books on design and old buildings, and several she’d bought because the covers were beautiful and had never finished. On the windowsill was the plant Rachel had given her the day she was promoted, which had outlived Northlight, a borrowed storeroom, two moves and a great deal of neglect. The table in the middle was old, from an antique shop in the old town, with a few scratches along one edge and a dark ring where somebody, decades ago, had put down a wet glass. She had chosen it because it reminded her of something. He had known exactly what, and hadn’t said a word.

On a quiet Sunday afternoon in late spring she sat on one side of it with a cup of tea and a book open in front of her, and he sat on the other side with a report, and she had been talking for eleven minutes.

“Rachel thinks we should hire another senior person. I agree, but she wants someone with real corporate affairs experience, and Calvin wants someone younger who can grow with us. I told them those aren’t necessarily opposites, and then Rachel said if we hire someone too junior she’ll end up training them on top of her own work and that’s not fair, which is true.”

He turned a page. Then he looked up. “What role?”

“Senior account manager. Maybe account director if we find someone good enough.”

“Candidates?”

“Two. One’s very experienced, but I’m not sure she’ll like a small agency. The other’s young, very capable, and needs another year before she runs clients on her own.”

“What does Rachel think?”

“She likes the first.”

“And Calvin?”

“The second.”

“Then interview both.”

“I know.” She drank some tea. He went back to his report. She waited, and went on. “Also we’ve run out of room over the restaurant. Fourteen people on two floors. Calvin’s working off the end of the coffee machine.”

He looked up again. “The floor above—”

“Is my aunt’s rice.”

“You could negotiate—”

“An Yu.”

He stopped.

“I am not asking you to buy me an office.”

“I wasn’t going to suggest that.”

“You were about to suggest that.”

He considered his words. “I was going to suggest you negotiate with your aunt for the rice floor.”

“Which I can do myself.”

“I know.”

She watched him for a second, and smiled. “Good.”

He went back to the report, and she went on talking. About a client who’d changed his mind three times about one headline. About Rachel’s new habit of bringing lunch from home in a tin with a tiger on it. About a restaurant she wanted to try, and a book she’d bought and suspected she’d never finish. He listened. Sometimes he asked a question. Sometimes he made one small dry remark. Sometimes he just let her talk while he read, the sound of her voice becoming part of the afternoon, like the light.

It was familiar. Not quite the school library, where she’d once filled every lunchtime while he sat opposite her pretending to study. But familiar in the way that mattered. She had never needed him to talk all the time. She had only needed to know that he was there.

After a while she shut her book. “Do you remember what I used to talk about?”

He put the report down. “At school?”

“Yes.”

“Most of it.”

She laughed. “You can’t possibly remember most of it.”

“Your chemistry teacher had handwriting, you said, like a man who wanted everyone to fail.”

She burst out laughing. “I did not say that.”

“You did. You also said the canteen’s fried rice got worse every week.”

“It did.”

“You complained about every maths test.”

“I was right to.”

“And you said the library was the only place in the school where nobody expected you to be interesting.”

Her smile changed. “I said that?”

“Yes.”

“I don’t remember.”

“I do.”

She looked at him. “What else?”

He thought. “You told me about your mother. Your father’s business. Where you wanted to go to university. Once you spent fifteen minutes explaining why a girl in your class was pretending not to like someone.”

“Who?”

“You never said her name.”

“That’s because you weren’t supposed to know.”

“I didn’t.”

She leaned forward on her elbows. “What did I say about you?”

“Quite a lot. That I was too quiet.”

“You were.”

“That I looked as if I was angry with the world.”

“You did.”

“That I probably liked maths more than people.”

“You did.”

“That I ought to try smiling occasionally.”

“You ought.”

He looked at her. “And you asked if I was lonely.”

Her smile went. The room was quiet. She remembered asking. She remembered the way he’d looked at her and not answered, and how at sixteen she’d taken that silence for a door shut in her face. She knew now it had been something else.

“I wondered,” she said.

“I know.”

“Were you?”

He didn’t answer straight away. He looked at the window, where the sun had moved across the floor.

“Yes. I didn’t know what to do with it. I had people round me. Family, teachers, boys in my class. But I didn’t know how to ask anyone to stay when they didn’t have to.” He looked back at her. “I liked the library because you came every day. I liked knowing you’d sit opposite me. I liked that you didn’t need me to turn into someone else before you talked to me. And I thought if I didn’t say anything, I couldn’t say the wrong thing.”

“So you said nothing at all.”

“Yes.”

“Which was the wrong thing.”

“It was.”

She reached across the table and put her hand over his. “I wish we’d had one more day.”

“So do I.”

She turned her hand over, and he laced his fingers through hers. “But we’ve got this one,” she said. “And tomorrow. And the day after.”

“I hope so.”

“Don’t say it as if you’re making a reservation.”

He laughed under his breath. “I’m trying to be precise.”

“I know.” She tucked one leg under her and settled into the chair. “Tell me something. Anything. Something you’ve never told me.”

He thought about it for a long time. Then he began.

He told her about Zurich: not the version he gave at dinners, the university and the years and the qualifications, but the first winter, and the flat that was too quiet, and the streets he didn’t know, and the first weeks when he’d believed he could organise loneliness into something manageable if he only made a good enough schedule. He told her about London, where he’d learned to be easier in rooms full of people without ever learning to like them. About the first company he’d worked for, and the afternoon he realised he wanted to build something of his own. About An-Tech’s first year, the long hours, the first six employees, the clients who didn’t pay, and the mistakes he’d made when he thought being decisive was the same as being right.

She listened. She asked questions, some serious and some absurd.

“Did you ever get lost?”

“Yes. Several times.”

“Did you ask for directions?”

“No.”

She stared at him. “Of course you didn’t.”

“I found the place eventually.”

“How long did it take?”

“Two hours.”

She laughed until she had to put her cup down and wipe her eyes, and he watched her, looking faintly pleased with himself.

“Did you think asking would make you look incompetent?”

“No. I thought I could work it out.”

“You’re still like that.”

“Less than I was.”

“Debatable.”

He told her about a project that had nearly sunk the company in its third year. About a colleague who’d stood up in a meeting and told him he was wrong, and been right, and whom he had promoted the next month. About standing alone in An-Tech’s empty first office one night after everyone had gone, wondering whether he’d made a terrible mistake. He told her things he’d never thought were important enough to mention, and she listened to all of them. She didn’t make a joke when his voice went quiet. She didn’t hurry him when he stopped to find the right words. She let the silences sit there without treating them as a problem.

Once he stopped. “What?”

“Nothing.”

“You’re looking at me.”

“I like listening to you.”

He looked down at their hands. “Even when I take too long?”

“That’s when I like it best.” She rubbed her thumb across his knuckles. “When I was sixteen I used to go home and replay our conversations in my head.”

“There weren’t many conversations.”

“Exactly. I had to do all the work. I’d go over what I’d said and wonder what you’d have said back. Sometimes I made up your answers.”

“What did I say?”

“Usually something very clever.”

“I’m disappointed.”

“Don’t be. You’re doing quite well.” She was quiet, and then, more softly: “I don’t have to imagine any more.”

His face went gentle. “No. You don’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The afternoon went dim. Someone, she didn’t remember which of them, switched on the lamp, and it made a warm circle on the table between them. She had given up on her book entirely. His report lay shut by his cup. Neither of them had moved to another room. She was telling him about a dream she’d had: a train she’d missed, a hotel with far too many staircases, and a angry cat.

“You don’t have a cat,” he said.

“I know.”

“Why was it angry?”

“Because I wouldn’t let it into the hotel.”

“Was it your hotel?”

“I don’t know. It was a dream.”

He nodded as if this were entirely reasonable. She narrowed her eyes. “Don’t look at me like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like you’re analysing the cat.”

“I was wondering why it was angry.”

She laughed, and then went quiet, and he waited. She looked at him across the table: at the man who’d once sat opposite her with a maths book and a silence she’d mistaken for not caring. He was older. His face was more settled. There were faint lines by his eyes that only showed when he smiled, and he smiled more now. But she knew him. She knew the way he listened with all of himself. The way his eyes dropped when he was thinking. The way his hand lay near hers on the table even when it wasn’t touching.

“An Yu?”

“Yes?”

“I’m happy. Not because everything’s perfect. Level’s busy, you’re busy, we argue about ridiculous things, and you still think vegetables can be cooked without seasoning.”

“They can.”

“They shouldn’t be.” She smiled. “But I’m happy. Because I get to tell you all of this, and you tell me yours, and we don’t have to wait for something important to happen before we talk.”

He looked at her. “I used to think I needed something important to say before I opened my mouth. I thought people were better off if I didn’t speak unless I was certain.” His eyes went to their hands. “I was wrong. I should tell you when the tea’s good. When I miss you. When I’m worried. When I’m happy. When I disagree.”

“And when you’re lonely?”

“That most of all. I don’t want you ever to have to guess again.”

She stood up, still holding his hand.

“What are you doing?”

“Coming round.”

She walked round the end of the table. He pushed his chair back to make room, and she stopped beside him and bent down and put both hands on his shoulders.

“Do you remember what I said, the first time I sat opposite you?”

“You asked if the seat was taken.”

“And what did you do?”

“I moved my books.”

“You didn’t say anything.”

“No.”

“Then I’ll ask again.” She looked down into his face. “Is this seat taken?”

His eyes held hers. “No.”

“Are you sure?”

He put his hands on her waist. “I’ve been keeping it for you since I was sixteen.”

She bent and kissed him, over the old table with the ring on it where somebody once put down a wet glass, the way every lunchtime of the year she was sixteen should have ended. It started gently, a familiar thing, and then he stood up into it without letting go of her, so that they were level, and her arms went round his neck and his hands spread on her back, and he kissed her slowly and deeply with the lamp warm on the side of her face, and for a moment they were back in that library in Shanghai: except that there was no maths book between them, and no bell about to end lunch, and no fear that one of them might leave without saying goodbye.

He kissed her again, slower still. When they came apart she rested her forehead against his.

“This,” she whispered, “is how every lunchtime should have ended.”

“I know.”

“You could have saved us a lot of time.”

“I know.”

“Do you regret it?”

He thought about it properly, as he always did. “I regret not speaking when I could have. I don’t regret the years that brought you back.”

“That’s a very good answer.”

“I’ve had a long time to think about it.”

She laughed, and kissed him once more, across the table, and then they sat down again in their own chairs on their own sides. She picked up her book. He opened his report. For several minutes the room was quiet. Then she started talking.

“Do you think we need another lamp, by the shelves? It’s dark when I read there. And maybe a small chair by the window.”

“That would fit.”

“Would it be too crowded?”

“Not if we move the plant.”

“Don’t move my plant.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were thinking about it.”

“I was considering the measurements.”

She laughed. He closed his report.

“Xi? Shall we choose a chair together next weekend?”

“Yes.”

“Good.”

She went back to her book. A moment passed, and she looked up again.

“An Yu. I’m going to tell you something.”

He put down his pen. “I’m listening.”

And she did. She talked about the chair and the plant and a book she wanted and a film they ought to see, and how Nainai, if she saw this room, would complain that the shelves were wrong. He listened. He asked questions. He laughed in the right places. And when she finally stopped, he told her what he’d been thinking about all afternoon: a morning in Zurich, a worry he hadn’t mentioned, and a small thing that had made him happy that morning when he woke and found her hand resting on his chest, the three rings warm against his skin.

She listened too.

Outside, the late light went slowly. Inside, two cups of tea went cold on the old wooden table. They sat opposite each other, the way they once had in a school library in Shanghai. Only now, when one of them had something to say, the other answered; and neither of them had to wonder whether tomorrow would bring another chance. They had a lifetime of lunchtimes in front of them.

chapters.title: The Bookmark
chapters.desc: A strip of squared paper with a lopsided face on it, given across a library table in 2014, and everywhere it went after.
chapters.content:
The bookmark was made from a page of maths homework.

Tang Xi tore it out of the back of her exercise book one lunchtime in November 2014, when she had run out of things to tell him about and decided that Wang An Yu’s textbook looked unbearably serious. It was a strip of squared paper, cut crooked, with one corner bent where she’d used her teeth to start the tear. At the top she drew a small face: two round eyes, a straight mouth, a pair of glasses, one lens noticeably bigger than the other. Underneath, in blue biro, she wrote For the person who never talks, and then sat looking at it, and crossed something out, and finally added: Don’t lose your place.

She leaned across the table and slid it between the pages of his book while he was in the middle of a proof.

He noticed. He noticed almost everything she did. He didn’t look up.

“I’m giving you something,” she announced. “You don’t have to thank me.” He turned a page. “Actually, you could say thank you. It would be a very good opportunity to practise.” Nothing. She leaned further. “Wang An Yu. Do you know what a bookmark is?”

He looked at her then, for perhaps a second.

She smiled in triumph. “Good. At least we’re making progress.”

When the bell went she packed up and left, talking to someone at the door about the canteen. He waited until the library was empty before he opened the book again. The strip of paper slid out onto the table. He read it. He looked at the small crooked face for a long time, and at the glasses, and at the bigger lens. Then he put it back between the pages exactly where she’d left it, which was the beginning of a chapter on probability he had already finished.

He would have liked to tell her that he knew what a bookmark was. He would have liked to tell her he was going to keep it. But the next day she arrived already talking about the fried rice, and he listened, and said nothing at all, and the moment went the way all his moments with her went that year.

✦ ✦ ✦

It lived in the maths book all through that winter and spring, at the start of the probability chapter, while he went on through the rest of the book around it. It survived the last Monday, when she sat down opposite him and said, “Good luck, Wang An Yu,” as if it were the end of term. It survived the Thursday he was at the hospital. It survived the empty chair, and the week he came back every day at twelve, and Mrs. Hua saying, “The cheerful one? Not this week, dear.”

In the last week of June another piece of paper fell out of the same book: a crane, folded too hard down one side, with writing inside it. He put the crane in wax paper and put it back between the pages. He put the bookmark in its place at the start of the probability chapter. The book went into a box when he left for Zurich, and both of them went with it.

He found the bookmark again on his first evening in his flat in Zurich, sitting on the floor among cardboard boxes, putting books on a shelf in the order he’d always put them in. He pulled out the maths book and it slipped onto the floorboards. For a second he didn’t know what it was. Then he saw the face. Two round eyes. A straight mouth. Glasses, one lens too big.

He sat on the floor. It was snowing outside, quietly, the way it seemed to do everything in that city. He could almost hear her. Do you know what a bookmark is? He remembered her asking if he was lonely. He remembered her chemistry teacher, and the strawberry milk she put on his side of the table without asking, and the way she’d stopped coming.

He put it back in the book. Not because he needed to keep his place. Because he didn’t know where else to put it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Four years later, when he left Zurich for London, he took it out of the maths book for good and put it in his wallet, behind his cards. He couldn’t have said why. The book could stay on a shelf. The crane could stay in the book, where she had put it. But the bookmark had been given to him across a table, in daylight, with her watching, and he found that he wanted it on him.

It went everywhere after that. Through London and three flats and the first terrible year of An-Tech, when the company was six people and a borrowed desk. Into a hundred meetings in his inside pocket while he negotiated with people who had no idea that the chairman across the table was carrying a strip of squared paper with a face on it. The edges went soft. The fold went thin. One corner turned almost translucent from being touched. The blue biro faded to the colour of a vein.

On the fourteenth of February 2025, in the archive on the forty-second floor, he took a square of wax paper out of that wallet and showed her a crane. He had taken the crane out of the book that week and put it in the wallet beside the bookmark, because he wanted to have it on him the first time he was alone with her in a room. She saw the crane. She never saw what was in the other slot.

✦ ✦ ✦

He showed her on their wedding day.

It was at her aunt’s restaurant, at the long table, after the speeches and before the soup; Nainai had just finished complaining about the length of everything, and Tang Xi’s mother had just put a dumpling on his plate, and he took his wallet out under the table, and the strip of paper out of the wallet, and laid it beside her bowl without a word.

Tang Xi looked down. Then she stared.

“Oh my God.”

The table went quiet around them. She picked it up carefully.

“You kept this?”

“Yes.”

“Since 2014?”

“Since the eleventh of November, 2014. It was a Tuesday.”

She turned it over in her fingers and looked at her own handwriting, a sixteen-year-old’s handwriting, and at the small face. It looked ridiculous now: the glasses lopsided, one eye bigger than the other, the mouth a stern little line.

“You kept this ugly thing for fourteen years?”

“I didn’t think it was ugly.”

“You’re being polite.”

“I’m not.”

“Where has it been? I’ve been through every drawer in your flat. I’ve seen the crane. I’ve seen the maths book.”

“In my wallet. Since London.”

Across the table Xing Yue put down his chopsticks. “You carry that in your wallet?”

“Yes.”

“I’ve seen you pay for dinner a thousand times.”

“Behind the cards,” said An Yu.

Tang Xi looked at it, and her face changed. She remembered making it. She remembered thinking he wouldn’t care, and wanting to leave something in his book that he might find after she’d stopped talking for the day. She hadn’t known he would keep it. She hadn’t known he’d carry it through two countries and a dozen flats and ten years of not knowing where she was, and into a lift and an archive and a school library and a registry office, without once telling her it was there.

“An Yu,” she whispered. “Why didn’t you show me? In the archive? In the library?”

He reached under the table and touched her fingers. “Because you’d have asked what it said.”

“It says don’t lose your place.”

“Yes.” He looked at her, and his face was entirely open, in front of thirty-eight people. “I didn’t. I wanted to wait until I could tell you that and have it be finished.”

She laughed, and her eyes went bright, and Nainai said loudly from the end of the table, “What is it?
