Show me,” and it went all the way down the table, from hand to careful hand, Nainai and Xing Yue and Elara and Yu Chen and Eliana and Rachel and Calvin and Mrs. Hua, who looked at it and said, “I told you off for tearing paper in my library,” and her mother, who looked at it, and at An Yu, and handed it back without saying anything at all. That was how Tang Xi knew it had reached her.

✦ ✦ ✦

After the wedding it moved house with them. It didn’t go back into his wallet. He bought a small archival sleeve, the kind museums use, acid-free, and slid it inside, and put it in the drawer of his desk in the study next to the crane in its wax paper.

She found it there one afternoon the next spring while she was looking for a pen. She held the sleeve up when he came in.

“You’ve given it a house.”

“It needed one.”

“It’s a piece of paper.”

“It’s an important piece of paper.”

“You’re very sentimental for someone who spent a year pretending he didn’t like me.”

“I never pretended that.”

“You didn’t exactly advertise it.” She leaned on the desk. “Do you know what I thought when I made it? That you’d use it for a few days and throw it away.”

“I never considered throwing it away. Not even when I moved.”

“Why?”

He took the sleeve out of her hand and checked that the paper hadn’t slipped inside it, and put it back in the drawer, and closed it. “Because for ten years it was almost the only thing I had of you.”

She went quiet. Then she came round the desk and put her arms round him.

“I wish I’d known,” she said into his shirt. “I’d have made you another one.”

He kissed her hair. “You did.”

She pulled back. “What?”

He looked past her, through the open door, down the corridor to the room at the end of the house: the old wooden table from the antique shop with the water ring on it, the two chairs, the shelves they’d filled together, his in order and hers in none.

“You gave me another one,” he said. “That’s where I keep my place now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the summer of 2029 she decided it was time to take it out of the drawer for good.

He found her at the dining table one Sunday with a small plain frame, a sheet of archival backing card, a soft brush, a pair of cotton gloves and the bookmark laid out on a clean white cloth.

“What are you doing?”

“Preserving history.”

“Is that necessary?”

“Yes. I don’t want it to disappear.”

“It won’t.”

“You don’t know that.”

“We’ve kept it for fifteen years.”

“You’ve kept it for fifteen years, in a wallet, with your credit cards, being sat on. It deserves better than a drawer.” She looked up at him through her fringe. “And I want to be able to see it.”

He sat down opposite her and watched. She worked slowly, the way she worked on anything that mattered, with the gloves on and the brush, laying the soft old paper flat on the card so that the face showed at the top and her biro underneath was still legible. For the person who never talks. Don’t lose your place. When she’d finished, she put the glass in and turned the clips and set the frame upright in the middle of the dining table.

He looked at it.

“Where should it go?” she asked.

“Here.”

“On the dining table?”

“Why not?”

“People will ask about it.”

“Then we’ll tell them.”

She smiled. “What will you tell them?”

He looked at the crooked little face. “That my wife gave it to me when we were sixteen. That I kept it. And that I was very happy she sat opposite me.”

Her face softened, and she reached across the table, and he took her hand.

For a while they just sat there with it between them. Then she started talking: about a client, and a book, and a restaurant, and something completely outrageous Rachel had said on Friday about Calvin’s new shoes, hopping from one thing to the next without caring whether they connected. He listened. And when she’d finished, he told her about something that had happened at An-Tech that week: the problem, what he’d decided, and the conversation he’d been turning over in his head since Wednesday. She listened too. The afternoon light moved slowly across the table. The bookmark stood between their cups.

It had started as a joke from a girl who couldn’t understand why a boy wouldn’t talk to her. It had become one of only two things she ever left him. It had gone with him through all the years when he didn’t know how to find her, and sat in his pocket in every room where he’d finally found the words. And now it stood on their table, in their house, between two people who no longer had to guess what the other was thinking.

“Do you still need a bookmark?” she asked.

He looked at the frame. “No.”

“Why not?”

He lifted her hand and kissed the gold band on it. “I know where I am.”

“And where’s that?”

“Right here,” he said, and she leaned across the table and kissed him, and the small paper face with its lopsided glasses watched them do what it had waited fifteen years to see: he talked, and she had nowhere else she needed to be, and neither of them ever lost their place again.

chapters.title: Nainai Approves of Nothing
chapters.desc: The day Tang Xi came north, from the other side of the tea tray. Nainai keeps a list of complaints and one entry that isn’t.
chapters.content:
Nainai had a notebook.

It was small and dark red, with a cracked leather cover and a brass clasp that hadn’t shut properly since 1987, and it contained twelve pages of complaints. She had started it as a young bride, on discovering that people were generally unreliable and that memory, though useful, wasn’t evidence. It had come with her through three houses, two wars inside the family, a great many hospital stays and more family dinners than she cared to count, and it recorded people who talked too much, people who talked too little, people who came late, people who ate the best piece without offering it round, and people who believed that being rich had made them clever. The last category ran to nearly two pages, and one of the entries on it was her son.

In September 2025 she put it in her handbag and came south.

She came every September, for the board, and she stayed with her younger grandson every time, because his elder brother lived on a ward and his father lived in a file. This year she had a further reason. In August, on the telephone, she had asked An Yu whether he was seeing anyone, and he had said yes, and she had asked who, and he had said a name, and then nothing else at all, which from An Yu was a confession.

She intended to investigate.

✦ ✦ ✦

Complaint No. 1. The driver. He was told eight o’clock and came at five to, which was acceptable, and then spent four minutes arranging her stick in the boot as if it were a bomb. She had been getting into cars with that stick for twenty years. She wrote it down at the traffic lights.

Complaint No. 2. My grandson doesn’t answer his telephone at a quarter past eight on a Saturday.

She rang him from the pavement outside his building. It took him three rings. When he answered, his voice was the voice of a man who had been asleep and wasn’t alone, and she heard, quite distinctly, a second voice behind his, a woman’s, saying “Who is it?”

She told him to come down and bring a jacket. It was twenty-six degrees. She wanted to see what he’d do. He came down in a jacket. Complaint No. 3. He is too thin.

He was. She told him so, and that he didn’t eat, and he said that he did, and she pointed her stick at him and told him not to lie to her before breakfast. In the lift she told him he was still not married. He said good morning to her, which was what he did when he had no answer, and she called him useless, and he took it, and she watched the numbers go up to thirty-eight and thought: there is a woman upstairs, and he hasn’t told her I’m coming, because he didn’t know himself, and he isn’t frightened. He is something else.

✦ ✦ ✦

The girl was standing by the kitchen counter when the door opened, straight, in a cream knit top, with her hair tied back in a hurry. She had a pleasant face and a careful smile and she said, “Good morning, Nainai,” before anyone had introduced her, which was either good manners or good nerve.

Nainai looked at her, and at her grandson, and back. She asked who this was. An Yu told her a name. Nainai said that told her a name, and pointed the stick at him, and told him what he’d said in August, and he said, “I didn’t know,” and she turned back to the girl, and the girl was trying not to laugh.

“You think that’s funny?”

“A little,” said the girl.

Complaint No. 4. The girl laughs at me. Nainai wrote it in the lift going down to look at the building’s lobby, which was too shiny, while An Yu ordered breakfast from the kitchen downstairs. Then she crossed it out. Underneath she wrote: At least one of them has a sense of humour.

✦ ✦ ✦

Complaint No. 5. Breakfast. Too much oil in the greens. She said so, and told them not to tell the kitchen, only not to order it again. The congee was correct. The buns were from a bakery and not from anybody’s hands, which she noted without comment. Complaint No. 6. The tea.

The girl had made it herself while they were downstairs. Jasmine. Nainai smelled it before she tasted it, and tasted it, and tasted it again, and the girl watched her do it without pretending not to.

“Who chose it?”

“I did. I thought something light, in the morning.”

It wasn’t too strong. The leaves hadn’t been stewed. Somebody had taught this girl to measure.

Nainai looked at her over the cup and asked how long she’d known him, and the girl said, “Since school. In Shanghai,” and Nainai’s cup stopped halfway to the saucer.

Shanghai. Ten years ago. A hospital bed, and a boy of sixteen sitting beside it all afternoon looking at the door. She had asked him what he was looking at. He had said nothing, and then, because she was his grandmother and had pins in her hip and nothing else to do, he had said there was a girl at school who sat opposite him in the library and talked. And Nainai, who had raised a son who never once in his life told her anything about his heart, had looked at her grandson and understood that he had just told her everything about his.

She put the cup down. “You’re the one who talks.”

The girl went pink to the ears. Nainai wrote nothing under Complaint No. 6. She left the space empty and turned the page.

✦ ✦ ✦

Complaint No. 7. The books. He has them in order by subject, like a library after a storm. She said so. He said they were organised. She said he was arguing with an old woman. He said he was explaining. She said that was the same thing. He let her win, which was correct.

She inspected the flat while the girl sat on the sofa and watched. The sofa was too low. The curtains were too grey. The lamps were the kind that made a room look like a hotel. In the bedroom, on the table beside the bed, there was a box, and in the box there was a schoolbook with a worn cover, and Nainai looked at it and knew it at once and didn’t open it. She had learned a long time ago that there are things in a person’s life you don’t put your hand into, even if you’re their grandmother, even if you could.

She sat down in the armchair and patted the seat beside her and asked the girl how old she was, and what she did, and whether she liked it, and then, because that was what she had come for, whether he bothered her.

The girl thought about it before she answered. Nainai noticed that. Most people answered that kind of question at once, with something pleasant, to get it over with.

“Sometimes,” said the girl. “He’s a little too determined to solve things. He means well. But sometimes he decides what’s best before he asks me what I want.”

“That’s an incomplete description,” said An Yu, from across the room.

Nainai rapped the floor. “Let her finish. Does he listen when you tell him?”

“He tries. He’s getting better.”

Nainai pointed the stick at her grandson and told him to listen properly. Not with his ears. With his head.

Complaint No. 8. She tells the truth about him in front of me.

She looked at that for a while, in the evening, and couldn’t decide which column it belonged in.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch the girl made a second pot, and Nainai stood in the kitchen doorway without her stick and watched her do it. Fewer leaves, because the water was hotter. She’d noticed the first pot was a little weak and corrected it without being told. Her mother had taught her, she said, and her mother made it better.

“Then learn from her.”

Nainai drank it. “Good. Not bitter.”

She went back to the sofa and didn’t say anything else about it. One word. She saw the girl stand at the counter afterwards for a whole minute without moving. Complaint No. 9. None.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three she got the album out of her suitcase, because the girl ought to know what she was dealing with. The photograph of the two boys at eight and fourteen, Xing Yue with his arm round his little brother and An Yu scowling at the camera with a scratch on his cheek. “You look exactly the same,” said the girl, and An Yu said he didn’t, and Nainai said he never smiled for photographs, and that he had always been quiet, and that he remembered everything.

Then she sent him off for her tea, though she didn’t want it, so that she could say the next part without him in the room.

“Good boy,” she said, watching him go. And then, more quietly, to the girl: “He was lonely when he was young. He had everything he needed. Schools. A family that cared for him, in its way. But his mother died when he was nine, and after that he was always somewhere else in his head. He doesn’t know how to ask people to stay.”

The girl looked at her hands. “I think he’s learning.”

“Did he tell you he was at the hospital with me? That day? In Shanghai?”

“In June. He told me in June.”

“Did he tell you he went back to that library every day for a week?”

“Yes.”

“And asked the old librarian about you?”

“Yes.”

Nainai looked at her. “Then he’s told you more than he ever told me,” she said, and the girl’s eyes filled, and Nainai pretended to be looking for her glasses.

Complaint No. 10. My grandson is an idiot. This required no further explanation, and she underlined it twice.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wanted to order dinner. She wanted something cooked. The girl offered to help, and he objected, and Nainai pointed the stick at him and said she could decide for herself, and so the two of them cooked together while Nainai sat at the counter and gave instructions that weren’t strictly necessary. Not so much ginger. More water. Don’t rush it. When he stood behind them doing nothing, she told him to sit down, and he sat down.

Steamed fish. Greens. A soup. Rice. Nainai asked about the girl’s family over it and got a careful answer: a mother who cooked at her sister’s restaurant in the old town, a father who did some consulting now. They lived. They knew about him. They hadn’t met him.

“Then he should meet them. Not at some point. When?”

“We’ll arrange it,” said the girl.

Nainai looked at her grandson. “Don’t make her do all the arranging.”

Complaint No. 11. He would have let her.

✦ ✦ ✦

At half past ten she announced that she wasn’t tired, asked for a glass of water, reminded him to shut the balcony door, and went to bed in the guest room, and lay down with the light off and her eyes closed and her breathing slow and even.

She heard the balcony door slide open. She heard their voices, low, and the city underneath them. She heard the girl laugh and say, “That’s terrible,” at something, and she heard what came after, which was a great deal of silence of a particular kind, the kind she hadn’t heard in a grandson’s flat in her life, and once a low sound from him that made her press her lips together in the dark so that she wouldn’t laugh, and the girl’s voice saying “Shh, your grandmother,” and him answering something she didn’t catch, and more silence.

Nainai lay in the dark and smiled at the ceiling. She hadn’t raised a child who could fool her by being quiet. She certainly hadn’t raised a grandson who could.

When the balcony door had slid shut and the flat was still, her door opened. He came in to check the lamp and straighten the blanket over her feet, the way he had done since he was nine.

“An Yu.”

She opened one eye. “That girl makes good tea. Don’t let her go.”

He stood still in the doorway. “I won’t.”

“Good. Now go to sleep.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, before anyone else was awake, she sat at his dining table in her dressing gown with the notebook open at the last page.

The first eleven were full: drivers and doctors and daughters-in-law, a cousin’s unforgivable wedding speech, the board, the family office, her son. She read the day’s entries through. Then she turned to the bottom of the twelfth page, where there was just enough room left, and took the cap off her pen, and thought about everything she could write. That the girl was polite. That she was clever. That she had a good voice and knew how to measure tea and hadn’t once looked at An Yu for permission before she answered a question. That she had told the truth about him to his own grandmother’s face, and he had agreed with her. That she hadn’t tried to make herself smaller.

But no. One word was enough.

Tang Xi. Good.

She looked at it for a while. Then she closed the notebook, and the brass clasp didn’t shut, as usual, and she put it in her handbag.

When he came out, dressed, she was drinking yesterday’s jasmine, cold, out of the girl’s cup.

“Are you ready to go to the board, Nainai?”

“In a moment.” She let him help her up, and took his arm, and at the door she looked back at the table, and the cup, and the flat that was too tidy and too grey and had, for the first time since she’d known it, somebody else’s hair tie on the kitchen counter. Twelve pages of things she didn’t approve of. A lifetime of them. And one word about the girl her grandson had waited ten years for without ever knowing how to ask her to stay.

She approved of nothing. But Tang Xi was good. That was different.

chapters.title: Brothers at Tea
chapters.desc: Summer 2022, under the persimmon tree. Xing Yue asks his little brother about love at first sight, and gets three papers and the good tea.
chapters.content:
Wang Xing Yue had never been particularly interested in love as a subject. He understood attraction. He understood companionship, and commitment, and the practical arithmetic of building a life alongside another person. He had spent enough nights on surgical wards watching people make enormous promises at three in the morning and break them by breakfast to have decided that love needed more than a dramatic beginning.

Which was why, when he asked his little brother whether love at first sight existed, he fully expected to be told it was nonsense. An Yu didn’t answer immediately.

It was July, the summer of 2022, and they were sitting in Nainai’s courtyard in the north hills under the persimmon tree, in the green heat, with the cicadas going like a machine somewhere above them. Nainai was asleep indoors; she had told them both they looked tired and gone to lie down to make her point. Between them on the stone table was a pot of tea that An Yu had brought up from the city himself and made himself, a dark aged tea with no label on the tin. Xing Yue had noticed the missing label. He had also noticed that his brother rarely made tea for anybody, and that this was the second pot.

“You’re being unusually generous with this,” he said.

An Yu poured. “You’re being unusually observant.”

“I’m a surgeon. It’s the job.”

“Then observe quietly.”

Xing Yue laughed. He was thirty, a senior resident who would be chief resident in September, with the permanently tired eyes of a man who had spent his whole adult life in hospitals. An Yu was twenty-four, six years younger, and in some ways exactly the same as he’d been at eight: quiet, composed, maddeningly hard to read. But recently Xing Yue had noticed something. His brother, who didn’t ask people questions, had started occasionally asking questions about people. Not many. Not obviously. Enough.

So today Xing Yue had decided to ask one of his own.

“Do you believe in love at first sight?”

“No.”

“That’s what I thought.”

“Why ask?”

“Because I saw someone.”

An Yu’s eyes moved to him. It was a small movement.

“You rang me at eleven o’clock at night last June,” An Yu said, “from a hospital car park, to tell me about a medical student who explained a drain to a frightened wife twice. You talked for nine minutes. You’d never rung me after ten in your life.”

Xing Yue stared at him. “You remember that.”

“You’ve rung me after ten twice since. Both times to ask about something else, and both times you mentioned her.”

“I did not.”

“Harbourside. Fourth year. You said she was a little stubborn.”

Xing Yue put his cup down and rubbed his face with both hands. “You’re very difficult to talk to.”

“You asked a question. I answered it.”

“I didn’t ask whether you believed in it as a philosophical position.”

“What did you ask?”

Xing Yue leaned back in the stone chair and looked up through the leaves. “I saw her for about four minutes a year ago, in a corridor, at another hospital, and I remember her. Not the way you remember a face in a corridor. I remember the way she talked to the patient’s wife. She wasn’t trying to sound clever. The woman was frightened, and didn’t understand the first time, so she stopped and explained it again, more slowly, and she didn’t make the woman feel stupid for needing it twice.” He looked down at his tea. “I remember thinking she was good at it.”

“That isn’t love.”

“I know.”

“It’s an observation.”

“I’m aware of that.”

“Then what are you asking?”

Xing Yue smiled faintly. “Whether it’s possible to know you want to see someone again before you know anything about them.”

An Yu looked at him, and for a moment seemed to take it entirely seriously.

“Yes,” he said.

Xing Yue blinked. “That was quick.”

“It isn’t a difficult question.”

“You just said you don’t believe in love at first sight.”

“I don’t. I believe in wanting to see someone again. Those are different things.”

Xing Yue studied him. “You’ve thought about this.”

“No.”

“Liar.”

An Yu refilled his brother’s cup and watched the tea settle. “Her name?”

“Lin. Elara Lin. She’ll be in her fifth year now. I don’t know if she’s still at Harbourside. I don’t know if she’s seeing anyone. I’ve spoken to her once, about a patient. I don’t even know if she’d remember me.”

“Then find out.”

“That’s your advice?”

“Yes.”

“Very romantic.”

“Would you rather I sent you poetry?”

“Honestly? Yes. I’m asking my little brother about love. I expect a certain level of emotional support.”

“You’ve come to the wrong person.”

“I know,” said Xing Yue, and laughed, and they sat for a while without saying anything, listening to the cicadas.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Have you ever felt like that?” Xing Yue asked eventually. “Seen someone, and remembered them?”

An Yu didn’t answer. His eyes went to the gate.

“Yes,” he said.

Xing Yue went still. “When?”

“A long time ago.”

“Did you see her again?”

“No.”

“Did you talk to her?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“I was sixteen.”

“That isn’t an answer.”

“It was the reason.”

Xing Yue looked at him more carefully then. He had known his brother for twenty-four years. He knew his habits and his silences and the particular way he walked round any question that touched something real. He had carried him on his shoulders when he was three, and stood next to him at their mother’s funeral when he was nine and Xing Yue fifteen, and watched him not cry, and not cry, and then not cry for about a decade. He knew when not to push.

“Do you regret it?”

An Yu was quiet. “Yes.”

It was so plain that Xing Yue stopped smiling. He only said, “I hope you get another chance.”

An Yu looked into his cup. “So do I.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Wait here,” An Yu said, and got up and went into the house, and came back after ten minutes with a few sheets of printed paper, warm from Nainai’s ancient printer, which had taken him eight of the ten minutes.

“What are these?”

“Papers.”

“I can see that.”

“Then why ask?”

Xing Yue took them. The first was a brain-imaging study from 2005 of people in the early, intense stage of falling in love: what lit up, and what didn’t, and how much of it looked like the reward system and how little like anything to do with judgement. The second was the old work on mere exposure, from 1968: that people come to like what they see repeatedly, faces and words and nonsense shapes alike. The third was about emotional arousal and memory: why something that happens to you in a moment of feeling is laid down harder and stays longer than anything ordinary.

He looked at the titles, and then at his brother. “You printed academic papers. About love.”

“About what you asked.”

“When did you find these?”

“Last night. You told me on the phone on Thursday that you wanted to ask me something about a person, and you sounded like that.”

“Like what?”

“Like the car park.”

Xing Yue laughed so loudly a bird went up out of the persimmon tree. “Most people would say, go and talk to her.”

“I did say that.”

“And then gave me three research papers.”

“Four. I didn’t print the fourth.”

“Why not?”

“It’s a study from Groningen, from 2017. They asked people who’d just met whether they’d felt love at first sight.” An Yu turned his cup a quarter turn on the stone. “Most of the time what they meant was that they’d found the other person very attractive. And the couples who said they’d fallen in love at first sight tended to decide it afterwards, looking back, once they were already together.”

Xing Yue looked at him. “You didn’t print it because it might put me off.”

“I didn’t print it because it doesn’t matter what you call it in the corridor,” said An Yu. “It matters what you do next. If you go and find her, and it turns into something, then in ten years you’ll say it was love at first sight, and you’ll be right, because you’ll have made it true. And if you don’t go and find her, you’ll only ever have the corridor.”

There was a long silence under the tree.

“That,” said Xing Yue slowly, “is the most romantic thing you’ve ever said in your life.”

“It’s in the paper.”

“It is not in the paper.”

“The discussion section,” said An Yu, with no expression whatever, and his brother put the printouts down on the table and laughed until he had to wipe his eyes.

There was something unexpectedly touching about it. An Yu had listened to a question, thought about it, and then done what he always did when something mattered: gone away, read everything, thought harder, and come back with something useful. He might not know how to comfort anybody in the ordinary way. But he had never in his life been careless with anything a person trusted him with.

“Thank you,” said Xing Yue.

“Read them before you decide anything. And don’t mistake a strong first impression for knowing her.”

“That sounds like real advice.”

“It is. And talk to her.”

“Yes, little brother.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The tea was nearly gone. Xing Yue turned his cup in his hands. “What is this? It’s very good.”

“An aged tea.”

“Which one?”

“Does it matter?”

“You’ve never labelled it.”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“I don’t want people asking for it.”

“Then why give it to me?”

An Yu looked at his brother. “Because you asked.”

When Xing Yue left for the train at five, with the papers folded into his jacket, An Yu came out to the gate after him and put the tin in his hand, the unlabelled one, more than half full.

“For when you go to Harbourside.”

Xing Yue looked at the tin and then at him. “You never give anyone this.”

“Make her a cup,” said An Yu, “if she lets you. Don’t tell her what it is. Let her ask.”

Xing Yue held the tin. Then he put a hand on his brother’s shoulder, which they hadn’t done since they were boys, and said, “I’m glad you told me. About sixteen. Whoever she was.”

An Yu’s face changed, just slightly. Not enough for anyone else to have noticed. But Xing Yue had known him all his life, and saw it.

“Don’t waste the tea,” said An Yu.

“I won’t.”

✦ ✦ ✦

When the car had gone, An Yu sat back down alone under the persimmon tree. The afternoon had gone quieter. The sun had moved off the stone table and lay in a pale strip across the courtyard, and the empty chair opposite him had the shadow of leaves on it.

He hadn’t told Xing Yue everything. He hadn’t mentioned a girl who sat across from him every lunchtime for a year and talked as though his silence were a small inconvenience she was prepared to work round. Or the crane. Or the maths book. Or the seven years he had spent remembering her voice, in Zurich, in London, in a dozen meeting rooms, without any idea at all where she was.

Some things didn’t go into a literature review.

He took out his wallet, and from behind the cards he took out a strip of squared paper, soft at the folds and gone thin at one corner, and laid it on the stone table in the last of the sun. A crooked little face with glasses, one lens bigger than the other. For the person who never talks. Don’t lose your place.

He had told his brother that it mattered what you did next. He sat for a long time looking at the bookmark, and thought about whether he believed it, and found that he did, and that he had no idea where to begin.

That evening Xing Yue sent him a message from the train.

Xing Yue (Calls After Ten): Read the first paper. It says familiarity can increase attraction.

An Yu: Under certain conditions.

Xing Yue (Calls After Ten): Don’t start.

Xing Yue (Calls After Ten): I’m going to Harbourside in September. When I start as chief. I might ask her for a coffee.

An Yu: Good.

Xing Yue (Calls After Ten): What if she says no?

An Yu thought about it for a long time, with the bookmark still on the table in front of him in the dark.

An Yu: Then you listen to her, and you respect it. And you don’t pretend you didn’t want to.

Xing Yue (Calls After Ten): Very romantic, little brother.

An Yu: Very important.

He put the phone down and the bookmark back in his wallet, and carried the cups inside, and Nainai, who hadn’t been asleep for one single minute of the afternoon, was sitting in the dark kitchen with her stick across her knees.

“Your brother has found someone,” she said.

“Maybe.”

“And you?”

He stood there with the cups in his hands. “I found someone a long time ago, Nainai. I lost her.”

“Then find her again,” said his grandmother, as if it were the simplest thing in the world, and went to bed.

chapters.title: The Lift
chapters.desc: Eleven lifts, ranked by the woman who kissed him first in ten of them. Number one has a stop button and his belt in it.
chapters.content:
“Eleven.”

Tang Xi looked up from her phone. It was a Thursday evening in December 2027, in the private lift at An-Tech, going down. He had a folder under one arm and one hand in his pocket, and he had just finished a call with his regional director and appeared to be thinking about something considerably more important.

“What?”

“Eleven lifts.”

“I’m sorry?”

“Eleven lifts we’ve kissed in.”

She lowered the phone slowly. “You counted.”

“No. I remembered.”

“That’s worse.”

“Rachel. In the account meeting this afternoon. She said the lifts in this building got unusually heavy traffic.”

Tang Xi stared at him, and then burst out laughing. “She meant the lobby. The morning rush.”

“She was looking at you when she said it.”

“And you took that as a reason to count how many times you’ve kissed your fiancée in a lift.”

“I was checking whether eleven was right.”

“I don’t know if it’s right. I haven’t been keeping a spreadsheet.”

“I could make one.”

“Don’t you dare.” She took the folder out from under his arm and put it on the little ledge by the panel. “Fine. Eleven. And?”

“Rank them.”

“Rank them?”

“From worst to best. I’d like to know.”

“You’re the chairman of a technology group. Haven’t you got anything better to do?”

“My meetings are finished.”

“Clearly.” She folded her arms and pretended to think about it. He leaned one shoulder on the brushed steel wall, watching her, and she reached past him and pressed the button for the car park, and then, after a moment’s thought, for the lobby instead, so that it would take longer. “All right. I’m ranking. You’re not allowed to argue.”

“I’ll try.”

“That isn’t a promise.”

“It’s an accurate assessment.”

“Eleven lifts,” she said. “Let’s see how well you remember.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Number eleven. Friday the fourteenth of February, 2025. Ten past eleven at night.

The lift down from the forty-second floor, after the security guard had finally come and let them out of the archive. Her mouth was still sore. His tie was in his pocket. Neither of them had said anything since the guard had looked at the two of them and the filing cabinet and pretended hard to be looking at his torch. They stood at opposite sides of the lift like two people who had met that evening. At the ground floor, as the doors began to open, she took one step across the lift and kissed him once, fast, on the mouth, and stepped back again before the doors were fully open.

“Good night, Mr. Wang.”

“Good night, Ms. Tang.”

And he let her walk out across the lobby into the rain alone.

“That’s why it’s eleventh,” she said now. “Because you let me go.”

“You wanted to go.”

“I did. You could still have asked me to stay.”

“I know.” He looked at her. “I didn’t know how, then.”

“See? You’ve learned something.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Number ten. Friday the twenty-first of February, 2025. Ten past six in the morning.

His building, not this one. The lift from the thirty-eighth floor down to the car park, the morning after the first night. She was in yesterday’s blouse with her hair still wet from his shower, and he had his car keys in his hand and was going to drive her home to change before work, and she’d told him not to, and he was doing it anyway, and at about the twentieth floor she turned round and pushed him against the wall and kissed him, slow and thorough and sleepy, until the doors opened on the car park and a man in running clothes stood there looking at them.

“Good morning,” said An Yu.

“Number ten,” she said. “Because I liked it, and it was too short, and the man in the running clothes was there.”

“He lived on the twelfth floor. He nodded to me every morning for a year afterwards.”

“He did not.”

“Every morning.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Number nine. Thursday the thirteenth of March, 2025. Nearly midnight.

Back from Singapore. The car park lift here, after the airport, both of them with suitcases, her hair still damp from the rain at Changi. She stood next to him watching the numbers.

“Do you know what I liked about Singapore?”

“The food?”

“The rain. Having an excuse not to go anywhere.”

“You had your own room.”

“Your room was better.” She took hold of his tie and pulled him down and he laughed against her mouth, actually laughed, a sound she had heard perhaps twice by then, and then stopped laughing, and it was warm and unhurried and made the long flight and the cancelled one go far away. When the doors opened she was still holding his tie, and didn’t let go, and he had to take her hand off it himself and lead her out by it.

“Number nine,” she said. “Because you laughed first.”

“You didn’t like that?”

“I loved that. I’m saving the good ones.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Number eight. A Tuesday in April, 2025. The wrong floor. He had arranged for a car to wait for her after a late review, after she’d told him she could get herself home. She found it outside and came back in and caught him at the lift.

“You said you understood.”

“I did.”

“Then why is there a car outside?”

“Because it was late.”

“I can take a taxi.”

“I know.”

“Then why?”

He was quiet. The lift stopped at twenty-nine and neither of them moved.

“Don’t do that,” she said. “Don’t go quiet because you don’t know what to say.”

“I thought it would make your evening easier.”

“You should have asked.”

“Yes. I’m sorry.”

She looked at him, and then kissed him, hard and short and furious, and when she pulled away she said, “I’m still angry. Don’t think this means you were right.” The doors opened. It was the wrong floor. She’d pressed twenty-nine at some point without noticing.

“See what you’ve done,” she said.

“Apparently.”

“Number eight. Because I was angry.”

“And kissed me anyway.”

“I contain multitudes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Number seven. Thursday the seventh of August, 2025. The day the agency was told. She came to An-Tech that afternoon for a scheduled account meeting, the new title three hours old, and he called her Ms. Tang in the boardroom as if nothing had happened, and was perfectly professional for an hour and twenty minutes. In the private lift afterwards he looked at her.

“Congratulations, Senior Account Director Tang Xi.”

She tried not to smile. “Thank you.”

“You earned it.”

“I know.” She turned round. “Is that all?”

“What else would you like?”

“Something that isn’t a sentence from an appraisal.”

He stepped closer. “I’m very glad it’s you,” he said, “and I’m very glad it had nothing to do with me.”

That was the first time she ever kissed him in a lift simply because she was happy. No argument behind it. No unfinished conversation. Just happiness, and his hand at her waist, and his mouth smiling against hers.

“Number seven. Because nothing was wrong.”

“That seems like a reason for it to be higher.”

“The good ones are coming.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Number six. Thursday the ninth of October, 2025. About eight in the evening.

The last one before anyone knew. A late review on the forty-second floor, and him waiting by the private lift, and the two of them going down together with an umbrella between them because it was pouring. She didn’t kiss him at the lobby. She kissed him at the thirtieth floor, because she was tired, and he was warm, and she liked the way he held the umbrella out of the way so it wouldn’t drip on her shoes. It was slow and tender and absolutely nothing special, and four days later a man called Mr. Quek told her agency he’d seen them walk out of the building together, and nothing was simple again for a long time.

He was quiet after she said it.

“Number six,” she said. “Because it was the last one that was only ours.”

“I’m sorry.”

“Don’t be. I’d do it again.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Number five. Wednesday the twelfth of November, 2025.

The day he said no to her in a meeting. She’d thanked him properly in the stairwell between forty-two and forty-one and told him to go first, so nobody would see them come out together. So he went. And she waited two minutes and walked down one flight and pressed the button for the lift on forty-one, and the doors opened, and he was standing inside it, alone, with his hands in his pockets.

“You were supposed to go first.”

“I did. I went to forty.”

“And came back up?”

“I wanted to see if you’d take the lift.”

She got in. The doors closed. “You’re ridiculous.”

“You told me to say no to you. You didn’t tell me I had to stay away from you afterwards.”

She laughed, and kissed him between forty-one and the lobby, slowly.

“Number five. Because you came back for me.”

“I was always going to come back.”

“You didn’t always know that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Number four. Tuesday the twenty-first of July, 2026. The flowers. She’d kissed him in the middle of his own lobby, which didn’t count, because it wasn’t a lift. Then they went down to the car park to go and fetch the lilies from Northlight, and in the car park lift he looked at her with an expression she had hardly ever seen on him inside this building.

“Was the lobby on purpose?”

“Of course.”

“In front of security.”

“In front of everyone. I don’t work for anyone you know any more.” She grinned. “I’m unemployable and I have three desks and a kettle, and I can kiss whoever I like in whichever lift I like.”

“Then,” he said, and kissed her first, for once, all the way down, and she kissed him back so hard she bumped her head on the handrail and didn’t care.

“Number four. Because you’d stopped being a client.”

“I was never your client.”

“You were my client’s chairman. It’s the same thing with worse lighting.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Number three. Monday the second of November, 2026.

The day after the letter. She’d come to his door the night before, and he’d kissed her before it shut, and in the morning she’d gone to work, and at one o’clock she walked into An-Tech’s lobby with a paper bag of her mother’s dumplings, for the first time since October, and asked reception for the chairman. He came down himself. In the private lift going up she didn’t say anything. She put the bag on the floor and put her arms round his neck and held on, and then she kissed him, slowly, the way you kiss someone you nearly lost and didn’t, and he held her so tightly that the dumplings were almost forgotten on the floor.

“I’m still hurt,” she said into his collar.

“I know.”

“I’m here anyway.”

“I know.”

“Number three,” she said now, quietly. “Because I’d decided to stay.”

He didn’t say anything to that. He took her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Number two. Friday the twenty-first of March, 2025.

“Not this building,” she said. “Mine. Northlight’s. Lift three.”

The café. The morning she found out he’d bought it so it would open at six. She’d stood in the lobby and told him it wasn’t about the money, it was about the choice, and that she wanted to be his girlfriend, not one more thing he managed. And then she’d marched him into lift three and kissed him with all of her anger and all of her affection knotted together, and he’d barely caught her by the waist before she was pulling him in, and she’d reached past him and hit the emergency stop.

“I wanted to kiss you without it arriving anywhere.”

“That isn’t how it works,” he’d said, and pressed the button again, and nothing happened, and she laughed into his shirt, and then he kissed her, slower than she had, with his hand along her cheek, and she could taste the coffee he hadn’t been allowed to give her, until a voice came out of the grille above the panel asking whether everyone in lift three was all right.

“We’re fine,” An Yu had said. “The stop was pressed by mistake.”

“It was not pressed by mistake,” Tang Xi said now.

“I know. I lied to building control.”

“Number two. Because I stopped the lift.”

“And the first time you stopped a lift for me, I said that isn’t how it works.”

“You did. You were very annoying.”

He looked at her. “Then what’s number one?”

She smiled slowly.

✦ ✦ ✦

Number one. Friday the fourth of June, 2027. Twenty-four minutes to eight in the evening.

This lift. This exact one. The night Level won the tender. She’d come up to his office to tell him herself, and watched his face, and asked him five times whether he’d interfered, and he’d said no five times. Then she’d taken him into this lift and pressed the stop button, and a calm recorded voice had told them the lift had been stopped and assistance was available, and she had said, “I haven’t congratulated you properly,” and taken hold of his tie.

He knew what had happened after that. He had been there. But she told him anyway, slowly, in the lift, with her mouth close to his ear, so that he would know she remembered it exactly.

How she had kissed him so hard against this wall that his head had touched the steel. How his folder had gone on the floor. How his hand had spread on the small of her back and pulled her in until she could feel his heart through his shirt and everything else through everything else. How she’d been laughing, and then hadn’t been laughing at all. How she’d got his tie off entirely, not loosened, off, and put it round her own neck so he couldn’t have it back. How her hand had gone from his chest to his belt, and stopped on the buckle, and stayed there, and how he had gone completely still against her and said her name in a voice she’d only ever heard in the dark.

“Are you sure?” he’d said. “Here?”

“I’m only holding it,” she’d said. “I’m holding it so you know I could.”

And he had laughed, helplessly, and kissed her again, deep and slow, while her fingers stayed exactly where they were on the cold buckle, not moving, for the longest four minutes of his life, until the recorded voice repeated itself and she took her hand away and pressed the button and let the lift go, and he had walked out into his own lobby with no tie, a ruined collar, his belt slightly crooked, and the expression of a man who had just been comprehensively defeated by somebody who had won a fair tender.

“Number one,” she said now, in his ear.

“Because of the stop button,” he said. His voice wasn’t quite steady.

“Because of the stop button.”

“And the tie.”

“And the tie.”

“And the belt.”

“Don’t get arrogant.”

“I’m confirming the ranking.”

She stepped back and straightened his tie, which was, today, still on. “It’s number one because you asked whether I was sure, while I was in the middle of it, with my hand on your belt. Because you wanted to be sure. Even then.”

“I always want to be sure.”

“I know. That’s why it’s number one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The lift was slowing for the lobby. She looked at him.

“Do you know what’s wrong with that list?”

“Tell me.”

“Eleven lifts. Two years and ten months. And in ten of them I kissed you first.”

He thought about it. “The car park in 2026.”

“One. Out of eleven. And only because I’d just kissed you in the lobby and you were in shock.”

“I can practise.”

“That’s a good idea.”

He reached past her, calmly, and pressed the stop button.

The lift jolted between the third floor and the second and hung there. The recorded voice began to say that the lift had been stopped. He took her face in both his hands, and kissed her first, without being asked and without asking, slow and sure and devastating, until she had to hold on to the handrail behind her, and when he finally lifted his head her lipstick was on his mouth and she couldn’t remember which floor they were on.

“Twelve,” he said.

“That doesn’t count. You’ve been told to.”

“You told me to practise. You didn’t tell me to do it now.”

She laughed against his mouth. “Where does it rank?”

He let the lift go. “You tell me. You’re the one keeping count.”

“I am not keeping count.”

“Then I will,” said An Yu, and the doors opened on the lobby, where a young man from the night security team was waiting with a trolley and found something interesting to look at on the ceiling.

An Yu picked up his folder. “Good evening.”

“Good evening, Mr. Wang.”

Tang Xi walked out beside him with her chin up and her hair slightly wrong. Somewhere in the building’s maintenance logs there were now two emergency stops recorded on lift one in six months, both with no fault found, and a note from the engineer suggesting that someone check the panel. Nobody ever did.

chapters.title: Her Team’s Group Chat
chapters.desc: Eight months of her team’s group chat about the chairman, read in bed. He wants their names. She says no.
chapters.content:
Tang Xi had made one mistake. She had shown An Yu her phone.

It was a Saturday night at the end of October 2025, two days after the second column, the one with her photograph, and they were in his flat because hers had a photographer’s car parked outside it on and off. She was lying on her side in his bed in one of his shirts. He was sitting against the headboard with his glasses on and a book open on his knee, a history of the Hanseatic League, which he claimed to be enjoying.

He had been reading for twenty minutes. She had been scrolling for twenty minutes. Every so often she laughed. The first time, he looked up. The second time, he asked what was funny.

The third time, he closed the book on his finger.

“What are you reading?”

“Nothing.”

“You’ve been laughing at nothing for twenty minutes.”

“It’s a group chat.”

“Your team?”

She smiled into the pillow. “Yes.”

“Something happened?”

“Not exactly.” She turned the phone round to him. “Would you like to know what my team has thought of you since February?”

An Yu looked at the screen, and then at her. “Since February.”

“It’s a long chat.”

He held out his hand. After a moment’s consideration, she put the phone in it.

And that was how Wang An Yu, chairman of An-Tech, discovered that for eight months he had been a recurring item on the agenda of a marketing agency’s private group chat.

✦ ✦ ✦

NORTHLIGHT — DO NOT FORWARD TO CLIENTS
Tuesday 11 February 2025

Rachel (Lunch Police): Emergency.

Calvin (One Last Thing): What happened

Rachel (Lunch Police): Chairman Wang just walked past reception.

Daniel (Boss, Technically): Why is that an emergency?

Rachel (Lunch Police): Because I forgot how to behave like a professional adult.

Calvin (One Last Thing): You were holding a sandwich

Rachel (Lunch Police): I KNOW.

Tang Xi: What does the sandwich have to do with anything?

Rachel (Lunch Police): He looked at it.

Calvin (One Last Thing): He looks at everything

Rachel (Lunch Police): Like he was calculating whether the sandwich was within the approved budget.

Calvin (One Last Thing): Or wondering why you were eating tuna at 9.15 a.m.

Rachel (Lunch Police): I hate all of you.

An Yu stopped. “Rachel.”

“Rachel.”

“Your account director.” He looked back at the screen. “Why was she eating tuna at a quarter past nine?”

“Because she had a meeting at ten and she’d missed breakfast.”

“Is that unusual?”

“For Rachel? No. For you, apparently everything’s a subject for investigation.”

He scrolled.

Thursday 20 February 2025

Rachel (Lunch Police): New observation.

Calvin (One Last Thing): no

Rachel (Lunch Police): Chairman Wang doesn’t walk. He arrives.

Daniel (Boss, Technically): Please stop describing our clients as weather.

Rachel (Lunch Police): I heard his shoes before I saw him.

Calvin (One Last Thing): That’s because the whole floor goes silent when he comes in

Tang Xi: You’re all exaggerating.

Rachel (Lunch Police): Xi, you’re not allowed an opinion. You have to sit opposite him.

Tang Xi: He’s perfectly normal.

Calvin (One Last Thing): That’s an extremely suspicious thing to say

Rachel (Lunch Police): Thank you Calvin.

Daniel (Boss, Technically): Everyone, please finish the quarterly report.

Rachel (Lunch Police): Yes boss.

Calvin (One Last Thing): yes boss

Tang Xi: Yes, boss.

Rachel (Lunch Police): See? Even Xi sounds frightened.

He lowered the phone. “I’m perfectly normal?”

“Don’t let it go to your head.”

“Twentieth of February.” He looked at her over the glasses. “That was the day before.”

She went pink, which she hadn’t expected to do in October. The twentieth of February had been a Thursday. She had sat at her desk and typed He’s perfectly normal into a group chat with her face entirely composed, and that night she’d gone to his flat for the first time, and not gone home until the morning.

“I was being professional.”

“You were lying to your team.”

“I was protecting my team. Give it back.”

“There’s more.”

“I gathered.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Wednesday 5 March 2025

Calvin (One Last Thing): Can someone explain why Mr Wang never blinks

Rachel (Lunch Police): He blinks.

Calvin (One Last Thing): Not in meetings

Daniel (Boss, Technically): I have never observed this.

At the corner of An Yu’s mouth there was something which in anyone else would have been called a smile. Tang Xi saw it.

“Don’t.”

“I haven’t said anything.”

“What is my face saying?”

“That you’re enjoying this.”

“I am.” He went on scrolling. “Calvin presented the media plan for the second quarter. Twenty-two slides. He was very good on slide nine.”

“Is that why you stared at him?”

“I was listening.”

“He thought you were going to have him killed.”

An Yu lowered the phone. “Slide twenty-seven.”

She blinked at him. “You remember that?”

“Of course.”

“What did I say?”

He said, without any hesitation at all, “That the regional budget shouldn’t be divided equally across the markets, because audience size and media costs differ by a factor of four between them. That we should allocate on expected reach and conversion, and then adjust after the first reporting cycle, rather than defending a split we’d chosen because it looked fair.”

She stared at him.

“You were right,” he said. “We adjusted after the first cycle. Malaysia came in eleven per cent over.”

“That isn’t the point.”

“What is?”

“The point is that everybody thinks you’re terrifying.”

“Do you?”

She put her head on one side and considered him: the glasses, the shirt open at the throat, the history of the Hanseatic League. “Sometimes.”

“Because you can look at someone for ten seconds and make them confess to things they haven’t done.”

“That’s an exaggeration.”

He thought about it. “I’ll avoid looking at Calvin.”

She laughed into the pillow until her eyes ran, and he waited, entirely composed, until she’d finished, and then went on reading.

An Yu had stopped scrolling. He read the October messages for a long time. Then he went back to the top of the October messages and read them again, more slowly. She didn’t say anything. She watched his face, which had gone still in the way that, at sixteen, she’d never been able to read, and now could.

“You didn’t tell me about this,” he said at last.

“You had enough of your own that morning.”

“You had Rachel on the phone at a quarter past seven.”

“And at the side door at half past eight. And Daniel at nine. And Calvin reading his gym contract out loud in a lift.” Her voice went a little uneven, and she steadied it. “I’m all right, An Yu. I was never by myself in it. That’s why I showed you.”

He took his glasses off. He folded them, and put them on the bedside table on top of the Hanseatic League, and he didn’t give the phone back.

“I want their names,” he said.

She sat up. “No.”

“I know their first names.”

“You know everything else too. You read the staffing plan. You know Calvin’s surname and Joanne’s start date and probably her CV.”

“I’d like to thank them.”

“No.”

“Why?”

“Because it would frighten them half to death.” She took the phone out of his hand. “Imagine it. Joanne opens her post and there’s a card from the chairman of An-Tech. Calvin’s gym is suddenly paid up for life. Rachel goes to lunch and it’s already been paid for at every restaurant within a mile of the office. They’d know you’d read the chat. They’d never write in it again.”

“I wouldn’t pay for Calvin’s gym.”

“You’ve thought about it.”

“For a second.”

“Wang An Yu.” She put both hands flat on his chest. “Those are my colleagues. They’re allowed to make jokes about you in a private group chat. They’re allowed to protect me without being thanked for it. That isn’t something you get to put your name on. It’s theirs.”

He looked at her, and she could see him understanding it, slowly, the way he understood everything that mattered, by turning it over until he’d seen every side.

“Then how do I thank them?”

“You don’t. You go to the next account meeting, and you’re perfectly normal.” She smiled. “And when Calvin presents, you tell him slide nine was good. Once. In front of everyone. And then you look at somebody else.”

“That’s all?”

“That’s everything.”

“All right.” He held out his hand for the phone again. “Is there more?”

“There’s always more. Rachel types like she’s being paid by the message.”

“Do you talk about me in it?”

Her smile went suspiciously innocent. “Of course not.”

He looked at her. She looked back. She lasted about four seconds.

“Sometimes.”

“What do you say?”

“Nothing important.”

“Xi.”

“Mostly that you’re difficult.”

“What else?”

“That you’re handsome.”

Something changed in his face, slightly. “Really.”

“Don’t look so pleased.”

“I’m not.”

“You are. Your ears have gone red.” She reached up and touched one to prove it. “That you’re annoyingly observant. That you remember too much. That you make people nervous by standing silently in doorways.”

“I don’t stand silently in doorways.”

“You’re doing it now. In bed. Somehow.”

“What else?”

She looked at him. “That you’re very good at kissing.”

He was quiet. Then he leaned down to her, close enough that she could feel him breathe.

“Did you tell them that?”

“No.”

“Why not?”

“Because that’s private.”

He kissed her, just once, as if he were checking. Then again, when she smiled against his mouth, slower, his hand coming up under her jaw to tip her face to him. The phone slid off the duvet somewhere. The shirt she was wearing was his, and had four buttons, and by the time he lifted his head it had one.

“See?” she whispered. “That’s why.”

“Why what?”

“Why I don’t tell them everything.”

He put his forehead against hers. “Good.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The next morning, Sunday, Tang Xi woke to her phone vibrating somewhere in the bedclothes. She found it under his pillow.

She looked at him for a long, suspicious moment. Then she typed, one-handed, with his arm round her.

She shoved the phone under the pillow and put her face in his shoulder.

She lifted her head. “Absolutely not.”

The corner of his mouth went up. “I thought I’d ask.”

“And you’re not allowed to turn up at our office just to see their faces.”

She laughed and lay back down on him, and he put his hand in her hair and kept it there until she’d fallen asleep again, which took about a minute.

Tang Xi looked at the man beside her. He was reading the Hanseatic League again, and he was smiling at a page about grain tariffs in Lübeck.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Wednesday, at the An-Tech account meeting on the forty-second floor, Calvin Seah presented the fourth-quarter media plan in nineteen slides, and was terrified throughout. When he had finished, the chairman of An-Tech looked at him for slightly longer than was comfortable.

“Slide nine was good,” said Wang An Yu.

Then he turned and looked at the head of procurement instead, and asked a question about payment terms, and didn’t look at Calvin again for the rest of the meeting.

Calvin didn’t say a word in the chat about it. He sent Tang Xi a single private message at 4.52 p.m., which was a photograph of the slide.

chapters.title: The Dumplings
chapters.desc: Six attempts in his kitchen and the seventh in her mother’s, with her mother watching, and a word he has waited twenty-one months to be allowed to say.
chapters.content:
The first attempt was too full. The second was strangled. The third was dry. The fourth looked like an envelope. The fifth was wet. The sixth was good.

An Yu considered this a reasonable progression. Tang Xi considered it the funniest thing that had happened to her in a year in which she had also hired nine people into two rooms above a restaurant and watched him eat forty dumplings at his desk.

“You know,” she said, leaning against his kitchen counter on the evening of the sixth, “most people learn to make dumplings without turning it into a six-month corporate development programme.”

“It’s been seven weeks.”

“Emotionally, it’s been six months.”

He looked down at the dumpling in his hand. It was a great deal better than the first. The edges were neat. The filling sat where it should. There were five pleats, not six, and they leaned the same way.

“That’s the sixth,” he said.

“Congratulations.”

“Your mother said the sixth was good.”

“She said it could be cooked.”

“That was the lesson in June. She said this one was good. I have it in writing.”

“You have a text message from a restaurant phone that says better.”

“Better,” said An Yu, “is in writing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It had started with a box of forty, in June, and a lesson in the restaurant kitchen at a quarter past eight at night, and her mother picking up his third dumpling and turning it over and saying, That one can be cooked.

He had said thank you. On the walk to the end of the street afterwards he had been quiet for so long that Tang Xi had asked what was wrong.

“Nothing’s wrong.”

“You’re doing the face.”

“Which face?”

“The one you do when a quarterly result is fine and you wanted it to be good.”

He’d thought about it. “She said it could be cooked.”

“That’s high praise, from her.”

“I know. I’d like to make one she says is good.”

“An Yu. She’s been folding them for thirty years.”

“Then I’ll need to practise.”

She’d stopped under the streetlight to look at him properly, and seen that he meant it in exactly the way he meant everything: entirely, with a notebook.

The recipe had never been written down, because her mother didn’t believe in writing down things she had made for thirty years. What she had given him in December 2025, across the back table of the restaurant while she decided whether he was trouble, was instructions. Wash the chives and dry them properly. Chop the prawns by hand, never in a machine, so they still bite. Scramble the eggs soft, let them cool, break them small. Ginger and white pepper, but neither should be the thing you taste. Stir the filling in one direction until it pulls. Chives in last.

He had asked her how much filling went in each wrapper.

“Enough,” her mother had said.

He had nodded as if this were a measurement. Tang Xi had laughed. Her mother hadn’t. That was the beginning.

✦ ✦ ✦

Attempt One — Sunday 4 July 2027

His kitchen had never seen so much flour. Tang Xi arrived at six to find the door already open and him at the counter with his sleeves rolled to the elbow, a bowl of filling at his elbow and flour on his shirt, on the counter, on the floor, and in some way she couldn’t account for on the back of his neck.

She stopped in the doorway. “What happened?”

“I’m making dumplings.”

“I can see that.” She came and looked into the bowl. The prawns had been chopped so finely they’d turned to paste. The chives were in long uneven lengths. There was a smell of raw ginger strong enough to make her eyes water. She put a finger in and tasted it, and made a face. “An Yu.”

“What?”

“It’s salty.”

“I measured the salt.”

“You measured it wrong.”

He accepted this without argument, and picked up a wrapper, and put a spoonful of filling in the middle of it that was approximately the size of a ping-pong ball.

“That’s too much.”

“It looked insufficient.”

“It’s a dumpling, not a suitcase.”

He folded it. The wrapper split down one side with a small, final sound, and they both looked at it. She started laughing. He looked at her.

“Don’t.”

“I’m sorry.”

“You’re not.”

She couldn’t answer. The second split. The third was so full the edges wouldn’t meet at all and he held it closed with two fingers like a man holding a wound. He looked at it for some time.

“It’s a filling problem.”

“It’s a you problem.”

He looked at her. She reached up and kissed his cheek, where there was also flour. “Keep going, Professor.”

He made eleven more. None of them survived the pot. That night he took a photograph of the bin and didn’t send it to anyone, and wrote in a small black notebook in his neat engineer’s hand:

4 July. Too much filling. Too much salt. Prawns to paste. Wrappers split. Don’t let her watch.

He crossed out the last line before he went to bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Attempt Two — Saturday 10 July 2027

He had corrected the filling. Less salt. Less ginger. The prawns cut into pieces the size of a fingernail, so you could still see that they’d been prawns. The chives in short even lengths, dry.

Tang Xi inspected the bowl. “Much better.”

He nodded and began to fold. He used less filling this time and the wrappers held. Unfortunately he sealed each one by pressing the edges together.

She picked one up. “Why are you strangling it?”

“It’s sealed.”

“It’s also dead.”

“It was never alive.”

“You know what I mean.”

He made eighteen, all sealed, all flattened at the edge into a hard little frill. They boiled them. The filling was good. The wrapper at the seam was thick as cardboard.

He took a bite, chewed, swallowed, and looked at the rest. “Too much pressure.”

“On the dumplings?”

“Yes.”

She leaned across the table and kissed him. “That’s the first time I’ve ever heard you admit it.”

That night he took a photograph of the best one and, after some thought, sent it to the number on a paper takeaway menu that lived in his desk drawer.

Attempt two. Too much pressure at the seal.

The reply came at ten to six the next morning, when the restaurant’s prep began.

Thumbs. Not fingers.

He read it nine times and wrote it in the notebook, underlined.

✦ ✦ ✦

Attempt Three — Sunday 18 July 2027

This time he got the pressure right. Tang Xi came into the kitchen to find him watching a video on a tablet propped against the kettle, with his hands in a bowl of dough.

“What are you watching?”

“Your mother.”

She stopped. “My mother sent you a video?”

“I asked.”

She came and looked. It was her mother, filmed by somebody who was plainly her aunt, at the steel counter at the back of the restaurant, demonstrating how to fold a dumpling. She didn’t look at the camera once. She looked at the dumpling.

“Not so much,” her mother said, to the dumpling. “You always put too much. Then press here. With your thumbs. No. Not there. Here.”

Tang Xi put her hand over her mouth. “She sounds exactly like herself.”

“Watch her fingers.”

“An Yu.”

“I’m watching.”

“How many times have you watched it?”

“Eleven.”

She leaned on his shoulder, and he paused it on the frame where her mother’s thumbs met in the middle of the wrapper, and they looked at it together.

“Your mother says the fold should be the same every time.”

“She also said you were too stiff. She told my aunt you look like you’re performing surgery.”

“That isn’t a bad thing.”

“It’s a terrible thing when it’s a dumpling.”

This attempt produced twenty-four, all intact, all pleated the same way. But when she boiled them the filling had gone tight and dry inside, and the prawns rubbery. She tasted one and he watched her face.

“Too long?”

“The water was boiling too hard. It thrashed them.”

He looked at the pot as if it had personally let him down, and wrote it down, and she picked up the notebook while he wasn’t looking. The pages were ruled into neat sections.

Filling: prawns by hand, not too fine. Chives completely dry. Egg soft, cooled. Ginger reduced. Stir one direction until it pulls.
Folding: less filling. Thumbs, not fingers. Five pleats.
Cooking: don’t thrash.
Ask about the cold water.

“What cold water?”

“In the video, after the dumplings go in, your aunt says something off camera about cold water. Your mother says three times. Then the recording stops.”

Tang Xi stared at him. “You’ve been listening to the background of my mother’s video.”

“It’s the important part.”

She put the notebook down and kissed his shoulder through his shirt. “Why are you so serious about this?”

He looked at her. “Because I want to make them properly.”

He didn’t explain further. He didn’t need to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Attempt Four — Saturday 31 July 2027

Every single one of them looked like an envelope.

Tang Xi stood over the tray with her hands on her hips. An Yu looked at his work.

“They’re consistent.”

“They’re rectangles.”

“Consistent rectangles.”

She covered her mouth.

“Don’t laugh.”

“I haven’t.”

“You’re about to.”

She laughed until she had to hold on to the counter. He sighed, and picked one up and turned it in the light. The corners were sharp. The filling was even. The seal was perfect. It looked like a small, well-drafted document.

“I tried making the pleats in half the time,” he said. “To be quicker. Like hers.”

“You folded it like a letter.”

“I’ve folded a lot of letters.”

She took a photograph before he could stop her. “I’m sending this to my mother.”

“Don’t.”

She already had. Her phone rang eleven seconds later.

“What is this?” said her mother, with no greeting at all.

“His dumpling.”

“Why is it square?”

“He’s practising.”

A small, disapproving sound. “Tell him not to fold paper. Fold dumplings.”

An Yu held out his hand, and Tang Xi, after a moment’s astonishment, put her phone in it.

“Good evening,” he said.

A pause. Then, in the voice she used to send suppliers away, her mother said, “Too much filling?”

“Not this time.”

“Then why does it look like that?”

He looked at the dumpling. “I’m still learning the shape. I was trying to be fast.”

“Don’t be fast. Be the same. Fast comes in ten years.” Another pause, and the sound of the extractor fan behind her. “And the cold water. You bring it to the boil. You put in a cup of cold water. It comes back to the boil, another cup. Then once more. Three times. Then they’re done. You don’t let it roll the whole time. The skin breaks and the inside goes hard.”

“Three times. Thank you.”

“Don’t thank me. Write it down.”

“I have.”

“Hm,” said her mother, and rang off.

Tang Xi stared at him. He handed the phone back with an expression she had last seen on him when Level won the An-Tech tender, which was to say no expression at all, carefully.

“She told you the water.”

“Yes.”

“She’s never told anyone the water. She told me the water when I was nineteen.”

“It’s three cups.”

“I know it’s three cups, An Yu.”

That night the notebook had a new line, and under it, small, a second line he thought she wouldn’t see.

Three times cold water.
She rang off without saying goodbye. Xi says that’s normal. Xi says that’s good.

✦ ✦ ✦

Attempt Five — Sunday 8 August 2027

The shape was right. The water was right. The wrapper was thin enough, rolled thicker in the middle and thinner at the edge, the way the video showed. But he had mixed the chives through too early, and salted the bowl afterwards, and by the time he came to fold, the filling was sitting in a little pool of green water and slid about in the wrapper like something alive.

Tang Xi found him looking into the bowl with the same expression he wore reading a quarterly report that had missed by a decimal point.

“What’s wrong?”

“The filling’s wet.”

She tasted it. “Yes.”

“I dried the chives.”

“Completely?”

He paused. “Apparently not.”

She sat on the stool beside him. “It’s all right.”

“I know.”

“You look offended.”

“I’m not offended.”

“You look as if someone’s betrayed you.”

“It was a preventable error.”

She laughed, and reached for his hand, which was still floury, and held it on the counter. “Listen. You don’t have to get it right.”

“I want to.”

“Why?”

He turned his hand over under hers so he was holding it.

“Because she made them for you when you were growing up,” he said. “When there wasn’t much else. You told me, the first time we went to the restaurant, that you ate them after school at the back table before you started your homework. You told me she’d been on her feet in that kitchen since six, and still made a batch to go home with you, and still asked whether you’d eaten.” He looked at the bowl. “I can’t give you anything you didn’t already have, Xi. You had all of that. But I’d like to be able to make you this. With my hands. The way she did.”

For a moment she had no teasing answer at all.

Then she leaned across and kissed him, slow and quiet, with her hand on his floury wrist, and he kissed her back with one hand at her cheek, leaving a white thumbprint there that she didn’t find until much later in the bathroom mirror. When she pulled away she had to wait a second before she could talk.

“You’re allowed to make ugly dumplings while you’re learning.”

“I know.”

“Even wet ones.”

“I know.”

“Even rectangles.”

He shut his eyes. “Xi.”

She laughed, and got up, and went to the fridge, and came back with a bottle of oil and a clean bowl. “Here. My aunt does this. Dry the chives, then before anything else, before the salt goes anywhere near them, you toss them in a spoonful of oil. It coats them. Then the salt can’t pull the water out.”

He looked at her. “You knew that.”

“Since I was eleven.”

“You didn’t tell me for five weeks.”

“You didn’t ask me,” said Tang Xi, pleased with herself. “You asked my mother. And a video. And the background of a video.”

He wrote it down. Then, after a moment, he wrote underneath it, Ask Xi first.

✦ ✦ ✦

Attempt Six — Saturday 21 August 2027

The sixth attempt was good. Not edible. Not acceptable. Good.

Tang Xi took the first bite standing at the kitchen island, with him on the other side of it, waiting, his hands flat on the marble. She chewed. She swallowed. She took a second bite without saying anything.

“Well?”

She looked at the dumpling, and then at him. “It’s good.”

He didn’t move. “Good?”

“Very good.”

He let out a breath. It was a small sound, and the whole of his back changed with it.

“You did it.”

“Not yet.”

“What do you mean?”

“The fold.”

She looked down. On the third pleat the dough had bunched a fraction, so that one side sat a little thicker than the other.

“An Yu. Nobody’s going to inspect it with a ruler.”

“Your mother will.”

“Probably.”

He took a photograph of the plate, the way he had every time, and sent it to the restaurant’s number with a single line under it.

Attempt six.

The reply came, not the next morning at ten to six, but four minutes later, on a Saturday night, during service.

Better.

And then, a minute after that:

Sunday after next. Come to the flat. Three o’clock. Bring prawns.

Tang Xi read it over his arm, and then read it again, and then turned and put both arms round his waist and her face against his chest.

“The flat,” she said into his shirt.

“Is that significant?”

“She’s never had anyone in her kitchen. Not my aunt. Not my father. Not me, since I was fourteen and dropped the steamer.”

He put his hand on the back of her head. “Then I’ll try not to drop the steamer.”

“You’re very brave.”

“I’m making dumplings.”

“Exactly,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Attempt Seven — Sunday 5 September 2027

Her mother’s kitchen was smaller than his. It was also warmer.

It was at the back of a third-floor flat two streets behind the restaurant, in a building with a lift that had been broken since the spring, and it had one window over the sink with a pot of spring onions on the sill growing out of their own cut roots, and a calendar from a fish wholesaler, and a rice cooker so old the buttons had worn blank. There were baskets of greens by the door. There was a bowl on the counter with a cloth over it. There was a pot of water already on the hob.

They came up the stairs at three with a bag of prawns and a bunch of chives wrapped in newspaper, and her mother looked at the bag before she looked at either of them.

“Good. You brought the right ones.” She lifted the newspaper and looked at the chives. “These are fine.”

“Thank you for having me.”

She waved a hand. “Don’t thank me yet.”

“Mum, be nice.”

“I am being nice.”

“You’re not.”

Her mother ignored this entirely and pushed the bag of prawns along the counter to him. “Show me.”

He rolled up his sleeves. He peeled the prawns and took the dark line out of each with the point of the knife, and chopped them. He didn’t hurry. He didn’t make them into paste. He cut them into pieces you could still recognise, and her mother watched, and didn’t say anything, which Tang Xi understood was a compliment so enormous it was almost unbearable.

He cracked the eggs and scrambled them soft in a little oil, and tipped them out to cool, and broke them small with the side of a spoon. He grated the ginger and put in half of what he’d grated. He put in the white pepper and the sesame oil and a little salt, and stirred, in one direction.

Her mother stood at his shoulder. “Not so fast.”

He slowed down.

“Until it pulls.”

“Yes.”

“Don’t stir because you think you should. Stir until it’s ready. You’ll feel it.”

He stirred. Tang Xi stood by the window with a tea towel she wasn’t using and watched the two of them, her mother half a head below his shoulder, with her arms folded and her eyes on the bowl, and the steam from the pot beginning to fog the bottom of the glass behind them.

Her mother had never in Tang Xi’s life let anyone else take over her kitchen. She worked with the certainty of someone who had spent decades doing things her own way, alone, since six in the morning, and she didn’t like being watched, and she didn’t like being helped, and she didn’t like anybody standing where she needed to stand. She was standing to one side.

She was correcting him without taking the bowl away. And he was listening to every word.

When the filling began to pull, a little, against the spoon, her mother put out her hand and stopped his arm. “Now.”

He took the chives, which he’d dried in a tea towel and then tossed in a spoonful of oil without being told, and her mother saw that, and her eyes went for one second to her daughter by the window, and back. He folded them through. Last.

“Now fold.”

He took a wrapper from the stack she’d rolled that morning. He put the filling in the middle, a small amount, and looked at it.

“Less,” said her mother.

He took a little out.

“Fold.”

He brought the edges up.

“Thumbs.”

He used his thumbs.

“Turn it.”

He turned it.

“Again.”

The second pleat. The third. The fourth. The fifth. The dumpling closed in his palm and sat there, leaning a fraction to the left, five pleats, all going the same way.

He put it on the tray. Her mother picked it up. She turned it over. She held it up to the window and looked at it against the light, the way Tang Xi had seen her look at fish at the market at half past five in the morning when she was a child. Tang Xi held her breath.

Her mother put it down. “Again.”

He made another. Then another. The kitchen went quiet except for the sound of wrappers coming off the stack and the scrape of the spoon in the bowl and the pot ticking on the hob. After a while her mother stopped saying thumbs and started saying nothing at all, and then she took a wrapper herself and stood beside him and folded too, quick and even, five movements, closed. His hands slowed down to watch hers. Hers slowed down, slightly, so he could.

Tang Xi watched them from the window, side by side at the counter, his sleeves pushed up and a little flour on his wrist, her mother’s hands moving the way they’d moved Tang Xi’s whole life, and his moving after them, half a beat behind, a little stiff, then less stiff. He had stopped treating each one as a problem to be solved. He was learning the movement. And her mother, who had never in thirty years slowed down for anybody, was letting him.

She found she had to look out of the window at the pot of spring onions for a while.

Eventually her mother picked up one of his, from the middle of the tray. She looked at it. She put it down.

“This one is good.”

He went entirely still. “Thank you.”

She turned to the hob. “Make more.”

Tang Xi laughed. “Mum, that’s approval.”

Her mother gave her a look. “I said it was good. I didn’t say anything else.”

“Yes, Mum.”

“Don’t make things up.”

An Yu took another wrapper. The corner of his mouth had gone up and stayed there, and he didn’t seem to know.

✦ ✦ ✦

They boiled them together. Her mother brought the water up and put the dumplings in and stirred once so they wouldn’t stick, and when it boiled she held out a cup of cold water without looking, and An Yu put it in her hand. When it boiled again she held out her hand and he gave her the second. The third time, she didn’t hold out her hand. She stepped back from the hob and looked at him, and he poured in the third cup himself.

Tang Xi made the dipping sauce at the table: black vinegar, a little soy, a few drops of chilli oil, a little grated ginger. Her mother put the first dumpling in front of him, on its own, in a bowl.

“Eat.”

He did. The wrapper was soft and held. The prawns had bite. The egg was soft, the chives bright and green, the ginger somewhere behind everything instead of in front of it.

Her mother watched him. “Well?”

“It’s very good.”

“Of course it is. I made the wrappers.”

“Mum!”

Her mother ignored her and put a second one in his bowl. “You pressed too hard on two of them.”

“I’ll remember.”

“Don’t remember. Practise.”

“I will.”

Under the table, Tang Xi found his hand. He turned his palm up for her and their fingers joined. Her mother looked at their hands, and then at her daughter.

“Don’t hold his hand while he’s eating. The vinegar will go everywhere.”

Tang Xi let go at once.
