An Yu looked down at his hand, and then across the table at her mother, and opened his mouth, and stopped, because he had been told in December 2025 not to call her Auntie unless she told him to, and she hadn’t, and he had spent twenty-one months carefully calling her nothing at all.

Her mother saw him stop. She put a third dumpling in his bowl.

“You can call me Auntie.” She said it to the bowl. “Eat.”

There was a short silence in the small hot kitchen. Tang Xi looked hard at the vinegar.

“Thank you, Auntie,” said An Yu.

“Hm,” said her mother, and ate a dumpling of her own, and that was all.

✦ ✦ ✦

After lunch he washed the bowls and she dried, and her mother wiped the counter, and when Tang Xi went to find the plastic boxes in the cupboard in the hall she heard her mother’s voice go low behind her, and stopped where she was, out of sight, with a stack of boxes against her chest.

“You’ve been practising a long time.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

He put a bowl away. “Because Tang Xi likes them.”

“She likes a lot of things.”

“I know.”

“You don’t have to learn all of them.”

“I know.”

Her mother stopped wiping. “When she was small, in Shanghai, she came into the kitchen after school and asked if there were any left. Every day. She liked the ones with more prawn. She used to pick them out of the steamer before anyone else could get them, with her fingers. She was greedy. And when we came here, at seventeen, she did it again, at the back table of the restaurant, as if she were still small.”

“I didn’t know that.”

“Now you know.” A pause. The sound of the cloth again. “When things were bad, after Shanghai, there were months there was nothing else much in that house. But there were always these. I made sure there were these.”

He didn’t answer. When he did, his voice had gone low and careful.

“I’ll make sure she gets the ones with more prawn.”

Her mother looked at him, and Tang Xi in the hall couldn’t see her face, and was glad, because she thought if she’d seen it she would have had to go in.

“Don’t give her all of them,” her mother said. “She’ll eat too much.”

“I’ll keep some for myself.”

“Good.”

It wasn’t a blessing. Her mother would never give one of those. But when they were leaving she packed a box of dumplings into Tang Xi’s bag and a second, bigger one into his. And at the door she took a folded piece of paper out of her apron pocket and held it out to him.

“What is this?”

“The recipe.”

He unfolded it. There were no measurements. Just the ingredients down one side in her handwriting, and beside them a few words each. Prawns — by hand. Chives — oil first. Egg — soft. Fold — thumbs. Water — three times. And at the bottom, underlined, in a slightly different pen, as if added that morning: Not too much.

“Thank you.”

“Don’t lose it.”

“I won’t.”

“And don’t use a machine for the prawns.”

“I won’t.”

She looked up at him. “Next time, make them here. With me.”

He held the paper in both hands. “I’d like that.”

“Go before the traffic,” said her mother, and opened the door.

They were halfway down the first flight when she called after him.

“An Yu.”

He turned on the stairs.

“Next time, make more.”

“Yes, Auntie,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

That evening Tang Xi found the recipe on his kitchen counter. He’d put it in a clear archival sleeve from the box in his study, and laid it beside the black notebook. She picked up the notebook. There were six dated entries, each with its corrections, and the lines he’d underlined, and the lines he’d crossed out. Below them was a seventh.

5 September. Her kitchen. Good.
Auntie.

And under that, in smaller writing:

Ask her to teach me the other things she made for Xi.

He was at the sink, rinsing the box. She came up behind him with the notebook and put her arms round his waist and her cheek against his back, and he turned the tap off.

“What is it?”

“You know you don’t have to learn every recipe my mother has.”

“I know.”

“Or every single thing I liked when I was small.”

“I know.”

She held on tighter. “Then why?”

He turned round in her arms and looked down at her.

“Because I want to know the things that made you,” he said. “And because I like making things for you with my hands. I didn’t know that about myself until this summer.”

Her eyes went bright. “Even when they’re ugly?”

“Most of all then.”

She laughed, damply, and pulled him down by the front of his shirt and kissed him, slow and thorough, there against the sink, until she’d forgotten what she’d been going to say, and his hands had gone into her hair and come out floury, and the box he’d been rinsing was dripping on the floor.

When she could, she touched his face. “Next time, I’ll help you.”

“I’d like that.”

“And I’ll teach you the dipping sauce properly.”

“I know how to make it.”

“You put too much vinegar in.”

“I adjusted the ratio.”

“You adjusted it wrong.”

He looked at her. She smiled.

“Don’t worry, Professor. We’ve got plenty of attempts left.”

He kissed her again. On the counter, the recipe lay in its sleeve beside the notebook. Seven attempts. One small hot kitchen. Five pleats, all going the same way, and a word he’d waited twenty-one months to be told he was allowed to say.

chapters.title: Singapore Again
chapters.desc: Singapore in the December monsoon, the same room by number, booked on purpose. No cancelled flight. No hurry.
chapters.content:
The first time they’d been in Singapore together it had been an accident.

Two rooms the first night, with a wall between them and a glass of strawberry milk knocking at her door at half past six from the room next door. Then a cancelled flight, a hotel with one room left, one king bed, rain against a wide window, and the discovery that being stranded together was a great deal more dangerous than either of them had planned for.

The second time, twenty-one months later, Tang Xi booked the room herself.

Same hotel. Same floor. Same room, by number, because she had rung the hotel in November and asked for it, and the reservations manager had asked whether there was anything special about 3108, and she had said, “The window.”

An Yu found out on the Monday before they flew. Ding had put the itinerary on his desk at nine: the Alder Vane review on Thursday, the regional operations team on Friday morning, the usual hotel near the bay, two nights. At four minutes past nine an email arrived on his personal address with no message in it at all, only a hotel confirmation.

Room 3108. Thursday 10 December and Friday 11 December 2026. One guest, one king bed. Corner window, high floor. Requested by guest: same room as March 2025.

He read it. He read the room number. He read the dates. Then he rang her.

She answered on the fourth ring. There was a printer going behind her, and Calvin saying “one last thing” to somebody, and the extractor fan of her aunt’s kitchen coming up through the floor.

“Why this hotel?” he said.

“Because it’s in Singapore.”

“It isn’t the closest to Alder Vane.”

“It’s closer to Halloway’s new property. My meeting’s on Duxton Hill. Yours is a taxi ride away. You can afford a taxi.”

“There are three hotels nearer the bay.”

“I know. Ding’s booked you into one of them.”

“You’ve seen my itinerary?”

“Ding sent it to me. In November you told him I’m allowed to know where you are.” A pause, and he could hear she was smiling. “Is there a problem with the arrangements, Mr. Wang?”

“No.”

“Good. I’m on the four o’clock flight on Thursday with Calvin. He’s staying at a hotel near the client. I’ll see you there.”

She rang off. An Yu looked at the confirmation for a while longer. Then he called Ding in.

“Could you cancel the hotel in Singapore, please.”

Ding looked at the itinerary in his hand, and then at the chairman, and then, briefly, at the ceiling, in the manner of someone who had made the original booking in March 2025 and the cancellation request for an extra night when the flight went, and had a long memory and good manners.

“Understood, Mr. Wang. Shall I tell the driver a different address?”

“I’ll send it to you.”

“No need,” said Ding. “I have it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was nothing accidental about any of it, and that was the point.

He flew on Wednesday night for the Alder Vane review, which had been fixed since September: a year since the regional partnership went live, a day of numbers, and a lunch where the chief executive made the joke about the summary slide that he’d made at every meeting since March 2025 — the slide a young woman from the agency had once stood up to correct in front of everyone. Somebody always laughed. An Yu never did. He did, this time, slightly, and the chief executive looked so astonished that he lost his place in the joke.

She flew on Thursday afternoon with Calvin and a suitcase of printed concept boards, and went straight from Changi to Duxton Hill, to a row of old shophouses Halloway was turning into twenty-two rooms, and spent three hours with the Singapore general manager and a heritage architect arguing about whether the launch should lead with the building or the people who looked after it. She won, which surprised nobody except the architect. Calvin said “one last thing” four times and got two of them agreed.

December was the monsoon in Singapore. Every afternoon at about three the sky went heavy and green-grey and then opened, for an hour or for the whole evening, and the streets went silver and the drains ran loud as rivers. It started on Duxton Hill at a quarter past three and didn’t stop.

At five past eight she let herself into 3108 with her hair wet, carrying her shoes.

He was already there. He had been there since six. He was standing at the window in his shirtsleeves, with his tie off and his jacket on the back of the chair, watching the rain come down over the city, and when he heard the door he turned round, and his face did something she would have given a great deal, at sixteen, to have seen even once.

She put her shoes down by the door.

“You’re early.”

“My meeting finished at five.”

“And you’ve just been standing here.”

“I was looking at the window.”

“For two hours?”

He thought about it. “I had a call. Then I looked at the window.”

She came across the room, past the desk and the sitting area and the wide bed, to where he stood. Everything was where it had been. The desk under the lamp. The little table by the glass where they’d eaten dinner over a revised travel plan. The window, floor to ceiling, the city beyond it smeared into light, the rain running down in long uneven lines.

“It’s the same,” she said.

“They’ve changed the carpet.”

“An Yu.”

“It was blue.”

She laughed and put her forehead on his chest, and he put his arms round her, and they stood like that, her damp hair soaking a patch of his shirt, for long enough that she felt him breathe out once, all the way, as if he’d been holding it in since he got off the plane.

“How was Duxton Hill?”

“Wet. I won. The architect wants the launch to be about the plasterwork.”

“And?”

“And now it’s about the woman who’s run housekeeping at Halloway’s first hotel for nineteen years. And her plasterwork.” She lifted her head. “How was Alder Vane?”

“Eleven per cent over plan in the first year.”

“That’s good.”

“They made the joke about the slide.”

“Did you laugh?”

“A little.”

She looked at him with great suspicion. “You laughed in a meeting.”

“I was thinking about who corrected it.”

She didn’t answer that. She went up and kissed him instead, because she couldn’t think of a single thing to say that would be better.

✦ ✦ ✦

They had dinner sent up, and didn’t hurry it. She changed into the soft grey dress she’d packed for the purpose and nothing else, and didn’t tell him, and he found out at about the moment he reached across the little table to take the pepper and she put her bare foot on his knee under it. He went on carefully grinding pepper onto a piece of fish that didn’t need it.

“I’ve been thinking,” she said.

“I can tell.”

“About the first time. In this room.” She looked out at the rain. “We were so busy pretending we’d been forced into it. The flight. The only room left. As if the weather had decided it, and we were just two people who happened to be standing in the way.”

“I knew it hadn’t.”

“I know you did. That’s why you asked if I wanted you to take the sofa.” She smiled. “I didn’t want you to take the sofa.”

“I gathered.”

“I booked it because I wanted one night in Singapore that nobody could say happened to us. Not a flight. Not a storm. Not your assistant and my agency’s travel policy.” She took her foot off his knee and stood up. “I chose it. The way you chose to stand at that window for two hours.”

He put his fork down. “Then it’s yours.”

“Ours,” she said. “Don’t be generous. I’m not in the mood for generous.”

“What are you in the mood for?”

She went to the window. She stood where she’d stood in March 2025, with the cold coming off the glass and the city drowned in light below her, and she turned round and leaned back against it, both her palms flat on the window at her sides.

“I want you to take your time,” she said. “All of it. We’ve got the whole night and a meeting at eleven and a flight that won’t be cancelled. Nobody’s coming. Nothing’s going to stop it. I want to see what you’re like when there’s no reason to hurry at all.”

He came and stood in front of her. He didn’t touch her. He looked at her, the way he’d looked at her from across a library table when she was sixteen and he hadn’t said a word.

“I’m always taking my time,” he said.

“No. You’re always being careful. That’s different.”

He was quiet. Then he put one finger on her collarbone, where the dress began, and drew it down, an inch, slowly.

“Like this?”

“Slower.”

He laughed, low, and kissed her.

There was no urgency in it anywhere. His mouth on hers as though he had all the time in the world and intended to use it; her hands on the glass behind her, staying there, because she’d decided they would. He kissed her until her lips were tender, and then stopped, and kissed the corner of her mouth, and her jaw, and the place under her ear that made her breath catch, and waited each time for the catch to finish before he moved again. The rain came harder against the window at her back. She could feel it through the glass: the cold, and the faint drumming of it, all down her spine.

When his hand went to the fastening at the back of her dress, he stopped.

“May I?”

“You don’t have to ask that any more.”

“I like asking.”

She shut her eyes. “Yes.”

He undid it the way he did everything that mattered, with complete attention and no wasted movement, and the dress slid off her shoulders and down, and caught at her hips, and he let it, and stood back half a step and looked at her against the window with the lights of Singapore behind her.

“What?” she whispered.

“Nothing.”

“That’s my answer.”

“I know.” His voice had gone rough. “You’re not wearing anything under it.”

“I was wondering how long you’d take.”

“Since the pepper.”

She laughed, and then she stopped laughing, because he’d knelt down in front of her on the new carpet, the way he had in this exact place twenty-one months before, and pushed the dress the rest of the way down to the floor with both hands, and she was naked against the glass and he was looking up at her from there, fully dressed, with his sleeves rolled to the elbow and his collar open, and his eyes dark.

“Hands on the window,” he said.

They were already there. She pressed them flatter.

He took his time. He’d said he would and he did, until she understood that every other time had been, in some way she hadn’t noticed, a little hurried. His mouth on the inside of her knee. Her thigh. The crease of her hip, his breath warm on her, and then away again, until she said his name in a voice she didn’t recognise, and only then his mouth on her properly, slow and open and patient, with one of his hands spread on her stomach holding her against the cold glass while the other hooked her knee over his shoulder. She shook. The rain came down. He didn’t speed up when she wanted him to, and he didn’t stop when she couldn’t stand it, and he didn’t do anything at all except exactly, devastatingly, the same thing, over and over, until her palms were squeaking on the wet glass and her head had gone back against it and she was saying please to the ceiling of a hotel room in Singapore, and he made her say it three times before he gave her what she was asking for, and she came apart with both her hands flat on the window and her whole body shaking against his mouth.

He held her up. He held her up until she could stand. Then he got to his feet and she slid down the window a little into his arms and he caught her.

“Was that slow enough?” he said against her temple.

She couldn’t speak for a second. “You’re a terrible person.”

“You asked.”

“I know I asked.” She fumbled for his shirt. “Take this off. Take all of it off. I’m cold and you’re dressed and it’s insulting.”

He let her. She was clumsy about it, her hands still unsteady, and he stood and let her be clumsy, one button at a time, and when she reached the last one she spread her palm flat on his chest and felt his heart going under it, fast and hard, nothing slow about it at all.

“Oh,” she said. “You’re not as calm as you look.”

“I’ve never been as calm as I look. Not with you.”

“Since when?”

“Since the library.”

She looked up at him, and then she pushed the shirt off his shoulders, and undid his belt, and the rest, and pushed him, gently, one hand on his chest, backwards, until the backs of his knees hit the armchair by the window, and he sat.

“Now you take your time,” she said, “while I take mine.”

She climbed into his lap. She took him in her hand and he made a sound she’d heard perhaps a dozen times in her life and wanted to hear a thousand more. She sank down onto him slowly, so slowly that by the end of it he had his head back against the chair and his eyes shut and his hands clenched on the arms of it.

“Look at me,” she said.

He opened his eyes.

“Don’t move.”

“Xi.”

“You said you’d take your time.”

She moved. Barely. A slow rise and fall that was hardly anything, and she watched every change it made in his face, the way he’d watched hers in this room once, asking her what she wanted when she was too far gone to tell him. Behind her the rain was loud on the window. In front of her he was coming undone in a way she had never once seen in a boardroom: his breath going ragged, his jaw tight, his hands finally leaving the chair and coming up to her hips and staying there, not pulling, not hurrying her, only holding on.

“Tell me,” she said.

“Tell you what?”

“What you want.”

He looked at her. And then the chairman of An-Tech, who had once needed a full evening and the threat of a cancelled flight before he could say a single thing he wanted out loud, told her. Precisely. In a low, uneven voice, against her mouth. Harder, and slower, and exactly there, and don’t stop, Xi, please, don’t stop. She made him wait for it once, on purpose, the way she had in March 2025. He laughed, breathless and helpless, and said her name in a voice that cracked down the middle, and she gave him every single thing he’d asked for, until neither of them was taking their time any longer, and he came with his face in her neck and his arms locked round her so tightly she could hardly breathe, and she followed him a few seconds later with her forehead against his and the whole wet city shining behind her.

For a long time after that, neither of them moved.

The rain went on. It had gone softer, steady, a long grey sound against the glass. She was still in his lap, still holding him, her cheek on his shoulder, and his hand was moving up and down her bare back, slowly.

“Better,” she said at last, into his neck.

“Than what?”

“Than the first time.”

“Why?”

She thought about it. “Because nothing trapped us here. We could have been in two hotels on opposite sides of the bay. You could have stayed where Ding booked you. I could have stayed with Calvin.” She lifted her head. “And I came here, and you were standing at the window.”

He pushed her hair back from her face. “I was always going to be at the window.”

“That isn’t what I meant.”

“I know what you meant.” He kissed her once, gently. “I wanted you here too. I wanted you to choose it. And you did.”

She smiled at him, slow and sleepy and entirely without defences. “Carry me to bed.”

“Is that a request?”

“It’s an instruction.”

“I’ll take it under advisement.”

“An Yu.”

He carried her to bed.

✦ ✦ ✦

She woke to rain. Grey light, the window beaded and running, the city pale beneath it. He was awake beside her on his side, watching her, the way he’d been watching her the first time she woke in this room. His phone was in his hand. He’d been reading an email.

She reached over without a word and took the phone out of his hand and put it face up on the bedside table, deliberately, the screen to the ceiling, where he could see it was there and not touch it.

“Good morning.”

“Good morning.”

“Work?”

“Something from Alder Vane.”

“Can it wait?”

“Yes.”

“Good.” She lay back against the pillow. “What time is your meeting?”

“Eleven. Yours?”

“Halloway at half past one. Calvin’s taking the concept boards back to the architect at ten so she can be angry about the plasterwork again.” She looked at the clock. “It’s ten to seven. We’ve got four hours.”

“That’s not long.”

“It’s very long, if nobody hurries.”

At seven o’clock there was a knock at the door.

He looked at her. She looked at the ceiling.

“Did you order something?”

“Get the door, Mr. Wang.”

He pulled on the hotel robe and went. An attendant stood in the corridor with a trolley: toast, a little plate of fruit, two warm egg sandwiches, a pot of black tea, and, in a tall glass, beaded with cold, a strawberry milk.

“Room 3108,” said the attendant. “From the lady.”

An Yu stood in the doorway in a hotel robe and looked at the glass.

He signed for it. He brought the trolley in himself. He put the strawberry milk on the bedside table on his side, beside the phone, and stood looking at it with an expression she couldn’t name.

“It’s yours,” she said. “I don’t even like it any more. I like it about once every two years. You always order it. You’ve never had one.”

“I don’t like strawberry milk.”

“I know. That’s what makes it funny.”

He sat down beside her. He picked up the glass, and he drank about half of it, steadily, without making a face, and put it down.

“Well?”

“It’s terrible.”

“Thank you for being honest.”

“I’m going to finish it.”

“Why?”

He looked at her. “Because you ordered it from the next room. Well. The same room.” He turned the glass a quarter turn on the table. “Nobody’s ever brought me anything at half past six in the morning because they remembered how I take it.”

“It’s seven.”

“Seven,” he agreed, and finished it, and put down the empty glass, and then he lay back down next to her in the robe, and pulled her against him, and said into her hair, “Thank you,” in a voice so quiet she almost didn’t hear it.

She held on to him. Outside, the monsoon was still coming down over the city in long silver sheets, and somewhere below them the traffic was starting, and in four hours they’d be in two different meetings on opposite sides of the island, being entirely professional. At six that evening they’d be on the same flight. It would leave on time.

She found, lying there, that she was almost disappointed about that.

“An Yu.”

“Hm.”

“Next time, let’s cancel it ourselves.”

chapters.title: The Gossip Columnist
chapters.desc: The column on page eleven stops appearing after An-Tech buys its publisher. She finds out from a trade newsletter, and is furious, a little.
chapters.epigraph: “You found a way to make him disappear without ever having to speak to him.”
chapters.content:
The column disappeared on a Thursday. There was no announcement. No correction, no apology, no final piece explaining that its author had decided to pursue other interests. On Thursday the third of September 2026, page eleven of The Exchange Weekly carried an interview with a shipping executive about container rates, and the column that had sat on page eleven every Thursday for six years was simply not there.

It was called Corner Office. It dealt in rumours dressed as observations and private lives presented as matters of public interest, in carefully weighed sentences that stopped exactly one word short of anything its lawyers couldn’t defend. Its author, Julian Rowe, had built a career on knowing which people were too powerful to name and which were small enough to name anyway. In October 2025 he had named Tang Xi.

Not at first. On a Monday he had written, on the website, about a young founder, a fast-growing agency and a convenient account. Ten days later, on a Thursday, in print, on page eleven, he had used her photograph, her full name, her title and enough of her career to make the insinuation impossible to miss. He had suggested that her promotion had been bought. A client had pulled out of a pitch she led. And for months afterwards she had been made to account for a relationship that was nobody’s business but hers.

An Yu had wanted to destroy him then.

He hadn’t. She had made sure of that, at two in the morning, standing at his desk in his cardigan with a legal assessment in one hand and a list of the magazine’s advertisers in the other. He had deleted the assessment. He had shredded the list. He had kept An-Tech and its lawyers away from the writer and the publication, as she’d asked.

He had listened. At least, he had believed he had.

✦ ✦ ✦

The opportunity came in February 2026, and it didn’t come looking like revenge.

A media holding group was selling off a portfolio of businesses. One of them was Tidemark Media, which owned three trade conferences, a market-data subscription service used by every shipping desk in the region, a handful of newsletters, and, as a small and increasingly expensive afterthought, The Exchange Weekly. The conferences made money. The data service made a great deal of money. The magazine lost a little more every year: print circulation down, advertisers drifting, and a column on page eleven that generated traffic and legal invoices in roughly equal amounts.

An-Tech’s investment arm wanted a services business with regular income. Tidemark was on a list of nine. The acquisitions team prepared a commercial assessment and it reached the chairman’s desk on a Tuesday afternoon with the rest of the week’s papers.

An Yu read it. He read the summary, and the revenue split, and the integration plan for the data business. On page thirty-four, under Editorial assets, he read the name of the magazine. On page thirty-five, under Contributor agreements and legal exposure, he read the name of the columnist.

He turned back to page thirty-four, and read it again, and then he rang the investment director.

“The magazine. Who owns the editorial rights?”

“The publisher. The columns are commissioned by the editor. The contributor agreements are separate and renewable.”

“Can a column be discontinued?”

“Subject to the contract, yes. Rowe’s is rolling, renewed every quarter. The editor has authority over commissioning.”

An Yu looked at page thirty-five. “What’s the proposed editorial structure after completion?”

“Still under review.”

“Then don’t assume the column’s continuation in the business plan.”

There was a short pause on the line. “Understood.”

“Assess the legal costs on their merits. If there’s no obligation to commission further work, it’s the editor’s decision.”

“Would you like to speak to the editor?”

“No.”

“Should we flag the title to the board as sensitive?”

“Yes. The transaction should be judged on its commercial merits. Make sure the process is documented.”

He put the phone down and went to his next meeting.

There had been no instruction. No request for anybody’s personal information. No call to an editor. No threat. Only a sentence about an assumption in a business plan, said on a recorded line by a man who knew exactly how much weight a sentence from him carried in his own company. It was, in every technical sense, defensible. That was what made it dangerous.

✦ ✦ ✦

The acquisition completed on Friday the twenty-eighth of August.

The new board of Tidemark met on Monday the thirty-first. The editor of The Exchange Weekly, a careful woman of fifty-five called Margaret Lau who had run the magazine for eleven years, presented the column’s figures. Readership. Complaints. Advertiser withdrawals. Legal fees, which in the previous twelve months had been four times the column’s fee. Under the business plan she had been given, the magazine would have to cut its costs by a fifth in a year, and nobody had told her the column was to be kept.

The board asked whether it could be redesigned. She said it could.

They asked whether it should be. There was no consensus. The decision was left to her.

On Thursday the third of September, page eleven carried an interview about container rates. On the tenth, a piece about port automation. By the third Thursday, readers had begun asking questions online, and the magazine’s account replied to all of them with the same line.

Our editorial programme is under review. We’ll share any changes as appropriate.

There were no changes to share. Julian Rowe rang the editor, and then the managing director, and then the editor again. Nobody gave him an answer he liked. His agreement wasn’t renewed at the end of the quarter. His old columns stayed online. His fees were settled to the last cent according to contract. He wasn’t accused of anything in public. He wasn’t dismissed in a press release.

He was simply no longer being published.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tang Xi found out on Friday the second of October, at twenty past four in the afternoon, from Calvin.

Level was eleven weeks old. It had three desks, two clients and a kettle, in a room above her aunt’s restaurant that smelled of ginger after twelve, and Calvin read the trade press every Friday afternoon because he said it was where clients went to complain about their agencies before they told them.

“One last thing,” he said, from the window desk. “Did you know An-Tech owns The Exchange Weekly now?”

The room went quiet. Rachel’s head came up.

Tang Xi looked at him. “What?”

“It’s in the media newsletter. Tidemark Media. Completed at the end of August. They’re merging the data business into An-Tech’s analytics arm.” He scrolled. “There’s a line at the bottom. It says Corner Office hasn’t appeared since the deal closed and the publisher won’t comment.”

She held out her hand for his laptop. He gave it to her.

She read it once, and then again. Then she opened a second article, and a third, and by the time Rachel said “Xi?” across the room she had understood more than enough.

“Did you know?” said Rachel.

“No.”

Rachel looked at her face. “Are you going to ring him?”

“No,” said Tang Xi, and closed the laptop, and gave it back to Calvin, and picked up her own phone. “I’m going to ask him in writing. So he has to write the answer down.”

An Yu was in a board meeting when it arrived.

Tang Xi: Did An-Tech buy the company that publishes Julian Rowe’s column?

He read it under the table. He didn’t reply. A regional director was presenting the revised operating structure for the north. An Yu listened, asked two questions, and approved the next item, and when the meeting ended forty minutes later he went back to his office and stood at the window and answered.

An Yu: Yes.

Tang Xi: Did you know which magazine it was when you bought it?

An Yu: Yes.

Tang Xi: We need to talk.

An Yu: I’ll come to you.

Tang Xi: No. I’ll come to you. I’d like to see your office when you explain it.

He looked at that. Then he asked Ding to cancel his six o’clock.

✦ ✦ ✦

She arrived at ten past seven. Ding met her in the lobby himself.

“Good evening, Ms. Tang.”

“Good evening, Ding. Is he up there?”

“Yes. He’s expecting you.” He paused at the lift, and then, which he never did, he said, “He told me on Tuesday the third of February that he’d read the file. He didn’t tell me what to do with it. I thought you should know that he told me.”

She looked at him. “Thank you, Ding.”

“I’ll be at my desk,” said Ding, “for a while,” and pressed the button for her.

An Yu was standing by the window on the forty-second floor when she came in. His jacket was on the back of his chair. On his desk, squared to its edge, lay a copy of the commercial assessment, open at page thirty-four. She didn’t sit.

“Did you buy the publisher because of him?”

“No.”

“Did you know it owned his column?”

“Yes.”

“Did that change anything about how you bought it?”

“The acquisition was already under consideration. Tidemark was on a list of nine. The case was the data business. It was reviewed by the team on its merits.”

She looked at him. “That isn’t what I asked.”

He was silent. “I knew the column was part of the business,” he said. “I knew what he’d written about you. I said, on a call with the investment director, that the column’s continuation shouldn’t be assumed in the business plan.”

“And?”

“And I didn’t instruct anyone to remove him.”

“An Yu.”

“The editor reviewed its costs and its legal exposure. The board left the decision to her. She made it.”

“Under a business plan you’d changed.”

“Under a business plan I’d made one remark about.”

“From you.” She came to the desk and looked down at page thirty-four. “Do you know how much a remark from you weighs, in this building? I’ve watched people rewrite a deck overnight because you raised one eyebrow at slide nine.” She put her finger on the page. “So you bought a company.”

“An-Tech’s investment arm bought a company.”

“And the column stopped.”

“Yes.”

She went to the window. For a long time she said nothing at all. The city was coming on below them, block by block, the way it had on the first evening she ever stood in this room, with a deck under her arm and her heart going like a drum.

When she turned back she was calm, which was worse than anything else she could have been.

“You found a way to make him disappear without ever having to speak to him.”

His face tightened. “He hasn’t disappeared. He can write anywhere else that will have him.”

“That isn’t what I mean.”

“I know.”

“Do you?”

He didn’t answer.

She came back to the desk. “You didn’t ring him. You didn’t threaten him. You didn’t send lawyers. You didn’t even tell the editor what to do.”

“No.”

“And now he hasn’t got a column.”

“Yes.”

She let out a short breath. “That’s almost worse.”

“Why?”

“Because you can tell yourself you didn’t do anything.” Her voice didn’t rise. “You can tell yourself it was a commercial decision. You can tell yourself the editor decided. You can tell yourself you followed every procedure.”

“I did.”

“I know you did. That’s what frightens me.”

He looked at her, and for once there was nothing composed in his face at all.

She sat down then, finally, in the chair opposite his desk, the client’s chair, and folded her hands in her lap so that he wouldn’t see them shake.

“Do you remember what I said, the morning the first column came out?”

“Don’t contact the writer. Don’t ask anyone to take it down. Don’t use An-Tech’s lawyers to make it disappear.”

“And did you?”

“No.”

“You wanted to.”

“Yes.”

“You had Ding make a list of the magazine’s advertisers. At two in the morning.”

“I shredded it.”

“You did. And I was grateful. I was more grateful than I ever told you.” She looked at him. “But I thought you understood why I asked. And I don’t think you did. You understood that I didn’t want you to interfere with the article. I don’t think you understood that I didn’t want you to use what you have to punish somebody because he hurt me. Not then. Not later. Not ever. Not through a lawyer, and not through a business plan, and not through a remark on a recorded line that someone else has to act on so you don’t have to.”

He looked down at the open file.

“I wouldn’t have bought a business that didn’t make sense to remove one columnist.”

“I believe you.”

“Then—”

“But you knew what was on page thirty-four.” She leaned forward. “You knew he was there. You knew what he’d done. And you knew that once you owned it, a sentence from you would decide whether he kept his column.”

He was quiet. “Yes.”

“Did you think about me?”

“Yes.”

“What did you think?”

He took a long time. “I thought he’d made money out of humiliating you,” he said. “I thought the magazine had made money out of it too. I thought it would be a very small thing to stop. And I thought that nobody, including you, would ever be able to say I’d done anything wrong.”

“And you were right. Nobody can.”

“Xi—”

“You didn’t ask me.”

“No.”

“You didn’t tell me. For eight months. You let me find out from Calvin, reading a trade newsletter, at the window, in front of everyone.” Her voice cracked slightly on everyone and she stopped, and waited, and went on. “Eleven weeks ago I sat in a room above my aunt’s restaurant with five desks and told two people that I’d built something nobody could say you gave me. And today they watched me find out that you’d quietly bought the magazine that said you had.”

He went white. He hadn’t thought of that. She saw him not having thought of it, all at once, the whole shape of it arriving in his face. He came round the desk, and stopped, and didn’t reach for her.

“Would you like me to reverse it?”

“Can you?”

“I can ask the board to review the editorial arrangements. I can recuse myself from anything to do with the magazine.”

“Would that bring the column back?”

“I don’t know.”

“Would it bring his job back?”

“I don’t know.”

“Then don’t offer me something you can’t promise.”

He nodded slowly. “All right.”

She was quiet for a while. Then she asked, “Did you enjoy it?”

“Enjoy what?”

“Knowing he’d wake up on a Thursday and find his column wasn’t there.”

“No.”

“Did you feel satisfied?”

He thought about it. The honest answer wasn’t a comfortable one, and she watched him decide to give it to her anyway.

“At first,” he said. “Yes. On the third of September I opened the magazine and turned to page eleven, and it was about container rates, and I felt satisfied. For about a minute.”

“And now?”

“Now I think I was far too comfortable with the fact that I could.”

She looked at her hands.

He sat down beside her, in the other client’s chair, with a little space between them. “I didn’t think about what it would mean for you to find out like this.”

She gave a small laugh with no humour in it. “You keep doing that.”

“I know.”

“You think about the outcome. Whether it’s legal. Whether it’s efficient. Whether you can justify it. And then you forget there are people inside the outcome.”

“I didn’t forget you.”

“No. You remembered me very well. You just didn’t ask me.”

That silenced him completely. For a long time they sat side by side in the two chairs facing his empty desk, like two people waiting to be seen by somebody.

“I don’t feel sorry for him,” she said at last.

“I know.”

“I don’t think he deserves another column. I don’t want to read another word he writes. I don’t care if he never writes about me or anyone else again.” She looked down. “But I don’t want you to be the reason he can’t. Not because he deserves protecting. Because I don’t want to be the reason you decide who’s allowed to speak.”

He was still. “I can’t undo the acquisition,” he said. “And I won’t lean on the editor to bring the column back just to prove something to you. That would be another decision made on your behalf, and another one on hers.”

She nodded slowly.

“But I can take myself out of every editorial decision at Tidemark, permanently. I can ask the board for an independent review of what I said in February and what happened because of it. I can put it in writing to the risk committee. All of it. The date, the call, the sentence. Why.” He looked at her. “The way you did, for Daniel.”

She went still. “Would you have done any of that,” she said, “if I hadn’t found out?”

He didn’t answer.

“No.”

“Thank you for not lying.”

“I should have done it in February.”

“Yes. You should.”

“Are you angry with me?”

She gave him a tired look. “Very.”

He nodded. “I’m sorry.”

“I know.”

“Would you like to go home?”

She looked at the window, and then at him. “Not yet.”

“All right.”

He stayed where he was. He didn’t reach for her hand until she put hers out, palm up, on the arm of the chair between them, and even then he waited a moment before he took it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He wrote the letter that night, at his desk, after she’d gone, and rewrote one paragraph of it four times.

On Tuesday 3 February 2026, in a recorded call with the investment director, I said that the continuation of the Corner Office column shouldn’t be assumed in the business plan for Tidemark Media. I made that remark knowing that the columnist had written about a person with whom I am in a relationship, and knowing that a remark from me would carry weight with the acquisitions team and later with the publisher. I didn’t declare that interest. I should have. I ask the committee to commission an independent review of the editorial decisions taken at The Exchange Weekly since completion, and I will take no part in any decision concerning the magazine from today.

On Monday the fifth he gave it to the chair of the risk committee by hand. The review was commissioned that week, from a firm with no connection to An-Tech. He didn’t ask for its terms of reference. He didn’t ask about Julian Rowe. When Ding brought him the governance documents for signature, he read every page before he signed.

“Is there anything else, Mr. Wang?”

“No.”

Ding hesitated in the doorway. “Shall I keep an eye on how the magazine responds?”

“No. The committee will deal with it.”

“Understood,” said Ding, and the next morning there was a cup of the good tea on the chairman’s desk at eight, which wasn’t something anybody had asked him to do.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Sunday she came to his flat. She found him in the kitchen making tea, and he looked up when she came in, and for a second neither of them knew what to say.

“Hi.”

“Hi.”

“Have you eaten?”

“Yes.”

“Tea?”

“Yes, please.”

He poured for her and she sat at the counter and watched him. “You sent the letter.”

“Tomorrow. It’s written.”

“Can I read it?”

He took it out of the folder by the kettle and gave it to her. She read it twice. When she put it down her eyes were wet, and she was cross about that, and wiped them with the back of her wrist.

“You rewrote the middle,” she said.

“Four times.”

“I could tell.”

For a while they talked about ordinary things. Level’s new pitch. Rachel’s conviction that the office printer had been designed to destroy her personally. A noodle place in the old town that Calvin swore by. Then she put her cup down.

“I’m still a bit angry.”

“I know.”

“Not because I think he deserved better.”

“I know.”

“Because I don’t want to have to wonder what you’ll do the next time someone hurts me.” She held the cup in both hands. “I don’t want to be the kind of person who reads a business page and wonders whether you’re in it because of me. Even if you can justify it. Even if everyone in your building tells me it was perfectly reasonable.”

“I don’t want you to have to wonder.”

“But I did.”

“Yes.”

He put his hand out across the counter, palm up, and left it there.

She looked at it. Then she put hers in it.

“I don’t want to become someone who thinks being able to do a thing means being entitled to it,” he said.

Her fingers tightened round his. “Then don’t.”

“I’ll try.”

“Don’t just try to be careful when I catch you.”

He looked at her. “No,” he said. “I’ll try when you can’t see.”

She stood up and came round the counter to stand in front of him. He didn’t pull her in.

“May I?”

She nodded. He put his arms round her, and she put her cheek against his chest and stayed there.

“I don’t miss the column,” she said into his shirt.

“Neither do I.”

“I never want him to write about me again.”

“I know.”

“But I don’t want you deciding who gets to speak.”

He put his chin on her hair. “I know.”

After a while she looked up at him. “Are you going to kiss me?”

“If you’d like me to.”

“I would.”

He kissed her, gently. It wasn’t a reward, and it wasn’t forgiveness, and it didn’t pretend to be either. It was only the thing she wanted from him that evening, and he gave it to her slowly and carefully and without asking for anything back, and when she pulled away she touched his face with her fingertips.

“Don’t make me regret trusting you with what you’ve got.”

“I won’t ask you to.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The review reported in January 2027. It found that the chairman’s remark had been made without a declaration of interest, that it had reached the publisher’s board as an assumption in the business plan, and that the editor had reasonably understood it as a signal. It found nothing else. It recommended a written editorial charter for every title An-Tech owned, with the editor’s independence on commissioning set out in it, and a standing rule that no executive with a personal interest could comment on content at all.

The charter was adopted in March. An Yu signed it last, under the editor’s name.

Margaret Lau was told in writing that she was free to recommission Corner Office if she chose to. She thought about it for a week, and then wrote back that she had read every column Julian Rowe had written for her in six years, that the legal costs and the complaints had been hers to manage long before An-Tech arrived, and that she had decided on her own judgement not to renew him. She asked for that letter to be placed in the file next to the chairman’s.

Julian Rowe began writing for smaller places: a business blog, a society magazine with good paper and few readers. His name appeared less often. The old columns stayed online.

There was never any public statement linking any of it to An Yu. Nobody announced that a chairman had taken his revenge. Nobody needed to.

And An Yu never mentioned the man again, until one evening in May, when Tang Xi was curled up on his sofa reading something on her phone and made a small noise of disgust.

He looked over. “What is it?”

“His new piece. It’s terrible.”

“Do you want to read it?”

“No.” She put the phone face up on the cushion, and looked at it, and then looked at him. “Do you know what?”

“What?”

“I think I’m bored of him. Finally.”

“Good.”

She leaned across the sofa and kissed him, and he kissed her back with his hand on her waist. When she’d settled against him again he said, “Are you still angry with me?”

“A little.”

He accepted that. “That’s fair.”

She put her head on his shoulder. “But I’m not thinking about him any more.”

He looked down at her, at her hair, at her hand lying open on his knee where she’d put it without noticing.

“Neither am I,” he said.

And this time, he meant it.

chapters.title: Her First Office
chapters.desc: A year to the day after three desks and a kettle: two floors over the restaurant, twelve people, and a better kettle.
chapters.content:
The first office had three desks.

One second-hand, with a long scratch down its left side. One lent by a friend who’d moved abroad. One new, bought after a fortnight of arguing about whether they could manage with two. A fridge that coughed every twenty minutes. A kettle that boiled itself dry that first summer, one evening when she was on the floor with An Yu and the noodles had gone cold. A printer that jammed at fourteen minutes past one on the first afternoon and had never fully been forgiven. And a glass door at the top of a narrow flight of stairs above her aunt’s restaurant, with five letters on it that she’d peeled off and put back a millimetre lower, so they’d be straight.

A notebook, open on her desk, with a list in it. Five rules. The fifth one said: We don’t take An-Tech as a client.

No clients. No contracts. No certainty that any of it would last a year. Just three people who’d decided to try, and a room that smelled faintly of rice.

A year later, to the day, there were twelve desks. And the kettle was considerably better.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Who bought this?”

It was ten past eight on Tuesday the twentieth of July 2027, and Tang Xi was standing in the kitchen on the second floor, which was a real kitchen now, with a sink, holding a kettle. It was a beautiful thing: brushed steel, a temperature dial, a little display that glowed blue, and a heating element so quiet she’d had to put her hand on it to make sure it was on.

Calvin, eating a pastry by the fridge, didn’t look up. “Rachel.”

“Rachel bought this?”

“Last Thursday. With her own money. She said if she had to listen to the old one scream for one more morning she’d throw it out of the window into your aunt’s bins.”

“It’s expensive.”

“It’s a kettle.”

“It’s a very expensive kettle.”

Rachel came up the stairs behind her with a cardboard tray of coffees. “We are twelve people. We cannot go on boiling water in something that sounds like a plane in distress.”

“It worked.”

“It took nine minutes.”

“Eight.”

“Nine.”

“Eight minutes and forty seconds.”

Rachel stared at her. “Do you hear yourself?”

Tang Xi put the kettle down gently, as if it might be offended. “I just think we should be careful with money.”

Rachel pointed at the room with a coffee cup. “Look around.”

She did.

They had two floors now. In June, after the tender, her aunt had moved her sacks of rice for the second time in a year, this time to a shed behind the restaurant’s kitchen, and announced that the second floor was available at the full rent and not a cent less, because they were a company now and she wasn’t a charity. They’d stripped it back to the boards and painted it white and put in a proper kitchen and a meeting room with a door that shut. The first floor, the original room, had eight desks in two rows under the windows. The second had four more, the meeting room, a small room for calls, and a cupboard that actually closed. Through the floor, as always, came the extractor fan and the clatter of the prep and, now and then, her mother’s voice telling somebody that the chives were wrong.

The lettering on the glass door downstairs was still straight. She checked it every morning.

“We’re allowed a good kettle now.” Rachel put the coffees down on the counter.

Tang Xi looked at it again. And then, against her will, she smiled. “Fine.”

“Thank you.”

“But if it breaks, it’s yours.”

“I bought it.”

“Exactly.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There were twelve of them because the work had become more than three people could carry, and because she had refused, for eleven months, to hire a single person before the work needed them.

Rachel had taken strategy and research. Calvin ran the client teams, and had discovered, to his own horror, that he was good at it. Tang Xi led the company, and all of its clients, and still wrote the first draft of every important proposal herself at the old desk at twenty to nine at night because she liked it best then.

They had hired, in order: an account manager in February, a researcher in March, a designer in May. And then, in June, after the tender, nine in eight weeks. A strategist, two account executives, a content lead, a production coordinator, a second designer, an analyst, and two juniors who’d come straight out of university and looked at Rachel.

Not all at once. Not to look bigger. Because the work had needed them.

Halloway House had launched in March and the retainer had doubled. Second Steep had come back for its autumn harvest and brought two other tea growers with it. A furniture maker had signed after a referral from Grace Tham. And on the fourth of June, Level had won the An-Tech group communications tender, through a two-envelope blind process run by an independent panel that the chairman of An-Tech hadn’t been permitted to enter, against three agencies each forty times its size.

The fifth rule was still in the notebook. She’d crossed it out on the evening of the fourth of June, with one neat line, and written underneath it, in the same pen: Until we’d built something nobody could say he built for us. We have.

She still remembered the first hiring meeting, in March, at the old desk. Rachel had wanted to move faster. Calvin had wanted to wait another month. Tang Xi had sat between them with the notebook and said, “We hire when the work needs it. Not when we’re excited about the idea of being bigger.”

They’d argued for an hour. Then they’d agreed. It was the way they did most things.

✦ ✦ ✦

At a quarter past nine the whole of Level crammed itself into the meeting room, which held ten comfortably, and stood round the walls.

Tang Xi stood by the screen with a printed agenda. “Before we start, I want to say something.”

Rachel, in the best chair, narrowed her eyes. “What?”

“Nothing bad.”

“That’s what you said before you changed the leave policy.”

“I gave everyone more leave.”

“Exactly. It was a shock. Some of us have hearts.”

A few people laughed. Tang Xi waited.

“It’s a year today,” she said. “A year ago this morning, Rachel stood on the landing and told me the lettering on the door was crooked, and Calvin was ten minutes late with breakfast, and the printer jammed at fourteen minutes past one.”

“The printer was not my fault,” said Calvin.

“You recommended it.”

“It’s a reputable brand.”

“It jammed on the first day.”

“It was a software issue.”

Rachel leaned towards the juniors. “He’s still defending it. A year later.”

More laughter. Tang Xi let it settle.

“I wanted to say thank you. For the move. For June, and July, which were chaos. For carrying desks up a staircase that was built for one person and a sack of rice.” She looked round the room. “And I wanted to say something else, now there are twelve of us, so that nobody new ever has to guess it. The office is bigger. The way we work doesn’t change because of that.”

The room went quiet.

“We don’t promise things we can’t do. We don’t hide a problem until it’s too big to fix. We don’t make clients feel stupid for asking a question twice. And we don’t ask anyone in this room to work hours that would make them ill, just so we can prove a small agency can beat a big one.” She put the agenda down. “We’ve already proved that. Now I’d like us to be good at the work. Not just busy.”

Nobody said anything for a moment. Then one of the juniors, Wen Hui, put up her hand.

“Can we still have Friday lunch together? Downstairs?”

“Of course.”

“Even when there’s a deadline?”

“We’ll plan round it.”

Rachel nodded with great satisfaction. “Excellent. The important policies have been protected.”

Calvin sighed. “Can we please discuss the actual agenda?”

“One last thing,” said Tang Xi, and the whole room turned to look at Calvin, and he put his face in his hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

At eleven, she found Wen Hui standing in the kitchen in front of the kettle with a mug, looking at the temperature dial.

“Something wrong?”

The girl jumped. “Nothing, Ms. Tang. I was just working out the setting.”

“Tea?”

“Green tea.”

“Eighty degrees. Not boiling. Boiling makes it bitter.”

“You know how to use it?”

“I spent four years making tea for a client who noticed if it was two degrees out.” Tang Xi turned the dial for her. “He’s very particular.”

Wen Hui filled her cup, and thanked her, and then, as Tang Xi turned to go, said, “Ms. Tang? Can I ask you something?”

“Of course.”

“Did you really start with three people?”

Tang Xi looked through the kitchen door at the second floor. Rachel was on a call with her feet on the radiator. Calvin was at the printer, which was in a corner nobody liked, apparently negotiating with it. The designer had pinned a new set of concepts for Second Steep along one wall and the analyst was standing in front of them with her arms folded, frowning.

“Yes,” she said. “Three people.”

“Were you scared?”

She thought about it. “Very.”

“You didn’t look scared when I met you.”

“I’ve had practice.”

“Was it hard?”

She thought about the first office. The borrowed desk. The first invoice, which had been for less than her old monthly salary and which she’d printed and stuck to the wall. The night in August when Second Steep’s money had been late and she had sat on the floor with her back against the old desk and done the sums three times and not told anyone. The day in October when she’d found out, from Calvin, reading a trade newsletter at the window, that the man she loved had quietly bought a magazine.

“Yes,” she said. “It was hard. And it was worth trying.”

Wen Hui nodded seriously. “Thank you.”

“Enjoy your tea. Eighty degrees.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At lunchtime Rachel found her standing at the window on the first floor, looking at the room.

“You’re doing it again.”

“Doing what?”

“Looking at the office as if someone’s about to take it away.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.” Rachel came and stood next to her, and they looked at it together: eight desks, sun on the floorboards, the extractor fan going under their feet, the smell of the lunch service coming up through the boards. Calvin, back from the printer, was showing one of the new account executives how to set up a project tracker. The researcher was explaining something to the strategist with a great many hand movements.

“Remember the first day?” said Rachel.

“The printer jammed.”

“The kettle died.”

“The Wi-Fi password was wrong. Calvin wrote it down.”

“We had one client meeting.”

“Two.”

“One was a coffee.”

“It was still a client meeting.”

Rachel smiled. “We were so sure we could do it.”

“We didn’t have any choice.”

“We did, Xi.” Rachel bumped her shoulder. “I could have stayed at Northlight and been head of strategy by now. Calvin could have stayed. You could have gone to any agency in the city with your name and your clients. We chose this. On purpose.” She looked at the room. “Look at us.”

“Twelve people.”

“And a kettle that doesn’t scream.”

“Please stop talking about the kettle.”

“Never,” said Rachel, and went back to her desk.

Tang Xi stayed at the window a while longer. In the corner, by the glass, under a hanging plant one of the designers had brought in, there was a small table that wasn’t a desk any more. A second-hand desk, with a long scratch down its left side. They’d repaired one leg and sanded the top and oiled it, and moved it to the window when the new desks came, and now people sat at it to read or think or eat their lunch. She’d kept it there on purpose. Not as decoration. As a reminder.

✦ ✦ ✦

An Yu arrived at twenty to seven, with nothing in his hands.

She saw him through the glass door at the top of the stairs before he saw her, standing on the landing in his shirtsleeves with his jacket over his arm, looking at the lettering. He looked at it for a while. Then he knocked, although the door was open.

Rachel, who was the only other person still on the first floor, looked up. “Oh.”

“Don’t,” said Tang Xi.

“I didn’t say anything.”

“You said oh.”

“It’s a very flexible word.”

He came in. “Good evening.”

“Mr. Wang,” said Rachel, with enormous formality.

“Rachel.”

Calvin put his head down through the stairwell from the second floor. “Mr. Wang.”

“Calvin. Slide nine was good.”

Calvin went back upstairs without a word, and they heard him sit down rather heavily.

Tang Xi stood up. “You’re early.”

“I finished early.” He looked round. He took his time. The eight desks. The window. The stairs up to the second floor, the meeting room, the kitchen. The old desk under the plant by the glass. He looked at that one for longer than the others.

Rachel looked at his empty hands. “You’ve come to Level’s anniversary with nothing?”

“I’ve ordered downstairs,” said An Yu. “Her aunt said fourteen minutes. She said if I brought food in from anywhere else she’d charge me corkage.”

“She would,” said Tang Xi.

“I paid in advance. She charged me corkage anyway, in case.”

Rachel laughed out loud. “How many did you order for?”

“Everyone who’s still here.”

“There are twelve people, Mr. Wang.”

He glanced up the stairs, where five people were still working, and then at her. “Then I’ve ordered too much.”

“Not a problem,” said Rachel.

Tang Xi took his jacket from him. “Don’t encourage her.”

“I’m not.”

“You are.”

The corner of his mouth went up.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate in the meeting room on the second floor: her aunt’s noodles, a plate of greens, a fish steamed with ginger, and a large bamboo steamer of chive and prawn dumplings, five pleats each, carried up the narrow stairs by her mother herself, who put them down on the table in front of An Yu and said, “You. Not too many,” and went back down without looking at anyone.

Rachel took the seat opposite him. “So, Mr. Wang. What do you think?”

“Of the office?”

“Of us. A year in.”

He looked round the meeting room. “It’s well organised.”

“That’s a diplomatic answer.”

“It’s also true.”

Tang Xi took the lid off the steamer. “He thinks the meeting room’s too small.”

He looked at her. “I didn’t say that.”

“You looked at the table.”

“I was looking at the table.”

“Exactly.”

Calvin laughed. Rachel leaned forward. “Should we get a bigger one?”

“No,” said Tang Xi immediately.

“I didn’t suggest anything,” said An Yu.

“I’m making sure.”

He put his chopsticks down, and looked at her across her aunt’s dumplings, and she saw him understand exactly what she was making sure of.

“It’s your office,” he said. “You’ll decide what it needs. And when.”

“Yes,” she said.

Rachel looked at them both for a second, and then down at her noodles. “That’s actually a very sensible answer, Mr. Wang.”

“Thank you.”

“Don’t get used to it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

After dinner the others went, one by one, down the narrow stairs and out through the restaurant, where her aunt gave each of them a box of something to take home whether they wanted it or not. Rachel was last. She collected her bag, checked the kettle was off, and stopped by the old desk under the plant.

“Tomorrow, nine?”

“Nine.”

“Don’t forget the Halloway call.”

“I won’t.”

Rachel looked at An Yu. “Make sure she eats breakfast.”

“Rachel.”

“I’m going. Good night. Happy birthday, Level.” She looked round the empty first floor, the eight desks and the window going dark, and her voice changed, just slightly. “It’s a good office, Xi. You did a good thing.”

“We did.”

“We did,” Rachel agreed, and went.

The room went quiet. Downstairs, the restaurant was closing: the shutters, the chairs going up on the tables, her mother’s voice and her aunt’s. An Yu stood by the window and looked at the old desk.

“You kept it.”

“Yes.”

“Why?”

She came and stood beside him and put her palm flat on the top of it, on the long scratch, which they hadn’t sanded out.

“Because I started here. On the first night. You came up the stairs at twenty to nine with nothing, the way you did tonight, and sat in the corner in a chair that didn’t match, and read my proposal for a tea company that couldn’t pay us. You didn’t change a word.” She traced the scratch. “I don’t want to forget what it felt like when there were three of us. I don’t want to be somebody who has twelve desks and can’t remember being frightened.”

“You won’t.”

“You sound very sure.”

“I’ve seen you remember much smaller things than this.” He looked down at her. “You remember the exact number of minutes a kettle takes to boil.”

She laughed. Then she turned and put her arms round him, and he held her, and for a while they stood in the dark first floor with the smell of tea and ginger in it, and eight empty desks, and the old one by the window.

“Tell me something true,” she said into his shirt. “About it. Not a compliment. Something true.”

He was quiet for long enough that she thought he wouldn’t.

“A year ago, I’d have bought you this building,” he said. “I’d have done it quietly, and called it an investment, and told myself it was to make things easier for you. I thought about it in July. Every day, for about a week.” His hand moved on her back. “I didn’t, because you’d have known. But I want you to know that I wanted to. And that I’m glad, now, that I didn’t. Because if I had, this wouldn’t be yours. It would be something I’d given you. And it isn’t. Not one board of it.”

She went still against him.

“And something else,” he said. “You didn’t build a company to prove you could. I used to think that was what you were doing. It isn’t. You built a place where a twenty-two-year-old asks you if she can still have Friday lunch downstairs, and you say yes. You made room for twelve people without forgetting the three. You got bigger without becoming anything you’re not.” He stopped. “I don’t know how to do that. I’d like to learn.”

She looked up at him. Her eyes were wet. “That’s a very good answer.”

“I know.”

She laughed, damply, and pulled him down by the front of his shirt and kissed him. He kissed her back with one hand at her waist and the other at the back of her head, slowly, against the old desk, until it creaked, and she broke away laughing.

“Not on the desk. It’s only just been mended.”

“I wasn’t going to.”

“You were thinking about it.”

“For a second.”

She kissed him again, softer. Then she put her forehead against his and stayed there.

“Take me home.”

“Yes.”

She switched off the lights. At the top of the stairs she looked back once: the desks empty, the kettle quiet in the kitchen upstairs, the old desk at the window with the streetlight on it. Twelve people would come up those stairs in the morning. There’d be emails, and revisions, and a call with Halloway at nine, and somebody would almost certainly complain about the printer.

She smiled, and locked the door, and checked the lettering, which was straight.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car, with the driver’s eyes politely on the road, An Yu held her hand on the seat between them.

“Have you decided what the next year looks like?”

She looked out at the old town going past, the lit windows, the shuttered shops. “Not yet.”

“Bigger?”

“Not necessarily.”

“More people?”

“Only if we need them.”

He nodded. She turned to look at him. “You’re not going to tell me to open a second office?”

“No.”

“Or hire a regional team?”

“No.”

“Or buy the building?”

He looked at her. “No.”

“Good.” She was quiet. Then: “Maybe next year we’ll need a second meeting room.”

“Then you’ll decide when.”

“And a bigger kitchen.”

“Because of the kettle?”

“Because of the twelve people.”

“All right,” he said.

She leaned her head back against the seat, still holding his hand. The first office had been three desks and a kettle that boiled itself dry. The second was two floors and twelve people and a kettle that didn’t scream. And Tang Xi, who had once been so afraid there’d be nothing left of her if she took the risk, found herself thinking about what they might build next.

Not because she had to prove anything to anybody. Because she wanted to see.

chapters.title: Anniversary in the Archive
chapters.desc: Their first wedding anniversary, the archive on the forty-second floor, and a door that only locks from inside.
chapters.epigraph: “Because this is where you found me again.”
chapters.content:
The first time they were locked in the archive, it was an accident.

A narrow room on the forty-second floor. A door that locked itself at ten o’clock and wouldn’t open again until someone from security came up with a key. A discrepancy in some old campaign records that had kept a junior account manager there long past the time she should have gone home, and a chairman who had come to find out why. She had asked him whether he remembered her. He had taken a paper crane out of his wallet. And then for fifty-seven minutes An Yu had tried with everything in him to stay composed, while Tang Xi discovered, one kiss at a time, how easily she could undo him.

Four years and two months later, she still remembered it with great fondness.

So did he. Which was why, when she said over breakfast on their first wedding anniversary, “Be at your office at eight tonight. Wear the grey tie,” he put his cup down and looked at her across the table with deep suspicion.

“What have you planned?”

“Lunch with my family. Then a nap. Then something.”

“What something?”

“Grey tie, An Yu.”

“It’s Sunday.”

“I know what day it is. I was there when we got married.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunch was at her aunt’s restaurant, at the long table, where they’d had their wedding lunch exactly a year before. Her mother put a dumpling on his plate before anyone else’s and said, “One year. Still too thin,” and her aunt brought out a fish with a red ribbon tied round the plate that made Tang Xi put her face in her hands. Nainai rang from the north at half past one to say that one year was nothing and she would be impressed at fifty. Xing Yue sent a photograph from the hospital of a coffee with a heart drawn in the foam by Elara, captioned She made me send this. Rachel sent a message that said only ANNIVERSARY followed by eleven exclamation marks and a reminder that she was still owed the second half of her bridesmaid’s speech, which she had cut on the day for time.

At five to eight that evening, An Yu was standing at the window of his office on the forty-second floor, in the grey tie, when the door opened behind him.

She came in in a dark green dress he hadn’t seen before, with her hair up and a small paper bag in one hand, and stopped just inside the door to look at him.

“You wore it.”

“You told me to.”

“You always do what you’re told?”

“Only by you. And only on Sundays.”

“Happy anniversary, husband.”

“Happy anniversary.”

He came across the room and kissed her. She let him, one hand flat on his tie, and when he drew back she straightened the knot, which didn’t need it, with enormous care.

“Is the building empty?”

“There’s a guard at the desk downstairs, and a cleaner on twenty-nine.”

“Good.” She lifted the bag. “Come with me. Somewhere you haven’t taken me in a while.”

He looked at the bag, and then at her face, and something in his own face changed.

“The archive.”

Her smile went slow and wide. “Very good, Professor.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The archive had been renovated in 2026. The tall steel shelving had gone, replaced by compact mobile stacks that ran on rails in the floor, each one moved by turning a three-spoked wheel at its end, so that the whole room was solid shelving with a single aisle you opened wherever you needed it. The lighting was kinder. The temperature was steady. And the lock had been changed, after a certain incident in February 2025 that the head of facilities still referred to only as the incident, so that it no longer locked itself at ten: now it had a keypad outside and a plain brass thumb-turn on the inside, and could only ever be locked by somebody standing in the room.

He keyed in his code. The door opened. She walked in ahead of him and stopped.

“It’s smaller than I remember.”

“It isn’t. It’s the same room.”

“Then perhaps you were more frightening.”

He let the door swing shut behind him. “Was I?”

“Terrifying.”

She went down the room, reading the labels on the ends of the stacks: years, departments, project codes. The air smelled of paper and the cedar lining of the new cabinets. At the far end they had kept the small table and the terminal. She stopped beside the last stack, which was labelled Corporate Communications 2019–2023, and put both hands on its wheel and turned it, hard. The stack rolled away along its rails with a low rumble, and an aisle opened up beside the table, exactly one person wide and a little more.

“There,” she said. “That’s where the shelf was. I counted it from the door the first time, while you were checking the panel. Eleven of my steps.” She sat down on the edge of the table, the way she had, and crossed her ankles. “I was sitting here when I asked you if you remembered me. You were standing there.” She pointed into the aisle. “A few feet away. With your tie perfectly knotted and your sleeves folded to the elbow, as if you’d come to audit me.”

He looked at the place she was pointing to, and then he walked into it and stood there.

“Like this?”

“Exactly like that.”

They looked at each other across a few feet of archive floor, the way they had four years before.

“You said you had something,” he said.

“I do.”

She took a small archival sleeve out of the paper bag. He recognised it before it was all the way out, and his hand tightened on the shelf.

The bookmark. A narrow strip of squared paper, soft at the folds, gone almost translucent at one corner, with a small crooked face at the top wearing glasses, one lens bigger than the other. And under it, in blue biro gone the colour of a vein, a sixteen-year-old’s handwriting.

For the person who never talks.
Don’t lose your place.

“You brought it.”

“I did.”

“I thought it lived in the study.”

“It does. In the drawer next to the crane, in its house.” She held it up between them. “I found it in March while I was looking for a pen. I’ve been planning this since.”

He took it from her carefully. For a moment his face did something she rarely saw on it any more: not sadness, exactly. Something quieter and older than sadness.

“You made this from your maths homework.”

“Yes.”

“You were meant to be doing it.”

“I’d finished.”

“You hadn’t.”

“I’d finished the important ones.”

“You drew the glasses badly.”

“I beg your pardon?”

“The left lens is bigger.”

“It’s artistic.”

“It’s inaccurate.” He looked at it. “It’s the most accurate thing anyone’s ever drawn of me.”

She stopped smiling. “Perhaps I should have brought the crane,” she said, a little unsteadily.

He caught her hand. “No. Keep this one here. Tonight.”

“Why?”

“Because this is where you found me again.” His thumb moved over her knuckles. “I’d had it in my wallet for six years by then. You were standing exactly there. And I didn’t show you. I showed you the crane, because the crane was the thing you’d left me, and I knew what to say about it. The bookmark was the thing you’d given me. I didn’t know how to say that yet.”

She looked at him. Then she stood up, and took the sleeve from him, and laid it flat on the shelf at shoulder height, between two boxes of 2021 press releases, where the light from the end of the aisle fell on the crooked little face.

“Then it can watch,” she said.

And she walked back down the room, past the wheel and the stacks and the kinder lighting, to the door, and turned the brass thumb-turn on the inside of it.

The click was small in the quiet room. It was also unmistakable.

He looked at the door, and then down the aisle at her.

“Xi.”

“Hm?”

“Did you just lock it?”

“Yes.”

“From the inside.”

“That’s the only side it locks from. Facilities changed it. After the incident.”

“I approved the change.”

“I know. I read the board paper.” She came back up the room towards him. “I’m being very careful this time. Nobody locked us in. Nobody’s coming at eleven with a torch. Nobody is going to rescue you.”

The corner of his mouth went up. “You’ve planned this.”

“Very thoroughly.”

“I see.”

“Do you?” She stopped in front of him in the narrow aisle, close enough to touch his tie, and didn’t touch it. “Then I’d like you to do something for me.”

“What?”

“Close your eyes.”

He looked at her. Then he closed them.

“Don’t open them until I tell you.”

“All right.”

“Now tell me,” she said, softly, “what I was wearing.”

There was a pause. Then, without opening his eyes, in the same steady voice he used to read out a set of figures to a board, he told her.

“A navy suit. The trousers, not the skirt. A white blouse with a collar that had come undone on the left side, and you hadn’t noticed. Flat black shoes, because you’d been on your feet since eight, and you’d kicked one of them off under that table before I came in. Small gold earrings. Your hair was up and coming down at the back. You had a pencil behind your ear that you’d forgotten about. You had ink on the side of your right hand from a pen that leaked.”

She had stopped breathing somewhere around the shoes. “And then?” she said.

“And then you asked me if I remembered you. And I couldn’t say anything. And you were angry with me for that, and you were right to be.” His eyes were still shut. “So you got off the table and took hold of my tie, like this—” his hand came up, without looking, and found her wrist, exactly, and put her fingers on the knot of the grey tie “—and you kissed me before I could make it any worse.”

“An Yu,” she whispered.

“You tasted of the coffee from the machine on forty, which is terrible. You put your hand flat on my shirt over my heart and kept it there as if you were taking my pulse. I didn’t know where to put my hands for about a minute. Then I knew.”

Her fingers were shaking on his tie. She undid the knot. She did it slowly, watching his face with his eyes shut, his jaw, the line of his throat moving when he swallowed, and she drew the tie free and wound it once round her own wrist and kept it there.

“Keep them closed,” she said. “Now I’ll tell you what I was thinking.”

She undid his top button. “I was thinking that I’d waited ten years for you to say one word to me, and you were still not saying it.” The second button. “I was thinking that you were taller than I remembered, and that your hands had got bigger, and that if you didn’t kiss me back in about three seconds I would die of embarrassment in a filing room and they’d find me in the morning under a pile of 2019 campaign reports.” The third. “And then you kissed me back. And I thought—” She stopped, with her hand flat on his bare chest now, inside his shirt, over his heart, where she’d had it four years before. It was going hard. “I thought, oh. You’re here. I thought you’d gone for good and you were right here, the whole time, in a locked room, with a crane in your wallet.”

He opened his eyes.

“I didn’t tell you to open them.”

“I know,” said An Yu, and kissed her.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was nothing like the first time and it was exactly like it.

He kissed her slowly, as if he knew how she breathed now and where she liked his hands and when a smile meant she was about to say something troublesome, which he did. Four years of knowing. One of being married. Her back went against the end of the stack and the shelving rocked slightly on its rails, and she laughed into his mouth, and he put one hand flat on the shelf above her head to steady it and kept kissing her.

His jacket was still on; he’d put it on to come down. She pushed it off his shoulders and he let it fall. She pushed his shirt after it and it caught at his wrists on the cufflinks, and she undid them one by one, without hurrying, and dropped them into the pocket of her dress, and then his shirt was on the floor of the archive and she put both her palms on him, his chest, his ribs, his stomach, the line of hair below his navel.

“Turn round,” he said, against her ear.

She turned. He found the zip at the back of the green dress and drew it down, slowly, the whole length of her spine, and the back of his knuckles followed it down, and she put both her hands flat on the shelf in front of her, on either side of a box of annual reports, and leaned her forehead against the cool edge of it while he kissed the back of her neck, and the top of her spine, and lower. The dress fell. She stepped out of it. She was in nothing but her underwear and his tie wound round her wrist, and the shelving was cold against her palms, and his mouth was warm, and it was too much and not enough at once.

“Tell me,” he said.

It was what she’d made him do on the night they wrote their rules, in his bed, with the notebook still open on the coffee table: say it, out loud, all of it. He’d gone first that night.
