Now she said it, with her forehead on the shelf and her eyes shut, every word of it, low and clear, in the room where she had once been too proud to tell him she’d missed him: what she wanted from his hands, and his mouth, and where, and how slowly, and that she wanted to see his face when he did it.

He turned her round to face him, so she could.

He went down on his knees in the aisle, on his own shirt. He drew her underwear down her legs and she stepped out of it, one hand braced on his bare shoulder, the other on the shelf, and he looked up at her from there, with that maddening, devoted attention, the same look he’d given her in a hotel in Singapore and on the floor above her aunt’s restaurant and in a hundred other places since. Then he lifted her knee over his shoulder and put his mouth on her.

She didn’t make jokes after that. She held on to the shelf with one hand and to his hair with the other and let her head go back against the end of the stack, and he was slow, and then not slow, and then slow again, exactly as she’d asked, reading every change in her the way he’d read the archive four years ago, until her thigh was shaking against his cheek and she was saying his name to the ceiling of the room where she’d first kissed him. When she came it was with her whole body arched off the cold steel and the tie round her wrist pulled tight in her own fist and the bookmark on the shelf beside her head, its lopsided face turned politely towards the boxes.

He stood up and caught her before her knees went.

“Still standing?” he said.

“No.” She was laughing, weakly, against his throat. “I’m being held up by a chairman.”

“Is that all right?”

“It’s the least you can do.”

She found his belt. She was clumsy with it, her fingers still unsteady, and he let her be clumsy, and when she’d got it open and the rest she put her hand round him and felt him go still against her, all of him, and let out his breath against her hair in a long uneven sound.

“Here,” she said. “Against the shelf. I want it here.”

He lifted her. She wrapped her legs round his waist and her arms round his neck, and he put her back against the end of the stack, and the shelving rocked on its rails, and she said, “Don’t you dare stop for that,” and he didn’t. He pushed into her slowly, all the way, and they both stopped, for one long breath, foreheads together, in the narrow aisle, and she felt him shaking slightly with holding still.

“Look at me,” she said.

He looked at her.

And then they moved, together, with nothing slow about it any more. Her back against the cold steel and his hand braced on the shelf beside her head and the whole stack humming on its rails with every movement, so that somewhere down at the far end of the room a box slid a centimetre and settled. He said her name. He said it in the voice she’d only ever heard from him in the dark, and then he said other things, against her mouth, the way she’d taught him the night they wrote the rules: what he wanted, and how, and that he’d wanted it in this exact room on the fourteenth of February 2025 so badly he’d had to count the shelves to stay upright. She laughed, and then couldn’t laugh, and held on to him, and came apart a second time with her face in his neck and her heels digging into the backs of his thighs. He followed her a moment later with a low, broken sound, and held her there against the shelf, both arms locked round her, for a long time after.

It didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later they lay on his jacket on the archive floor, between the stacks, with her head on his chest and her dress pulled over them both like a blanket. The aisle she’d opened was just wide enough for the two of them if he kept one arm round her. Above them, on the shelf, the bookmark lay where she’d put it.

“Do you think security knows?” she said.

“Knows what?”

“That the archive’s occupied.”

“They know I have access.”

“That isn’t what I asked.”

“No,” he agreed.

She laughed into his skin. “Good.”

He ran his thumb along her shoulder. “Are you comfortable?”

“Very.”

“Cold?”

“No.”

“Do you want to go home?”

“In a minute.” She tilted her head to look up at the shelf. “When did you first find it again? After I’d gone. In the book.”

“The first evening in Zurich. On the floor, unpacking. It fell out of the probability chapter.”

“You never told me that until the wedding.”

“I kept it.”

“That isn’t the same thing.”

“I know.”

She came up on her elbow. “Why didn’t you ever tell me? Not at sixteen. Later. In the archive. Any time.”

He thought about it, the way he thought about everything she asked him, all the way to the bottom.

“Because you’d have asked me why I kept it,” he said. “And I didn’t know how to tell you that I kept everything you ever gave me. The bookmark. The crane. The way you took your tea. The name of the chemistry teacher you hated. The eighty-seven.” He touched her face. “I didn’t know how to say that without it sounding like something you’d have to carry.”

“You could have just said you liked me.”

“I could have.”

“You could have said thank you.”

“I should have.”

“You could have asked for my number.”

“I should have done that too.”

She put her head back down on his chest and laughed, a little wetly. “Luckily, you got another chance.”

“Luckily,” he said, and kissed her hair.

✦ ✦ ✦

They dressed slowly. She found his tie still wound round her wrist and unwound it and held it up.

“Should I put this back on you?”

“Would you like to?”

“Not particularly.”

He took it from her and hung it round his neck, untied. She found his cufflinks in her pocket and gave him one and kept the other, and he looked at her.

“That’s mine.”

“It’s ours. You’re getting it back at home.” She took the bookmark down off the shelf in its sleeve and held it a moment. “I’m going to take this home after all.”

“I thought it was staying here tonight.”

“I changed my mind.”

He nodded, gravely. “That’s allowed.”

She looked at him, delighted. “You remember the amendment.”

“We’re allowed to change our minds.”

“And rule eight?”

“We don’t use silence to get out of hard conversations.”

“And the other amendment. Mine.”

“We’re allowed to ask again.” He looked at her. “Xi. Are you happy?”

“You asked me that this morning.”

“I’m allowed to ask again.”

She stood in the narrow aisle in her green dress with her hair coming down at the back, holding a strip of paper she’d drawn on at sixteen, and looked at her husband with his shirt half-buttoned and his tie round his neck and his face wide open, the way it was now almost all the time, with her.

“Yes,” she said. “Ask me again next year.”

“I will.”

She put the bookmark back in the paper bag. He turned the stack’s wheel and the aisle closed, slowly, with a low rumble, the place where she’d stood and the place where he had stood rolling together until there was no gap between them at all.

At the door he turned the brass thumb-turn and opened it. She caught his sleeve before he could step out.

“One more thing.”

He looked back. “What?”

She kissed him. Not hurriedly. Not secretly. Just once more, in the doorway of the archive, before they went back out into the ordinary world.

When she pulled away he touched her cheek. “Ready?”

“Yes.”

The corridor was empty and the lights were on their night setting. They walked to the lift together, his hand at the small of her back.

“Do you know what I liked about tonight?” she said.

“What?”

“That we came on purpose. Nobody locked us in.”

“I liked that too.”

“And next year?”

“Wherever you want.”

“Careful,” she said. “I might choose the archive again.”

“I wouldn’t object.”

“I’ll need to read another board paper first.”

The lift came. They stepped in. He reached past her and pressed the button for the car park, and then, without any expression whatever, pressed the button for the lobby instead, so that it would take longer. She laughed all the way down.

That night the bookmark went back into its sleeve and its sleeve into the drawer of his desk in the study, beside the crane in its square of wax paper: the two small things that had come through the years before either of them knew what to call any of it. In the summer she would take it out again for good and put it in a frame on the dining table, and he would tell her he knew where he was.

But for one evening it had been where it began, between the two of them, on a shelf in a locked room.

And this time nobody had locked them in. They had chosen to stay.
